events.summary: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang presents Vera computers. Sean Gallup/Getty Images It could be about to get harder for some countries to access Nvidia's advanced AI chips. The US Commerce Department released an interim final rule aimed at preventing remote access to advanced AI chips that circumvent the country's export controls. "Rapid advancement in cloud computing and SI infrastructure have made it increasingly possible to access advanced American computing capabilities remotely, including through data centers located outside countries subject to US export restrictions," the statement said. The move comes as Nvidia faces intense scrutiny over the export of its AI chips in the wake of a scandal that led to CEO Jensen Huang's resignation . events.title: Uncertainty deters green investors from Africa's biggest economies
events.summary: Many of Africa’s biggest economies remain unattractive for major renewables investors because of legislative, regulatory, and security uncertainty, the head of one of the continent’s biggest clean energy developers told Semafor. Infinity Power, a privately owned joint venture between Infinity and the UAE’s Masdar, has been fast expanding its green power generation targets in Egypt, and sees Côte d’Ivoire and Senegal as attractive markets for growth. But Ethiopia, Kenya, and Nigeria — among the continent’s biggest economies — are not as much of a draw, Nayer Fouad, Infinity Power’s co-founder and CEO said in an interview. Kenya had recently renegotiated the terms on its power-purchase agreements, causing unease among prospective investors, while Ethiopia and Nigeria carried security risks.

events.title: Nvidia fallout: Commerce cracks down on third-country loophole that allowed China to use computing power
events.summary: The Commerce Department moved to close a loophole that has allowed Chinese companies to lease Nvidia's computing power from locations in other countries. Commerce's action is the first U.S. policy response to the scandal at Nvidia that led CEO Jensen Huang to resign last week. And it came after rising criticism of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who has been accused of not doing enough to prevent possible diversion of Nvidia's most advanced chips to China in violation of American export controls. The Commerce Department moved on Monday to close a loophole that has allowed Chinese companies to lease Nvidia's computing power from locations in other countries. Commerce's action, in the form of an interim final rule issued by its Bureau of Industry and Security, is the first U.S. policy response to the scandal at Nvidia that led CEO Jensen Huang to resign last week. The department said in a press release that the rule was "written by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council." The rule came after rising criticism of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who has been accused of not doing enough to prevent possible diversion of Nvidia's most advanced chips to China in violation of American export controls. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, in an interview on Friday with CNBC's "Squawk Box," blamed the Commerce Department for not putting Megaspeed, the Singapore-based company at the center the Nvidia scandal, on the so-called entity list, which would restrict certain exports to it. events.title: MTN eyes $2B takeover of state-backed rival Telkom
events.summary: Telecoms giant MTN revived its $2 billion pursuit of state-backed rival Telkom, a buyout that would present a tricky choice for South Africa’s government and regulators. A deal would confront South Africa’s coalition government with a choice over the future of Telkom, in which the state owns a stake of about 40%. It would also test competition regulators’ willingness to accept a more concentrated market, with MTN and Vodacom a de facto duopoly in exchange for the prospect of a larger entity pumping more money into digital infrastructure. The two companies said they had started early-stage takeover talks that could see MTN making a cash-and-shares offer for Telkom, reviving a courtship that collapsed three years ago. Investors have already started pricing in the possibility of a deal; they sent shares in Telkom soaring 15%. — Tiisetso Motsoeneng

events.title: A major NFT marketplace is shutting down—5 years after the boom, there's a lesson for investors
events.summary: Save and Invest Do funds for wealthy investors perform better? Not recently Save and Invest How parents can help Gen Alpha manage money On The Job NYC's 'Baklava Guy' brings in $20K/month selling Turkish pastries Startups A pickle startup valued at $8.5 million? Thank its Gen Z branding Save and Invest 52% of Gen Z investors have redirected investing money to sports bets Five years ago, NFTs seemed to be everywhere. Although the digital collectibles, known as nonfungible tokens, had existed since 2014, they exploded in popularity in 2021 alongside the cryptocurrency boom, becoming status symbols for celebrities and wealthy collectors. Weekly NFT trading volume across major blockchains surged from about $4.4 million in late 2020 to a peak of $3.2 billion in August 2021, according to CryptoSlam data published by The Block . Today, much of that trading activity has disappeared. Weekly NFT trading volume has fallen more than 99% since August 2021, and several major NFT marketplaces have closed. On Thursday, Blur, once the largest marketplace for Ethereum-based NFTs, shut down its website. At the height of the boom, Twitter co-founder Jack Dorsey sold an NFT of his first tweet for $2.9 million , while a digital artwork by an artist known as Beeple fetched $69.3 million at Christie's. Paris Hilton and Jimmy Fallon showed off their Bored Ape NFTs on "The Tonight Show," and even McDonald's released NFTs celebrating the return of its McRib sandwich. Back then, some buyers believed NFTs represented the future of digital ownership, while others bet they could resell them at higher prices. But as enthusiasm faded, so did the demand that had driven the digital tokens' values higher. The NFT boom and bust shows how quickly speculative investments can unravel when demand dries up. For investors, it's a cautionary tale about spotting the warning signs before buying into the next craze, financial experts tell CNBC Make It. Part of the initial appeal of NFTs was the promise of a new way for artists and other creators to make money from their work. Using blockchain technology, NFTs allowed creators to sell digital collectibles with verifiable ownership records and potentially earn royalties on subsequent sales through smart contracts. More broadly, NFTs were touted as part of the future of digital ownership, with the potential to transform how people bought, sold and traded digital assets. But establishing ownership of a digital collectible was different from creating lasting demand for it, says Evan Mills, a financial advisor at wealth management firm Scholar Advising. "NFTs tried to manufacture that demand," he says. "Blockchain could establish who owns the token, but it couldn't guarantee that anyone would really value the ownership at the end of the day." In practice, many of the NFTs that attracted attention were relatively simple digital images, such as cartoon animals or promotional artwork featuring beer cans. Traditional collectibles, such as paintings, antiques and baseball cards, have established histories and communities of collectors that can sustain demand, Mills says. NFTs, by comparison, became enormously popular in a relatively short period. Unlike many traditional collectibles, however, NFTs could be created in virtually unlimited quantities. While individual collections might contain a limited number of tokens, there was little stopping creators from launching new series. At the height of the boom in 2022, roughly 500 new NFT collections were being created every day , according to blockchain analytics firm IntoTheBlock. The rapid rise in NFT prices helped fuel expectations that buyers would continue paying more for them. But as enthusiasm faded, so did the pool of potential buyers. And unlike stocks or bonds, most NFTs didn't generate income, meaning buyers hoping to turn a profit generally depended on someone else being willing to pay more for them, says Martin Mulyadi, the YHB Endowed Chair in Accounting at Shenandoah University. "Most NFTs paid nothing, so the only way to make money was finding a next buyer at a higher price," he says. "When the buyers stopped coming, there was nothing holding up the price." For everyday investors, the NFT bust is a reminder that an asset's popularity doesn't necessarily make it a worthwhile investment . One common justification for buying risky investments like collectibles is that they make up only a small portion of an otherwise diversified portfolio . Financial advisors often recommend limiting speculative holdings to money an investor can afford to lose. But keeping an investment small doesn't necessarily make it worthwhile, Mulyadi says. "While keeping a bet small limits the damage, it doesn't turn a weak asset into a good one," he says. Mills argues that investors can also confuse speculation with diversification. "Diversification is not just owning more things," he says.

events.title: Mazama Energy has a solution for geothermal’s biggest drilling problem
events.summary: Success in geothermal energy is guided by two basic goals — drill fast and drill deep. Hit both targets, and geothermal startups have a good chance at being cheaper than nearly every other source on the electrical grid. But while the goals might be straightforward, they’re anything but easy. Drilling fast generates heat, which damages equipment, and so does drilling deep. Those two foes are what led Mazama Energy to develop a new technology, called Carbon Chill, that uses carbon dioxide to cool the drill bit and bring cuttings to the surface. The technology will not only let the company drill deeper, but also faster. The startup gave TechCrunch an exclusive look at Carbon Chill. “Our rate of penetration increased 20% over the already very high rates we were achieving,” Sriram Vasantharajan, co-founder and CEO of Mazama Energy, told TechCrunch. Speed has other advantages in geothermal. Drilling represents about 25% to 30% of the total cost of building a power plant, so reducing drill time can bring costs down significantly. If geothermal startups succeed in drilling faster and cheaper, they stand to help reshape the grid in the 2030s. Hyperscalers are already planning the facilities that will enter operation at the end of the decade. Mazama has been working on the problem for years now. In October 2025, the Khosla-backed startup said it had drilled a well in Oregon that reached 629˚ F (331˚ C), and a more recent well has surpassed 700˚ C, Vasantharajan said. In September, the startup raised $135 million in a round led by Centaurus Capital and Doerr Capital. Mazama hopes that its new carbon dioxide-based cooling technology will help it prove that geothermal energy from super-hot rock is a viable contender in the electricity market. Already companies like Google and Meta have started to explore the use of geothermal energy, in part because the potential is enormous: a report from the National Laboratory of the Rockies said that geothermal could generate between 26.5 to 57 terawatts of electricity in the U.S. alone. If just 10% of the conservative estimate were developed, it would more than double the U.S.’s peak generating capacity. Geothermal experts have identified super-hot rock — in which temperatures exceed 752˚ F (400˚ C) — as a promising way to improve the performance of individual wells. At those temperatures, water turns “supercritical,” a gaseous-like liquid state which carries five to ten times more energy than water from traditional geothermal wells. By harvesting more energy from a each well, developers have to drill fewer of them, bringing costs down. Accessing that heat can be challenging for traditional drilling methods. Most geothermal drillers use “mud” — a combination of water and other compounds to keep the bit cool and clear cuttings from the borehole. But mud can only bring temperatures down so much. Eventually, they become so hot that electronics in the drill bit, which help keep it on course, start to fail. High temperature-rated electronics exist, but they’d be cost prohibitive, Vasantharajan said. Instead of mud, Mazama injects liquid carbon dioxide down the center of its drill string. As it is travels deeper, it gets heated by the rock around it, which turns it supercritical, too. Then, just before it reaches the drill head, Mazama has it flow through a valve that looks a lot like a rocket nozzle. As the gas expands, it escapes through the cone-shaped nozzle, rapidly cools, absorbing heat from the electronics and the drill bit. “I look at [carbon dioxide cooling] as a binary,” he said. “Without such technologies, I am, today, not able to drill these horizontal wells at super hot rock temperatures.” That capital injection will help Mazama drill more wells deeper. By next year, Vasantharajan said his company hopes to complete a single well that’s capable of generating up to 15 megawatts of electricity. “What was just a dream or a quest, I can tell you with confidence is now a promise,” he said. “We see a path towards this commercial super-hot rock geothermal.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. Tim De Chant is a senior climate reporter at TechCrunch. He has written for a wide range of publications, including Wired magazine, the Chicago Tribune, Ars Technica, The Wire China, and NOVA Next, where he was founding editor. De Chant is also a lecturer in MIT’s Graduate Program in Science Writing, and he was awarded a Knight Science Journalism Fellowship at MIT in 2018, during which time he studied climate technologies and explored new business models for journalism. He received his PhD in environmental science, policy, and management from the University of California, Berkeley, and his BA degree in environmental studies, English, and biology from St. Olaf College. Google documented this attack in its fourth-quarter 2026 AI threat tracker, and said it marks a significant advance in how attackers use LLMs for fully autonomous vulnerability discovery and exploitation compared to Q3. In this case, the threat hunters found an exposed staging server hosting a multi-agent vulnerability research and weaponization framework that integrates with multiple frontier and local models. The framework, called exploit_agent, used Russian-language tooling, and was configured to conduct continuous differential analysis of “popular web application software,” according to the report . This includes comparing code before and after security updates, identifying potential vulnerabilities, developing exploits, and then automatically executing them without any human involvement. The server also contained data stolen from victim organizations, and “multiple” post-compromise scripts that allowed attackers to perform nefarious activities including internal reconnaissance, brute-forcing, installing webshells, and removing other attackers’ webshells. “Victim telemetry on the server suggests the operator was specifically interested in targeting French websites associated with the media and entertainment industries, as well as the education sector,” according to the report. The report also documents other instances of attackers moving beyond manual LLM prompting during cyberattacks and instead deploying autonomous, multi-agent offensive security frameworks to carry out multi-stage intrusions. These include both financially motivated cybercriminals and cyber-espionage groups. In addition to the recent attacks involving the open source penetration-testing tool ARTEX, attackers have also used other AI-powered offensive frameworks, including CAIRN , CyberStrikeAI , HexStrike AI , and PentAGI. In another instance, GTIG observed attackers using PentAGI alongside proxy services to target the aerospace sector. “We have observed several threat actors separately experimenting with use of these frameworks and harnesses, including financially motivated, as well as suspected espionage threat actors with a PRC nexus,” the Googlers wrote. “Given the low barrier to entry, ease of integrating new exploits, and massive scaling potential, we believe it is highly likely that threat actors will continue to use these frameworks in campaigns targeting organizations globally.” ® Marvell and Penguin Solutions aim to end the RAMpocalypse with photonic memory fabric Appliances can share 16 TB of DRAM and half a terabyte of HBM across up to 16 systems Your AI agent is only as good as your endpoint data PARTNER CONTENT: Real-time endpoint data keeps AI-driven IT operations accurate, fast and under control The Jensen Huang saga could be the beginning of the end of the AI bubble – or just a boon for competitors There could be no greater irony than if the misdeeds of one of AI's biggest names brought the whole house of cards crashing down We don't need no education platform evolution.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Appliances can share 16 TB of DRAM and half a terabyte of HBM across up to 16 systems Los Alamos boffins to put NextSilicon's Maverick-2 through natural selection in Darwin testbed 1 hour ago Datacenters' share of UK planning applications nearly triples in three years 1 hour ago Elon Musk leads Silicon Valley's campaign to put Jensen Huang back in charge at Nvidia 2 hours ago Chinese AI labs are training models on Nvidia's Blackwell despite export controls, says ex-OpenAI engineer 2 days ago HPE debuts hybrid storage configs: Rising SSD costs hit supercomputing 2 days ago Celestial AI’s dream of high-bandwidth memory (HBM) at a distance will soon be a reality as part of a new collaboration between Marvell Technology and system integrator Penguin Solutions to build a photonic memory fabric. Marvell acquired the underlying technology for the fabric from Celestial AI for $3.5 billion in February. It comprises a memory expansion module with two stacks of HBM3e totaling 72 GB along with support for eight channels of DDR5 stacked atop a silicon photonic interposer with 7.2 Tbps (900 GB/s) of bidirectional bandwidth. “What we provide in this appliance is what we call a Photonic Fabric memory module… We provide these modules to Penguin, and they build the box, do all the power management, do the software, and all the management layer,” Preet Virk, senior VP of Marvell’s photonic fabric biz, tells El Reg. Penguin’s first appliances based on the tech will support 16 of these memory modules for up to 16 TB of DDR5 and 1 TB of HBM, with future systems capable of scaling to twice the DDR5 capacity. With 57.6 Tbps of bandwidth distributed via a Marvell-designed optical fiber shuffle, each appliance supports up to 16 servers either via a network interface card, or via co-packaged (CPO) or near-packaged optical (NPO) modules. If you’re not familiar, CPO modules are typically integrated directly into the compute or switch ASIC, while NPO modules are a sort of half measure. They connect electrically to the host, whether that’s a CPU, GPU, or some other ASIC, and the rest of the fabric optically. NPO is expected to play a major role in the next generation of rack-scale systems from Nvidia and AMD, as it provides better serviceability and lower blast radius than baking photonic chiplets directly into CPUs or GPUs. Through a software layer, which we’re told was developed by Penguin, each system can access the entire shared memory space, similar to how systems connecting to network-attached storage would have access to the appliance's full capacity. As we understand it, a lot of this functionality is made possible today through CXL 3.1 compatible NICs and host CPUs, like AMD’s shiny new Venice CPUs. However, for NPO- and CPO-based memory, Virk tells us that CXL can be bypassed entirely. Memory godboxes could offer relief from the RAMpocalypse Amid the AI-fueled memory crunch, will Compute Express Link finally have its moment to shine? The implications of this tech should be obvious. If memory can be shared and pooled across multiple servers, each of those servers doesn't need as much of its own DRAM, possibly saving some money. In addition to facilitating communications, Virk says, the software also allows for several memory tiering modes by which customers can expose the resources to connected systems. For the most part, these follow typical CXL memory tiering conventions, with the exception of an HBM cache-through mode that Virk says will enable users to extract the performance of HBM with the capacity of DDR5. This mode essentially treats the HBM as a read/write cache. Frequently accessed files are written to and read from HBM first before being pushed into standard DDR5 as they get stale. Marvell and Penguin are positioning the new memory appliance as an alternative to storage-based key value (KV) cache offload. AI inference generates large KV caches, which are used to track model state across chat sessions, and long-running agents.

events.title: 'We slept here': Flight delays linger as airlines recover from ground stop, but schedule improves Monday
events.summary: U.S. flights disruptions eased Monday, but hundreds of additional flights were canceled. Flight disruptions continued through the weekend after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded departures nationwide for more than four hours. Airlines waived change fees and fare differences and offered pilots and flight attendants extra pay to ease the delays. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the issue on a router in Arkansas that overwhelmed systems that feed radar and other data for air traffic control. U.S. flights delays eased on Monday as airlines scrambled to get back on track after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded departures nationwide for more than four hours on Friday. Nearly 300 U.S. flights were canceled and close to 1,000 were delayed Monday, a fraction of Sunday's disruptions, according to FlightAware data. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy over the weekend tied the issue that prompted officials to call for the ground stop to a router in southern Arkansas and work to update copper wires to a fiber-optic system overseen by L3Harris Technologies . FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said the upgrades were part of "routine" maintenance to switch over to fiber optic. Officials ordered the ground stop before 4 p.m. on Friday and it lasted until after 8 p.m., marking the longest halt to U.S. flight departures since 9/11. Hundreds of thousands of travelers were stranded and about 18,000 U.S. flights were canceled from Friday through Monday morning, according to FlightAware. Over that period, American Airlines had the most cancellations with 5,367 flights, close to 22% of its schedule, followed by Delta Air Lines with 3,434 cancellations, or 17% of its schedule, according to aviation data firm Cirium. Southwest Airlines and United Airlines each canceled more than 16% of their schedules. Bad weather on Thursday and Friday had also contributed to disruptions before the ground stop. DOT Sec. Duffy ties router in southern Arkansas to issues that led to nationwide ground stop Hundreds of flights into Newark, New York, Philadelphia disrupted after Verizon fiber line cut The government shutdown is over. The air traffic controller shortage is not 'Seconds count': Avoiding airplane collisions at airports could come down to cockpit alerts Aviation industry pushes Congress for air traffic improvements, more hiring Why the U.S. doesn't have enough air traffic controllers FAA system outage disrupts thousands of flights across U.S. On Sunday, disruptions lingered but were starting to improve. "We slept here," said Beth Martin, who was trying to travel home to Birmingham, Alabama, from New York's LaGuardia Airport on Sunday at the end of her daughter's birthday trip. The two were booked for Saturday night, and when delay announcements started rolling in from Delta, they decided to make good use of the extra time: After strolling through Central Park, they went window shopping on Fifth Avenue. But when the flight was canceled, the standby list for a backup flight looked grim and their original Midtown hotel was charging about $700 for an additional night, the two slept at LaGuardia on Saturday. She said they found wheelchairs to sleep in outside security. Customers told CNBC they were booked on several flights before getting on board. Justine Fritz, who works in sales for a consumer goods company, was in New York for a business event on Friday. She tried five different flights before getting on one to Houston, then flew four hours out of her way to get back to Minneapolis after her Saturday flight was canceled. Fritz said she had so many boarding passes that TSA wouldn't let her through security at first. "It's been bananas," she told CNBC at the gate. Fritz said she made the best of it by shopping and getting a haircut, but she's still disappointed. "I'm missing the first hour of the Vikings game," she said. Martin said her trip home with her daughter will take even longer. Delta booked them to Memphis, and her husband will drive the four hours from Birmingham to pick them up. Officials are investigating the root cause that led to what the FAA described as "instability" in data feeds. Duffy said Sunday that two routers, the original one detected as a problem in southern Arkansas, and another in Amarillo, Texas, are in an L3Harris lab in Florida. "We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel," L3Harris said in a statement Saturday afternoon. Shortly after the ground stop, Duffy pushed Congress for as much as $50 billion for upgrades to the aging U.S. air traffic control system. A day later, Democratic lawmakers pushed back, citing unspent money from existing funding, which includes Congress's approval last year of $12.5 billion for airport and air traffic control improvements over five years.

events.title: US limits remote access to advanced AI chips; Jensen Huang ‘discusses comeback as Nvidia CEO’ – business live
events.summary: Introduction: Huang's considering comeback as Nvidia chief (!) Good morning and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets and the world economy. Just days after his dramatic defenestration, Jensen Huang is considering a comeback as Nvidia’s chief executive. In what would be one of the more impressive returns since Lazarus, Huang is attracting support to be reinstalled at the head of the chip giant, despite the scandal which led to his resignation last Thursday. News broke over the weekend that Huang’s allies in Silicon Valley are campaigning for his return to the top job, even though an investigation into his conduct has barely started. According to the Financial Times , “Huang has discussed with confidants the possibility of returning”, following his resignation last week after revelations he had at least two extramarital affairs, one with a woman accused of spying for China and another with a subordinate. The drama has knocked around $600bn off Nvidia’s value, so far. Nvidia’s board named chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim CEO last week. But now, an open letter calling for Huang’s reinstatement has attracted more than 165,000 signatories. The list includes Elon Musk , Tim Sweeney , founder and CEO of video game publisher Epic Games, Garry Tan , president of business incubator Y Combinator, and Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick . More than 7,500 signatories identify themselves as Nvidia employees – which, if true, would equatae to around 18% of the company’s workforce. It only adds to the pressure on Kress, who will be presenting Nvidia’s latest financial results tomorrow afternoon…. 10am GMT: Eurozone production output for September 1.30pm GMT: New York Empire State Manufacturing Index 22m ago US announces new rules to limit remote ccess to advanced AI chips 2h ago Insurance industry workers: how is climate-related risk managed in your company? 3h ago San Jose Denny's reinstalls plaque honoring former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang 4h ago ECB warns of market risks if AI boom stalls 5h ago UK bond yields rise after interest rate rise hints 5h ago Nvidia shares down in pre-market trading 5h ago UK stock market nearing record high 6h ago Japan's economy stagnates in Q3 6h ago Georgieva: it's been the year of AI - whether you love it, hate it, or fear it 6h ago US dollar hits 19-month high 6h ago Megaspeed insists it’s a ‘legitimate and lawful business’ 7h ago Bessent: Nvidia needs a 'dramatic shake-up' 7h ago AI sell-off resumes as Kospi and TW50 slide 7h ago Introduction: Huang's considering comeback as Nvidia chief (!) US announces new rules to limit remote ccess to advanced AI chips Newsflash: The US Commerce Department has issued a new rule to limit remote access to advanced artificial intelligence chips by certain third countries. The interim final rule (IFR) is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries, the US government says. The IFR will require licenses to reexport advanced AI chips to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil. This move follows reports that Singapore-based Megaspeed , the company where suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang worked, had transferred advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese companies. The Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry & Security explains: Rapid advancement in cloud computing and SI infrastructure have made it increasingly possible to access advanced American computing capabilities remotely, including through data centers located outside countries subject to U.S. export restrictions. This IFR addresses this evolving technological landscape by further aligning protections governing remote access to advanced computing capabilities with existing controls on the physical shipment of sensitive American technology. Marketwatch’s Mark DeCambre has three questions for anyone considering taking up the CEO’s role at Nvidia: What am I inheriting? What has the board learned about the export concerns and Nvidia’s financing deals? What’s still unresolved? How much of the company do I actually get to run? Who‘ll be on the board a year from now, and will they back me if I change a strategy that Jensen put in place? Who can I count on to stay at Nvidia? If Jensen goes to work for a competitor, which of the people I need at Nvidia might take his call? Insurance industry workers: how is climate-related risk managed in your company? Whether you’re a modeller, actuary or underwriter, we’d like to hear how the insurance industry is dealing with climate risk – click here for more : Tensions are building in the markets ahead of the stockmarket float of AI firm Anthropic. Anthropic is due to launch its shares onto the stock market on Thursday. And having initially hoped for a $2tn valuation, it may come to market at a lower valuation of $1.5bn, or even less….

events.title: At Cantor’s crypto summit, a window into Tether’s ambitions and a warning on cyberattacks
events.summary: Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong once sent an executive from San Francisco to New York with the goal of making inroads with the storied Wall Street firm Cantor Fitzgerald. It did not go well. Arriving alone, the executive recalls he was greeted by Cantor’s then-CEO Howard Lutnick and a dozen lieutenants, who ridiculed his General Manager title: “So I sat down with this big, sharp-elbowed financial company, trying to work a deal…The CEO laughs at me and goes ‘Hey GM, are you going to make my coffee?’ I came out to New York and got my ass handed to me by old-school traders.” That anecdote, which I recount in my history of Coinbase’s early years, took place in 2016. A decade later, things are a little different. In Miami last week, Lutnick’s son Brandon presided over Cantor Converge, an annual summit dedicated to blockchain and other new technology—where this year’s keynote speaker was none other than Brian Armstrong. I sat down with the younger Lutnick, whose dress and appearance are every inch that of a Wall Street banker, but who speaks fluent crypto. He revealed that he is bullish about four parts of the sector in particular: Bitcoin, stablecoins, remittances, and exchanges like Coinbase that are crypto native but now offer everything from tokenized equities to prediction markets. In the long term, I suspect he’s correct on all four counts. But it is his and Cantor’s ties to stablecoins, and in particular Tether, that are most intriguing. Those include an arrangement that saw Cantor become the custodian for Tether’s massive reserves, receiving a small stake of the stablecoin giant in return. As part of this tie-up, Brandon Lutnick has seen the workings of Tether up close. That includes a stint in Switzerland where he physically examined a hoard of gold bars used to back Tether’s gold stablecoin, which currently has a market cap of around $3 billion. As for the company’s flagship USDT product, Lutnick views it not only as the world’s biggest stablecoin, but also as a strategic asset—one that cements the influence of the U.S. dollar in countries around the world. (He is not alone in that view .) In one of the more memorable moments from last week’s Miami conference, Tether’s CEO Paolo Ardoino took the stage with a background showing larger-than-life AI images of the future. Those images included a hologram of Hari Seldon, the protagonist from Isaac Asimov’s acclaimed Foundation sci-fi series, as well as scenes of decentralized cellphone and AI infrastructure in Africa. In his address, Ardoino made the case that, just as stablecoins offer a form of money beyond control of the state, it’s possible (and perhaps urgent) to build out a host of other decentralized technologies. The presentation left some in the standing-room audience (including the Polish equities analyst at my table) looking puzzled. But elements of it also provided a valuable look into the mind of Tether’s CEO and his global ambitions. Cantor’s shindig also included appearances by Binance founder Changpeng Zhao and CFTC Chairman Michael Selig, who reaffirmed his position that crypto and other new financial technologies should be built in the U.S. The most notable moments for me, though, came in the form of comments by Armstrong and the CEO of quantum computing firm IonQ, Niccolo de Masi. Both chief executives warned that the recent wave of cyberattacks are going to persist, with Armstrong stating matter-of-factly that there is an employee at every company—including his own—with malware on their computers. For his part, de Masi said that cyber attackers currently have the upper-hand over defenders, and that there is not much time left to secure our networks from quantum-based exploits. Whether we like it or not, cybersecurity is going to be in the news a lot. Jeff John Roberts jeff.roberts@fortune.com @jeffjohnroberts This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: International student enrollment drops sharply, putting more U.S. colleges in financial jeopardy
events.summary: Changing immigration policies have contributed to a sharp decline in the number of international students studying on U.S. college campuses this year, according to the Institute of International Education. International enrollment is an important source of revenue for colleges and universities, experts say. Institutions with large graduate and STEM programs may be hardest hit, according to an analysis from Fitch Ratings. Amid changing visa policies and rising degree costs, significantly fewer new international students enrolled at U.S. colleges this year — a shift that could have financial repercussions for colleges, students and the broader economy. In the fall 2026 semester, the tally of new international students studying in the U.S. sank 15% compared to the prior academic year, according to a fall snapshot released Monday from the Institute of International Education, an international education nonprofit. Over the 2025-26 academic year, the number of new international students in the U.S. fell more than 17%, largely because fewer graduate students came from countries such as India and China, the IIE's report found. A growing number of U.S. colleges said that international student recruitment was a top concern, but the report also cited the high cost of a U.S. degree relative to other countries — along with uncertainty around new rules ending the traditional "duration of status" system and limiting most F-1 and J-1 visas to four years — as significant barriers. IRS announces 2027 401(k) contribution limits, raises savings cap Why Nvidia stock drop isn't a big deal for many ETF, mutual fund investors Social Security could pay benefits until 2059 if payroll kept pace with GDP: AARP CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 ranked CNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026 Even though the Department of Homeland Security's new visa restrictions are currently on hold under a federal court injunction, experts say questions about the changing policies may have already discouraged some prospective international students. "At a time when countries around the world are competing for talent, the United States should be strengthening our ability to attract the best and brightest, not creating new barriers to it," Fanta Aw, executive director and CEO of NAFSA: Association of International Educators, said in a Sept. 14 statement after a federal court temporarily blocked the Department of Homeland Security's new visa rules. Foreign students typically pay full tuition, making international enrollment an important revenue source for colleges and universities, according to Robert Franek, editor-in-chief of The Princeton Review. With fewer tuition dollars coming in, there are fewer resources for U.S. students, particularly for financial aid, he said: "There are going to be fewer research dollars, fewer scholarship dollars for students here in the states." International students also contributed nearly $40 billion to the U.S. economy during the 2025-26 academic year, according to a separate NAFSA analysis . This year's enrollment decline is expected to cost the economy roughly $2.4 billion. "The data again reflect the harsh reality that the barriers the U.S. government is putting in place to block talented international students are having a real impact," said NAFSA's Aw. "All Americans will feel the effects as international students' tuition payments, local spending, and contributions to U.S. excellence in research and innovation diminish." Although the fallout extends well beyond college campuses, other research shows that colleges and the students they serve will bear the brunt of the impact. Recent changes to F-1 student visa rules could heighten financial risks for some U.S. colleges and universities, particularly those that rely heavily on students from abroad, according to an analysis from Fitch Ratings released in August. "Sustained drops in new international student enrollment can have outsized revenue effects, as international students often pay full tuition or receive less institutional aid than domestic students," Fitch analysts said in the report. "Lost revenue is hard to replace quickly." Specifically, universities with large graduate and STEM — science, technology, engineering and math — programs, where time to degree completion can exceed four years, will have a harder time sustaining the enrollment pipeline and "may incur higher costs to address overseas recruitment challenges," the analysts wrote. Most international students — 57% — study in STEM fields, according to IIE's report, so enrollment declines can have an outsized financial impact on schools with large engineering and computer science programs. Underscoring the importance of those students, 91% of colleges and universities said recruiting international students in STEM fields is now a key priority, according to IIE's fall snapshot, which was based on a survey of 809 institutions.

events.title: A Ukrainian drone maker says that if it had to do business facing Western levels of bureaucracy, it wouldn't exist
events.summary: Ukrainian drone maker TechEx says the West should rethink its level of regulation to be fast and agile enough for modern, large-scale war. Pavlo Bahmut/Ukrinform/Sipa USA via Reuters Connect Ukraine's defense industry works differently from the West, with less bureaucracy. One key drone maker said that with such heavy levels of regulation, "we wouldn't exist." The West wants to learn from Ukraine's speed and flexibility, and questions some bureaucratic steps. A Ukrainian drone maker said it wouldn't exist if it had to grapple with Western-style weapons regulations, warning that cutting the red tape can be key to keeping pace in modern warfare. Ukraine's defense industry operates at speeds that many Western partner nations admire and say they ought to learn from. The pace is born in part from authorities allowing companies to bypass traditional structures to work directly with units. Many Ukrainian companies have warned that their Western partners ought to adopt a less rigid, more flexible approach if they are going to be ready for a possible large-scale conflict, TechEx, which makes fiber-optic and interceptor drones, works with more than 100 units and was the first Ukrainian company to receive NATO codification for fiber-optic FPV drones . Its team started experimenting in 2022, and it was formally registered in 2024. Oleg, a TechEx executive, told Business Insider that had it needed to adhere to strict pre-war regulations similar to those governing defense companies in the West, "we wouldn't exist." Ukraine's experience suggests that "the regulations and the amount of the bureaucracy or the paperwork required for those things to launch or to produce anything should be definitely reduced," he said. If Russia attacks Europe, Oleg said, "there will be no time for the bureaucracy. There will be no time for the paperwork or any kind of approval to 100 levels by the checking authorities." After Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, Ukraine pivoted away from its old system for procuring weapons and arming troops, toward more decentralized operations. Ukraine still has certain regulations, but troops have better access to industry and vice versa. Key weaponry like drones, electronic warfare, and robotics is dominated by agile firms that are allowed to work directly with units to test, request, and buy what they need. Defense products can be authorized for use without meeting traditional peacetime testing requirements as long as they meet the manufacturer's declared specifications, and a manufacturer-issued quality certificate can be sufficient for procurement, with manufacturers responsible for quality. With the freedom for troops and defense tech companies to engage one another directly, TechEx receives constant feedback from Ukrainian units . The company offers technical support, makes weekly updates to its products, and believes that if it doesn't make those updates, a product could become obsolete and outdated in as little as three months. It takes requests directly from combat units, even manufacturing specific variations of its drones with added features that it doesn't intend to mass-produce. Ukraine's defense companies have a much closer relationship with front-line units and soldiers than their Western counterparts typically do. Wolfgang Schwan/Anadolu via Getty Images Unlike Ukraine, its Western partner nations are not fighting a war for their survival. Still, some officials warn that their peacetime processes could leave them unprepared for the demands of modern warfare. Ukraine urges the West to act differently TechEx is not alone in warning that Western industry needs to work differently to meet today's needs. Yaroslav Filimonov, the CEO of Ukrainian electronic warfare company Kvertus, told Business Insider that for many partner nations, processes like identifying a need, building, and testing, "are still too slow." "A five-year R&D cycle is just an obsolete concept and will not survive in the reality of modern warfare," he said. Oleg Fedoryshyn, the director of R&D for Ukrainian defense company DevDroid, told Business Insider his company can develop , test, and field new features in a week. Some Western firms that use his technology might take months, he said, explaining that it's "because of bureaucracy." Davyd Aloian, the deputy secretary of Ukraine's National Security and Defense Council, told Business Insider that a key thing partners can learn from Ukraine is its "deregulation processes," which he described as "really very beneficial" for companies to rapidly develop and scale production. Western partner nations are responding to these recommendations. NATO's Rapid Adoption Action Plan, for instance, is a Ukraine-inspired effort to get new gear faster, with allies "embracing more risk at early stages to achieve better results, faster." Wes Streeting, the UK's defense minister, said last month that "Ukraine has changed the character of conflict forever," including by being able to deploy new technology in weeks instead of years. "The old model of procurement that involved defense giants and lengthy specs, tortuous legal compliance, and endless form-filling is obsolete," he said. Latvian military officials told Business Insider that they want to draw lessons from Ukraine's rapid weapons development and close cooperation between troops and manufacturers. There are efforts on the eastern flank and elsewhere within the alliance to make that a reality, but NATO Deputy Secretary General Radmila Shekerinska said in August that the alliance's efforts to boost weapons production must happen "much quicker." The West will need to decide how much it is willing to change in peacetime before it faces the pressure of war. Oleg said that ultimately, " allies have this time to prepare for this, to learn, to prepare and to absorb this knowledge from what we are learning." He described it as knowledge won at an extremely high price, "the lives of our soldiers." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: 'Bad lighting, dry skin': Bill Ackman has an explanation for haters who said he looked 'grizzled'
events.summary: Bill Ackman said a tennis injury and poor sleep explained why he looked “grizzled” in a recent interview. Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images Bill Ackman said a tennis injury and poor sleep explained his "grizzled" appearance in an interview. After he spoke on Bloomberg TV on Friday, X users criticized Ackman's appearance. The hedge fund billionaire also said he wasn't helped by bad lighting and having dry skin. Bill Ackman has an explanation for why he looked "grizzled" in an interview last week: a tennis injury, two sleepless nights, dry skin, and bad lighting. After a clip of Friday’s interview circulated on X, commenters questioned the Pershing Square founder's appearance, saying he looked older. "Markets have really done a number on Bill here?" one user wrote. Another asked whether it was "really Bill Ackman" and why he looked "so old and out of shape." A third said he appeared to have "aged 20 years in the last 6 months." In a Sunday post, Ackman, 60, set the record straight. His explanation involved no dramatic market losses: He had hurt his back playing tennis, slept badly, and the lighting in the interview did him no favors. The post was pinned to the top of his X account. Yesterday, some of you in the @X community expressed concern about my health based on how grizzled I looked in a Bloomberg interview I did on the street this past Friday. I explained to those concerned that I had pulled out my back, couldn’t work out for a week, and had trouble… https://t.co/fq9I0y23Ks — Bill Ackman (@BillAckman) November 15, 2026 He had trouble sleeping because of the pain, he said, and joked that the resulting look made him seem a decade older. The tennis-loving Ackman then joked that he looked like John McEnroe, who is seven years his senior. The interview that sparked the commentary had focused on AI. Ackman told Bloomberg he was sad to see Jensen Huang leave Nvidia and said he was impressed by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s presentation at the company’s New York IPO road show. Those remarks, however, took a back seat to a debate about his face. Ackman followed up with a recovery report. He said the team at VOSK Center, a luxury New York-based performance and longevity club, helped him return to exercise with electrical stimulation, work on his back and hip muscles, and weights. VOSK, which called Ackman one of its founding members , shared a video of him taking on a pull-up challenge. "The back is still stiff but I can walk again," Ackman wrote, thanking people who had checked on him. He also said he does not take GLP-1 medications, which are used to treat diabetes and obesity. "I don’t like drugs," he wrote. He later acknowledged that avoiding them made the back pain harder to manage. Ackman ended his update with a plea for people to look out for one another. events.title: Fed up with the healthcare industry, this red state capped insulin prices for patients
events.summary: The Kritzberger family has farmed in the Red River Valley for more than a century. They once had livestock. Now they grow sugar beets, soybeans, and grains. Like many farmers, they labor to balance the books. “We’re in an incredible amount of debt,” Ang Kritzberger said as she walked the farm on a recent fall morning. For the past 10 years, the Kritzbergers have had another worry. Their daughter Nina has Type 1 diabetes. That’s landed the family in a national debate about how to protect patients from high insulin costs. Nina was diagnosed when she was 7. “I slept by her bedside for the first 60 days,” Ang Kritzberger said. “And I had to stick her finger every two hours, 24 hours a day, to make sure that she was OK.” The Kritzbergers also pay a lot out-of-pocket every year for medical care, despite having insurance — at least $8,000 for drugs, supplies, and medical appointments. That’s not uncommon. Soaring insulin prices for years forced people with diabetes to pay hundreds, even thousands, of dollars. Many rationed insulin, with sometimes deadly consequences. But today, there’s a growing movement across the country to cap what people with diabetes pay for insulin. That’s brought together Democrats and Republicans, tapping an emerging consensus that the government should protect people from high drug prices. “Typically, Republicans are more on the free-market side of things, Democrats are more supportive of intervening,” said North Dakota state Sen. Sean Cleary, a Republican. “But in this case, I think there was broad-enough agreement that this market just wasn’t functioning for folks.” Cleary co-sponsored legislation last year to cap patients’ insulin bills at $25 a month. North Dakota is one of 29 states that have enacted such measures. The cap limits what patients have to pay out-of-pocket every month for insulin — even if they have a high deductible that might force them to pay thousands of dollars before coverage kicks in for other healthcare, such as physician visits, hospitalizations, or other prescriptions. Patient advocates, including the American Diabetes Association , began pushing for out-of-pocket caps and other protections amid spiking insulin prices and stories of patients who had died because they couldn’t afford their medicine. About a fifth of the estimated 40 million Americans with diabetes depend on insulin. The drug has been in use for a century. But steep price hikes boosted patients’ out-of-pocket costs, which hit an average $470 a year in 2018 for people with private health insurance, according to federal data . Prices have since moderated as drug companies faced a public backlash. Average yearly out-of-pocket costs for people with private insurance declined to $220 in 2025 . But for many families like the Kritzbergers, the prospect of a government cap offered protection from future price hikes and some relief from the anxiety of a serious disease. Nina Kritzberger, now 17, said she already has a lot to worry about. “I have to make sure I have insulin, a spare pump, a spare Dexcom,” she said, ticking off the equipment that patients with diabetes rely on. “Oh, what if my pump doesn’t work, or my Dexcom? Then I have to bring a testing kit. What if I go low? I need Gatorade, glucose.” A missed dose of insulin could land her in the hospital. “My body would start attacking itself and start shutting down,” she said. “And then I would die.” The price cap strategy initially caught on with Democrats. In 2019, Colorado became the first state to enact what was called an insulin copay cap. State-regulated health plans there cannot charge patients more than $100 for a 30-day supply of the drug. In 2022, President Joe Biden signed legislation that capped insulin prices for Medicare enrollees at $35 a month. Biden and congressional Democrats wanted to extend the cap to people with private health insurance, including Americans with employer-provided coverage. But Republican opposition sank that proposal. In North Dakota, state Sen. Tim Mathern led the effort to enact an insulin copay cap for health plans regulated by the state. For a long time, Mathern struggled to find supporters. He’s one of only five Democrats in the Senate. There are 42 Republicans. “One is very lonely being a Democrat,” Mathern said, “especially if you espouse the more progressive end of public policy.” Health insurers and the state chamber of commerce said price relief for people with diabetes would mean higher insurance premiums for everyone else. “We do not make health insurance more affordable by passing coverage mandates,” Blue Cross Blue Shield of North Dakota lobbyist Megan Hruby told lawmakers. The industry tapped into many lawmakers’ skepticism about regulation, said Janelle Moos, a state lobbyist for AARP. The nonprofit advocacy group for older Americans supported the insulin bill. “It wasn’t the role of government,” Moos said she was told by many GOP lawmakers. “In a state like ours, we hear that all the time.” Ang and Nina Kritzberger joined other families driving hours across the state to testify at the Capitol in Bismarck. It was intimidating at first, Ang Kritzberger said. “It was me and six other lobbyists that were going to be giving their testimony against me,” she recalled. But supporters of the insulin bill showed that a similar measure that limited out-of-pocket costs for state employees with diabetes had little impact on insurance premiums. It also became clear that many lawmakers, including Republicans, had grown very frustrated with drugmakers, health insurers, and others in the healthcare industry. “Why are folks paying hundreds of dollars a month for a drug that’s been commercially available for decades?” asked Cleary, the state senator. “I just kept coming back to the fact that this market seems so broken and these families are having to make impossible decisions about rationing medication or skipping treatment.” State Rep. Carrie McLeod is also a Republican, and a diabetes educator. She said the healthcare system had become too focused on the bottom line. “The insurance companies started out to really help people with catastrophic needs, but things have gotten out of control,” McLeod said. When the insulin bill came up for a vote last year, it passed with overwhelming bipartisan support. The cap won’t suddenly make healthcare affordable. For one thing, states can regulate only some health plans. Health insurance provided by larger employers is typically regulated by the federal government. But polls suggest government regulation of healthcare prices is drawing Americans together. About 7 in 10 U.S. adults — including 68% of Republicans and 77% of Democrats — said in a KFF survey earlier this year that there isn’t enough government regulation to limit the price of prescription drugs. Congress is now considering a national cap on insulin prices. Among the bipartisan list of co-sponsors is Sen. Kevin Cramer, a North Dakota Republican. Back on her farm, Ang K

events.title: Beyond the Horizon: Searching for Kenya’s elusive black leopard
events.summary: Maasai photographer Latei Moses searches Kenya for the rare wild cat, telling his own story through his lens. Maasai photographer Latei Moses is on a journey across northern Kenya to fulfil a lifelong ambition: to photograph the elusive black leopard, known locally as Giza. Believed to inhabit the remote region of Laikipia, the wild cat has long been the subject of local stories. Latei’s search takes him across difficult terrain, as he faces repeated setbacks and exhaustion. But his journey is about more than wildlife. The Maasai are among the most photographed communities in the world, often depicted through the eyes of outsiders. As a Maasai photographer, Latei is reclaiming the power of the camera, documenting his people on his terms. But can his persistence help him find Giza? Beyond the Horizon: Searching for Giza is a documentary film by Mohtadi Ali Ahmad, Mohamad Ali Ahmad and Christelle Saade. events.title: The Jensen Huang saga could be the beginning of the end of the AI bubble – or just a boon for competitors
events.summary: KETTLE Jensen Huang is out at Nvidia after a trio of affairs that include an alleged Chinese spy and two of his subordinates, turning the week into one that's shaken the tech sector. You can listen to the latest episode of The Kettle right here on this page, as well as on Spotify , Apple Music, or YouTube . Those platforms also let you subscribe to The Kettle, so you are always notified when the latest episode goes live. What will become of Nvidia now that its only leader in 33 years, and one whose vision shaped the company into one of the largest in the world, is gone? Who will take charge? Will other chipmakers take advantage of the chaos to surpass the Geforce maker? Will Jensen be the one to put a pin to the AI bubble? Join host Brandon Vigliarolo, systems editor Tobias Mann , and reporter Dan Robinson to talk about the Jensen Huang affair(s) and how the misdeeds of one of AI's biggest names could reshape the entire industry on this week's episode. A lightly edited transcript is included below: Brandon (00:01) Hey everyone and welcome to another episode of The Register ’s Kettle podcast. I'm your host, Reg Reporter Brandon Vigliarolo, and the big news on the tech industry's mind this week is the ouster of Nvidia founder, CEO, president, and board member Jensen Huang over allegations that he not only had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, but also at least two Nvidia employees who were his subordinates. Nvidia's been shaped into one of the most valuable companies in the world over the past thirty-three years, and Huang has played a pivotal, if not the pivotal, role in that ascension, meaning his controversial departure is going to rock the industry, if not the greater world. With me to discuss this is our systems editor Tobias Mann and Reg reporter Dan Robinson. Thanks to you both for coming on. Dan Robinson (00:42) Hi. Tobias Mann (00:43) Good to be here. Brandon (00:43) Quite the week, huh? It seems like we went from Jensen’s just going to survive this spy kerfuffle to the board basically seeming to demand his resignation in the course of a few days, right? So Dan, bring us up to speed on the timeline here, what happened? Dan Robinson (01:01) Well, it all happened over the last couple of weeks. That was when the story first surfaced, or it was first reported in the media, of an affair with an alleged Chinese spy who happened to work for this company in Singapore that bought a lot of Nvidia's products. Brandon (01:30) Right, company was Megaspeed, right? And her name's Alice Huang, no relation to Jensen, coincidence. Dan Robinson (01:36) So it's all happened fairly quickly, but like you say, at the start of this week, it all seemed like Jensen could weather the storm. We were discussing this in our editorial chat and we thought that basically there isn't really anybody who could replace him, or so we thought. He practically is Nvidia, and it's been his vision that's driven the company for so long. But then he came out and he confessed and said he was sorry to all the Nvidia employees. Then the second affair came to light and very quickly, on November 11th actually, Wednesday, he handed in his resignation and it was accepted by the board. So we got to hear about it yesterday [Thursday] when they announced it and it was filed with the SEC. Brandon (03:03) And since then a third affair has come out, right? The New York Times published a finding. Tobias Mann (03:06) Just a few hours later, yeah. Dan Robinson (03:08) It seems so. Makes you wonder how many others may be about to come out in the following days. Brandon (03:13) We're not going to speculate, but my gosh, it seems like that leather jacket really made him irresistible. It’s kind of crazy, right? It seems like the internal affairs with Nvidia employees are the ones that sort of broke the board's back, right? The spy affair seemed like it was kind of like…. Apparently American authorities have basically said they've found no direct evidence to say she is a spy. Dan Robinson (03:44) Exactly. Brandon (03:45) It could just be that she runs a chip company too, or at least a company that is dealing in servers and datacenters. So she has a business reason beyond politics to potentially want to get involved with Jensen. What do you guys think? Was it the internal elements that finally kind of broke the camel's back here and forced the board to act? Dan Robinson (04:08) I think that was the final straw. I think quite possibly he could have weathered the storm as we were saying, if it had just been the one affair outside the business. Brandon (04:20) Outside the business, right? Because now like you were saying, Tobias, not only do you have potentially an international spy affair, but you also have an HR issue to contend with. Tobias Mann (04:29) Right. And I do think that the board could wave their hands around an alleged honeypot scenario. “He was targeted, this was a deliberate act, they preyed on his insecurity.” Brandon (04:44) “It wasn't as big as it's made out to be in the media.” Tobias Mann (04:47) They could make up any number of excuses that they wanted in order to wave their hands over it and keep him CEO or if their arms were twisted by US intelligence services they could have taken him out of an executive role and pushed him into a chairmanship. They had options. And then you had the HR kerfuffle of him allegedly sleeping with another employee. And at that point now there's a pattern. I do sort of question once the news came out that he had an extramarital affair with an employee, whether or not that had influenced him being targeted by Megaspeed and or the Chinese intelligence service, assuming those allegations prove out. Brandon (05:42) We don't know the timeline on one or the other, do we? Tobias Mann (05:46) Right, no. And so it could be that the Chinese intelligence service became aware that this was an avenue that could be exploited and they took it. It's not lost on anybody that he spent most of the last year and a half lobbying to get his chips back into China. And largely successfully on the US side of things. It's been held up by Beijing, which kind of undermines that theory a little bit. events.title: Trump arrives in the Philippines, a key ally in resisting Chinese aggression
events.summary: President Donald Trump’s trip to the Philippines ahead of the APEC summit this week takes him to a key US ally on the front lines of resisting alleged Chinese aggression in Asia. Though Trump has upended relations with many longtime partners throughout his second term, ties with Manila have remained sturdy, with joint military drills increasing in scope and sophistication. Washington sees the Philippines — a potential launchpad for American defense of Taiwan were China to attack the self-ruled island — as a key linchpin in projecting its power across the East, The Wall Street Journal reported. Trump should expect a warm welcome: Almost 70% of Filipinos said they trusted him to do the right thing, the highest level of 36 countries polled. — Jeronimo Gonzalez

events.title: Russian attacks kill three in Ukraine, EU accuses Moscow of prolonging war
events.summary: EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas says Russian President Vladimir Putin is making maximalist demands. Russian attacks have killed at least three people in Ukraine, as the European Union accuses Moscow of stalling talks aimed at ending the war. Russia carried out several attacks on Monday, including in the village of Sadove in southern Ukraine’s Kherson region, killing a man on a moped, according to Governor Oleksandr Prokudin. list 1 of 3 Estonia to close border crossings with Russia after attack on drone maker list 2 of 3 Prince Harry in Ukraine meeting Invictus 2027 hopefuls list 3 of 3 ‘NATO will collapse’: Russia stalls Ukraine talks, seeks to divide Europe Another person was killed in a Russian attack in Dnipro city in central Ukraine, according to Oleksandr Hanzha, the head of the Dnipropetrovsk region’s military administration. Elsewhere, a 59-year-old man was killed in a Russian drone attack in the village of Bilenke in the southern region of Zaporizhia, said Mykhailo Semikin, the acting head of the region’s military administration. Monday’s attacks come as EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs Kaja Kallas accused Russian President Vladimir Putin of making maximalist demands in a bid to extend the conflict. After negotiations in Abu Dhabi last week, the United States encouraged Ukraine and its backers to agree to a Russian demand for a new security framework for Europe, suggesting that it might help bring peace. But the Europeans see that as a Russian attempt to weaken NATO by obliging the military alliance to pull troops and equipment back westward, similar to the way they were deployed before the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland joined in 1999. “In 2021, Russia’s demands were a pretext for war. In 2026, they are pretext to keep the war going,” Kallas said in a post on X. “A ceasefire must come first. It must be the basis to start the talks about anything else. With EU Foreign Ministers, we will discuss our own demands on Moscow to reply to the maximum demands that Russia is presenting.” Meanwhile, Ukrainian drone attacks in the Belgorod region of southwest Russia killed one person on Monday, local authorities said. The Russian Defence Ministry said on Monday that it had intercepted 1,336 drones during overnight attacks by Ukraine. Kyiv received $1.88bn from the European Commission on Monday to buy drones, ammunition and air ⁠defence systems. The money is part of a larger $99bn loan approved in February. Separately, the EU approved its largest-ever single payment to Ukraine, about $8.7bn. “Thank you to [the] EU Commission and EU Council for approving the largest-ever single payment to Ukraine under the Ukraine Facility, amounting to nearly €8 billion [$8.7bn],” Zelenskyy said in a post on X. “I thank President Von Der leyen for her personal efforts to expedite the preparation of this payment, given Ukraine’s growing budgetary needs ahead of winter and intensified Russian attacks on our energy, heating, water supply, and other critical infrastructure.” The EU is currently pushing for a ceasefire followed by a lasting peace agreement to end the four-and-a-half-year conflict. The bloc on Monday imposed more sanctions on Russia, targeting nearly 50 banks and financial institutions. Several businesspeople with links to the energy sector, the trade in oil, and petroleum products were also sanctioned. Dozens of others accused of spreading pro-Russian propaganda and disinformation were also hit with travel bans and asset freezes. Last week, two days of talks between Russian and Ukrainian officials were held in the United Arab Emirates. The discussions were mediated by the US and led to an agreement on a prisoner exchange. However, they failed to make a breakthrough on ending the war.

events.title: China's economic activity slows more than expected
events.summary: China’s economic activity slowed more than expected last month, a sign that Beijing’s efforts to bolster growth are having limited impact. Retail sales and industrial output missed forecasts, feeding fears that the country could slip into deflation. Meanwhile, investment plummeted in the worst monthly drop outside the COVID-19 pandemic. Policymakers fear conditions will worsen further in 2027 and 2028 , prompting them to hold back some stimulus to weather those headwinds. The disappointing data weakens Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s hand ahead of this week’s APEC summit in Shenzhen. Elsewhere, Japan’s economy unexpectedly cooled , too, as it reeled from higher energy prices sparked by the war in the Middle East. — Jeronimo Gonzalez

events.title: Beckham firm sues after fragrance found for sale in Poundland
events.summary: Brand reacted with ‘shock and dismay’ after products were also found in a ‘bargain bin inside a gas station’ David Beckham’s company reacted with “shock and dismay” after discovering his branded fragrance range was on sale in petrol stations and in Poundland, court documents have revealed. The former England football captain’s brand, DB Ventures, has launched a lawsuit against the distributor of the products, arguing it allowed them to be sold in stores that had not been agreed upon. DB Ventures claimed to have discovered the perfumes for sale in the troubled UK budget retailer and in a “bargain bin inside a gas station” at an unspecified location, according to court papers filed in New York. Lawyers acting for Beckham’s company said it reflected “desperation and greed” by the perfume company, Coty. Coty, which is headquartered in the Netherlands, has worked with Beckham’s brand for more than a decade and has produced more than 30 different fragrances bearing his name. In the UK, they sell at about £20 per bottle. Lawyers claimed that Coty sold at least $24m (£18m) of Beckham products through “unapproved distribution channels”. In the court filing, they said: “DB Ventures, the licensor of the David Beckham brand, ensures that all of its brand licensing partnerships maintain the lifestyle and luxury image of the brand that Sir David has carefully cultivated for decades. “Imagine, then, the shock and dismay experienced when DB Ventures discovered that David Beckham products were being offered for sale in a gas station. How could this possibly have happened? Desperation and greed.” The legal documents, filed at the supreme court in New York and first reported by the Daily Mail, allege that Coty had “distributed David Beckham fragrances through the budget retailer Poundland , allowing the product to be sold for dollar store prices and associating the David Beckham brand with cheap, discount products.” The lawyers asked for compensation and damages totalling $41m. They also claimed Coty under-reported net sales by $123m, which would mean that DB Ventures lost $6m in unpaid royalties. Coty filed its defence, asking for the case to be dismissed. It denied that it had ever sold the fragrances in Poundland , but argued that it had the right to decide where it wanted to sell its David Beckham range. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Beckham, who retired from professional football in 2013, has built a multimillion-pound business empire, DRJB Holdings, around his brand. The group is made up of three divisions, the largest of which is DB Ventures, which covers most of his commercial partnerships with brands such as Hugo Boss. The Seven Global division contains licensing agreements with companies such as Adidas, and the remainder of the business is Studio 99, the production studio that made Netflix documentaries about the lives of himself and of his wife, the former Spice Girl and fashion designer Victoria Beckham. This year David Beckham received a $51m dividend from the group, after a series of lucrative brand deals for the Fifa World Cup. He appeared in about a dozen ad campaigns during the tournament this summer, working with brands such as Lenovo, McDonald’s and Bank of America. The Beckhams are together worth an estimated £1.2bn, according to the most recent Sunday Times Rich List. DB Ventures and Coty were approached for comment.

events.title: Average diesel prices are under $6 per gallon for the first time in months
events.summary: Data: AAA; Chart: Ben Geman/Axios Average U.S. diesel prices inched below $6 per gallon on Monday for the first time since Sept. 10 amid lower oil prices recently, per AAA data. Why it matters: Diesel soared even more than gasoline during the Iran war, and those costs rippled throughout the economy. Democrats featured high prices, especially for farmers, en route to midterm wins in typically red agricultural states. Zoom out: The worldwide diesel supply crunch remains acute even as the broader oil market is starting to fitfully stabilize. Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, damage to Middle Eastern production and shipments, throttled oil supplies, and expanded U.S. exports to meet overseas demand helped raise domestic costs. The bottom line: Prices are now far below the Sept. 22 record of nearly $6.53 per gallon. The recent relief is real, but it's limited. Average U.S. prices remain well above the prior record $5.82 per gallon set in 2022.

events.title: How Rockstar's 'GTA VI' release could reshape gaming, streaming and even paid time off
events.summary: "Grand Theft Auto VI" launches Nov. 19, with third-party estimates pointing to exceptional preorder demand and Wall Street expecting tens of millions of copies sold by March. Creators, streaming platforms, food delivery services and Miami tourism could all feel the impact or see spending shift with the game's launch. The game could pull holiday attention from streaming and movies in the week before Thanksgiving. It's been 13 years since the last installment of Grand Theft Auto , and fans are getting ready for what analysts say could be the biggest video game launch of all time. The latest game in the franchise, "Grand Theft Auto VI," is set to launch on Nov. 19, after Take-Two Interactive's Rockstar Games delayed its launch twice. Roth analyst Eric Handler estimated the game maker spent more than $1 billion developing the game. Sales figures could end up breaking records. Sensor Tower estimated over 12 million preorders through Nov. 13, and Morgan Stanley forecast the game could sell 40 million copies by March 2027. Beyond launch week, the Grand Theft Auto, or GTA, franchise has a track record of lasting engagement over many years. Even 13 years after launch, "Grand Theft Auto V" is one of the top five most viewed games on Twitch this year. In anticipation of the game's launch, investors have been taking note: Take-two's stock has more than doubled since the beginning of 2023. The release is seen as not only a monumental moment for developer Rockstar Games and parent company Take-Two, but also a massive opportunity for the entire gaming industry. Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick addressed demand in a recent "Squawk Box" interview , saying, "We tend to be pretty judicious when we talk about this sort of thing, but our expectations were high and they are being vastly exceeded so far." Streamers and creators across the digital ecosystem are looking at the launch as a massive opportunity to drive engagement with their content and fuel subscriber and ad revenue growth. A creator who goes by the name Deansocool, who has 375,000 followers on Twitch and posts content to YouTube and other social platforms as well, said "GTA VI" will enable creators to grow their audience and provide a massive opportunity for newer streamers to make a name for themselves. "This game is going to make a lot of millionaires in 2027. A lot of creators gotta understand this is it. This is that golden ticket. This is like a hundred times bigger than Fortnite," he said in an interview with CNBC. "It goes beyond this launch moment into this sustaining opportunity for them to grow, build, engage and retain their audience and ultimately support themselves by making money," said Twitch Chief Product Officer Mike Minton. The release of the latest Grand Theft Auto title could draw so much attention that its impact will be felt beyond just the world of gaming. BambooHR, an HR software platform where workers manage time-off, reported that paid time off requests for the "GTA VI" release date are nearly 13% higher than equivalent days in 2024 and 2025. It also noted that nearly one in five workers are planning to take time off for the launch. PwC issued a report examining all the different sectors of the economy that could benefit from the game's launch — or be hurt by it. The firm projected that food delivery companies could see a surge from hunkered-down gamers, and Miami tourism could benefit. PwC noted that foreign visitors to Seoul's Bukchon Hanok Village, which inspired a location in the hit Netflix movie KPop Demon Hunters, increased 118% in the four weeks following the movie's debut. Music streaming also looks set to get a boost. Tom Petty's "Love Is a Long Road," which appeared in the first "GTA VI" trailer in December 2023, reportedly saw Spotify streams jump by more than 37,000%. On the downside, the game could distract from movies and streaming entertainment. "How are people spending Thanksgiving? There's a lot of sports on TV, but you've also got a pretty solid group of your demographics that are going to be focused on playing 'GTA VI,'" said Bart Spiegel, who leads PwC's Global Entertainment & Media sector. "You're going to start to pull eyeballs away from video streaming platforms. "I think you're going to hear a lot of analyst calls in the first quarter of 2027 saying, 'Hey, listen, some of our numbers were down because of the release of this game,'" Spiegel added. Rockstar Games declined CNBC's interview request. Watch the video above to learn more.
