events.title: Create more jobs for under-25s by cutting National Insurance, key report urges
events.summary: Salon owner: 'We have parents offering to pay their kids' wages' National Insurance (NI) paid by firms on under-25s should be gradually lowered to help create more jobs, a major report will urge. There are nearly one million 16-24 year-olds not in employment, education or training (Neets) in the UK, official figures show. Reducing NI costs for firms starting with retail and hospitality firms - which provide almost 40% of jobs for these people - will help improve their opportunities, the report will suggest. Collette Osborne, a hairdresser who owns three salons in Nottingham, said she feels "suffocated by employment costs" including NI and while she used to employ eight apprentices a year, now she cannot afford to take on any. Alan Milburn's report will also make recommendations on cutting the benefits bill (file photo) Her workforce has more than halved to 21 staff. Osborne told the BBC it costs "around £60,000 to train an apprentice before we can actually start allowing them onto customers' heads". She said she has had parents so desperate for their children to find employment at her salons that some have even offered to pay their wages. "I'm inundated with applications - and I mean inundated - which is heartbreaking because I can't take them on," she said. Osborne does not feel she is getting help to offer jobs to youngsters. "I feel like the government's foot is firmly on my neck," she said. "They promise breathing space. I feel suffocated, suffocated by employment costs." The independent report by former Labour minister Alan Milburn has been in the works for a year and will be published on Tuesday in full. He has already unveiled some of his proposals including: Reducing benefits - under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of UK-wide Universal Credit or personal independence payment (Pip), which is the main disability benefit in England and Wales A legal guarantee of a job, training or employment support with those who refuse to take up potentially losing their benefits. Doubling the threshold at which businesses start paying NI for 21 to 24-year-olds from £5,000 to £10,000. At the moment, businesses pay no employer NI contributions for workers younger than 21 or for apprentices under 25 – unless they earn above a threshold of £50,270. However, for non-apprentices aged 21-24, employers pay 15% on annual earnings above £5,000. This has been the situation since April 2025, after the then Chancellor Rachel Reeves increased the rate from 13.8% and lowered the threshold from £9,100. Under Sir Keir Starmer, the government raised NI for firms but Milburn will say the Neets issue was not started by the increase. Immediately axing NI for 21 to 24-year-olds would cost £5.1bn, according to research by the Resolution Foundation, a left-leaning think tank. Milburn is set to say that an immediate across-the-board cut in employer NI is not the best use of several billions of pounds of public money. But shadow work and pensions secretary, Helen Whately, said the government should "just stop doing the taxing". Milburn told the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg programme he supported the government subsidising wages to encourage businesses to take on young workers. "Because young people today are walking into the workplace often with a mental health problem, ADHD or anxiety, if you're a small business that's a cost that you've got to absorb," he said. "The state has a responsibility to help them with that." On Sunday, Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said the government would extend its subsidised jobs guarantee scheme for 18 to 24-year-olds who are claiming Universal Credit. People who have been on benefits for 12 months will be eligible, down from 18 months and the scheme would be available for people in England, Scotland and Wales. McFadden said the scheme, which guarantees workers a six-month job, "will help more than 90,000 young people into work by March 2029". events.title: We retired on a budget to Georgia. A nearby nudist resort came with some surprising perks.
events.summary: The author and her husband bought their retirement property sight-unseen. It turned out, there was a bit more for them to see once they moved in. Courtesy of Jamie Hubbard. My husband and I gave up snowy winters for a warmer retirement and bought our place sight-unseen. When we moved in, we discovered the neighboring community was clothing-optional. The eye-opening experience came with some surprising perks, like an inexpensive meal plan and new friends. "So, how's retirement?" Everyone asks the same question, expecting stories about leisurely mornings , coffee on the porch, pickleball, and sunset cocktails. I smile and say, "It's been an education." My husband and I retired on a limited budget at the youthful age of 67. After years of enduring Chicago winters and a decade in upstate New York, we were ready to trade snow shovels for hiking gear. Our three grown children and grandchildren live throughout the Midwest, but we had had our fill of icy sidewalks and snowdrifts that lingered until Mother's Day. We wanted sunshine — just not Florida sunshine. North Georgia checked all the boxes: milder winters , mountain trails, friendly people, and charming small towns. After selling our business and packing decades of memories, we leased an affordable two-bedroom apartment— sight unseen — and headed south. In retrospect, that sight-unseen part of our plan probably could have used a bit more of our attention. Details matter We had missed one little detail: our new community was near a clothing-optional resort . When someone mentioned "the resort," I assumed golf or a spa. They did not. My husband commented, "Well, that's — different." The author (not shown) said she wasn't sure what she and her husband had gotten themselves into when they discovered who their new neighbors were. Lucy Lambriex/Getty Images Different was not on my retirement bucket list . My imagination went into overdrive. I pictured awkward morning walks and accidental detours into the wrong parking lot. Would I ever hear "community amenities" the same way again? I was worried that we'd made a big mistake. Everyone was so friendly Something surprising happened. Almost nothing changed — except my assumptions. The neighbors we met were ordinary people from all walks of life. They talked about grandchildren, joint replacements, grocery prices, restaurants, and good plumbers. We even learned a thing or two about poker. The only difference was that some neighbors enjoyed the resort au naturel. I had an eye-opening experience A month after we moved in, one of our new neighbors, a former librarian, invited us to spend the day at the resort. My first reaction was "Absolutely not." My second was "Well, maybe once." After moving halfway across the country and starting over, a pool without swimsuits seemed like a minor hurdle. I spent three days worrying about etiquette. Do you look people in the eye? Bring a towel? What do we wear, or in this case, not wear? Instead, we found people playing water volleyball and debating the best potato salad. It was less about clothing and more about friendship and community. People were young and old, every shape and size, with surgical scars, wrinkles, and age-softened profiles. Nobody seemed concerned about appearances. That surprised me. For years, I had focused on every extra pound and wrinkle as a sign of aging, including the few pounds I'd gained during menopause. Yet these people seemed comfortable in their own skin. The judgment I had feared was in my own head. It's hard to ignore some of the perks Another unexpected perk: an affordable yearly membership that includes meals six days a week. This is what's available to us, even though we don't officially live in this community. On our budget, the price was hard to beat. Tasty food, good company, and one less grocery bill. Who knew this was possible? We signed up. We did not become converts overnight, and we still spend plenty of time in hiking clothes, but the resort next door has become part of our retirement story. I've learned that life's best things sometimes turn up in places you would never have considered. Retirement did not just change our address. It changed how I perceived people, including myself. Starting over at this age is not easy. But new friendships, unexpected experiences, and laughing at yourself can make life worthwhile and exciting. Happiness is not about recreating your old life in a warmer ZIP code. It is about staying curious enough to embrace something unique. Even when unique happens to live right next door. These days, when someone asks, "How's retirement?" I smile and answer honestly. "It's been eye-opening." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Nvidia stock falls as investors price in fallout from Jensen Huang's resignation
events.summary: Nvidia shares were down in premarket trading on Monday after a tumultuous week when CEO Jensen Huang resigned. Nvidia announced Huang was stepping down as CEO on Thursday, amid reports of extramarital affairs, including with a woman whom U.S. intelligence reportedly believes to be a spy for China. The stock was down around 2.7% in premarket. Nvidia 's stock continued its slide on Monday, after the chip giant lost hundreds of billions in market cap last week amid the fallout from Jensen Huang resigning as CEO. The company was 2.7% down in premarket trading on Monday as of 8:07 a.m. ET. Huang resigned from Nvidia, the company's board announced on Thursday, after mounting scrutiny following reports that he had a relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy. Huang told employees he had an affair in an email on Nov. 8. It was later reported that Huang had romantic relationships with two Nvidia employees. Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Friday. An online petition calling for Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO has drawn more than 170,000 signatures , as prominent tech executives, including Elon Musk, rallied behind him. Meanwhile, U.S. lawmakers are pushing to launch comprehensive investigations into the scandal. Huang cofounded Nvidia in 1993 and led the company through its meteoric rise to becoming the world's most valuable company, with its AI chips underpinning the technology's boom. Nvidia's Colette Kress confronts key questions in first earnings report since Jensen Huang's exit The tech world's calls for Huang to return to Nvidia are growing Nvidia stock slides as investors weigh Huang resignation Megaspeed says Alice Huang left in 2025 as it launches internal probe Howard Lutnick's sons' Nvidia ties amid Huang China spy scandal Nvidia appointed longtime finance chief Colette Kress as interim CEO and said its board would consider both internal and external candidates in its search for a permanent successor. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday called for a "dramatic shakeup" at Nvidia, adding that the board should look outside the company for its next chief executive. He also suggested other Nvidia executives should face scrutiny over the chip giant's compliance with U.S. export controls.

events.title: Warren Buffett lets his money do the talking, announcing a $5.5 billion donation in a short Thanksgiving letter
events.summary: Warren Buffett gave more and wrote less this Thanksgiving. Daniel Acker/Bloomberg via Getty Images Warren Buffett is ramping up his giving as promised, but not saying much about it. He's donating $5.5 billion of his Berkshire Hathaway stock to four of his family foundations. In his Thanksgiving letter, Buffett advised thanking one's teachers and paying it forward, too. Warren Buffett is saying less but giving more. The legendary investor is donating $5.5 billion worth of Berkshire Hathaway stock to four of his family's foundations, a press release revealed on Monday morning. Buffett will give a total of 9.225 million Class B shares, with 3.69 million going to The Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation, named after his late wife, and 1.845 million shares going to each of his three children's foundations: The Sherwood Foundation, The Howard G. Buffett Foundation, and NoVo Foundation. The former Berkshire chairman and CEO donated shares worth about $1.35 billion to the same four foundations last year. Buffett said in a press release that the gift was "consistent" with his plan to accelerate his donations so that his three children can distribute his entire Berkshire fortune of over $160 billion to good causes by 2034. He wrote that as his shareholders "heard plenty" from him in September about his confidence in Berkshire, he would "keep this Thanksgiving message short." "Last Thanksgiving I wrote that kindness is costless but also priceless," Buffett wrote. "A year later, I would only add that it compounds, and at a better rate than anything Charlie and I ever bought," he added, referring to his late business partner, Charlie Munger. Buffett wrote that he and Munger received "beyond measurement costless benefits" from teachers and mentors such as Benjamin Graham and Tom Murphy. "Because of this we not only prospered mightily but were able to pass along many of the benefits we received," he continued. "This Thanksgiving, thank one of those selfless people in your own life," Buffett wrote. "Better yet, be a benefactor for someone else." Berkshire stock has surged by over 19% this year to record highs of above $593 a share, trouncing the S&P 500's 10% gain, and valuing the conglomerate at close to $1.3 trillion. events.title: The Download: testing tech promises and searching for cognitive immortality
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Are we there yet? Six technologies that promised to change the world How do you measure progress towards the future? In the Impossible issue of MIT Technology Review , our series “ Are we there yet? ” examines how far six potentially transformative technologies have come after years of promises. We spoke to experts, researchers and engineers to find out what’s holding them back, then scored each on a progress meter from zero to ten. Find out how we rated each of these technologies—and how close they are to delivering on their promise. Nuclear-powered spaceships Exercise in a pill Interspecies communication Solid-state batteries Cleaning up PFAS Eliminating traffic deaths Subscribe now to get every issue of our print magazine as soon as it lands. Inside the quest for cognitive immortality Could technology keep your brain going beyond death? Far-thinking technologists are exploring ways to make it happen, from gradual brain replacement to uploading memories to the cloud. MIT Technology Review’s latest Roundtables event explores these ideas and how close they might be to reality. Join science editor Mary Beth Griggs and senior editor for biomedicine Antonio Regalado for this subscriber-only discussion tomorrow. Tune in live on Tuesday, November 17 at 5:00 p.m. GMT / 12:00 p.m. EST / 9:00 a.m. PST . events.title: Who inherits Jensen Huang’s empire? The Nvidia CEO contenders facing an extraordinary test
events.summary: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang spent more than three decades building an enterprise whose technological ambitions, commercial relationships, and very identity became inseparable from his leadership. Yet for a company that demonstrated extraordinary foresight in anticipating the future of computing, the absence of a deep internal bench capable of succeeding its founder raises uncomfortable questions about the board’s long-term stewardship. With longtime CFO Colette Kress serving as interim CEO, attention has turned to an eclectic field of potential outside successors. Their varied credentials underscore just how difficult it will be to replace a leader whose influence permeated virtually every dimension of the business. Fortune senior writer Sheryl Estrada examined the potential contenders , finding an array of accomplished executives whose qualifications are matched by significant questions about their suitability—or willingness—to take the helm. Arm CEO Rene Haas offers perhaps the closest connection to Nvidia’s foundations. He spent seven years at the company, understands its culture, and now leads a business whose architecture underpins Nvidia’s Grace and Vera CPUs. But Haas left in 2013, before Nvidia’s ascent to AI dominance, and would be returning to an enterprise vastly more complex than the one he knew. Another option is AMD CEO Lisa Su, who brings formidable semiconductor credentials and a proven record of corporate transformation. Since 2014, she has rebuilt AMD into a major force in processors and an increasingly credible challenger in AI chips. Her technical authority would carry weight inside Nvidia, although persuading her to abandon the company she revitalized presents an obvious hurdle. Former Apple CEO Tim Cook offers an unusually relevant precedent, having succeeded Steve Jobs and subsequently presided over Apple’s expansion into a global technology powerhouse. His command of supply chains, international relationships, and operational complexity could prove invaluable as geopolitical tensions reshape the semiconductor industry. President Trump has endorsed Cook, though his continuing role as Apple’s executive chairman complicates the prospect. Then there’s Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian, who brings intimate knowledge of the hyperscalers and whose enormous AI investments underpin Nvidia’s growth. His experience managing cloud infrastructure and working closely with Nvidia could prove valuable as the company expands its influence across the computing stack.  Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora, meanwhile, offers extensive experience in enterprise technology, global sales, and corporate strategy, although his career has been less closely tied to semiconductor innovation. Taken together, the candidates illuminate the competing priorities confronting Nvidia’s board and the difficulty of finding those capabilities in a single executive. But the more consequential head-scratcher is how a company indispensable to the global AI economy arrived at this moment without an apparent heir. For all Huang’s extraordinary achievements, the ultimate test of his legacy may be whether Nvidia can sustain its ambitions without him. Ruth Umoh ruth.umoh@fortune.com This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Not paying Tesla's $299 Cybercab subscription turns it into a shiny gold lawn ornament
events.summary: Tesla said on Friday it would begin invite-only sales of the Cybercab for personal use. Ying Tang/NurPhoto via Getty Images Lucky Tesla fans invited to buy a Cybercab should read the fine print. Tesla can buy back a Cybercab "at any time" and can remotely brick it if owners try to sell it, per the T&Cs. Opting out of the $299 "autonomy subscription" will also turn your Cybercab into a shiny gold lawn ornament. Tesla's Cybercab comes with some pretty important T&Cs. Elon Musk's EV giant said on Friday that select customers were now being invited to buy Tesla's steering-wheel-less robotaxi for their own personal use. For the lucky few who have received an invite, the Cybercab starts at $29,990, with an "autonomy subscription" of $299 a month. Opting out of that subscription will turn the Cybercab into a shiny gold lawn ornament. The autonomous EV "will not operate" without an autonomy subscription, according to Tesla's Cybercab order and subscription agreements, which were uploaded to Tesla's website over the weekend. Those who get the green light to order a Cybercab will also only be able to drive it within the limits of Tesla's Robotaxi ride-hailing service . Right now, that includes parts of Austin, Dallas, and three other cities in Texas, as well as Miami, Orlando, and Tampa in Florida. But owners will not be able to add their Cybercabs to the service and make money from them, a key part of the robotaxi pitch Musk has been making for nearly a decade . That's not the only catch. Like other limited-edition vehicles Tesla has released, Cybercab owners are barred from reselling their robotaxis without the company's permission. Those who do face a $50,000 penalty, and Tesla might also remotely brick your vehicle. More unusually, the Cybercab's order agreement says that Tesla can repurchase the vehicle "at any time," at a fair market value determined by the company. A replacement is not guaranteed, and owners have to pay the cost of shipping their Cybercab back to Tesla. Tesla Cybercabs on a lot in Austin, Texas. Jay Janner/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images Other details buried in the fine print include a ban on modifications, including wraps and tinted windows. Would-be Cybercab owners should also be aware that Tesla will be collecting their data. That includes personally identifying data such as location data and "cabin camera image data" recorded by a camera above the rear-view mirror, per the autonomy subscription agreement, which states that the data will be used to provide ride support and improve the product. It's unclear whether Cybercab owners can opt out. Tesla's tech pivot The Cybercab is not the first Tesla vehicle to come with major strings attached. Early adopters of the company's Cybertruck pickup also faced a $50,000 penalty if they tried to resell it within a year, and Tesla told customers who spent $250,000 to reserve the rocket-powered Roadster last month that it "cannot guarantee" the flying EV will ever be delivered. The subscription-only model of the Cybercab, however, is the latest sign that Tesla is pivoting toward a business model closer to a tech company than an automaker. Musk announced this month that Tesla would discontinue the Cybertruck , after the company sunset the Model S and X earlier this year. The billionaire CEO has said that in the future, most of Tesla's revenue will come from robotaxis, autonomous driving subscriptions, and the company's Optimus humanoid robot. Early invitees to order the Cybercab, which Tesla estimates will begin deliveries in December, include YouTuber Marques Brownlee. The tech reviewer once bet that if Tesla delivered a sub-$30,000 Cybercab by the end of 2026, he'd shave his head. Marques Brownlee has a bet with Elon Musk. Diego Donamaria/SXSW Conference & Festivals via Getty Images In a series of X posts over the weekend, Brownlee said that his hair was safe as the Cybercab was not publicly available, before posting a screenshot of a confirmed order after some goading from Musk. He added that the fact that the Cybercab is geofenced to a small number of locations meant Tesla has so far not delivered on Musk's promises of personal robotaxis. "It's a paperweight if I take this thing home," Brownlee said. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: After dodging death, battery startup Our Next Energy is now going public
events.summary: It’s never been easy to run a battery startup in the U.S. There have been more failures than successes over the last 20 years, and whipsawing federal policy has caused more than a few battery companies to shut shop. Not all of them die, though. Our Next Energy (ONE) had some close calls, but soon it will go public via SPAC, the company exclusively told TechCrunch. ONE says it is valued at $600 million pre-money, and it expects the merger with Wen Acquisition Corp. will bring $400 million in gross proceeds assuming no redemptions. The combined company will trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker “ONEE”, and the pro forma implied equity value is $1 billion. Over the years, ONE has raised $483 million, according to PitchBook, and at one point was valued at $1.3 billion. It has also received tens of millions of dollars in incentives tied to investments and job creation in Michigan. ONE is the brainchild of former Ford and Apple engineer Mujeeb Ijaz, who designed a way for electric vehicles to draw power from two batteries of different chemistries. In ONE’s first setup, it paired lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) and with a manganese-rich chemistry , which would let each chemistry play to its strengths: LFP could be used day in, day out, while the more fragile but energy-dense, manganese-rich one would work for long, infrequent road trips. An initial prototype traveled over 600 miles on a single charge. But the EV market didn’t take off as quickly as anticipated, and automakers wanted to buy at lower prices (usually from China). Both of those reasons helped sink ONE’s first attempt at a Series C in late 2023. The startup had to lay off a chunk of its staff, and eventually vacated its lease for a planned $1.6 billion factory in Michigan. The rough patch led to Ijaz’s ouster as CEO in December 2023, only to have him return to the position in March 2025 after a new round of funding closed. (His brother’s investment firm co-led the round.) Part of the critique aimed at ONE during Ijaz’s first tenure as CEO was that the company spent too much time developing new products instead of focusing on one or two, as most startups tend to do. When Ijaz came back to the helm last year, he said that ONE would leave the automotive market and focus on grid-scale batteries. ONE isn’t alone in pivoting away from vehicle batteries. American automakers, which had similarly rosy views of EV adoption, also bet big on battery factories and supply chains. When sales didn’t pop in the U.S. like they have in China or Europe, they had to find an outlet for that capacity, and the grid started looking like the obvious target once it started groaning under the weight of AI data centers. Both Ford and GM have announced their own energy storage products. Many new grid-scale batteries use LFP, which is safer and cheaper than those used in most EVs in the U.S., and Ijaz saw an opportunity for ONE there as well. “We go back to the origins of LFP in this country and even to some of the factories that are in China,” he said. Indeed, just over a decade ago Ijaz led the automotive division at A123 Systems, the company that first commercialized the chemistry. Soon, Ijaz saw other opportunities for ONE’s batteries, including defense and locomotives. The defense play isn’t surprising. Nearly every battery company I talk with these days mentions defense, in part because it’s a market that Chinese companies can’t play in. Building an American supply chain means that a company can sell batteries at a premium, shielded as they are from Chinese competition. It’s a higher-margin market, though much smaller than EVs. My recent conversation with Ijaz last week was the first time I’d heard a company pitch rail companies as potential customers, though. Ijaz said ONE is “finding a lot of traction in” that market. The company has built a hybrid locomotive that uses a 2.8 megawatt-hour battery, and another he calls a micro-hybrid, which uses a smaller battery to start the diesel engine faster, similar to a stop-start system on a fossil fuel car or truck. “Our customers are seeing a 50% improvement in diesel fuel consumption, which is a big deal,” Ijaz said. Currently, ONE has three business lines, which could be a sign of its old culture creeping back into the picture. But Ijaz said the addition of defense and rail were driven by the bottom line: Grid-scale battery customers are also “very much like automotive customers, where they were willing to buy from China as long as the price was low enough,” he said. “Believe me, I would have loved to have made that grid business into the single business of the company. But the customers would look and then be taken away to a Chinese option because of the pricing, and the tariffs also leading them to that conclusion,” Ijaz said. “And so we decided that we needed a more durable market, and we looked for who in the customer base valued an American battery company.

events.title: Bedrock Energy raises $24M to build more AI-enabled geothermal drill rigs for enterprise buildings
events.summary: Dig deep enough, and the temperature of the ground remains steady year round, a fun trivia fact that has the potential to improve efficiency and slash costs for heating and cooling across the country. Geothermal heat pumps, which use the ground as a heat source in winter and heat sink in summer, have been around for decades, but they’re underutilized. Just a fraction of all buildings in the U.S. use them in part because it’s expensive to drill into the earth. But one startup, Bedrock Energy , says its AI-directed rigs can slash drilling times by up to 80%, significantly reducing costs. That time savings recently helped Bedrock raise a new $24 million funding round, the startup told TechCrunch. Previously, it raised a $12 million Series A in 2025 and an $8.5 million seed round in 2023. Bedrock has focused mostly on commercial properties to date, since they benefit from deep, accurate boreholes which maximize the use of their small footprints. But the startup has also been talking with data center developers, Joselyn Lai, co-founder and CEO of Bedrock Energy, told TechCrunch. Some might use it for cooling server racks, but others are interested in the technology’s flat load profile — deploying it on neighboring properties can open up significant capacity on the grid. “We had someone in Michigan say, if we could free up a few megawatts, I think we might be able to operate that many months or even a year earlier,” Lai said. “A year of revenue for a data center is very meaningful.” Bedrock says its modernized approach to shallow geothermal drilling — up to 1,0000 feet or so — sets it apart. Most geothermal heat pump drillers use rigs that are similar to those used for water wells. They work fine, but they’re crude instruments. Instead, Bedrock uses directional drilling techniques borrowed from the oil and gas industry, guiding them using its own models of the subsurface. That combination allows them to optimize drilling and placement, the company says, helping to ensure performance and longevity. Sensors in the boreholes help to refine those models. The startup currently operates in Utah, Colorado, New York, Alberta, and its home state of Texas, and the new round will help the company expand into New England, New Jersey, the upper Midwest, and additional states in the West, Lai said. To power that expansion, Bedrock will add more rigs to its fleet to serve customers in those regions. Currently, it has drilled boreholes in nine sites, and it has secured payments from new customers in anticipation of drilling in the next year or two, she added. Once up and running, a geothermal heat pump requires far less maintenance than traditional HVAC systems. “You only have to install it once and then it works for a very long time, which is very good for infrastructure from a financial perspective,” Lai said. The new round was led by Clean Energy Ventures and Clearvision Ventures with participation from GVP Climate, Susquehanna Sustainable Investments, Catalytic Capital for Climate and Health by Temasek Trust, MUUS, Great Wave Ventures, Autodesk Foundation, Titanium Ventures, Energy Impact Partners, Wireframe Ventures, Elemental Impact, and SFV Capital. events.title: Los Alamos boffins to put NextSilicon's Maverick-2 through natural selection in Darwin testbed
events.summary: The US Department of Energy (DoE) is deepening its relationship with HPC-first chip startup NextSilicon. During Supercomputing 2026 in Chicago on Monday, the Israeli startup revealed that the agency had deployed its second Maverick-2 cluster in the Darwin testbed at Los Alamos National Laboratory (LANL). The deployment comes just six months after Sandia National Laboratories powered on NextSilicon’s first supercomputer, which features 64 nodes and 128 of the company's “runtime-configurable” accelerators. NextSilicon’s latest DoE system is comparatively smaller, comprising just four accelerators, yet for LANL, the system is arguably more important despite its size. Darwin, LANL’s chief scientist Galen Shipman, tells El Reg is a “long-lived testbed environment where we bring in newer technologies for evaluation.” “It gives us the ability to work with the technology much more quickly, and integrate it with other components of our architecture in our environment,” he explained. Smaller systems like the Maverick-2 cluster now deployed in Darwin allow LANL to validate and port a wider array of codebases to the chips, identify problems, and work with NextSilicon to not only address them, but directly influence the capabilities of future chips, Shipman explained. In other words, Los Alamos’ interest in Maverick-2 is the first step toward larger scale deployments of NextSilicon silicon in future DoE supers. For this, hands-on access is kind of important as many of LANL’s most important workloads can’t exactly be run on public systems. A compute chameleon LANL is one of several labs tasked with ensuring that the US’ nuclear deterrent remains effective decades after underground testing was banned. The lab is also responsible for running simulations on energy sources like fuel candidates for future fusion reactors. Both of these workloads, Shipman tells us, fall into a category called multi-physics simulations. These workloads aren’t really one workload, but multiple simulations that can have wildly different compute requirements. A “good example is inertial confinement fusion. At the National Ignition Facility at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, you're using lasers to implode a fuel capsule, and the goal is to generate more energy through yield than you do from depositing energy to the capsule,” Shipman explained. “That's inherently multiphysics.” There are simulations for the lasers, the hydrodynamics within the fuel capsule, and the chemistry and material interactions taking place during the fusion process. The problem, Shipman explains, is that a system that’s ideal for one of those simulations may not be well suited to others. “Identifying one specific platform that is optimal for that type of simulation is challenging.” CPUs, he says, are well suited to workloads with large serial sections, irregular access patterns, and jobs that benefit from deep cache hierarchies. Meanwhile, GPUs are fantastic for dense, matrix-multiplication heavy workloads. "Where NextSilicon fits in is being able to reconfigure to match the workload, on demand,” Shipman said. “The hope is that we won't have to make these rigid determinations upfront like, ‘we need this much CPU or we need this much GPU.’ We can use a much more adaptable, reconfigurable architecture to meet the workflow where it is at.” A closer look at Maverick 2 Despite some visual similarities to Nvidia’s current crop of GPUs, Maverick-2 is not a GPU. Instead it employs a dataflow architecture which overlaps communication and computation. Rather than waiting for load-store operations to shuffle data around as you would with a conventional CPU or GPU, the chips themselves comprise a grid of arithmetic logic units (ALUs) which are configured to perform an operation like addition or multiplication in the order that they’re needed. Data is computed as it moves from one ALU to the next, a bit like how a ball moves through a Rube Goldberg contraption. This can make dataflow architectures extremely efficient in bandwidth-bound scenarios, which has implications not only for HPC and scientific computing but also for AI. It’s why we’re seeing dataflow accelerators, like Nvidia’s Groq, Cerebras’ WSE-3, and SambaNova’s SN50, being deployed as decode accelerators in AI inference clusters. Where NextSilicon stands out is that its designs, so far, have been specifically tailored toward sparse double-precision FP64 workloads. Real FLOPS are rarely advertised Programming dataflow architectures, historically, has been a challenging endeavor. To overcome this, NextSilicon claims to have developed a compiler that can decompose any existing C, Python, Fortran, or CUDA codebases into a graph that can run directly on its chips. So far, NextSilicon has managed to validate its systems against the High Performance Conjugate Gradients (HPCG) benchmark, the LAMMPS molecular dynamics test suite, and the Sparta Monte Carlo simulation suite. But as NextSilicon CEO Elad Raz notes, the roofline performance of Maverick-2 is different from one workload to another, and so the company has opted not to advertise peak theoretical performance the same way GPU vendors like Nvidia or AMD have traditionally done. That’s not to say NextSilicon is shy about Maverick’s performance characteristics. Rather than advertising peak performance that the chip may not be able to hit in the workloads its customers actually care most about, it published performance figures across a swath of HPC benchmarks. For example, in HPCG, one of the closest watched HPC benchmarks after High Performance Linpack (HPL), NextSilicon says a single Maverick achieves 600 gigaFLOPS of performance, which it says is on par with contemporary GPUs but at half the power. That’s just fine and dandy as far as Shipman is concerned. He tells us peak advertised performance is rarely a useful proxy for real-world performance. “The thing that my team spends the most time on is how do we generate representative proxies, representative kernels; how do we generate specifications that communicate our needs to the broader ecosystem so that vendors like NextSilicon can meet us and co-design with us.” ®

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters EVENT: Peers compare how they're cutting duplicate storage without ripping anything out, over dinner with The Register. Pick any busy project folder and count the copies. There's one on the file server, one in a cloud bucket and one on each laptop that needed it at a usable speed. If a team got fed up with sync and built its own workaround, there's another in there too. The storage bill pays for every one of them. The Register and LucidLink are hosting senior technology, infrastructure and data leaders at the Covent Garden Hotel on Tuesday 24 November to compare how they're bringing that number down. Joe Fay of The Register is in the chair. Nobody keeps duplicates for fun. They're what people do when files have to move between sites faster than sync allows. Every copy IT can't see into is a security question as well as a cost, so the duplicates you don't know about matter most. What the table wants to hear is how others got the copies down without ripping out storage they've already paid for, or the governance built around it. The evening runs under the Chatham House Rule, so people say what worked and what didn't. Alan Marshall, Strategic Director, EMEA at LucidLink, joins a small group of peers. Nobody presents. events.title: I'm a dietitian and mom of 2. These 11 Costco buys help me quickly throw together balanced dinners during the week.
events.summary: As a dietitian and mom, I grab a few staples on most Costco trips so I can get dinner on the table for my family fast. Kristen Carli Our family of four tries to eat dinners that are delicious, quick to make, and fairly balanced. I buy many staples at Costco , like Kirkland Signature rotisserie chicken and seasoned pork chops. My family also likes Safe Catch tuna burgers and Amylu's cranberry-and-jalapeño chicken meatballs. Our family needs dinners that are fast, healthy, and delicious — a tall order for any weeknight, especially when feeding two working parents and two picky toddlers . As a dietitian, I also aim for our meals to be well-rounded, containing protein, starchy carbohydrates, and vegetables. Luckily, we've found a handful of dinners that check all three boxes, and Costco is my favorite place to stock up on shelf-stable and frozen staples that help us throw them together quickly. Here are a few of my go-to Costco purchases . Kevin's Natural Foods' heat-and-serve proteins help me get dinner on the table fast. Kristen Carli There's often a variety of heat-and-serve meals from Kevin's Natural Foods available at Costco, and my family has enjoyed most of the ones we've tried. The Thai-style basil beef is our current favorite because of its delicious, sweet-and-savory sauce. It couldn't be any quicker to prepare: Simply warm the fully cooked beef on the stovetop for five minutes, then stir in the sauce. The beef has 20 grams of protein and fairly simple ingredients, which I also appreciate. Even my picky eaters enjoy the Pura Vida Thai red-curry flame-grilled vegetable skillet. Kristen Carli One way I can ensure my kids eat their veggies is by adding flavor. Frozen vegetable mixes like this one from Pura Vida make that super easy. The broccoli, bell pepper, carrot, cabbage, and onion are already flame-grilled and simply need to be warmed through. Plus, this mix comes with a curry sauce that's packed with flavor but mild enough for kids' palates. I throw these veggies over some brown rice and top with a protein, like Kevin's Thai-style basil beef (above), and dinner is done. Minsley's cooked brown rice is a huge time-saver on weeknights. Kristen Carli Cooking rice in a saucepan with water isn't very hard, but it often takes too long for the average weeknight. I love these pre-cooked packs of organic brown rice from Minsley because they can be warmed through in the microwave in under two minutes. Of course, I love a $5 Kirkland Signature rotisserie chicken. Kristen Carli I'd be remiss if I didn't mention the famous Costco rotisserie chicken . The $5 bird is endlessly versatile. Put the chicken into tacos with salsa and refried beans, stir it into vegetable noodle soup, or toss it with a Caesar-salad kit. Or keep it simple and serve it with ketchup, steamed broccoli, and dinner rolls. Whatever gets the job done. Amylu's cranberry-and-jalapeño chicken meatballs pair well with mashed potatoes and broccoli. Kristen Carli Don't let the jalapeño scare you; these are not spicy and are a major hit with my kids. After eight minutes in the air fryer, these fully cooked meatballs from Amylu are ready to serve. We like pairing them with instant mashed potatoes and steamed broccoli for a more well-rounded meal. Safe Catch tuna burgers are a go-to lean protein in our house. Kristen Carli When we are looking to substitute ground beef for lean protein, these Safe Catch tuna burgers are my top choice. They're packed with omega-3 fatty acids and 33 grams of protein per serving. I feel good about serving these to my kids. Russet House sweet-potato fries are an easy side. Kristen Carli When we need a side for those tuna burgers, we usually opt for these frozen sweet-potato fries, which we crisp up in the air fryer. I love them because they are full of vitamin A and fiber, and my kids love them because, well, they're fries. I like that they're ready in under 20 minutes, so I can get dinner on the table fast. The Path of Life sweet root vegetables are a great mealtime shortcut. Kristen Carli This vegetable assortment from Path of Life is a staple in our house for two reasons: The mix comes pre-chopped and pre-seasoned. We just open the bag, dump the frozen veggies on a baking sheet, and roast for 20 minutes. Anyone who's tried to hack through a raw butternut squash knows what a gift it is to have it pre-cut. The mix also includes seasoned sweet potatoes, parsnips, and red onion. I like stocking up on Kirkland Signature's seasoned boneless pork chops. Kristen Carli Costco's prices never fail to impress me when I'm buying meat in bulk . I tend to stock up, portion out what I won't use right away, and freeze the rest. One of my go-to buys is the Kirkland Signature boneless pork chops that come pre-seasoned with souvlaki seasoning. After a few minutes on the grill, these are ready to serve for dinner alongside the sides of our choice. Del Real chicken tamales with red sauce are a hit in our house. Kristen Carli Being local to Arizona, we eat a lot of tamales, but almost never make them from scratch. These Del Real tamales are my pick when we want authentic Mexican flavor without the effort. We typically just steam them on the stovetop for 10 minutes, then let them cool for about two more. Each tamale contains 14 grams of protein, and we like serving these with a side of refried beans for an added fiber boost. Rosarita organic refried beans are my kids' favorite. Kristen Carli As a dietitian, I always keep my pantry stocked with canned beans of every variety, but these Rosarita refried beans are my kids' favorite. Since they're already seasoned, we just heat these beans up, and they're ready in minutes. We serve them alongside tamales, quesadillas, or tacos for an easy boost of fiber, as they contain 6 grams per ½-cup serving. events.title: VC Bradley Tusk decided to offer startups services instead of cash. How’s that working out?
events.summary: Good morning, it’s Finance Editor Jeff Roberts in for Allie. In the course of my career, I’ve interviewed hundreds of venture capitalists, and I have an observation: Many VCs regard themselves as unconventional thinkers, but when it comes to the norms of their industry, they are highly conformist. Bradley Tusk is not one of those VCs. Brash and outspoken, Tusk made his name as the chief of staff for former New York City mayor Mike Bloomberg, and by helping Uber in its early battles with city officials and the taxi industry. Soon after, he leveraged his reputation as a political fixer to launch Tusk Ventures, which helped startups like Lemonade, Bird, FanDuel, Ro, and Coinbase navigate various regulatory minefields. In 2025, Tusk made another bold bet. Despite a successful run as a conventional VC, which saw Tusk raise $300 million over three funds, he decided to abandon the model in favor of something novel: taking equity in exchange for services rather than cash. “I took half a step back and asked, ‘What do I and don’t I like about this process?’ I like two things: I like legalizing disruptive shit, and I like betting on and working with founders who are interesting. What I did not like was raising money, dealing with LPs, taking board seats, and portfolio construction. I also didn’t like giving someone else 80% of my profits,” Tusk explains. In practice, Tusk says the pivot means his firm spends almost all of its time on a few core areas. Those include helping startups obtain licenses and navigate regulations, and turning up on fundraising calls to assure would-be investors that the government won’t cripple an up-and-upcoming sector. Tusk Ventures also provides comms advice that allows startups to avoid blowing cash on pricey PR retainers, and makes introductions to other CEOs. This model suits Tusk on a personal level, but it also looks like a shrewd choice in light of a challenging era for conventional VC firms. As Allie noted last week, venture firms are being buffeted by a scary confluence of slow exits, nosebleed valuations, and climbing interest rates. In this context, Tusk’s pivot may have been driven as much by necessity as by choice. The question is whether that pivot is working. So far, it appears it is. Tusk says his firm is currently supplying its equity-for-services arrangement to around 21 startups. “Our fees are between $50,000 and $200,000 a month in preferred equity, scaled to whatever the valuation of the company is. Engagements are usually about 18 months,” he explains, adding that the equity is typically paid out of a pool set aside for employees, and is less than 2% of the overall supply. One upside of this arrangement, and it’s a big one, is that the firm can cut its losses if a startup hits the skids. As Tusk observes, the firm will have expended time and internal resources for naught, but that’s a better outcome than watching $5 million or $10 million in cash go down the drain. This model, which Tusk describes as an “equity-for-services-at-scale fund” (he admits it’s a terrible name), may be a tempting one for other VC firms given the current venture climate. The catch, of course, is that it requires a hefty supply of capital to give it a go. “If we can generate, say, $20 million to $30 million a year in earned equity over a 10-year investment period, that’s $200 million to $300 million,” Tusk said. “That’s like the equivalent of a $200 million fund, but times five, because you keep all of it. Obviously I have costs a normal venture fund doesn’t have, because I have to pay everyone every two weeks without management fees to offset it.” Even as Tusk makes these large early outlays, he is also devoting some of his fortune to a number of civic-minded ventures. Those include a bookstore on Manhattan’s Lower East Side called P&T Knitwear , in homage to a schmatta store run in the same neighborhood by his grandfather, a Holocaust survivor. Tusk admits he is losing a bushel of money on the venture, but that he views the bookstore as a form of philanthropy. In the coming year, Tusk says he plans to move part-time to Los Angeles, where his firm has a satellite office. I suggest that, when he arrives, he employ his considerable political skills to solve one of the city’s most intractable problems: completing a monorail that has been fully built around LAX, but has been unable to start operating due to ongoing problems related to L.A.’s dysfunctional government. Tusk says he’ll consider it. See you tomorrow, Jeff John Roberts jeff.roberts@fortune.com @jeffjohnroberts Submit a deal for the Term Sheet newsletter here . events.title: Current price of oil as of November 16, 2026
events.summary: As of 7:30 a.m. Eastern Time today, oil sold for $96.68 per barrel (using Brent as the benchmark, which we’ll get into momentarily). That’s 42 cents lower than yesterday morning and approximately a $32.60 rise over the past year. Oil price per barrel % Change Price of oil yesterday $97.10 -0.43% Price of oil 1 month ago $107.61 -10.15% Price of oil 1 year ago $64.09 +50.85% Will oil prices go up? It’s impossible to predict the future of oil prices. Several factors determine the movement of oil, but it ultimately boils down to supply and demand. Again, when threats of economic downturn, war, etc. are high, the oil trajectory can turn rapidly. How oil prices translate to gas pump prices When you pay for gas at the pump, you’re paying for more than just the crude oil itself; you’re also springing for links along the chain, such as the refineries and wholesalers—not to mention taxes and local gas station markups. Still, the crude oil aspect affects the final price most dramatically, as it typically accounts for more than half the price per gallon. When oil prices spike, so do gas prices. And frustratingly, when oil prices drop, gas prices tend to take their time drifting down to the lower price (sometimes referred to as “rockets and feathers”). The role of the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve In case of emergency, the U.S. has a store of crude oil known as the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Its primary purpose is energy security in case of disaster (think sanctions, severe storm damage, even war). But it can also go a long way toward softening crippling price hikes during supply shocks. It’s not a long-term answer—more of an immediate relief to assist the consumer and keep critical parts of the economy running, like key industries, emergency services, public transportation, etc. How oil and natural gas prices are linked Oil and natural gas are both major energy fuels. A big change in oil prices can affect natural gas by extension. For example, if oil prices increase, some industries may swap natural gas for some segments of their operations where possible—which increases demand for natural gas. Historical performance of oil When examining oil’s performance, there are generally two major benchmarks: Brent crude oil is the main global oil benchmark. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) is the main benchmark of North America. Between the two, Brent better represents global oil performance because it prices much of the world’s traded crude. And, it’s often the best way to track historical oil performance. In fact, even the U.S. Energy Information Administration now uses Brent as its primary reference in its Annual Energy Outlook. Looking at the Brent benchmark across several decades, oil has been anything but steady. It’s seen spikes due to factors such as wars and supply cuts, and it’s also seen crashes from global recessions and an oversupply (called a “glut”). For example: The early 1970s brought the first big oil shock when the Middle East cut exports and imposed an embargo on the U.S. and others during the Yom Kippur War. Prices dropped in the mid-1980s for reasons such as lower demand and more non-OPEC oil producers entering the industry. Prices spiked again in 2008 with increased global demand, but it soon plummeted alongside the global financial crisis. During the 2020 COVID lockdown, oil demand collapsed like never before—bringing prices below $20 per barrel. All to say, oil’s historical performance has been anything but smooth. Again, it’s hugely affected by wars, recessions, OPEC whims, evolving energy initiatives and policies, and much more. Energy coverage from  Fortune Looking to stay up-to-date regarding the latest energy developments? Check out our recent coverage: Son of ex-Alamo Rent a Car owner went from hip hop label founder to lithium leader Future of U.S. renewable energy rests on Nextpower—the backbone of the growing solar sector Standard Chartered profit jumps 46% as CEO bets on a fragmenting global economy Frequently asked questions How is the current price of oil per barrel actually determined? The current price of oil per barrel depends largely on supply and demand, including news about potential future supply and demand (geopolitics, decisions made by OPEC+, etc.). In the U.S., prices also move based on how friendly an administration is to drilling, as it can affect future supply. For example, 2025 saw the Trump administration move to reopen more than 1.5 million acres in the Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge for oil and gas leasing, reversing the Biden administration’s policy of limiting oil drilling in the Arctic. How often does the price of oil change during the day? The price of oil updates constantly when the “futures” markets are open. A futures market is effectively an auction where people agree to buy or sell oil in the future. As long as people and companies are trading contracts, the oil price is changing. How does U.S. shale oil production affect the current price of oil? In short, shale is rock that contains oil and natural gas. Think of shale as energy yet to be tapped. The more shale the U.S. accesses, the more energy we’ll have—and the more easily oil prices can keep from spiking as much thanks to a greater supply. How does the current price of oil impact inflation and the broader economy? When oil is expensive, it tends to make everyday items cost more. This can be related to energy (your heating, gas utilities, etc.), but it’s also due to the logistics involved with making those items accessible to you. Shipping, for example, can affect the price of things at the grocery store, as it’s more expensive to get those products from warehouses and farms onto the shelf. events.title: Who is Leo KoGuan, the Singapore-based billionaire backing Nvidia’s Jensen Huang?
events.summary: Indonesia-born investor Leo KoGuan has also backed Elon Musk’s Tesla. Leo KoGuan, a Singapore-based billionaire, said he would not buy more Nvidia shares without Jensen Huang, whom he called “the supreme creator”. Huang’s exit after reported affairs and a 33-year run shook Nvidia, sent shares down 12.8%, and sparked calls from tech leaders for his return. KoGuan built his fortune through SHI International and Tesla, and has made major Singapore buys, including the Dysons’ Wallich Residence penthouse and 21 Carpenter hotel. SINGAPORE – Billionaire investor Leo KoGuan on Nov 13 said that he would not buy more Nvidia shares without co-founder Jensen Huang at the helm. This came a day after the US chipmaker announced Huang’s resignation. KoGuan, who called Huang “the supreme creator” in posts on X, argued that his achievements should count for more than his mistakes and said that he had invested about US$1.3 billion (S$1.7 billion) in Nvidia. The artificial intelligence and semicon heavyweight has a market capitalisation of about US$3.9 trillion as at Nov 16. KoGuan’s backing for Huang comes as prominent tech figures push for his return to Nvidia. Elon Musk, Epic Games founder Tim Sweeney, Y Combinator president Garry Tan and Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick were among the signatories of an open letter urging Nvidia’s board to reinstate him. More than 7,500 signatories reportedly identified themselves as Nvidia employees, equivalent to 18% of the company’s workforce. Huang’s abrupt ouster from Nvidia followed reports of three extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a former executive of Singapore-based Megaspeed whom US authorities suspect of spying for China. His departure ended a 33-year run at the helm of Nvidia, the company he co-founded and whose chips now power much of the AI boom. The company named chief financial officer Colette Kress interim chief executive officer. Amid the turmoil, Nvidia shares fell 12.8% in the week to Nov 13, closing at US$162.85, even as chip stocks as a group rose about 8% the same week, noted Kenneth Goh, director of private wealth management at UOB Kay Hian. He added that the shares could remain under pressure until Nvidia’s board names a successor who has the confidence of key stakeholders. “KoGuan is saying out loud what a lot of investors feel. Many of them bought Nvidia because of Jensen Huang,” Goh said. “His own holding is small, well under 1% of the company. He has also only said he will stop adding. He has not said he is selling.” KoGuan first drew wider attention for his bet on Tesla. In Singapore, he made headlines for his high-profile property purchases, such as that of the Dysons’ Wallich Residence penthouse. KoGuan, 71, was born in Indonesia to Chinese parents. He moved to the US, where he earned a master’s degree in international affairs from Columbia University and a law degree from New York Law School. In 1989, he and his then wife, Thai Lee, paid less than US$1 million for a struggling New Jersey software reseller with five employees and about as many customers. The business became Software House International, now known as SHI International. SHI has since expanded beyond software reselling into hardware, cloud computing and cybersecurity services. It serves more than 17,000 customers, including Boeing, Johnson & Johnson and AT&T, and employs about 7,000 people worldwide. KoGuan told Bloomberg in 2021 that he had stepped back from day-to-day operations around the turn of the century. He remains chairman, while Lee is president and chief executive officer. In October 2025, SHI said it reached US$16 billion in gross sales over the preceding 12 months. It also announced an investment in AI engineering consultancy NStarX, giving clients of its New Jersey AI and cybersecurity lab access to NStarX’s data scientists. KoGuan began buying Tesla shares in 2019. He built a concentrated position through shares and options. Bank records showed that he held 6.3 million Tesla shares and 1.8 million options as at September 2021. The options gave him the right to buy Tesla shares at prices ranging from US$450 to US$550 apiece. He was one of the carmaker’s largest individual shareholders at the time. As the stock rallied, the value of his Tesla holdings climbed to more than US$7 billion by October 2021. In 2024, KoGuan said he was cutting his Tesla stake and buying three-month US Treasury bills. He said in a post on X that he still planned to hold Tesla for the long term but feared a stock market crash on the scale of 1929, which was the catalyst for the Great Depression. In March 2026, the 71-year-old said he was “still mostly in Tesla” and Treasury bills. He had grown more critical of Tesla and its CEO, Elon Musk, including over a pay package that could be worth up to US$1 trillion. He declined to say how much of his Tesla stake he had sold. On March 3, KoGuan said he bought one million Nvidia shares.

events.title: Ex-Barclays CEO Bob Diamond on investing in the Gulf and the irrelevancy of Bitcoin
events.summary: The News Speaking from the Bahrain capital Manama, which a few months earlier had been bombarded in Iranian attacks, Bob Diamond, chief executive of private equity firm Atlas Merchant Capital, says he’s still optimistic about the outlook for the Gulf’s future, the US economy, and the prospect to raise more capital to consolidate the banking industry around the world. Panmure Liberum, a UK investment bank he’s invested in, is expanding into the Gulf. Wall Street investors increasingly see the region as a place to invest, not just a place to raise money, and the war isn’t deterring that. “This is a really serious economy,” he said. Diamond has experience in the region spanning decades. His contacts in Abu Dhabi and Qatar helped secure a £11.8 billion bailout for Barclays during the Great Financial Crisis, enabling the bank to avoid a taxpayer-funded rescue. He left Barclays in 2012 in the wake of a scandal around its role in manipulating interbank rates, and has since reinvented himself as a private equity investor, backing bank consolidation deals and fintechs. He is also chairman of the advisory committee of the Export-Import Bank of the US and chairman of Abu Dhabi’s tokenization platform Finstreet. Diamond also said that Bitcoin, the most well-known and biggest digital asset by market capitalization, is “irrelevant” (though useful as a store of value untethered from governments) and that the future of finance is tokenization — an industry is being led by the US as well as the Middle East. Q&A Matthew Martin: You just announced Panmure Liberum, the UK investment bank you own, is expanding into the Gulf — how do you think about the opportunities in the Gulf now, particularly with the conflict that’s still going on? Bob Diamond: I don’t mean to be dismissive of the severity of the situation here for a second, with the invasion of Iran, but when you’re here, as you and I are today, it feels pretty normal. For people who have not spent time in this region, I don’t think there’s a recognition of how developed the economies are, how developed the leadership is. And then I’d say that since we started Atlas Merchant Capital just over 10 years ago, I’ve been as interested in investing Middle Eastern money in other parts of the world as I have been in how we can find ways to help develop business here on the ground. I think there’s just a tremendous opportunity in this region for an on-the-ground advisory and M&A business for middle-market and family-owned businesses, because, as we are seeing here, the entrepreneurial spirit is very, very strong in many of these countries. Financial services here is a great example of an industry where the vast majority of banks are ultimately state-controlled. As governments need to redirect capital to other things in the wake of the war, is there an opportunity for private equity investors to come in and play more of a role in the financial services industry in the Gulf? One hundred percent. But I think you hit on a key issue, which is that traditionally that state control made things more opaque, so you couldn’t get outside investment because it was opaque. And two, it was intrusive and more focused on subsidized business. And you can see why, right? Because as the Middle East was growing, much of the commercial real estate, for example, had to be “if we build it, they will come.” So some of the unbelievable commercial real estate, whether it’s in Abu Dhabi or Dubai or Qatar, or the financial services center that was built in Riyadh, was done really with strategic impetus, if you will, as opposed to pure commercial activity. And I think that’s changing, because a lot of those initial strategic investments have been done. I think it was the same in the early days of the development of Singapore. You could say the same thing, that it was strategic investing, but if you go to Singapore today, it’s a very commercial city. You don’t see commercial buildings being put up. What impact do you see the conflict in the region having on how Wall Street sees the Gulf? I think sometime around 2024, 2025, we hit an inflection point where the Middle East being seen purely as a source of funding for the Western world changed to “this is a really serious economy.” Going forward the Gulf will be focused much more on inward investment, as well as outward investment. I think it probably happened already with Saudi Arabia, and they’ve been a little bit ahead of it. But I think it’s really true across the region. But there are still significant pools of capital in this region — if you just look at the sovereign wealth funds, that’s the best example but not the only example — for investment in good ideas wherever they happen to be. Dubai and Abu Dhabi are both making this big play into fintech and tokenization. How much are you getting involved in that, and what do you see as the chances of centers in the region becoming hubs for this new asset class? I feel very strongly. Bitcoin’s irrelevant. It’s not that Bitcoin isn’t going to go up or down, and I’m not questioning whether Bitcoin’s going to have a significantly higher price or not. I’m personally not an investor, but I have a number of close associates who believe strongly. My point is different. In its best version, Bitcoin is a store of value away from a government, much as gold is. And if it doubles or triples or quadruples in value, it doesn’t have a single strategic implication for financial services. It’s just made somebody money, and it’s a good store of value. Compare and contrast that to stablecoins, basically making payments electronic institutionally for the major currencies around the world. Compare and contrast that to blockchain, which is 24/7, instantaneous settlement, a permanent record of every transaction that happens, everything at the speed of the internet and a fraction of the cost of conventional financial services. That’s the future. That’s the underpinning of financial services going forward: blockchain, and finally tokenization. In the last two to three years, the US has moved very, very aggressively forward in terms of recognizing Circle, USDC, stablecoins, payments. Under Gensler at the SEC, it was just ignored. Nothing was approved. Outside of the US, we’re not seeing the same kind of attitude in London or Europe, but we are seeing it in the Emirates and in the Middle East. Abu Dhabi’s only a few hours’ time difference from London and Europe, and I think it has a real chance to emerge as a more important financial center with the progress of tokenization and the advance of digital. events.title: Africa’s power drive is short of developers, Gridworks CEO says
events.summary: The News Africa has plenty of investors ready to finance much-needed electricity projects, but too few developers with the expertise and early funding to get them off the ground, the head of a UK government-backed power developer told Semafor. More than 40% of sub-Saharan Africans lack electricity, with private investment central to a World Bank and African Development Bank push to connect 300 million across the whole continent by 2030. “People spend a lot of time talking about a lack of capital for infrastructure projects in Africa. There is not a lack of capital,” said Chris Flavin, chief executive of Gridworks, which develops and invests in electricity networks across Africa. The issue for him is that investors generally want to get involved once projects are ready for construction, leaving the four or five years of preparatory work harder to finance. Gridworks, which has electricity projects in countries including Uganda and Mozambique, is set to become the majority shareholder in a planned $300 million power line linking Zambia’s grid to DR Congo’s copper-mining region, under an agreement signed in October. Lenders have shown “very strong interest” in the line, Flavin said. When it develops its own projects, though, Gridworks faces the same hurdles as others despite its UK backing, he added, from permits and environmental approvals to years of planning “before you even get close to the financing.” In DR Congo, for example, commercial banks will not lend at that stage, said Archip Lobo, co-founder of Nuru, a solar mini-grid operator in the country’s east. “They will take the risk on something that exists,” he told Semafor. Instead, Lobo highlighted the existence of state support for early development costs and World Bank Group insurance against political risks. But the World Bank’s own evaluators are less sure capital is plentiful. They found in a recent review that private financing remained too limited to meet Africa’s electrification needs. The narrow pool of investors, such as development lenders’ private arms, government-sponsored funds, foundations, and impact funds “are unlikely to meet the scale of financing needed for electrification growth,” the group said. Industrial advantage Private power projects in Africa are easier to develop when they serve large industrial buyers, such as mines, rather than households and small businesses, Flavin said. A mine with a strong balance sheet and known electricity consumption gives developers a clear customer to design around. For projects aimed at individual customers “the challenge is one of guaranteed demand.” In southeastern DR Congo, CrossBoundary Energy, a Mauritius-based power producer, commissioned a 233-megawatt solar farm with battery storage in August to supply Kamoa-Kakula, a copper complex co-owned by Ivanhoe Mines. “Kamoa’s books are very good,” Auguy Bakome, a project manager at the mine, told Semafor in an earlier interview. He said its expected 40-year operating life and a 15-year contract to buy the electricity helped reassure lenders. Utilities must estimate consumption across tens of thousands of customers. Building networks to serve them is “at the much harder end of the spectrum, full stop,” Flavin said. Moyi Power, a Gridworks-backed utility planned for three cities in northern DR Congo, relies on donor grants for about a quarter of its $190 million first phase and is not expected to deliver electricity before 2029. Notable Africa’s shortage of reliable power is stalling its industrialization , Bloomberg reported, citing World Bank data that put manufacturing at 11% of sub-Saharan Africa’s GDP , half East Asia’s share.

events.title: Lovable chief people officer: How to lead a company where ambition has somewhere to go
events.summary: Imagine a front desk coordinator who builds her ideal check-in software in an afternoon, shaped exactly to how her company welcomes people. After greeting hundreds of visitors, she knows the flow better than anyone: where guests get stuck, what hosts need to know, and which steps exist only because the old system required them. She can picture a better experience. In the past, getting there meant comparing a dozen visitor-management vendors, picking the closest fit, and bending her process to what the software could do. Today, she can use AI to create a working first version in an hour, show it to colleagues for feedback, and keep improving it based on what guests tell her. As the chief people officer at Lovable, I don’t have to imagine this at all. Our front desk coordinator built our visitor check-in system after understanding what the old process lacked. The system she created from scratch checks guests in, alerts their hosts in Slack, handles signed NDAs, and syncs with the calendar for expected visitors. It also counts how many guests are coming in, so we can see a busy lunchtime ahead and order enough food in advance instead of scrambling on the day. And when our needs change, she updates it in seconds with a single prompt. To me, this is a glimpse into a very exciting future for work, one where talent is unlocked to do their best and most meaningful work. A résumé tells you where someone has been, but rarely their curiosity, their judgment, or their eye for what’s broken. Now those qualities can show up as something real. That’s what happens when the person closest to a problem has the room to act. And yet, new data* from Lovable shows more than 2 in 3 (68%) business owners and senior leaders say a good idea at their company has been dropped or never built because no one with the right skills, time, or budget was available. Leaders have the power to change that. You decide whom to hire, how to empower them, and what conditions to create so they can question how things are done. Lovable turns two today, meaning two years of building a company on the belief that anyone with a good idea should get the chance to act on it. Here are three things I’d encourage leaders of tomorrow to do to meet this moment, along with some mistakes we made along the way so you can avoid them. Hire for craftsmanship If you want people to take ownership, look for evidence that they care deeply. The curiosity, judgment and taste to shape something genuinely useful. In an interview, don’t over-index on whether a candidate knows every tool on the market or has built a zillion agents. Early on at Lovable, we quickly saw that skill with the tools, on its own, told us very little about who would build something useful. That lesson changed how we hire. Now, we look for relentless curiosity and expert judgment in the candidate’s field. A strong finance operator understands the exceptions that complicate a purchasing decision. An experienced recruiter knows where a hiring process loses good candidates. Candidates can pick up new tools. What they bring from their field is harder to teach. Craft grows by doing real work, so give people a real problem as early as you can. Start before day one: new hires get Lovable credits and a short starter brief ahead of time, so they arrive already using the product. A slow ramp can feel like a time-out for someone who’s eager to contribute. On their first day, every new employee spends two hours building something real alongside an experienced colleague. They turn an idea into something that works, share it with their cohort, and get feedback before the day is over. The experience gives them confidence to try the next thing and shows them how work gets done here. About 90% of our new hires ship a first contribution in their first week . That’s a practical leadership choice that we carry through every day after. Across every function, managers give new direct reports meaningful problems to tackle and agree on which decisions they can make themselves and where they’ll need support. Trust people with meaningful responsibility early, and you’ll be surprised by what comes back. Let the people closest to the problem build the solution Leaders too often fall into the trap of being the bottleneck. Not for the decisions that truly need you, but for the improvements that don’t. A team lead wants a better way to track performance of a campaign. Someone wants to automate a weekly report. Someone else wants to retire a legacy tool that no longer fits how their team works. Each request lands on your desk for a sensible reason. Along the way, you become a gatekeeper for your people to improve work they understand well. Your new task is to champion and unblock the people closest to the problem. Look for the first movers, your ““intrapreneurs:” people who think like founders without the title and who see a gap and close it themselves. Not everyone needs to be a world-class builder, but most teams have at least one if you look closely. Give this person time to build and space to get it wrong. Guardrails make that freedom possible. The worry I hear most from leaders is what happens to our data, and who’s responsible when something breaks. The companies doing this well don’t answer it by saying no. They change IT’s job. At Pendo , a software company that helps product teams improve the products their customers use, the data and engineering team builds a secure foundation connected to the company’s data, and frontline leaders shape the last 20% to fit how they work. Nearly 300 employees there built over 1,400 apps in under five months, with the data team keeping full governance. Decide who controls data access before anyone builds, give every tool a named owner and a plan for maintenance or retirement, and build on what already works so you don’t end up with forty versions of the same spreadsheet app. The results can be large. At Nursa , a workforce management solution for healthcare, one VP built an entirely new business line in mere days, and it set the tone for a new way of working. From there, the CEO encouraged all 200-plus employees to build. One credentialing specialist made a verification tool the company estimates would once have taken six months and half a million dollars. The same is true on my own People team. Headcount planning used to live in separate spreadsheets across finance, recruiting, and department heads, and keeping them in sync took weekly reconciliation meetings. The people who lived with that problem, across all those functions, worked together to build a single live view, connected to our HR and recruiting systems, so no one has to cross-reference duplicate spreadsheets anymore. Leadership can now adjust workforce plans as fast as the business changes, and recruiters can see which roles are opening soon so they can prioritize and build a pipeline early. It helps us bring the best people to Lovable, and we estimate it saves about 10 hour
