events.title: Freshworks alums raise $53M to take on Salesforce, HubSpot with AI-native CRM
events.summary: Dreamteam , a startup founded by former Freshworks executives, has raised $53 million to challenge Salesforce and HubSpot with its AI-native CRM, betting that AI can finally shake up a market where established players have so far proved difficult to dislodge. The funding comprises seed and Series A rounds, led by Together Fund and Accel respectively, with participation from Premji Invest. The San Francisco-based startup declined to disclose the size of each round or its valuation. Traditional CRMs depend on salespeople to manually record customer interactions and keep deal information up to date. That often leaves businesses with incomplete or outdated information. Dreamteam aims to eliminate much of that work by automatically capturing context from sources including emails and customer conversations. It also uses AI agents to handle tasks such as follow-ups, meeting preparation, and pipeline monitoring. Dreamteam co-founder and CEO Anand Venkatraman (pictured above, right) told TechCrunch that he had repeatedly encountered problems with traditional CRM platforms over more than 25 years in enterprise software, including at Salesforce and Freshworks. Salespeople spent considerable time updating records, yet managers still struggled to get a reliable picture of their business. “In all these years, I have never come across an instance where I could click a button and get a forecast from the CRM,” he said. That experience led Venkatraman to co-found Dreamteam in 2025 with Senthil Kanthaswamy (pictured above, center), who spent more than nine years at Freshworks, most recently as a product leader at Freshservice, and Ramesh Parthasarathy (pictured above, left), who previously worked on AI and platform engineering at Freshworks. At the heart of Dreamteam’s CRM is what it calls the Company Brain. This acts as virtual memory, pulling together information from emails, meetings, and other customer interactions to build a shared record of customer relationships. Four built-in AI agents use that information to research prospects, draft follow-up emails, flag potential risks to deals, and configure CRM workflows, with sales teams retaining control over what gets sent to customers. Dreamteam has signed up more than 100 customers across 13 countries in the three months since it began actively selling its product, with most paying for the service, Venkatraman said. The startup has also replaced established CRM platforms at several businesses, including Salesforce at healthcare company DMS Health and HubSpot at other customers. The advertising sales team at media streaming company Plex also chose Dreamteam over HubSpot and other AI-native CRM alternatives, Venkatraman told TechCrunch. Plex’s co-founder and chief product officer Scott Olechowski said Dreamteam’s ability to integrate with AI tools already used across the company was a “game changer.” Replacing established CRM platforms at scale may prove more difficult. In a blog post earlier this year, venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) argued that while AI could transform how businesses manage customer relationships, existing CRMs are likely to remain the systems where customer records are stored, with a new generation of AI-powered tools capturing much of the value by working on top of them. Venkatraman acknowledged that Salesforce and HubSpot are unlikely to disappear anytime soon, but noted that their entrenched positions do not guarantee they will dominate the next generation of CRM software. “We see this as an electric-car moment for systems of record,” he said, adding that AI requires a fundamental rethink of how CRMs are built — not simply adding new features to existing platforms. Kanthaswamy believes startups have a window of two to five years to gain ground before established CRM providers can fully adapt to AI. Rebuilding software around a fundamentally different architecture takes time, he stated, giving newer companies an opportunity to attract customers while incumbents work to overhaul their existing products. Dreamteam also plans to expand beyond sales into other parts of the customer lifecycle, including onboarding, customer support, and upselling. The startup already has a feature called Magic Apps that allows users to create custom applications and dashboards within the CRM using natural-language instructions, without writing code. Currently, Dreamteam employs more than 35 people, with its engineering team based in Chennai and its go-to-market operations in the United States. Kanthaswamy said the startup aims to reach eight figures in annual revenue by the end of 2027, though he declined to disclose the startup’s current revenue. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Double capture eludes company for now as booster fumbled Amazon loses first batch of broadband satellites launched on custom rocket 12 hours ago Microsoft lifts Indian cloud prices by 15 percent, cuts costs in China 14 hours ago Scientists check their work and confirm it with update on iconic black hole image 4 days ago NASA asks Earthlings to wave as Voyager 1 reaches a light-day away 4 days ago NASA keeps its PROMISE to raid Mars testbeds for parts 6 days ago SpaceX caught its Starship upper stage returning from orbit on its first attempt, but the Super Heavy booster ended its flight in an explosion after recovery was aborted. The catch was a remarkable achievement: Starship returned to the same launch tower it had left almost a day earlier, settling into its giant mechanical arms. Flight 15 began well, with the 33 Raptor engines of the Super Heavy booster launching the stack from Pad 2 at Starbase, Texas. Hot staging followed, and the booster performed its directional flip maneuver. Thirty-two Raptor engines relit for the boostback burn, intended to return Super Heavy to the tower for another catch. The booster had managed the maneuver on flight tests 5, 7, and 8, but this time something went wrong. "The boostback burn ended early due to low fuel mass," SpaceX said. The booster automatically aborted its return to the tower and diverted offshore. It completed a landing burn, briefly hovering above the Gulf before its engines shut down and the flight termination system delivered an explosive finale. Starship reached orbit under the power of its six Raptor engines and deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites. Unlike the previous flight's brief orbital stint, this mission lasted almost a day. Following a deorbit burn, Starship returned to the launch site 22 and a half hours after it left. Many more development flights remain before SpaceX can deliver its promised fully reusable launch system. NASA's Space Shuttle came close, but the large external tank was expended with every launch, and the orbiters never matched the cadence SpaceX reckons it can achieve with Starship. SpaceX boss Elon Musk admitted that "many small fixes are needed to achieve immediate reusability (like an airplane)." Cadence will be key if Starship is going to meet NASA's needs for the Artemis missions. Somewhere between 6 and 22 launches (depending on who you ask) will be required for a lunar mission, and SpaceX has yet to demonstrate in-space propellant transfer between vehicles. Next year's Artemis III mission also calls for docking tests between NASA's Orion spacecraft and a test version of SpaceX's Starship Human Landing System (HLS) in low Earth orbit. The booster fumble shouldn't obscure what the engineering teams achieved. events.title: Nvidia stock falls on reports Jensen Huang is plotting a comeback—and 40% of prediction market bettors think he’ll return by next year
events.summary: It hasn’t even been a full week since Nvidia’s former CEO and founder, Jensen Huang, resigned after admitting to an extramarital affair with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy. And yet, major investors in the chipmaker are already talking about Huang making a comeback. Huang resigned last Thursday, but by Saturday, both Brad Gerstner, CEO of Altimeter Capital, and Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker had written to Nvidia’s board to ask them to consider leaving “all options” on the table, “including the potential return of Jensen Huang.” Some speculators are inclined to agree. At the time of writing, Polymarket users assigned a 40% probability to Huang rejoining Nvidia by December 2027. 12% suspect he’ll be back before the end of this year. Over on Kalshi, the odds of Huang’s return as CEO are more muted. At the time of writing, 18% of users say Huang will be the next CEO of Nvidia, trailing only Rene Haas, the CEO of Arm Holdings. Haas, who leads the British semiconductor and software design company, has reportedly been approached for the role. A “Stand with Jensen” campaign has also been launched, with Elon Musk—CEO of SpaceX and Tesla—at the top of the petition. Of nearly 180,000 signatures, nearly 9,000 are reportedly “current Nvidians.” But while petitions and speculators online can be waved off, major Nvidia shareholders are harder to ignore. Altimeter holds approximately $1.9 billion in shares, and Atreides approximately $250 million. The letter did not call for Huang’s immediate reinstatement (the company is currently led by interim CEO Colette Kress, formerly CFO), but added: “If after all the facts are known the Board decides that it is not in shareholders’ best interest to have Jensen Huang back as CEO, that is the Board’s prerogative.” “But the founder and long time incredible leader of this extraordinary company has earned the right for a deliberate process that avoids any needless rush to replace him before all the facts are known.” The Financial Times reported over the weekend that Huang had discussed a return with close confidants, citing multiple sources familiar with the matter. This letter was sent to the Nvidia Board today which we believe outlines the minimum acceptable standards the Board owes shareholders as it manages this difficult situation. Onward. 🫡 pic.twitter.com/fIsyXVQ5tR — Brad Gerstner (@altcap) November 13, 2026 Stock wobble Nvidia’s stock continued to slide this weekend, and fell another 2% overnight , to just over $158 per share. Some market analysts see Huang’s return as impossible. Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives, wrote yesterday : “After this global scandal the old Jensen with the black leather jacket and rock star persona is gone for good …. that cannot be replicated and any talk of a damaged Jensen coming back to Nvidia is ridiculous in our view.” He added: “We see no chance Jensen comes back to Nvidia as CEO.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Elon Musk joins 'Bring Jensen Back' campaign to reinstate the ex-Nvidia boss
events.summary: SpaceX boss Elon Musk and Nvidia's former chief executive Jensen Huang Published 16 November 2026, 11:45 GMT Allies of Jensen Huang are trying to rally support for the former Nvidia boss to get his job back after resigning last week over a scandal involving extramarital affairs, one involving an alleged Chinese spy. SpaceX boss Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, chief executive of Fortnite-maker Epic Games, are among those backing a campaign to get the AI chip giant's board to "Bring Jensen Back". Huang resigned as chief executive of Nvidia after the emergence of two affairs, one of whom was with a woman suspected of spying for China and another allegedly with one of his employees. It has created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms which is a key part of the AI industry and its huge expansion. An open letter calling for Nvidia's board to give Huang his job back while an internal probe is conducted has received more than 175,000 signatures, including Musk and Sweeney, according to a website named "Stand with Jensen". The campaign group said it is made up of current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters. "We write with gratitude for Jensen Huang and with a clear demand to the board: bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts, unless and until you can provide compelling evidence that his removal is in NVIDIA's best interests," the letter said. Allies of the ex-Nvidia boss wrote they were "concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process". Huang had been expected to weather the storm following the revelation of an affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy. However, he resigned last Thursday after a second extra-marital relationship emerged, this time allegedly with an executive at Nvidia who reported to him. The scandal-hit tech boss is now discussing a possible return to Nvidia with confidants, according to the Financial Times. , external The newspaper quoted one ally saying that a "war room" of Silicon Valley executives was being convened to lobby for the former Nvidia boss's reinstatement. A representative for Jensen Huang declined to comment on the report. The so-called war room also wants to get support for Huang from the White House. While President Donald Trump recently spoke in glowing terms about Huang , the scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end Nvidia chips to Alice Huang's former firm, Megaspeed. It has raised questions about the possibility that the chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions. The former Nvidia boss has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China . The BBC understands that the likelihood of Huang being reinstated is low while the Nvidia's internal investigations are ongoing. The FBI is also investigating the affair between the former Nvidia boss and Alice Huang, according to Trump. Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation. "Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract. "Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost," he posted on X. , external He later added: "If Jensen gave me his word about compute delivery or I asked for components to be accelerated, he always came through." If Huang was reinstated, it would face scrutiny from Washington. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company. In an open letter to the board, Brad Gerstner, founder of Altimeter Capital and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker called for management to leave "all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang". Lord Sarfraz, a member of the UK's House of Lords, has also written to Nvidia's new chair, Harvey Jones, urging the firm's directors to give "serious consideration" to Huang's return following the investigation. For the moment, Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress is leading the firm and will present the company's results on Tuesday. events.title: Warren Buffett donates $5.5 billion, says kindness 'compounds' in Thanksgiving letter
events.summary: Buffett converted 6,150 Class A Berkshire shares into 9,225,000 Class B shares and gave 3,690,000 of those to The Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation. He also gave 1,845,000 shares to each of The Sherwood Foundation, The Howard G. Buffett Foundation, and NoVo Foundation. Berkshire chairman emeritus still owns 182,140 Class A shares — roughly $162 billion — following the donations. Billionaire Warren Buffett donated Berkshire Hathaway shares worth about $5.5 billion to four philanthropic foundations, stepping up his annual charitable giving from the prior year. Buffett, 96, converted 6,150 Class A Berkshire shares into 9,225,000 Class B shares and gave 3,690,000 of those shares to The Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation, and 1,845,000 shares to each of The Sherwood Foundation, The Howard G. Buffett Foundation, and NoVo Foundation — the foundations run by his three children, Susie, Howard and Peter Buffett. Following the donations, the chairman emeritus of Berkshire still owns 182,140 Class A shares — roughly $162 billion. "Last Thanksgiving I wrote that kindness is costless but also priceless. A year later, I would only add that it compounds, and at a better rate than anything Charlie and I ever bought," wrote Buffett, who was succeeded as chairman in September by his son Howard, in his annual Thanksgiving message. The letter was much shorter than his message last Thanksgiving. Charlie Munger, former vice chairman of Berkshire, passed away in November 2023. Berkshire shares have been on a tear recently, up more than 19% since the start of the fourth quarter and ending last week with four consecutive record high closes. That compares with the S&P 500's decline of 1.2% so far for the fourth quarter. Berkshire has been seen as a safe haven as investors have worried about the AI buildout, corporate drama and geopolitical risk. The shares are now outperforming the S&P 500 for the year by about 7.5 percentage points. In his letter, Buffett reiterated that all of his Berkshire shares eventually will be donated to the four foundations, with the goal being to increase the size of the grants each year. Buffett wrote that the gifts were a signal of his confidence not only in his three children, but also in Berkshire CEO Greg Abel: "My children have given thoughtfully to worthy causes for decades, and I trust 100% both their abilities and their fidelity...You heard plenty from me in September about my confidence in Berkshire. That confidence is as strong as ever," he said. Referring to Munger and himself, Buffett added, "Both of us received beyond measurement costless benefits from a few teachers such as Ben Graham, Joe Rosenfield and Tom Murphy. Because of this we not only prospered mightily but were able to pass along many of the benefits we received." "Warren continues to share his wisdom with us all during this holiday season. His example reflects the kindness he encourages in all of us," said CEO Abel of the letter. Buffett closes his message with this advice: "This Thanksgiving, thank one of those selfless people in your own life. Better yet, be a benefactor for someone else."

events.title: Which cricket teams can qualify for the LA 2028 Olympics and how?
events.summary: Six men’s and six women’s teams will compete for the medals in Twenty20 format as cricket returns to the Olympics in 2028. Cricket has moved one step closer to its Olympic comeback with the unveiling of a qualification process in advance of the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics, where the sport will feature in its shortest format. Eight men’s and women’s teams will have one last chance to feature in the Twenty20 competition at the LA Games, according to the plan announced by the International Cricket Council (ICC) on Sunday. list 1 of 4 South Africa centre bid in Durban for first Olympic Games on the continent list 2 of 4 Kenya’s 2029 World Athletics bid: A win for Africa under scrutiny list 3 of 4 Swiss commentary on Israeli Olympic bobsleigh team termed ‘discriminatory’ list 4 of 4 Irish European athletics champion and Olympian Ciara Mageean dies aged 34 The world’s second-most popular sport has billions of followers around the world, particularly in South Asia, which has secured five of the 10 men’s T20 world championships. Despite its global popularity, cricket has not featured at the Olympics since 1900, when Great Britain defeated France in the only match played. The sport’s Olympic return was overwhelmingly approved in October 2023 in what was described as a “win-win situation”. “The Olympic Games will give cricket a global stage and the opportunity to grow beyond the traditional cricket countries and regions,” then president of the International Olympic Committee, Thomas Bach, said after the IOC announced its decision. Here’s everything to know about the Olympic qualifiers: Six men’s and six women’s teams will feature at the Olympics. Four teams automatically qualify based on ICC rankings in the Asia, Europe, Oceania and Africa regions. One spot goes to the host nation (USA), subject to the side being ranked 15th or better in the Twenty20 International (T20I) standings during the qualification period. The sixth and final place goes to the team winning its qualifier. When and where are the Olympic cricket qualifiers? The men’s qualifiers will take place from February 5 to 13, 2028, in Bangladesh, followed by the women’s qualifiers from February 26 to March 5 in the United States. Which teams have qualified for the Olympics? Four women’s teams — India, Great Britain (through England), Australia and South Africa — have already qualified after finishing as the top-ranked sides in Asia, Europe, Oceania and Africa, respectively, in the women’s T20 World Cup this year. No men’s teams have qualified yet. The highest-ranked sides from the four regions as of December 31, 2026, when the qualification period ends, will secure spots. What’s the format of the qualifiers? Both the men’s and women’s tournaments will feature a total of eight teams divided into groups of four. Each team will play the other teams in their group once. The group winners will progress to the final, with an Olympic berth at stake. Are any teams ineligible to compete at the Olympics? Yes, the West Indies will not be able to compete at the Olympics because the team consists of multiple Caribbean nations, which are represented by their respective national Olympic committees (NOCs), not a unified one. If the West Indies rank among the eight highest sides yet to qualify, a dedicated Caribbean tournament will be organised to determine which nation will represent the region at the qualifiers. Where and when will cricket be held at LA28? Cricket will be played at the $21m, 15,000-seat Knight Riders Cricket Ground in Pomona, about 31 miles (50km) east of downtown Los Angeles. The women’s tournament will be held from July 12 to 20, followed by the men’s tournament from July 22 to 29. The purpose-built venue hosted its first competitive match in July when the Los Angeles Knight Riders took on Washington Freedom in Major League Cricket. Which sports are making their Olympic debut at LA 2028? Squash, lacrosse and flag football will feature at the games for the first time. Will cricket be a permanent feature of the Olympics? Cricket is not yet confirmed for the 2032 Games in Brisbane, Australia, but the ICC is hopeful the sport will make the cut.

events.title: Lutnick faces questions over Nvidia spy scandal. His sons' firm has ties to the chipmaker
events.summary: Cantor Fitzgerald’s reported Nvidia share count fell by nearly half between September 2025 and March 2026, a CNBC analysis found. That was the period when, according to Axios, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick faced pressure from administration officials to address suspected smuggling of Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China. The Wall Street firm, which Lutnick formerly chaired and is now run by his sons, maintained extensive commercial ties to Nvidia, helping arrange billions of dollars in financing for companies in its AI business universe and repeatedly hosting its top executives. Those relationships have come into sharper focus following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and revelations about Lutnick’s handling of national security concerns involving the chipmaker. There is no evidence that Cantor's business interests influenced Lutnick's decisions. In late September, Cantor Fitzgerald hosted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and other top executives from the chipmaker for investor meetings in New York, according to a Cantor research report reviewed by CNBC. The Wall Street firm liked what it heard. "We continue to view NVDA as the best risk/reward in our coverage," Cantor analyst C.J. Muse and his colleagues wrote in a research report dated Oct. 3 that maintained a $350 price target and overweight rating on the stock. Yet the firm, formerly run by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and now led by his sons, Brandon and Kyle, reported a nearly 50% decline in the number of Nvidia shares it held between September 2025 and March 2026 , according to a CNBC analysis of securities filings that excludes options. Nvidia had been one of the largest stock positions reported in Cantor's filings. The decline coincided with White House and U.S. intelligence officials pressing Lutnick to crack down on Megaspeed , a Singapore-based company suspected of funneling Nvidia's advanced artificial intelligence chips to China . Lutnick repeatedly resisted those efforts, Axios reported Nov. 11. By the time Cantor hosted Huang in New York, Lutnick had also received a classified intelligence warning, according to a Nov. 10 Axios report, about Huang's ties to a suspected Chinese spy and had appeared alongside the CEO at a G20 technology summit in North Carolina. Even as Cantor pared back its Nvidia stake, it continued doing business across the chipmaker's AI empire. A CNBC review of securities filings, corporate announcements and Wall Street research found the firm has helped arrange billions of dollars in financing for Nvidia's business partners while maintaining close ties to the chipmaker's leadership. Those ties have drawn fresh scrutiny following Huang's resignation Thursday and Axios' reporting that Lutnick repeatedly resisted a crackdown on companies suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, despite President Donald Trump authorizing new export restrictions on those companies for a third time on Nov. 5. An ethics expert said the relationship between Lutnick and his former firm's investments may raise questions, given what the secretary knew about Nvidia. Nvidia's Colette Kress confronts key questions in first earnings report since Jensen Huang's exit The tech world's calls for Huang to return to Nvidia are growing Nvidia stock slides as investors weigh Huang resignation Megaspeed says Alice Huang left in 2025 as it launches internal probe Howard Lutnick's sons' Nvidia ties amid Huang China spy scandal Richard Painter , the former chief White House ethics lawyer for President George W. Bush and now a corporate law professor at the University of Minnesota, said that while "there's no proof of" Lutnick sharing nonpublic information with Cantor Fitzgerald, "the appearance doesn't look great." "His conversations with his sons better be about publicly available information," Painter told CNBC. There is no evidence that Lutnick's sons had advance knowledge of the intelligence concerns, that changes in Cantor's reported holdings were tied to any warnings or that the firm's business interests influenced their father's decisions. "Cantor has to date from time to time had only immaterial stand-alone proprietary positions in Nvidia, unlike the positions reflected in 13F filings which were entered into in the ordinary course of business in connection with client swap transactions, that are common in institutional markets," a Cantor spokesperson told CNBC. Cantor declined to answer CNBC's other questions. The Commerce Department, the White House, Howard Lutnick, Brandon Lutnick and Kyle Lutnick did not respond to CNBC's requests for comment or detailed questions about the findings. As scrutiny of Huang intensified, Cantor Chairman Brandon Lutnick was publicly praising the chipmaker's leadership. "Nvidia is one of the great companies on the planet, and they have an amazing leadership team," Brandon Lutnick told Fox Business on Wednesday. Trump is standing by Howard Lutnick.

events.title: Cantwell urges Lutnick to stop AI chip sales to China ahead of Xi meeting
events.summary: Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., the ranking member on the Senate commerce panel, is urging Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to use his authority to stop the flow of advanced AI chips to companies with ties to China. Lutnick has drawn scrutiny since news broke about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy and reports that the commerce secretary slow-walked attempts to crack down on the sale of restricted chips to China. Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., who chairs the Senate banking committee, has called Lutnick to testify before Congress in December. Sen. Maria Cantwell , the top Democrat on the Senate commerce committee, alleged in a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Sunday that the department under his leadership failed to prevent China from accessing the U.S.'s most advanced artificial intelligence chips. In the letter, Cantwell prodded Lutnick to enforce export controls and stop the flow of AI chips to companies barred from receiving the technology. She sent the missive ahead of a planned meeting this week between U.S. officials and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, in China. Her urging comes as Washington reels from revelations that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy named Alice Huang. Nvidia is the leading U.S. company designing advanced AI chips. Nvidia's Colette Kress confronts key questions in first earnings report since Jensen Huang's exit The tech world's calls for Huang to return to Nvidia are growing Nvidia stock slides as investors weigh Huang resignation Megaspeed says Alice Huang left in 2025 as it launches internal probe Howard Lutnick's sons' Nvidia ties amid Huang China spy scandal Alice Huang was an executive at Singaporean technology company Megaspeed that allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China. Lutnick, meanwhile, has come under fire for stalling efforts to crack down on chip sales to China and for his close personal relationship with Jensen Huang, who was a vocal opponent of export controls. "The Department of Commerce has resisted efforts to restrict companies flagged as national security threats, weakened safeguards, and left open pathways for the PRC to train advanced AI models using sensitive American technology," Cantwell wrote to Lutnick. "These failures to carry out the law help give away America's technology advantage in AI." The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday. Cantwell called on Lutnick to use his authority to enforce a 2018 law, known as the Export Control Reform Act , which gives the Commerce Department broad latitude to enforce export controls and protect sensitive American technology. She also cites potential financial conflicts involving Lutnick's sons , who control Cantor Fitzgerald, which she said held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time of his nomination. And she notes the Trump administration's 25% fee on certain Nvidia chips sold to China, which she said could create "a perverse financial incentive to approve exports of sensitive American technology." "America's national security and AI leadership cannot be compromised by family business interests or a policy that generates federal revenue from exporting technology critical to our competitive edge," Cantwell wrote. Both Democratic and Republican members of Congress have ramped up pressure on Lutnick and other Commerce Department officials after a Nov. 9 New York Times report alleging the department may have slow-walked an investigation into Megaspeed. On Thursday, Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., summoned both Huang and Lutnick t o testify before his committee in December. Lutnick has agreed to appear before the panel, Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said in a statement last week. And Democrats, who will take control of both the House and Senate in January, have signaled they will investigate Jensen Huang and Commerce officials. On Wednesday, Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., the top Democrat on the Senate banking panel, and Sen. Chris Coons , D-Del., the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations subpanel with jurisdiction over East Asia and the Pacific, sent a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller instructing them to preserve all documents and communications related to Nvidia's exports of "advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China." The letter gives all three officials until Nov. 17 to confirm that preservation directives have been issued.

events.title: How Nvidia turmoil and a Democratic Congress could reshape the AI trade, according to ETF experts
events.summary: The largest technology stocks linked to the artificial intelligence trade could stand to benefit the most from Nvidia's woes and a Democratic-controlled Congress pushing back on data centers, according to investing experts interviewed on CNBC's " ETF Edge " earlier this week. "We may have been put in an environment, as much as investors have sort of been looking for areas outside of Big Tech, where net-net Big Tech ends up as the winner once again," said Roundhill Investments CEO Dave Mazza, whose firm manages the Magnificent Seven ETF ( MAGS ). Part of his bull case: Other players in the AI trade are positioned to fill Nvidia's chip demand if investors lose trust in the company after a tumultuous week that saw its iconic founder and CEO Jensen Huang resign. "If we get into an environment where people can't trust … Nvidia, they're going to look for other sources for these chips because they need them," Mazza said during the "ETF Edge" interview, which occurred Monday as the Nvidia scandal grew but before Huang had resigned. Nvidia's Colette Kress confronts key questions in first earnings report since Jensen Huang's exit The tech world's calls for Huang to return to Nvidia are growing Nvidia stock slides as investors weigh Huang resignation Megaspeed says Alice Huang left in 2025 as it launches internal probe Howard Lutnick's sons' Nvidia ties amid Huang China spy scandal Discussing recent fund flow activity for the MAGS ETF, as well as for the Roundhill Neocloud ETF ( NCLD ) — which focuses on smaller market cap, specialized cloud computing companies — Mazza said, "In a weird way, [hyperscalers] may continue to benefit from this because they have the compute available. It's going to be more valuable if the demand is there." The Roundhill Magnificent Seven ETF ended the week in the green, albeit with a gain of less than 1%, while the Roundhill Neocloud ETF was up over 1%, though earnings from top holdings Coreweave and Nebius presented a mixed picture. CoreWeave had its best day since April 2025 on Wednesday after its latest quarterly results, while Nebius shares sank after its Thursday report. The neocloud ETF remains deeply in the red since its August 2026 launch, down 39%, amid concerns about balance sheet strength, which could linger given Nvidia's role in financing the AI buildout. CoreWeave shares sank again on Friday, and Nvidia posted its longest losing streak since 2012 after its latest weekly losses. Nvidia's interim CEO and current chief financial officer Colette Kress will have her first opportunity to reassure the market when Nvidia reports its third-quarter earnings next Tuesday. "Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders," Kress said in a statement issued on Thursday morning when the company announced Huang's exit. Yorkville Ives partner and senior managing director Dan Ives said on "ETF Edge" on Monday that the market will remain optimistic about other AI chip players, like AMD and Alphabet, if Nvidia faces prolonged headwinds. Ives helped create the Dan IVES Wedbush AI Revolution ETF ( IVES ) while at Wedbush Securities, where he served as the managing director and global head of technology research before departing Wedbush to form his own firm earlier this year. AMD finished trading this week up close to 13%, with Broadcom posting similar gains. The tech-heavy Nasdaq index posted its best week since August as Nvidia's slump reshuffled the AI trade. Yorkville Ives lowered its price target on Nvidia to $225 from $300 on Thursday after Huang's resignation, but maintained a buy rating on the stock, which finished the week at $162.85 per share. "Nvidia remains the clear leader in GPU chips for the AI Revolution. They are roughly 2-3 years ahead of the nearest competitor and the demand trajectory the next few years is not changing because Jensen is gone," Ives wrote in a note to investors on Thursday. "The strategic roadmap is already essentially built around the next few family of chips and physical AI with 42k employees driving it. ... Valuation at roughly 10x 28 EPS is way too cheap once Nvidia gets through this storm and emerges on the other side." The compute that does exist could become even more indispensable against the backdrop of a potential slowdown to the data-center buildout by Congress after the Democratic Party gains of Nov. 3 swept control of Congress, Mazza said. Ives estimates that the "blue tidal wave" in Congress could mean 10% of planned data centers won't materialize on the low end, and 15%-20% on the high end, but he added that demand still outstrips supply four to one. "The compute is just that much more valuable in the capacity today than it was a week ago. So I could argue just more and more bullish, strong, get stronger," Ives said. "The game is going to change for Big Tech. It will slow it down. But there's no overbuild, no bubble concerns. And I view that as actually a positive thing," he added.

events.title: Datacenters' share of UK planning applications nearly triples in three years
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Supercomputing BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features SC 26 Supercomputing Month 2026 Nvidia GTC Berlin 2026 Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Councils waving through majority of proposals as government turns on the AI-friendly planning taps Marvell and Penguin Solutions aim to end the RAMpocalypse with photonic memory fabric now Elon Musk leads Silicon Valley's campaign to put Jensen Huang back in charge at Nvidia 2 hours ago Jensen Huang's self-sabotage sends Nvidia into a midlife crisis 3 days ago US bit barn boom sees energy needs grow 10x as fast as grid capacity 4 days ago AMD winds up Zen 6 cores for faster clock speeds 5 days ago Datacenters made up nearly three times as large a share of UK planning applications in the year to September 2026 as they did three years earlier, with councils receiving 59 submissions. The figures come from planning data site Plota, whose Q3 2026 Planning Index draws on applications from every council across the UK. Plota has logged 416 datacenter applications since 2016, though these include extensions and alterations, not just new bit barns. Estimates put Britain's existing fleet at between 477 and 602 facilities. The peak for volume came in the 12 months to March 2021, when 63 campus applications were filed. However, overall planning applications were also higher then, so datacenters accounted for just 1.1 in every 10,000 filed. In the current period they equate to 1.4 in every 10,000. The figures show that applications for building new server halls are about as high as they have been over the past decade, and close to their recent peak as a share of all applications. Even so, the application numbers don't show the dramatic jump that the steady stream of bit barn announcements might suggest. Nor do they tell us how many facilities are actually being built. Applications did bounce around the middle of 2024, when the current government - and its fetish for all things AI - was elected. But it didn't publish the AI Opportunities Action Plan , which recommended "AI Growth Zones" with streamlined planning to speed up datacenter builds, until the start of 2025. Plota links the rise to datacenters being recognized as critical national infrastructure (CNI) in September 2024, and a December 2024 update to the planning framework that told councils to identify suitable sites for them. The facilities are getting larger. One site being built for Equinix near London's M25 motorway will feature three data halls with more than 250 MW capacity, while another planned for Havering in East London could go up to 600 MW. Both were billed as being among Europe's largest campuses. According to Plota, just 3.3 percent of datacenter applications decided between 2016 and 2024 were refused, against 11.3 percent across all applications. The government has also overturned some local council refusals, controversially, as at a site near Abbots Langley in Hertfordshire last year. Slough leads Plota's tally of applications since 2016 with 28, followed by Tower Hamlets in East London with 16, Leeds with 12, and West Northamptonshire with 11. Developers in England can also ask ministers to bring qualifying datacenter projects into the nationally significant infrastructure planning regime , shifting the consent decision from the council to central government. Projects taking that route fall outside Plota's council-based figures. A recent report found UK ministers met with representatives from 137 different businesses between July 2024 and June 2026 to discuss datacenters, while there were no meetings with environmental or community groups about them.

events.title: Big-ticket holiday items may be harder to find as shipping costs rise
events.summary: Experts expect higher transport and carrying costs this holiday season will mean retailers have lower inventory of big-ticket items like large TVs and grills. Transportation executives said they're seeing retailers be cautious on their holiday inventory strategy. Meanwhile, interest in last-minute delivery is ticking up, and drone company Flytrex said retailers are exploring using drones for holiday delivery. This holiday season, big-ticket items are expected to be in short supply with diesel prices near records, trucking rates close to a post-pandemic level and carrying costs hitting multidecade highs. All of that is forcing many retailers to rethink their holiday inventory strategy. "We are going to have some of the lowest inventory levels on some of these big-ticket items we have seen in history," said Deborah Weinswig, CEO of retail analytics firm Coresight Research. Weinswig said retailers she is working with are holding less inventory of big-screen TVs, grills, large consumer appliances like washers and dryers, and other items that take either big amounts of space or cost a lot of money to hold. "It's freight getting it from there to here; it's carrying costs; then it's just the trucking to get it into the stores," Weinswig said. "We're talking three different pieces right here and each is up significantly year on year." The surge pricing for supply chain services is being caused by domestic and international policy. According to Evercore ISI, the rates for general trucking have increased more than 47% year over year during the week of Nov. 2. Industry experts say a large factor has been a crackdown by the federal government on non-citizen truck drivers and non-U.S.-based truck drivers operating in the U.S. That has created a capacity crunch that has raised rates and is expected to continue to create upward pressure. At the same time, fuel surcharges are spiking. Most transportation providers charge customers an extra fuel surcharge to offset changes in the cost of diesel fuel. That surcharge has spiked 64% year over year, according to Evercore ISI data, as diesel prices have hit new record highs due in part to the U.S.-Israel war with Iran. And inventory holding costs — or the total expense of storing unsold goods, which could include the costs for capital, service, storage and other risk factors — are closely tied to the yield on the 10-year Treasury note, which exceeded 5% in October and remains at multiyear highs in November. Collectively, the higher costs could mean bigger discounts for shoppers willing to wait, according to Bill Catania, CEO of logistics technology company OneRail , which powers same-day delivery for companies such as FedEx and Lowe's . "You're going to see more discount and price promotions as we get closer to the holiday to liquidate inventory, so they're not having to transfer it or dispose of it or position it some other way," Catania said. Retailers are also facing a conundrum in their holiday inventory strategy when it comes to shipping costs versus opportunity costs. In other words, is it worth it to stock up now, or wait it out in hopes that shipping rates will come down some but potentially miss out on having the right product mix? It's leading to a wait-and-see approach for stocking shelves after early holiday sales in October, executives said. UPS CEO Carol Tomé said on the company's earnings call on Oct. 27 that it's "just starting to get peak season forecasts from our customers." Similarly, Derek Leathers, CEO of Werner Enterprises, a trucker for big-box stores and major retailers, said retailers are cautious. "When rates are higher and the cost of capital is more expensive, you are going to have a much more intense focus on not having excess inventory," Leathers said. Still, 2026 holiday sales are expected to top $1 trillion as inflation drives growth and customer spending is expected to remain healthy, according to Bain & Company's annual forecast . Leathers said even with the surge in trucking and shipping rates, he's seeing that retailers are willing to pay up to stock up. "The bigger concern right now is wanting to make sure they have their capacity locked in. There is way more dialogue around the assurance of having a truck or whatever mode that needs to be secured," Leathers said. "Not saying they are price insensitive, because they are certainly always concerned about price. But you can't sell it if it's not on the shelf." ShipMatrix, a data analytics firm for the logistics industry, forecasts 2.4 billion packages will be delivered during the 2026 holiday peak, a 4% increase year over year. It's an increase that will likely lead retailers to increasingly use gig delivery, especially later in the holiday peak. Gig workers allow retailers and delivery companies to adjust to changes in order flow and accommodate surges of last-minute shopping without spending time and money onboarding new team members. "Gig economy delivery is great.

events.title: Zoox robotaxis are now on the Uber app in Las Vegas
events.summary: Zoox robotaxis are officially available through the Uber app in Las Vegas, marking the Amazon-owned autonomous vehicle company’s first partnership with a third-party ride-hailing platform. The launch on Monday is a milestone for both companies. Uber gets to add another partner to its app as part of its broader strategy to become the primary purveyor of autonomous vehicle technology in North America, Europe, and the Middle East. Uber has partnered with more than 30 companies developing autonomous vehicle technology for sidewalk delivery robots, self-driving cars, robotaxis, and drones — though not all of those have turned into commercial deployments yet. For Zoox, the partnership and launch gives it access to more potential customers who might otherwise not try its robotaxi, a needed boost as it trails market leaders Tesla and Waymo. The partnership is expected to extend beyond Las Vegas. Zoox will begin initial robotaxi operations in Los Angeles this year (introducing the robotaxi and opening rides to Zoox employees, family, and friends), but commercial service will not begin until 2027. Rides will be available via the Uber app next year as well. For now, all eyes are on Las Vegas, Zoox’s first commercial market and a city where Uber has ambitious robotaxi plans. The two companies also announced a multi-year partnership with MGM Resorts International: they’re rideshare and robotaxi partners for MGM Resorts properties in Las Vegas. Uber and Zoox said they’ll work with MGM Resorts to improve pickup and drop-off locations, along with signage to help riders navigate sprawling MGM properties and find the robotaxis. Earlier this year, the Nevada Transportation Authority unanimously approved a permit that allowed Uber to deploy up to 1,000 robotaxis in Clark County — home to Las Vegas — through its partnerships with Hyundai subsidiary Motional and Zoox. Zoox’s addition to the Uber app comes with some initial limitations. Customers won’t be able to select a Zoox robotaxi — at least initially. Instead, people who request an UberX, Uber Comfort, Uber Electric, Uber Comfort Electric, or Wait & Save ride may be matched with one of Zoox’s custom-built robotaxis once they hail a ride. Customers can increase their chances of getting a Zoox robotaxi by opting for autonomous rides through “ride preferences” in the Uber app’s settings. Uber plans to introduce a dedicated autonomous option in its app as “availability and reliability improve,” Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said during the company’s third-quarter earnings call in November. “Las Vegas will become the first U.S. city where riders can access two fully driverless partners through the Uber app,” he said on the call. “We will begin with limited fleets and expand supply over the coming months, with plans to introduce a dedicated autonomous option in our app.” The plan to offer a dedicated autonomous option marks a shift in Uber’s approach to robotaxis, including its partnership with Waymo. That exclusive partnership, which matches Waymo robotaxis with Uber riders in Austin and Atlanta, will end in January 2028. Waymo plans to offer its rides directly through its own smartphone app as it does in other cities. TechCrunch previously confirmed with Uber that it still plans to host Waymo robotaxis on its app for as long as the two companies agree. And unlike its partnership with other AV developers, Uber told TechCrunch that it will not provide maintenance and other services for Zoox in the Las Vegas market. events.title: Great Britain’s oldest renewables projects could rake in nearly £9bn next year
events.summary: Subsidy scheme, which is paid via taxes and energy bills, must be reformed, ECU analysis finds Great Britain’s oldest renewable energy projects are likely to rake in a near £9bn windfall next year because of soaring market prices, according to independent analysis. The research has revealed that almost a third of the UK’s wind and solar farms that rely on the government’s legacy renewables subsidy scheme are in line for soaring subsidy payments as officials grapple with plans to lower the country’s energy costs. Renewable energy projects built between 2003 and 2014 are expected to claim £4.5bn in subsidies over the next financial year, on top of £4.2bn in wholesale market revenue. The analysis showed developers will receive almost 50% more than before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine sent gas prices soaring in 2022. The analysis by the Energy Competitiveness Unit (ECU), a non-partisan research and policy project, said the legacy support scheme – which is paid via taxes and energy bills – must be reformed “if we are serious about getting costs of the electricity system down in the short and medium term”. Unlike newer renewable energy projects that earn fixed-price subsidies for their generation, older projects access support via the renewables obligation (RO) scheme, which provides payments on top of what developers earn via the wholesale market, meaning that higher gas market prices lead to higher subsidy costs for renewables. The scheme was credited with kickstarting the UK’s renewable energy industry when it was put in place almost 25 years ago, but the ECU said it “has been allowed to persist unsustainably”. Andrew O’Brien, the ECU director, told the Guardian that the rise in wholesale prices over recent years has meant that many renewable energy developers are earning “well above what they could reasonably have expected” when first taking the decision to invest in the projects. The government announced last year that it would remove three-quarters of the RO scheme’s costs from home energy bills, and move these levies into general taxation from April 2026 to help temper the steep rise in energy bills. The government later warned that legacy generators could face higher windfall taxes unless they give up the existing RO scheme in favour of a new partially fixed subsidy contract as part of its plans to protect bill payers. The ECU believes that the government’s consultation on plans to fix the generators’ wholesale revenues to help to weaken the link between volatile global gas markets and the UK’s electricity costs “falls short”. It argues ministers should go further to fix their subsidy payments and create a new scheme. Since 2013, renewable energy developers have been required to compete in an auction to secure a contract for a fixed price for each megawatt-hour of electricity generated, known as a contract for difference (CfD), which means costs remain fixed regardless of global markets. Under an alternative proposal set out in the ECU’s research, the government could cut electricity costs by £3.8bn next year, and £9.2bn over 10 years, if all generators moved on to an entirely fixed-price contract, which it calls a fair value CfD. The new private law contracts could also offer a degree of legal protection against the political risk that any potential future net zero sceptic government could dismantle renewable energy support through the government’s RO scheme, a threat signalled by the rightwing populist Reform UK party . Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning “It is in the interests of everyone – investors, generators, businesses, households and government – to get a credible long-term plan in place that can withstand shocks in this increasingly uncertain world,” the ECU said. In his budget speech last month, the chancellor, John Healey, said : “We will further break the grip of international gas prices on our bills by moving more of our old renewables on to fixed-price contracts.” Tara Singh, the chief executive of RenewableUK, said the renewable energy projects were still helping to keep a lid on bills by “pushing expensive gas off the system”. Singh said: “UCL found wind has saved consumers £100bn since 2010 even allowing for support schemes like the RO by reducing the need for expensive imports.” She added that the government’s windfall tax, which took effect from July, has meant that renewable energy projects using the RO scheme pay the Treasury up to 80p of every additional pound it earns from market prices above £82.61 per megawatt hour. “To put this into context, the average wholesale price of electricity over the last 12 months is over £100 per megawatt hour, and frequently higher than that,” she said. “The fastest way to protect consumers from future price shocks is to build more cheap, homegrown renewable power.”

events.title: Zambia's mining investor seeks to borrow $700M
events.summary: The News Zambia’s majority state-owned mining and energy investor plans to borrow about $700 million by 2028 to expand its business, its CEO told Semafor, as Africa’s second-largest copper producer seeks a bigger share of the wealth from its minerals. The money, which ZCCM Investments Holdings has yet to secure, will help fund a $2.7 billion investment proposal it unveiled on Monday. Over the next decade, the company looks to back new infrastructure including a coal-fired power plant in southern Zambia and to raise its stakes in copper mines , among them a project led by Bill Gates-backed Kobold Metals. “We don’t want to be a quiet minority shareholder,” CEO Kakenenwa Muyangwa said. He added that any changes would be negotiated on commercial terms, and that “investors who share the ambition will find us a committed long-term partner.” ZCCM-IH holds stakes in mines run by other companies and earns much of its income from their dividends, which depend on what is left after the mines pay their costs and debts. “For a country that owns a share of its mines, that is not good enough,” Muyangwa said. The company now aims to earn more from royalties, a share of a mine’s sales that is paid regardless of profit. Its only such arrangement, with Canadian miner First Quantum’s Kansanshi mine, will bring in more than $990 million over the next decade, the company forecasts. ZCCM-IH aims to add at least one more later this decade. The investment company said it now owes $5 for every $100 of its own capital, down from about $66 in 2021. Muyangwa said a cleaner balance sheet had put ZCCM-IH in a strong position to fund its expansion. Trading ambitions ZCCM-IH also plans to negotiate with its mining partners to get a share of the copper produced at each mine, which it would then sell directly. That would give the company “a trading income on top of its investment income” and build “the skills to market Zambian metal from Zambia,” Muyangwa said. The plan comes as state-backed companies across Africa’s copper belt seek a more influential role over the trade of the metal. In neighboring DR Congo, state miner Gécamines sells copper through a venture with Swiss trader Mercuria. Zambia’s state-owned Industrial Development Corporation also has a trading venture with Mercuria, which last month named ZCCM-IH as a regional partner. The goal is greater control over the money countries earn from their minerals, Ekpen Omonbude, a senior policy adviser at the International Institute for Sustainable Development, told Semafor. As demand for critical minerals grows, governments are looking to take a more active role in their sale, an approach he said is more common in oil and gas than in mining. Notable Zambia’s copper output rose just 1.5% in the first nine months of the year , far short of what it needs to meet its goal of 3 million tons a year by 2031.

events.title: Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if Trump trade talks fail
events.summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry PHNOM PENH, Cambodia -- Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry. Carney’s comments in Cambodia on Monday came ahead of a planned meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week in Shenzhen, China, where Chinese auto manufacturing is expected to be discussed. The two leaders reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs. “We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters in Cambodia. “That market has become less integrated because of U.S. trade actions.” Carney said Saturday in Manila, Philippines, that any trade agreement with Washington must leave Canada with a viable auto industry. He said Monday that negotiations with the United States remain his priority, but their outcome could determine whether Canada pursues alternatives involving European, Chinese or Japanese automakers. Asked whether potential Chinese investment was leverage in the U.S. negotiations, Carney replied: “It’s not leverage. But action, reaction.” “If they’re not fully utilized in a North American context, that provides other opportunities,” Carney said of Canada’s auto workers and manufacturing assets. “Canada is going to move forward either way.” The Detroit Three — Ford, General Motors and Stellantis — operate factories across Canada, the United States and Mexico, with parts sometimes crossing borders multiple times before a vehicle is completed. Trump has repeatedly pushed automakers to move production to the United States from Canada. Carney said any Chinese investment would have to involve substantial manufacturing in Canada rather than simply assembling imported parts. He said it would require proper labor standards, manufacturing facilities and domestic supply chains that expand over time, including Canadian critical minerals used in electric vehicles. In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola. Carney said at the time that he expected the agreement to attract Chinese investment in Canada’s auto industry and create jobs. The deal drew criticism from Ontario Premier Doug Ford, whose province is the center of Canada’s auto industry. Ford warned that allowing Chinese electric vehicles into Canada could threaten Canadian jobs and jeopardize access to the U.S. market. Trump’s tariffs have disrupted Canada’s auto industry, which relies heavily on cross-border production. Canada recently threatened to sue Stellantis after the automaker shifted planned Jeep Compass production from Brampton, Ontario, to Illinois and agreed to sell its idled Canadian assembly plant. Carney said Saturday that he had spoken at length with Trump and senior U.S. officials and that the two countries were making progress toward a possible trade agreement, although differences remained. events.title: Welcome to 'Grandthropic', the day the gaming and AI industries get tested
events.summary: Anthropic's IPO and "Grand Theft Auto VI" drop the same day. Rockstar Games; iStock; Tyler Le/BI This post originally appeared in the Business Insider Today newsletter. You can sign up for Business Insider's daily newsletter here . Grand Theft Anthropic. GTA VI(PO). Grandthropic. Call it whatever you want. Just don't call it boring. Grand Theft Auto VI's release and Anthropic's market debut arrive this Thursday. Not since "Barbenheimer" — when "Oppenheimer" and "Barbie" premiered the same weekend — have we had two cultural and business phenomena collide on the same day. I'll start with Anthropic, since that's the easier sell. A valuation as high as $1.4 trillion with as much as $90 billion raised makes it a behemoth (and potentially record-breaking) IPO. It's also the first major test of investor appetite for a company focused solely on AI . Then there's GTA. The last installment — GTA V — surpassed $1 billion in sales within the first three days of its release in 2013. It remains a top-selling game to this day, with almost 235 million units sold overall. GTA VI is already off to a hot start. Presale estimates have reached 12.13 million units, totaling $1.18 billion in revenue, according to SensorTower data . The impact also extends to companies' PTO calendars . (Or your favorite newsletter writer; I'll be out next week.) Workforce management tech company UKG said time-off requests for the week of GTA 6's release are up roughly 20% compared to the same week in previous years. Some companies are even leaning into it . 'Grandthropic' comes with some incredibly high stakes. For Anthropic, the fate of the wider AI trade rests on its shoulders. And that was before one of the industry's mascots — Jensen Huang — blew up spectacularly. The AI giant's public debut represents the cleanest bellwether for AI. This isn't an offshoot of the AI ecosystem, like a chipmaker or data center, or a company leveraging AI atop a mature business. Anthropic is as pure-play of an AI company as you'll ever find. Which raises the question: If investors don't support Anthropic, why have any confidence in the wider AI trade? I argued that point on my Instagram . For GTA 6, it's tough to compare it to the rest of the video game industry because its incredible success makes it an outlier. But with the threats posed by artificial intelligence and high hardware costs , GTA's success could serve as the anchor that keeps gamers engaged, bridging to other games. As if that wasn't enough pressure, waiting 13 years for a new edition also created lofty expectations. (And an incredible meme: We got X before GTA 6. ) Strauss Zelnick , CEO and chairman of Take-Two Interactive, the company behind GTA, is well aware of that. At BI's The Long Play event last month, he spoke to my colleague Sarah E. Needleman about how his company's mission "is to make the best entertainment on Earth." The full interview is worth a watch . events.title: Who is Ahmad Tibi, the Arab MP elected deputy speaker of Israel’s Knesset?
events.summary: Will Israel’s election change life in Gaza? Ahmad Tibi, a veteran Palestinian-Israeli politician and doctor, has built a career fiercely advocating for Arab rights while defying Israel’s right-wing establishment. Ahmad Tibi, chairman of the Arab Movement for Renewal (Ta’al) party, has been elected deputy speaker of the Israeli Knesset. The appointment marks a significant milestone for the seasoned lawmaker who has long represented Palestinian citizens of Israel. Speaking to Al Jazeera following his election, Tibi framed the moment as a victory against far-right parties that have led or been part of Israel’s government in recent years. “This is a rightful achievement for the Joint List, which secured 11 seats,” he said, referring to an alliance of Arab-majority parties. “Likud and Ben-Gvir attempted to prevent my election, but they failed despite their reckless incitement,” Tibi added, referring to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s party and far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir. Born in the city of Taibe on December 19, 1958, to a family displaced from Jaffa during the 1948 Nakba, Tibi initially pursued medicine, graduating with top honours from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem in 1983. However, his political activism soon overshadowed his medical career. In 1984, Tibi met Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) leader Yasser Arafat in Tunis, Tunisia, defying Israeli laws that classified it as a “terrorist organisation” at the time. Although interrogated by Israeli police upon his return, he was never formally charged. Tibi later served as a political adviser to Arafat between 1993 and 1999. He acted as the Palestinian delegation’s spokesperson at the Wye River summit in Maryland, United States, in 1998. Benjamin Netanyahu, the longest-serving Israeli prime minister, was then in his first stint in power. At the summit, Israel agreed to withdraw its forces from parts of the occupied West Bank, while the Palestinian Authority (PA) agreed to a further crackdown on armed factions of the Palestinian resistance movement. Like other Israel-Palestine accords, the Wye River Memorandum was soon abandoned by Israel. Tibi founded Ta’al in 1996 and was first elected to the Knesset in 1999. Identifying himself as an “Arab Palestinian with Israeli citizenship”, he advocates for a two-state solution and the right of return for Palestinian refugees. He consistently challenges Israel’s definition as a “Jewish state”, describing it instead as an “apartheid state” and advocating for a “state for all its citizens”. His outspoken positions and on-the-ground activism have repeatedly made him a target of the Israeli government and violent far-right activists. During the second Intifada in September 2000, his right hand was broken while confronting Ariel Sharon, who would become prime minister the following year, during his provocative storming of the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound. In 2002, Israel stripped Tibi of his parliamentary immunity after he entered the Jenin refugee camp during a military offensive and confronted soldiers. Tibi is also renowned for his dramatic parliamentary protests. In 2016, he famously raised the Islamic call to prayer inside the Knesset chamber to protest against a proposed Israeli bill aiming to ban loudspeakers in Jerusalem and the occupied Palestinian territory.

events.title: Dar Global launches $267m project in Jeddah amid Saudi expansion push
events.summary: London-listed real estate developer Dar Global is launching a new mixed-use development in Jeddah , with an estimated value of about 1 billion Saudi riyals ($267 million) as part of its expansion plans in the kingdom. The project will be developed on a plot of land acquired for $56 million and forms part of Dar Global's programme to expand its Saudi Arabia portfolio by up to 4 billion riyals, the company said on Monday. On completion of the programme, the company's worldwide development pipeline is expected to reach about $24 billion, it added. A new international luxury brand will be introduced to Jeddah as part of the development, as the company plans to announce more land acquisitions in the kingdom. Dar Global has partnerships with more than 10 brands, including the Trump Organisation, Aston Martin, Automobili Lamborghini, Missoni, Pagani Automobili and W Hotels, among others at its developments. “With buyers from 61 nationalities already investing in our Saudi portfolio, we are witnessing accelerating international confidence in the country's real estate sector,” said Ziad El Chaar, chief executive of Dar Global. “This new development marks another significant milestone in our global expansion strategy.” The Arab world’s largest economy is looking to boost home ownership for Saudi citizens as part of its Vision 2030 programme. It has also opened up the property sector to foreign ownership, a move expected to attract increased demand. However, buyers remained “selective” in the kingdom during the third quarter amid regional uncertainty triggered by Iran war, a recent report by JLL said. In the July to September period, sale transaction volumes in Riyadh fell by about 30 per cent year-on-year to 9,100, while values decreased 51.8 per cent to 8.5 billion riyals. Residential transaction volumes in Jeddah fell by 25.8 per cent on an annual basis to 3,100. Transaction values fell by 5.8 per cent to 3.9 billion riyals, JLL said. With a presence in 14 international cities across nine countries, Dar Global’s portfolio of 4,200 units completed or under construction, spans the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Oman, Qatar, the UK, Spain and Greece. It is building three residential projects in Saudi Arabia in partnership with the Trump Organisation, including a $1 billion Trump Tower in Jeddah and a Trump-branded ​luxury project in Wadi Safar in the capital. Dar Global and the US President are also in partnership for the development of a $1 billion Trump Tower on Dubai 's Sheikh Zayed Road. Other international developers, including UAE-based Arada, are also expanding to Saudi Arabia. Last month, Arada unveiled a Dh14 billion ($3.8 billion) residential project in Riyadh, with plans to build 100,000 homes in Saudi Arabia over the next three to five years. Up to 3,500 villas and townhouses will be built in Al Rimal district in Riyadh's north-eastern growth corridor on a 2.5 million-square-metre plot.

Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen's blunder will rock the world 2 days ago Elon Musk and a bunch of Silicon Valley heavyweights want Jensen Huang back at Nvidia, and they've decided an online petition is the way to make it happen. An open letter addressed to Nvidia's board had attracted more than 173,000 signatures at the time of writing, just four days after Huang's departure following revelations about his personal relationships, including an affair with a woman suspected of spying for China. The campaign, launched under the banner "Stand with Jensen," calls on Nvidia to reinstate its co-founder and former CEO while an independent investigation establishes the facts, give him a chance to respond to the allegations, and publicly explain why he was forced out. "For thirty-three years, Jensen poured his heart and soul into building Nvidia," the letter reads. "He bet it on ideas that most of the industry dismissed, carried it through years when the bets looked foolish, and stayed long enough to see them change how the world computes. "Many of us joined because of him. Many of us stayed because of how he treated the work: as something worth getting right, together, at whatever hour it took. This company is the work of his life. That deserves more than gratitude after the fact. It deserves fairness now." Among the supporters are Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, Y Combinator boss Garry Tan, and Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick. More than 8,000 signatories also identify themselves as Nvidia employees, equivalent to roughly a fifth of its workforce. However, how many of those signatures are genuine is anyone's guess. The site doesn't verify names or employers, so there's nothing stopping someone from signing as Musk, Huang, or Nvidia's entire board if they fancy it. The campaign follows Huang's resignation on November 12 , ending his 33-year reign at the GPU giant he co-founded in 1993. His departure came after reports of an affair with Alice Huang , a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed who US intelligence suspects of spying for Beijing, and a separate alleged relationship with an Nvidia employee. Nvidia CFO Colette Kress has been handed the unenviable job of running the company while its board searches for a permanent replacement. Huang's departure has left the chipmaker facing something of an identity crisis , with rivals undoubtedly watching the chaos with interest. Huang himself may not be ready to hang up his leather jacket. According to the Financial Times , the former CEO has discussed a possible comeback with associates, while an ally is reportedly assembling a "war room" of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his return. The effort could even involve seeking support from the White House, although Washington appears rather less enthusiastic about the prospect. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Sunday that Nvidia needs a "dramatic shake-up" and should look outside the company for its next chief executive. He also wants answers about whether Nvidia knowingly allowed advanced AI chips to reach China in breach of US export restrictions. None of that seems to have put off Huang's supporters. "He has erred, yes – to err is to be human – but I do not believe anything he has done rises to the bar of separating him from his company," Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick said.

events.title: As homes seized, Jericho’s Palestinian residents fear settler takeover
events.summary: Will Israel’s election change life in Gaza? Palestinians are assaulted and their homes are levelled in pogrom in occupied West Bank. Jericho, occupied West Bank – On November 4, Israeli settlers seized eight Palestinian homes in Jericho after a months-long secretive operation spearheaded by the internationally sanctioned Nachala settler movement and with the support of the settlement council in the northern West Bank. As soon as we arrived at the area, known as Diyouk al-Tahta, we encountered Mustafa. Israeli settlers had barred him from his land, beating him and his elderly father, who had to be treated in hospital. His uncle and cousins faced the same abuse, and other Bedouin families who live in the area were also assaulted and forced to leave their homes in the pogrom . Many of their houses were later razed by residents of Israeli settlements, which are illegal under international law. list 1 of 3 Israeli settlers seize 8 Palestinian homes in Jericho, displacing dozens list 2 of 3 Israeli settlers seize Palestinian homes in Jericho, displacing dozens list 3 of 3 Palestine Weekly: West Bank on fire – and Gaza’s tents under water While we were talking to Mustafa, a settler’s car sped past, and we had to quickly move out of its way. When the dust settled, a settler had left the car and appeared to be cornering a child. He slapped the boy before he managed to get away on his bike. I asked him what happened. The child’s eyes were red. He was struggling to hold back tears. “The settler slapped me. He was speaking in Hebrew. I didn’t understand anything. I didn’t even see him coming!” I asked the child about his name, but he sped away. Perhaps it was fear or embarrassment, or both. Many of the homes taken over by settlers in the area were under Israeli demolition orders. A government decision this year allowing settlers to buy Palestinian property inside Palestinian-controlled areas laid the groundwork for Israeli settlement outposts to pop up in the middle of cities, which in turn would bring the Israeli army and movement restrictions to the streets of cities like Jericho. This is what makes the precedent set in Jenin different from other settler takeovers. In occupied East Jerusalem and the Old City of Hebron, where the army maintains direct control, settlers have taken over homes by alleging they bought the properties or claiming historical Jewish ownership predating the establishment of Israel. Palestinian owners take their battles to Israeli courts and often prove that the documents presented by settler organisations are forged. But they rarely, if ever, succeed in keeping their homes. While Jericho is run entirely by the Palestinian Authority, the Israeli settler presence here is upending people’s lives and is in effect reversing Palestinian control. The Palestinian Authority has launched an investigation into the takeovers, trying to ascertain if anyone facilitated them via sales to settlers, and several arrests have been made. According to the law, Palestinians may not sell their homes in the West Bank to Israelis. Legal experts told Al Jazeera that even if money changed hands in these cases, the sales would be illegal under Palestinian and international law. These are not real estate deals. They are part of a takeover campaign. “It’s a campaign to uproot us just as they did with others in al-Mughayyir and Turmus Aya and other villages across the West Bank,” Mahmoud Abu Fkheida told me. The Jericho farmer inherited this land from his father, who inherited it from his. Working this land is their life. “When I leave my home to tend to my farm for an hour, I stay worried. I’m now afraid when my phone rings. I keep wondering if it’s news of them burning or attacking my home,” Mahmoud told me. As we were filming, Israeli settlers, some of them covering their faces with cloth hoods, ambushed us. They told us that our presence is a provocation and demanded we leave. The settlers are armed, and they have Israeli army protection. We could not challenge their orders or argue with them, so we walked away towards the homes still inhabited by their Palestinian owners. Jericho is a city that depends on tourism. Today, the cable cars leading to the Mount of Temptation run empty while the city’s facilities below waste away. Fear is ever present, as are the settlements and outposts that surround Jericho. On the eastern edge of the city, a new settlement towers over the rubble of Palestinian villas while the fields lie barren. We met Abdel Qader Abu Khashan, who has been overtaken by a sense of loss and dread. “Look around you. All these homes are now under threat,” he said. Abdel Qader says what is happening in Jericho foretells a dead-end future for Palestinians. “It’s not fear that I feel. It’s about hope and the future. I don’t want to say they’re disappearing, but they’re becoming distant,” he said. Back at Diyouk al-Tahta, the scene was paradoxical.
