events.title: SIA logs 3.5% rise in October passenger traffic; sees ‘healthy’ demand for semiconductor shipments
events.summary: SIA and its budget arm Scoot carried 3.7 million passengers during the month, up 4.5% from a year ago, the group said in a bourse filing. SIA reported a 3.5% rise in October passenger traffic, with 3.7 million travellers and an 87.8% passenger load factor, showing resilient demand for air travel. Scoot kept strong momentum, with a 91.6% load factor for its fourth straight month above 90%, while both airlines added new services to Madrid and Guiyang. Cargo traffic rose 10.1% as demand stayed healthy, especially for semiconductor and cloud-computing shipments, lifting cargo load factor to 59.1% despite slightly lower capacity. SINGAPORE – Singapore Airlines on Nov 16 reported a 3.5% rise in passenger traffic in October from the year-ago period amid “resilient” demand for air travel. The group’s October passenger capacity concurrently rose 2.9%, while the passenger load factor (PLF) – the percentage of available seating capacity occupied by passengers – was up 0.5 percentage point at 87.8%. SIA recorded a monthly PLF of 86.8%, thanks to “robust growth” across all regions, including East Asia, Europe and the South-west Pacific, where “traffic marginally trailed capacity increase”. Scoot’s PLF stood at 91.6%, making October its fourth consecutive month with a PLF exceeding 90%. Both airlines had launched new services during the month: SIA to Madrid in Spain, and Scoot to Guiyang in mainland China. Cargo loads rose 10.1% in October amid “healthy, broad-based demand across all verticals, particularly for semiconductor and cloud-computing shipments across the Pacific”, SIA said. Cargo capacity for the month was lower by 0.4%, translating to a rise in cargo load factor of 5.6 percentage points to 59.1%. The group’s passenger network as at end-October covers 138 destinations in 35 countries and territories; SIA serves 79 destinations, while Scoot serves 85 destinations. The cargo network comprises 141 destinations in 36 countries and territories.

events.title: Microsoft blames monster email outage on software defect introduced in July fix
events.summary: Microsoft has blamed last week's epic outage on a change it made in July that lurked in the network gateway servers until a surge in load and a drop in capacity triggered the defect, giving the Microsoft 365 world a day off from email. According to a preliminary post incident report published by Microsoft on November 15, the defect was introduced in July 2026. The update looked fine at the time, Microsoft says, having passed load testing and been deployed without any impact. However, the testing wasn't good enough. Microsoft's report states: "Our load testing tended to focus on weaker hardware with fewer cores." The defect caused "lock contention inside an internal Windows process which caused the machine's resources (CPU & memory) to be exhausted." "The contention issue is worsened on machines with more cores and newer hardware." The fix containing the defect was prepared specifically for Microsoft 365 network gateway servers. Then two things happened at once. Teams failed over to the "primary" gateway that supports Exchange Online, creating a surge in load that was not, in itself, particularly unusual. At the same time, almost 14 percent of server capacity for the networking gateway was out of service, which wasn't a problem by itself either: it was on its way to being restored and, according to Microsoft, "the service had sufficient capacity headroom." Together, they pushed the gateway into the defect and chaos ensued. It was a classic cascading failure scenario. When a server loses connectivity, traffic gets routed to the next healthy endpoint. Which encountered the same problem. So traffic was rerouted again and… you can see where this was going. Within two hours, the defect was encountered across Microsoft's fleet. "At its lowest," the report states, "more than 80 percent of servers were unresponsive." So, what to do? Bringing servers back to service didn't help – they were immediately overwhelmed and fell over again. "Our normally automated recovery processes were not designed to restore service from this broad unresponsive state." A straightforward rollback was also not possible because the defect was months old. Instead, engineers developed patch for the patch or, in Microsoft's words, "an update that returned the code path to the previously known good state in Windows." The patch was applied to groups of servers and service was gradually restored. The timings show the pain customers experienced and the floundering in Redmond as Microsoft tried to work out why Exchange Online and other cloud services were so poorly. The Teams failover, which turned out to be a factor in the outage, happened at 0107 UTC on November 12. During the day, the load began to ramp up until, at 1603 UTC, Microsoft's connectivity anomaly detection monitor identified an increase in connectivity issues. At 1633 UTC, the first support case came in. It is not difficult to imagine the stress engineers felt as, over the next 15 hours, nothing they tried resolved the issue. All ongoing and planned deployments and configuration changes were paused while the team attempted to resurrect the service. Extra capacity was added. Traffic was rerouted. Yet servers kept falling over. "Those services that were able – like Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint, and Office apps – failed out of the faulty network gateway infrastructure," the report says. "But not all services, like Exchange Online, can fail out of this network gateway for scale reasons." Hence the length of time for which Exchange Online (or, from the perspective of many users, Outlook) was out of action. By 0030 UTC on November 13, Microsoft had identified connection negotiation as the main culprit for the access failures and concluded that competing processes were preventing connections from being handled. However, it took until 0720 UTC before "We identified a mitigation and applied the mitigation – an update that reverted the defective change." At 1610 UTC, Microsoft confirmed that things were once again looking healthy and, at 0415 on November 14, issued its final customer update. A final post incident report is due on November 20. However, the preliminary report will do little to calm jangling nerves. An update applied three months ago managed to cause Exchange Online (and other services) disruption on a global scale? With load testing that didn't reflect scenarios under Microsoft's control? The engineers who worked feverishly to restore services deserve commendation and will hopefully never have to buy their own beverages in Redmond again (or at least escape the next round of firings). However, the processes that led to an update with a latent defect reaching production deserve a long, hard look. ®

events.title: I went to a math class at Caltech. The professor no longer grades homework because everyone's using AI.
events.summary: I went to a math class at Caltech, where the specter of AI loomed large. Truman Dickerson I attended an intro math class at Caltech, an elite STEM university in Pasadena. I didn't understand the material, but I did understand that AI was looming large. The professor, Yi Ni, said he no longer grades homework because students use AI to do it. Professor Yi Ni had no laptop or projector. He instead rapidly filled eight blackboards with chalk scrawl during an introductory math class at Caltech on Friday. Though the instruction was entirely analog, the specter of AI loomed large. Ni, a professor at Caltech for 17 years, told me that he no longer grades homework on accuracy because students are using AI to complete it. Now, he grades it only on completion. "There is a problem in the education process," Ni said. "Virtually all the homework in college math, you can use AI." Chatbots, once derided for their inability to perform such basic tasks as counting the r's in "strawberry," can now do math as well as a graduate student. And if you're an undergraduate student, that's kind of a big deal. Some, Business Insider has reported, are reconsidering whether to study math at all . From my perch near the back of the lecture hall on Friday, however, I didn't see any students prompting ChatGPT. In many ways, the class resembled a typical early morning university lecture (for undergrads, 10 a.m. is basically the crack of dawn). Sweatshirted students arrived late and filtered in the upper rows, while the overachievers sat in the front and asked questions. Many bent their heads over large iPads and took furious notes while Yi filled up blackboard after blackboard with formulas and practice problems. Some had no note-taking materials to speak of. A couple closed their eyes for extended periods. The class is a "core requirement" in Caltech's curriculum, meaning everyone at the school has to take it. Students I spoke to afterward gave a variety of majors, but none said they were comfortable speaking on the record. So later on I spoke with Sathvik Redrouthu, a sophomore who'd taken the class last year. Redrouthu, a math major , said he didn't use AI because he wanted to understand the concepts. "I was interested in the class," he said, adding that mainlining the homework with AI is like "shooting yourself in the foot" for when an in-person exam comes around. "I personally think that if you leave AI out, then it pushes the average student to learn properly," he said. If you're not interested in math, though, Redrouthu said you'd probably turn to AI — and you'd get away with it, until the exam at least. Ni told me that, as a professor, he can't tell whether a problem set he assigns is completed using AI. It's unlike AI-generated writing, which is usually a pretty obvious amalgamation of short sentences, em dashes, and hypophora. But math is all numbers: the specialty of AI programs . Caltech has no unified guidance for how math professors should plan around AI now. Redrouthu said that this year, some of his classes come with an auspicious caveat: "AI allowed." "Syllabuses are changing," he said. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Stocks decline on tech sell-off as concerns over the Nvidia fallout persist
events.summary: World shares are mixed, with Asian shares mostly declining Monday due to a tech sell-off HONG KONG -- World shares were mixed and Asian shares mostly declined Monday on another tech sell-off, as investors’ worries over the future of the artificial intelligence trade extended into another week following Nvidia’s fallout . U.S. equity futures were lower. Investors and traders are closely monitoring any signals on what is next for the AI industry ahead of Nvidia’s earnings report due Tuesday and Anthropic’s massive stock market debut set for later this week. In early European trading, Britain's FTSE 100 added 0.3% to 10,935.36. Germany's DAX was up less than 0.1% to 26,756.19, while France's CAC 40 rose 0.3% to 8,390.11. Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO last week after his extramarital affair sparked U.S. national security concerns shook global markets. Huang has been one of the biggest advocates for AI and his downfall triggered questions over how the global AI boom could be impacted. Those worries have spread to Asia, where AI hardware stocks are prominent on markets including in South Korea and Japan. South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index lost 3.6% to 5,100.50. Shares fell for memory chipmaker SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics , two of its most valuable companies. SK Hynix plummeted 7.9%, while Samsung Electronics gave up 4.5%. Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell 2.4% to 59,662.02 after official data Monday showed Japan’s economy contracted in the latest quarter . Several of Japan’s big AI stock names also traded lower. OpenAI investor SoftBank Group slipped 3.7%, while memory maker Kioxia Holdings dropped 7.7% and chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron dipped 7.1%. Also a beneficiary of the global AI frenzy, Taiwan’s Taiex sank 6%, with shares of its leading chipmaker TSMC, or Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., falling 5.7%. There have been increasing concerns that the robust growth of the AI capital spending may slow, analysts have said, even before the Nvidia episode. For one, uncertainties surrounding developments of AI data centers in the U.S. were also growing following the U.S. midterm elections. “The market was already worried about this risk before what happened at Nvidia,” Zhiwei Zhang, president and chief economist at Pinpoint Asset Management said in a commentary Monday. “Now the risk has become even more serious.” Hong Kong’s Hang Seng index rose 0.5% to 23,753.84. The Shanghai Composite index declined 0.9% to 3,602.57 following latest Chinese official economic data released Monday, including on retail sales and industrial production, that disappointed analysts. Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech Authorities investigate 'credible' unknown device threat at Illinois plant Microsoft apologizes for email disruption, says AI agents not responsible Australia’s S & P/ASX 200 edged down 0.4% to 9,044.70. On Friday, Wall Street’s benchmark S & P 500 dropped 0.4% . The Dow Jones Industrial Average edged 0.1% higher, while the technology-heavy Nasdaq composite fell 0.9%. Nvidia lost 2% Friday, after falling 4.3% Thursday as the company announced Huang’s resignation. Some of its rivals’ shares were also lower, with Broadcom declining 4.8% Friday and AMD, or Advanced Micro Devices, giving up 8.8%. In commodities trading, oil prices stabilized as tensions in the Middle East dragged on while oil flows in the Gulf were recovering from prewar levels. The International Energy Agency said last week that Gulf exports “recovered much faster than global oil demand.” Brent crude, the international standard, declined 0.3% to $95.55 per barrel, still much higher than the approximately $72 a barrel in late February before the Iran war began. Investors are also looking for updates this week as U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin are expected to meet Thursday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China. Meanwhile, the minutes from the Federal Reserve’s latest policy meeting is set to be released Wednesday, which could offer more detail on the decision-making processes on rates as it attempts to cool inflation in the U.S. The U.S. dollar was trading at 159.61 Japanese yen and was almost unchanged. events.title: Why Silicon Valley is backing Nvidia ex-CEO Jensen Huang after his ouster
events.summary: Huang’s peers, including Elon Musk, have praised his business acumen and potential risks to the US’s AI goals. Some of the biggest names in the United States tech sector have launched a campaign to back former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who stepped down last week after reports of an extramarital affair with a woman suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy. Billionaire Elon Musk and several others praised Huang on social media and urged the Nvidia board to consider reinstating him. Failing to do that, they warned, could hurt US aspirations and business deals within the burgeoning artificial intelligence (AI) sector. list 1 of 4 Nvidia scandal: What’s next for the US tech company? list 2 of 4 How will the US deal with Nvidia scandal? list 3 of 4 Microsoft says affected services fully recovered following worldwide outage list 4 of 4 Trump, Xi and Putin to hold first three-way summit in China Huang founded Nvidia, which manufactures advanced chips used to power AI, in 1993. The company has since become one of the most valuable in the world and is a cornerstone of the US push to secure AI dominance over China. After Huang’s resignation, Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress stepped in as interim CEO. Since last week, Nvidia’s shares and those of some of its partners have suffered significant losses. An online petition, meanwhile, gathered tens of thousands of signatures from Huang’s peers, former and current Nvidia employees, the company’s stakeholders and other supporters. Elon Musk, the world’s richest man and CEO of SpaceX, has been a vocal supporter. He praised Huang’s business acumen in a post on his X platform on Saturday, arguing that Nvidia could lose business without him. “Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia, but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract,” he wrote. “Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost.” In an open letter to the board, Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker, the CEOs of investment firms Altimeter Capital Management and Atreides Management, said Huang was an “incredible leader” and deserved a measured investigation. The firms are shareholders in Nvidia. “Given the extraordinary success of Jensen Huang’s leadership over a long period of time and given the massive uncertainty associated with recent events surrounding his departure, we believe it is in the best interest of all stakeholders and certainly the shareholders of Nvidia for the Board to pursue a slow, measured and deliberate process regarding the future leadership of Nvidia that leaves all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang,” they wrote. What is the ‘Stand with Jensen’ campaign? Dozens of major tech leaders also signed an open letter titled “Stand With Jensen” calling for Huang’s return. They included Musk, Garry Tan, CEO of venture capital firm Y Combinator, and Steve Chen, cofounder of YouTube. The letter, which has garnered more than 172,000 signatures, said Huang was “forced out without due process and without even a few days to make his case”. It asked the board to reinstate the CEO, investigate the allegations and then publicise its findings and decisions, including how it will weigh employees’ and shareholders’ interests when taking further action. “We are concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process,” the letter read. “We have not been shown evidence substantiating the allegation that the woman at the centre of this controversy was a spy.” “Thirty-three years of leadership do not place anyone above accountability. But accountability requires evidence, a fair hearing, and a reasoned decision. Jensen deserves due process, not mob justice,” the letter said. Some Nvidia employees also showed solidarity with Huang who they said fostered a supportive company culture. Darrell Dai, who identified himself as a robotics engineer, said in a LinkedIn post that he resigned in support, saying he was struggling to understand Huang’s departure “before receiving an explanation that helps me understand it”. Huang is discussing a possible return with close confidants, according to the Financial Times. But he faces hurdles. The US restricts Nvidia from selling chips to China, but lawmakers are now looking into whether Huang’s alleged affair may have affected the US’s own AI goals, and more seriously, whether the issue has national security implications. At least two Congressional committees have asked Huang and senior White House officials to attend hearings in the coming weeks. US President Donald Trump’s administration has faced criticism for allegedly failing to scrutinise Nvidia’s deals strongly enough, amid the AI race with China, with some pointing to a $25m Nvidia donation to Trump’s White House ballroom project. The Financial Times newspaper reported that the board has already reached out to Rene Haas, CEO of British chipmaker Arm Holdings, as a potential successor.

events.title: Silicon Valley’s head-on collision
events.summary: The timing of Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World this week, which brings together global business and political leaders at the intersection of technology and geopolitics, could not feel more urgent. When we came up with the name of the California convening this spring, the phrase was meant to represent a broad sense that AI and geopolitics were on a collision course. Policymakers and CEOs were starting to come to terms with the pressing need to talk to one another. Then, here in the US, they spent a long bitter summer campaigning for and against each other. Thirteen days ago, that collision course became a head-on collision. The US is preparing to inaugurate a new Congress deeply skeptical of the tech industry and its leaders, and — perhaps more consequential — new governors from Texas to Ohio who have pledged to stop data center construction. Similar sentiments are rising in Europe, but much of the rest of the world is rushing to get in on the action, and eager to pick up data-center investments forced out of North America. And now Washington is facing questions about how it managed the interactions between its main geostrategic rival, China, and one of the world’s most valuable companies, Nvidia, and what, if any, involvement it had in the undoing of the CEO atop an American chip champion. There are, of course, far more than two sides to this story: Silicon Valley is divided on the fundamental questions of how fast to develop new technology, on open- versus closed-weight models, on the role of startups and hyperscalers, and on the correct place for regulation. Washington, too, is balancing the promise of AI against the impact it could have on citizens. And senior officials from Singapore to South Africa bring their own pressing agendas. You can join us live here for conversations with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy, and dozens of other CEOs and world leaders. We don’t have all the answers, but you can be sure we’ll be asking the right questions.

events.title: Advanced Metrology for Defect Detection, Tool Health, and Semiconductor Yield Enhancement
events.summary: In advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar shows how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis. In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work. In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling. What You Will Learn: How surface scan metrology in station monitors tracks tool health and supports the qualification of thin film deposition processes How baseline signatures and real-time monitoring detect particle generation, hardware degradation, and process drift before production is affected How in-line scans on patterned wafers reveal layer-level defects and show how they propagate through multi-layer device structures When offline 3D optical profilometry should follow in-line inspection, and how it measures dimensions and separates sample defects from foreign material How correlating tool health data, inspection results, and electrical performance links physical defects to yield loss and guides targeted improvement projects Register now for this free webinar!

events.title: Nvidia Was Already in Trouble Before the Jensen Huang Mess
events.summary: Nvidia played a key role enabling the AI gold rush thanks in large part to its recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang . Huang was a master of foreseeing technological changes , investing in chips to train AI earlier than most. But just as he’s leaving , the company has a growing list of competitors with a range of new, advanced technology breathing down its neck. For Nvidia , where CFO Colette Kress has now taken the reins, the timing isn’t great. “Everything sold today was designed two-to-three years ago,” says the CEO of a large AI company, who spoke to WIRED on condition of anonymity to avoid hurting business relationships. Kress, or whoever replaces her permanently, will have to chart the course that the chip industry will take two years from now, the CEO says. Already, competitors have started to move in. Nvidia dominates the market for AI accelerators, capturing 80 percent of sales, according to Silicon Analysis. Longtime nemesis AMD is now making a concerted effort to build competitive AI chips. Its share of the market has crept up from just two percent in 2022 to between 7 and 10 percent in 2026. Big US cloud players—Google, Amazon, and Microsoft—are all developing more specialized chips to power the training and serving of AI models. Each has seen similar gains. These companies are designing their own silicon to reduce costs and to gain some independence from Nvidia. Several startups now offer more specialized chips that promise improvements over Nvidia’s core products. Cerebras, for instance, sells giant ones meant to power giant AI models. AMD recently bought Taalas, a company that burns models’ weights into silicon to make computations ultra efficient. Using these chips requires rewriting a lot of code, however, to make them work with cutting-edge AI models. Patrick Moorhead, chief analyst at MoorInStrat, a company that tracks the chip industry, says the rise of AI agents makes inference, or running models that have already been trained, more important. That’s an area where Nvidia has less of an edge compared to cloud hyperscalers and startups. Nvidia did, however, acquire a startup making specialized chips, called Grok, in December of 2025. And because of the rise in AI assistants and agents, there’s also growing demand for general purpose central processing units (CPUs), Moorehead said, an area where Nvidia barely competes. Nvidia still maintains a huge lead in AI thanks to Huang’s foresight. Huang cofounded the company in 1993 to design graphics chips for PCs. In the mid-2010s, he saw the promise of AI. He funded academic research on the topic, developed software to support AI engineering, and gave hardware to labs and startups. In 2022, ChatGPT took AI mainstream and sales of Nvidia chips skyrocketed. The company’s revenue went from $26.91 billion in January 2022 to $215.94 billion in January 2026. The challenges it faces may not be existential—but they do add up, especially on a global scale. While Nvidia’s fortunes have risen in the US, they have declined in the world’s other big market for AI, China. Washington is trying to restrict access to its most advanced chips, while Beijing is trying to develop its own chip industry. Nvidia is not allowed to sell its most powerful chips in China, but it can sell previous generations. Sales of these chips as well as non AI chips doubled over the past year, but China now accounts for only eight percent of the company’s overall revenue, compared with 20 percent in 2024, according to its fillings. It remains unclear how many chips exported to other countries may either end up in China or end up being used remotely by Chinese firms. Huawei, a Chinese tech giant targeted with US sanctions for several years, has developed new kinds of supercomputers that harness many more chips than usual to train and run AI models. Some Chinese AI companies, such as Z.ai, which makes one of the world’s best open source models, say they’ve trained their models entirely using Huawei’s chips. If Chinese open-weight models gain traction in other countries, it could create a market for Chinese chips elsewhere. Huang’s dealings with China played a major role in his downfall. He had a romantic relationship with Huang Le, also known as Alice Huang, a Chinese executive at a Singaporean company called Megaspeed who the US government suspects of being an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. Megaspeed and its subsidiaries have reportedly imported between $4.6 and $7.5 billion Nvidia chips into southeast Asia. Reports suggest that the company may have provided access to the chips to Chinese AI firms. Babak Minovi, a senior analyst at the Eurasia Group, a consultancy that focuses on technology and geopolitics, says Huang was right to point out that cutting off access to China would empower domestic rivals. “Huang was taking a pragmatic line, and he knows competition,” he says. Even in markets that it dominates, Nvidia may turn out to be a victim of its own success.

events.title: Corporations Are Using Trump’s Tariff Refunds on Bonuses Rather Than Reimbursing Consumers
events.summary: President Donald Trump announces tariffs at the White House in April 2025. Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images When Stanley Black & Decker, one of the world’s largest tool companies, got hit with President Donald Trump’s tariffs last year, the firm made clear that it would be sharing the pain with its customers. The Connecticut-based company raised prices again and again, moves its executives said were necessary because of the new fees on imports.  Now, after the Supreme Court struck down Trump’s most sweeping tariffs earlier this year, the company is getting at least $298 million refunded. Instead of sharing that bounty with its customers, however, the firm has chosen different recipients:  Its own leaders.  The company is one of at least nine that have disclosed that they are using their refunds not to pay back the cash-strapped consumers who generally covered much of the tariff costs through higher prices, but to give bonuses, according to a ProPublica analysis of thousands of securities filings and earnings calls for publicly traded companies. Other recognizable companies include the owners of discount department stores TJ Maxx and Marshalls and the golf equipment brand Titleist. Dozens of other firms have said little about how they plan to use the money other than to characterize the windfall as the kind of earnings they use to determine executive bonuses. The Trump administration has not publicly detailed which companies are getting the roughly $170 billion in refunds or how much they’ve asked for, and it has denied ProPublica’s requests for this information. But reporters found some of these details while reviewing the disclosures of thousands of publicly traded companies. Some have described vague plans to pay the money forward by, for example, “returning tariff refunds to our members through pricing,” though they generally don’t say whether that involves price cuts or limiting future increases. Others are paying back businesses they sold products to because they had itemized receipts that detailed the tariff markups. But consumers hoping for refunds appear to be largely out of luck. With the help of artificial intelligence, ProPublica identified companies that said they planned to refund customers with their tariff windfalls. Almost all of them deal with other businesses, not consumers.   “Executive bonuses are probably the least just way to use this money because it wasn’t anything the executives did that they should be rewarded for. It was a government mistake that resulted in a refund,” said Gregory Germain, a corporate law professor at Syracuse University. “It really explains why it’s so important for the government, when they’re doing something like this, to think it through to make sure consumers don’t pay extra money and not get it back.” The chain reaction that led to these bonuses began in the first months of Trump’s second term. In February 2025, Trump declared a national emergency over illegal drugs coming in across the border and unilaterally announced new tariffs on goods from the countries he deemed responsible: Canada, Mexico and China.  Then, in April, he declared a second national emergency, this one over the U.S. trade deficit — the fact that the U.S. was importing more than it exported. Declaring it “Liberation Day,” Trump unveiled a poster in the Rose Garden detailing his most sweeping tariffs yet on goods from more than 100 countries. “Executive bonuses are probably the least just way to use this money.” Gregory Germain, corporate law professor at Syracuse University Those tariffs remained in place, with some tweaks, until earlier this year when the Supreme Court struck them down, ruling that Trump had needed congressional approval to impose them.  That left the federal government scrambling to figure out how to refund billions in duties it had collected over the prior year on more than 53 million imported shipments. U.S. Customs and Border Protection set up an online application system. But only the direct payers of the tariffs — called the “importers of record” — are eligible to apply, not the businesses and consumers who took a hit downstream.  The New York Federal Reserve Bank, which analyzed the prices of a broad swath of goods, found that 26% of the tariff costs were eaten by American customers; a study from Harvard Business School put the estimate at 43%. One study estimated that Trump’s tariffs cost typical American households about $1,000 last year. The administration and Congress have not placed constraints on how companies use the tariff refunds, though there have been calls to do so. After the Supreme Court ruling, a group of Democratic senators wrote to the president , asking if he would require companies to pass along part of their payments to consumers and assign penalties to those that did not. Doing otherwise, said Sens. Elizabeth Warren, Cory Booker and Peter Welch, would render the refunds “a giveaway to giant corporations that amounts to theft from the middle class.”  Though Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has denied that the tariffs resulted in significantly higher prices, he has acknowledged the fundamental unfairness of only importers of record getting the refund. “I got a feeling the American people won’t see it,” he said in February at an Economic Club of Dallas event. Bessent has made the argument that it’s the Democrats who challenged the tariffs in court, not the administration that imposed the tariffs, who are responsible for the transfer of wealth from American consumers to companies.  “The Democratic attorney generals who filed a ridiculous lawsuit against this administration wanted the money to go back to the payer of record,” he said at a press conference . “If I hear another Democratic legislator make the inane remark, ‘The American people should get the money’ — the American people had the money in the U.S. Treasury and we were forced to give it back.” “I got a feeling the American people won’t see” the refund money. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent In some cases, companies have said that they will be splitting at least some of their refund checks with their customers. ProPublica’s analysis shows these companies’ customers are generally other businesses, not average consumers. Among them is Varex Imaging Corp. in Utah, which sells X-ray imaging components for medical businesses and cargo screeners. Varex and firms like it have not elaborated on why they are passing along refunds, but trade experts suspect these business-to-business vendors have detailed contracts that itemize tariff costs. Shipping companies, like UPS and FedEx , have set up online portals for customers seeking refunds. Though the firms are technically importers of record, they imported goods on behalf of businesses and individuals that paid them to ship products. events.title: Apollo exec says firm plans to lower annual head count growth, mainly because of AI
events.summary: Scott Kleinman, co-president of Apollo Global Management, said that he expects the firm to reduce headcount growth to 2-5% annually. Lauren Justice/Bloomberg via Getty Images Apollo's Scott Kleinman said the firm expects to lower its annual hiring rate to 3-5% from its typical 12-15%. The Apollo Asset Management co-president said AI has been the "primary driver" of that reduction. He said the firm doesn't need as many new hires to target its 20% annual growth. Apollo Global Management is considering slowing down on hiring, thanks to gains from artificial intelligence. Scott Kleinman, co-president of Apollo Asset Management , said at a summit in October for the firm's nonprofit arm, that Apollo Global Management plans to grow its head count by 3% to 5% annually moving forward. That's a decrease from its typical 12% to 15% rate, he said. The company employs over 6,140 workers as of a December 2025 financial filing. Kleinman, who co-leads Apollo's day-to-day operations, including all of its revenue-generating businesses and enterprise solutions across its investment platform, said the company plans to hit a 20% annual earnings growth target. However, the firm doesn't need to hire the same number of people to do it, he said. "We don't need to throw more bodies at it," Kleinman said in a follow-up conversation with Business Insider. This is part of a series of stories from Business Insider's conversation with Scott Kleinman, co-president of Apollo Asset Management and chair of the Apollo Opportunity Foundation Board. To be alerted when the next piece publishes, follow reporter Ana Altchek here. Apollo is sharing its private-equity playbook with nonprofits Kleinman said AI has been the "primary driver" of that shift in hiring expectations. The co-president said that AI tools allow workers to "cover more ground" and be more productive across multiple parts of the business. "AI is doing a lot of the work, and so that frees up our people to do more," said Kleinman. Kleinman said Apollo hasn't reduced its hiring yet, but it will aim to cut back moving forward. The executive's comments came days before Apollo partner and chief economist Torsten Sløk released a report focused on a macro view of corporate America which stated that AI has so far delivered "zero financial payoff" outside the tech industry. The company has been investing in AI for a couple of years, but up until recently, only "tidbits of productivity" were seen from the tools, Kleinman said. "Companies are now starting to know enough of what AI can and can't do to say, 'OK, this is where I'm actually going to be able to hire those people,'" Kleinman told Business Insider. Apollo CEO Marc Rowan said on the company's third-quarter earnings call in November that the company will incur roughly $350 million in planned expenses over the next 24 months to replace legacy software and systems and adopt new technologies. Matthew Breitfelder, partner and global head of human capital at Apollo, said the company assesses its hiring needs on an ongoing basis, considering a number of factors, including AI. "As a high-growth company, we are continuing to grow our team in a number of different areas, including our new strategic innovation hub in Austin, Texas," Breitfelder said in a written statement. As AI reshapes work and drives efficiency gains, many companies are rethinking headcount — and what hires they make. Paul Griggs, PwC’s US senior partner and CEO, said the Big Four firm hired fewer consultants and accountants this year than it did two years ago. Meanwhile, a handful of companies, including Uber, Snap, and Block, have directly cited AI as a reason for layoffs . Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: I graduated from Columbia Law and became a corporate lawyer. After getting laid off, I built a $19M hot dog business.
events.summary: Denys Gorbatiuk was laid off in 2008 and started his own company. Courtesy of Denys Gorbatiuk Denys Gorbatiuk worked in mergers and acquisitions in New York City. After being laid off, he founded a hot dog company and later expanded into other meats. He says being able to figure out challenges on the fly has helped him succeed. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Denys Gorbatiuk, founder of The Grumpy Butcher . It has been edited for length and clarity. When I met my now-wife during high school in Moldova, she told me right away that her family was planning to immigrate to the US. I knew she would be my wife from the beginning, so I'd have to figure out a way to live in America. Sometimes, ignorance is bliss. After we graduated from high school, we moved to Kyiv , where I went to law school, and my wife went to medical school . Then, her family was approved to move to the US. At the time, I didn't speak any English, and I knew nothing about practicing law in the US. The only thing I knew was that Harvard Law was a good school. So, I moved to Boston and spent a year learning English. When I applied to American law schools , I was accepted everywhere, except Harvard. I graduated from Columbia Law and started working in New York City, focusing on mergers and acquisitions. My wife was practicing medicine in the city, and it felt like we had, in fact, figured it out. A particularly delicious hot dog led to a business idea Then, the 2008 financial crisis hit. I was a midlevel lawyer at the time. Like most other midlevel lawyers doing mergers and acquisitions, I was let go. Getting another law job at that time felt impossible. Looking back, I can also see that I wasn't particularly happy. I was a good lawyer , and I enjoyed the attention to detail that law required. And yet, law was boring. When you follow the established protocol, there's not much deviation in what you can do. Food has always been my passion. Around that time, I made my wife an interesting meal: a hot dog that was so much more. It was a 45-minute production, complete with homemade pineapple chutney and toasted buns. It was so delicious that I was mesmerized — and soon began wondering if I could make it a business. My business never really took off After tons of experimenting, I distilled my 45-minute stove-top cooking process into a 45-second microwavable product. In 2011, I launched Den's Hot Dogs. Everyone who tried them was wowed, and by 2017, Den's Hot Dogs were sold in more than 400 Walmart stores . Looking back, it would have been better if the hot dogs had been an overnight flop. What happened was a slower failure. The hot dogs were sold individually with the bun and condiment. Since people are used to buying hot dogs in multipacks, we needed a lot of consumer education. During that time, the business was mostly generating losses, and I didn't have a couple million dollars to spend on the advertising we needed. The pandemic presented the chance to pivot We were still hobbling along until the pandemic hit. By that point, Den's Hot Dogs had a loyal online following, but our factory had shut down. I thought we were done for. Then I met someone with the opposite problem: he was a food distributor serving restaurants that were now closed. As we vented to each other about our business troubles, we realized we each had what the other needed: I had customers, but no product, and he had product, but no customers. It was a marriage of necessity. In 2022, we launched The Grumpy Butcher brand within Den's Hot Dogs, selling meats and prepared meals. Being willing to adjust has helped me succeed There was a steep learning curve about how to safely ship perishable foods. Still, The Grumpy Butcher was immediately more successful than the hot dogs. We didn't need to educate consumers, because they already understood the product. Last year, we started selling The Grumpy Butcher on Temu, becoming the online retailer's first frozen food vendor. That opened up a younger demographic than our typical customer, and it now makes up about 20% of revenue. In 2025, we did about $19 million in gross sales. I've always been someone who can keep going when the first idea doesn't work out. I have the perseverance to keep adjusting. I don't mind that the hot dogs didn't pan out. I'm just glad that we found success with The Grumpy Butcher, and the future is bright. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: NATO member Estonia to close Russia border after attempted 'sabotage' of drone maker
events.summary: Estonia says it will shut border crossings with Russia after blaming Moscow for an attempted arson attack on a drone maker. Tallinn says the attack fits Russia's wider hybrid campaign against NATO states. The move adds to fears Russia is escalating pressure on Europe after nearly five years of war against Ukraine. NATO member Estonia says it is preparing to close road border crossings with Russia from Dec. 1, as it blames Moscow for an attempted "sabotage" of one of its defense companies. Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said on Sunday that Russia's military intelligence service GRU had ordered an arson attack against Estonian drone maker Threod Systems in the early hours of Saturday morning. Authorities said the attempted attack did not cause significant damage and eight people were detained in connection with it. Estonia, which shares a 294-kilometer (183-mile) border with Russia, said closing the crossings would help to reduce Moscow's ability to conduct hostile activities against it and mitigate risks related to sanctions circumvention. Tallinn has frequently raised the alarm over sabotage attacks against NATO countries that have been supporting Ukraine since Russia launched the full-scale invasion of its neighbor in February 2022. "This weekend's attempted sabotage against an Estonian defence company, attributed by our security authorities to Russia's GRU, is yet another reminder that Russia's hostile activities extend far beyond Ukraine," Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said Sunday via social media. "Estonia is preparing to close its road border crossings with Russia in response. Hostile actions must have consequences." Tsahkna said he had informed his Finnish, Lithuanian and Latvian counterparts of the decision. Russia's foreign ministry said it would assess Estonia's plans to close its border crossings, adding that if these plans were to come into force, it would be seen as "yet another bout of aggressive and unbridled Russophobia," according to state news agency Tass . It did not directly comment on the accusation that Moscow is responsible for the attack on Threod Systems. "Estonia is building walls. Many countries, as history shows, have built walls that have brought no good to their creators," Kremlin spokesman ​Dmitry Peskov said Monday, according to comments reported by Russian state news outlet Ria Novosti . Estonia PM: 'We will not be intimidated' Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal said the attack was part of Russia's broader "hybrid war" against Europe. "We will not be intimidated. Estonia is preparing for the possibility of closing its border with Russia to reduce the risks to our people and national security," Michal said Sunday via social media. The latest incident follows an arson attack in mid-August against Milrem Robotics, an Estonian defense company that supplies Ukraine with unmanned military vehicles. Estonian authorities later blamed Russia for the attack. Moscow denied the allegation. European security officials and lawmakers have previously warned about Russia's hybrid warfare. In September, Danish intelligence officials said Russia could launch a "limited" military attack against a NATO member in the coming months, saying the Kremlin appears more willing to take risks after more than 4½ years of war against Ukraine. The Danish Defence Intelligence Service, or DDIS, identified a "low but growing risk" that Russia could carry out isolated strikes with long-range weapons on infrastructure that is critical to the support of Ukraine.

events.title: Thai central bank pushes back against proposed legal changes
events.summary: “No changes can be made that would undermine the next governor’s independence,” Bank of Thailand governor Vitai Ratanakorn told a briefing. Thailand’s central bank said the 2025 review found the Bank of Thailand Act still fits international standards and does not need changes. It warned that linking governor performance reviews to dismissal grounds could weaken independence and invite pressure from political or interest groups. Governor Vitai Ratanakorn said, “No changes can be made that would undermine the next governor’s independence,” while Finance Minister Ekniti Nitithanprapas said the government should not interfere but must coordinate. BANGKOK – Thailand’s central bank on Nov 16 defended its current governing rules and warned against changes that could undermine the governor’s independence, as it responded to criticism from its board chairman over the slow progress of legal reforms. The Bank of Thailand (BOT) said its 2025 review found the current Bank of Thailand Act remained appropriate and in line with international standards, with no need for changes. It said the BOT board had not approved any amendments to the act, though chairman Somchai Sajjapongse later pushed for changes. Among the issues previously raised and studied was whether the governor’s performance assessment could be used when seeking grounds for dismissal. Under the current law, performance assessments and grounds for dismissal are separate. The BOT said linking performance reviews to grounds for dismissal could undermine the central bank’s independence and expose it to pressures from political or interest groups. “No changes can be made that would undermine the next governor’s independence,” BOT governor Vitai Ratanakorn told a briefing. On Nov 14 , Somchai said the board called for a legal review last June, but after 18 months only one section had been proposed. He said the review should have involved outside agencies, including the Finance Ministry and the Council of State, not just BOT officials. On Nov 16 , Finance Minister Ekniti Nitithanprapas said the government should not interfere with the central bank’s operations, but the two sides need to coordinate. REUTERS

events.title: Employer health cost crunch is worse than projected
events.summary: There's new evidence that double-digit health cost increases were hitting employers well before the forecasts of big spikes for 2027 — forcing big changes in workplace coverage for millions of Americans. Why it matters: The findings offer a higher-resolution view of how much health spending is putting a drag on the labor market and increasing affordability concerns for the approximately 160 million Americans who get coverage through work. They also show how factors like surprise billing disputes, more cancer diagnoses and expensive specialty drugs are combining to exert cost pressure, with no immediate relief in sight. Driving the news: A new Gallagher benefits survey of more than 3,700 firms found 36% of the companies reported premium increases of 10% or more during their most recent renewal. Pharmacy costs account for a quarter or more of some companies' total health spending. Cancer care is the No. 1 cost driver for about 7 in 10 firms. The survey, fielded from January to March, also found employers are trying to avoid saddling workers with a disproportionate share of rising costs while struggling to balance the quality of care with their financial risk. "The last two renewal cycles have been unlike anything we've ever seen before," said Robby White, Gallagher's U.S. benefits business line leader. "It's unsustainable, obviously. Every additional dollar that an employer spends on health care, they can't spend on their employees." Between the lines: The 2027 coverage year was already shaping up to be painful for many employers. Projections are showing premium spikes due to rising demand for health services, more chronic disease and increased use of drugs like GLP-1s. In fact, double-digit premium increases for both the 2026 and 2027 plan years suggest there are more underlying causes, according to benefits experts. One leading factor is chronic disease: More people are being diagnosed with cancer at a younger age, and advanced treatments and related care can result in $10,000 a month in expenses or claims. Drug costs also are surging — and not just because of demand for GLP-1s. The high cost of specialty drugs for chronic or rare conditions is prompting companies to scrutinize the way formularies are designed and how well pharmacy benefit managers administer their benefits. White said another big cost driver is the No Surprises Act, which shielded consumers from large, unexpected medical bills but also created an expensive arbitration process. The arbitration has added administrative costs and is giving providers big payouts, which add millions in costs for large employers that self-fund their health plans. That's an assessment shared by big health insurers, which say the surprise billing law is creating unintended financial consequences. "The [independent dispute resolution] process has now become a top-three single driver of health care cost increases for employers," Aetna president Steve Nelson told Axios, adding the company wants to work with Congress to overhaul the system. The big picture: In a volatile health market, more employers are self-insuring and directly paying medical claims to have greater visibility and control over health costs, the Gallagher survey finds. As workers get tired of high deductibles, some employers are testing copay-only plans, which vary out-of-pocket costs by medical service and steer workers to providers deemed to be providing the most value. Part of this involves more digital tools to help patients decide. They're also re-evaluating their relationships with pharmacy benefit managers in response to rising drug costs, leading to what White says is a "huge shift" away from the big three PBMs — CVS Caremark, Optum Rx and Express Scripts. On GLP-1s, Gallagher says the question isn't whether the drugs are effective, but whether coverage is financially sustainable. More companies are exploring direct-to-consumer sales through outside vendors and giving employees debit cards or defined subsidies. What we're watching: Benefits experts are waiting to see how much congressionally mandated changes to PBMs' business practices bring down drug prices and improve transparency. They're also watching the growing number of worker lawsuits against plan sponsors, alleging they breached their fiduciary duty by failing to negotiate reasonable prescription drug prices or keep fees reasonable. Caitlin Owens contributed to this story .

events.title: Lebanon’s second airport could provide economic and political benefits
events.summary: The establishment of a second airport in Lebanon gives the war-devastated country more options for air travel. Beirut, Lebanon – Lebanon’s second airport is scheduled to begin operating test flights on Independence Day, November 22, in what experts and analysts say could prove to be a boon to the country after years of war and an economic collapse. In June, Prime Minister Nawaf Salam and other officials took a test flight from Beirut to Rene Mouawad airport, located in the northern town of Qlayaat. Lebanese officials hope a new airport will stimulate growth in one of Lebanon’s poorest and most underserved regions. list 1 of 3 ‘Greater Israel’: Christian Zionism’s role in US policy list 2 of 3 More than one million people in Lebanon face acute food shortages, UN says list 3 of 3 UNRWA funding cuts deepen hardship for Palestinian refugees in Lebanon Qlayaat airport was originally set to open mid-2026, but Israel’s war on Lebanon delayed it. The beginning of commercial flights was deferred to November 22, but it was pushed further to mid-December, when many in the Lebanese diaspora return home for the winter holiday, due to construction delays. Commercial flights are now expected to start on December 14. Rafik Hariri international airport, Lebanon’s only functioning airport, located just south of the capital, Beirut, has been sensitive to political and regional disputes. Supporters of Hezbollah, the Iranian-backed Shia armed group, have at times weaponised the vulnerabilities of Rafik Hariri airport’s location by blocking the road connecting it to the capital. In February 2025, Hezbollah supporters blocked the road when two Iranian planes were prohibited from landing in Beirut. A new airport in the north, outside Hezbollah’s traditional zone of influence, could potentially weaken this logistical chokepoint, said Bassel Doueik, a Lebanese political analyst. “Whenever tensions rise between them and the government, they [Hezbollah] tend to block the inbound and outbound [traffic] on the Beirut airport road through protests, and this is a strategic advantage for the group,” Doueik, a Lebanese political analyst, told Al Jazeera. “I don’t think the new airport will remove this strategic advantage, but it will actually decrease it to a certain extent because the [Qlayaat] airport is small and it cannot substitute for the current airport.” Hezbollah has been the strongest military and political actor in Lebanon in recent decades, but its role has come into open debate in the country following the 2024 ceasefire with Israel and the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s regime in Syria, the group’s key regional ally. The opening of a new airport is not expected to change internal political calculations, but analysts say it gives the state alternatives in the event of future conflicts. “The state gains manoeuvrability and alternatives by opening a second airport. But in terms of Hezbollah’s arms or anything else, it doesn’t change much for the state,” Marcel Baloukji, a Lebanese political and security analyst, told Al Jazeera. “This airport becomes a factor in any potential future war. Beirut airport could be shut down, but alternatives [to fly in and out] would still exist, especially for foreign nationals and diplomatic missions present in Lebanon.” But officials say the reason for opening a second airport is economic rather than political. Lebanon’s economy has struggled to recover from the 2019 economic crash due to Israel’s ongoing assault on the country and the US-Israel war on Iran. Inflation is expected to hit 17.5 percent this year, and the World Bank predicts Lebanon’s economy to contract by 6.4 percent in 2026. Previous estimates suggest Lebanon has suffered damage estimated at more than $14bn since 2023. Still, Dania Arayssi, assistant director of the New Lines Institute for Strategy and Policy, told Al Jazeera that she believes there is a legislative angle for the establishment of a new airport as well. “Successfully managing a facility that can generate significant public revenue could help rebuild citizens’ trust in state institutions,” Arayssi said. “It would show that the government can enforce its authority, protect public assets from Hezbollah’s interference, and lead on delivering services that benefit the country as a whole.” South Lebanon, where an Israeli invasion has turned into an occupation that analysts believe could last years , has been the worst-affected part of the country as a result of Israel’s war. But other parts of Lebanon are also struggling and have a history of state neglect. Qlayaat, on the other hand, is located in the northern Akkar region, just 6km (3.7 miles) from the Syrian border. Officials believe the new facility would serve much of Lebanon’s north, as well as important Syrian cities like Homs, Latakia and Tartous, with the northern neighbour struggling to modernise its dilapidated airports.

events.title: Inside Acwa’s clean power battle plan
events.summary: The Scene Samir Serhan had an unenviable start at the helm of Acwa, one of the world’s top clean energy developers: The day before saw the first fusillades of the war in Iran. Acwa, which is part-owned by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, operates power and desalination plants across the Gulf, and Serhan quickly understood they could become targets. Sure enough, some of the company’s assets were damaged in the war, although for security reasons it hasn’t disclosed exactly what was hit. Acwa’s net income rose 0.6% in the first nine months of the year compared to the same period last year, but was held back as the war slowed its pipeline of new projects and raised its shipping costs in the region ten-fold. But Serhan remains defiant: “You take the cards you’re dealt and make the best out of it,” he said in an interview on the sidelines of COP31 in Türkiye. Acwa operates nearly 100 gigawatts of gas and renewable power projects in more than a dozen countries, as well as the world’s largest privately held fleet of water desalination plants. At the summit, it was involved in one of the summit’s biggest clean power announcements, a commitment by eight financial institutions to back two gigawatts of solar plants Acwa will build in Türkiye. That plan followed Serhan’s belief that the key to global electrification, COP’s main theme this year, is to go as big as possible, so the unavoidable headaches of project development lead to a worthwhile payoff for investors and consumers. But Serhan is clear-eyed about the challenges ahead, including investors skeptical about its extensive reliance on Chinese supply chains. And only a few weeks after Acwa jointly launched a $4 billion plan to buy and build clean power projects in the US, with a focus on AI infrastructure, it ran into more unexpected headwinds: A new Congress adversarial to data centers, and an industry shaken by Jensen Huang’s ignominious departure from Nvidia. But Serhan still isn’t worried: “The demand is massive, and these things will be built.” The View From Acwa Tim McDonnell: Let’s start with Plenum, your initiative with EIG to invest $4 billion in US power projects with a focus on data centers. Since that was announced in October we’ve had the US election, which involved a lot of pushback against data centers, and then Jensen Huang stepping down from Nvidia, both of which have raised questions about a possible slowdown in the pace of the AI buildout. Is that a risk for Plenum? Samir Serhan: We’re operating today in five regions in the world, and with Plenum we’re entering the US market. The drive behind it is really the demand for clean electricity. Our main focus right now is to acquire immediately operating assets, instead of building greenfield projects, which take a lot longer. I know the stock market is reacting in a negative way to what’s happening with the Democratic majority and with the personal affairs of the CEO of Nvidia. It’s a shame, but I think this is just going to be a blip. The demand is there. People are seeing the value of AI and of industrial growth, which all need electricity. There might be some little bit of a slowdown in the US, but it will really happen. So none of this news has changed your capital allocation strategy. We are committing around $4 billion and we really see the value there. And we’re not just a financial investor. When we typically build an asset, we also operate it, we invest in it, and we stay in for 20, 30 years. So these ups and downs happen sometimes, but the long-term signal definitely is very strong. Why the focus on acquisitions instead of greenfield projects? Time, and the risks of construction, and honestly because of all of this demand for data centers means there isn’t enough labor force in the [US]. EPC contractors and supply chains are a problem. There’s just not enough to feed the frenzy. If we buy a platform of projects, we immediately get a footprint. And we see the energy transition is not a sprint, it’s a marathon. So some of the major oil and gas companies are going back to investing in their traditional assets. They also want renewable power, but they can hire someone like Acwa to build and operate it, and supply it to them, instead of them becoming a power company. And with the hyperscalers, they have a nice balance sheet and they’re in a big race to lead on AI technology. So there are some dislocations in the market and we’re trying to capitalize on this. Switching focus, you took this job just as the war started in Iran, correct? What do they say? Timing is everything. With my announcement, basically, the fireworks started. What were those first days like? Definitely it’s uneasy. It’s not comfortable to see this thing happening in the region where you’re operating. But you just have to focus on what you can manage. It’s unfortunate, but we’re managing it for the best. Our people are safe. And hopefully this conflict will be behind us soon, inshallah. You reported in your shareholder filings that some assets were damaged. Yeah. From a security perspective, I can’t really share what happened. But definitely there were some attacks that impacted some of our facilities. We have a 24-hour command center to monitor the situation and make sure we are proactive and be ready for how to staff our plants that are in the conflict… do we need to go to half staff, or whatever, but keep the asset running. Were you worried about your assets being targeted from the very beginning? No doubt about it. That was openly communicated by the people within the conflict. They didn’t make it a secret that they’re targeting critical infrastructure. So definitely that heightened our risk. How did that impact the business? You take the cards you’re dealt and make the best out of it. Across the company, the pipeline [of possible projects] is very strong. So we had to basically now become more selective about the opportunities we go after in the whole world. We still want to grow, but we want to focus more on quality growth. And some costs are creeping into our supply chain; in the Gulf region now you’re talking about a factor of 10 to bring a container from China to the Middle East. The cost of financing is going up. And that’s all going to become reflected in our pricing. But we hope this is only going to be temporary. What does it mean to be more selective about the projects you go after? Are there certain types of projects or geographies where you think, this one’s not for us? No, we’re really trying to not be biased. If we see an opportunity that has the right risk profile… At the end of the day, these projects need to be bankable, because this is not corporate finance. This is all project finance. So you need to make sure that the government, wherever you’re operating, has a clear mandate. events.title: The chain-reaction era: Constant shock and awe
events.summary: It was random, but related, that we were hit with a tectonic election result, an epic AI-and-spy scandal , and the dramatic FAA shutdown in just over one week. This is our new reality: constant shock and awe, igniting chain reactions across politics, media, AI, business and culture. Why it matters: This month's three shocks hit separately. But their speed and spread are our new reality. Politics, AI, media and business are now one wired system: A jolt in one sets off the other three, instantly. We call this post-processable velocity : Change is moving faster than any person, company, market or government can absorb. People's fears about AI are now mushrooming into jitteriness about civilization's connective tissue. An AP story on Sunday asked: "Could everything be broken?" Images of empty European supermarket refrigerators , cleared of spoiled food after a spate of mysterious cyberattacks, added to the sense that our connections are crumbling, with the simplest conveniences in danger. What makes all this so disorienting for all of us is how interconnected politics, AI, business and media have become. The Nvidia spy scandal is a vivid example: Media, last weekend: The New York Times reports that Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned President Trump that Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang was tied to a suspected Chinese spy. Social media erupts. Business, Monday: Nvidia stock falls more than 4% at the open and keeps sliding. Fears of economy-wide AI fallout follow. Politics, all week: Trump's top team gets dragged into a "what did they know and when" frenzy. Democrats demand hearings. Policy, now: Lawmakers are scrambling to untangle the web of spies, lies and AI, and are racing to tighten China's access to Nvidia chips that gave Huang the power he's now surrendered. Tech, going forward: AI companies are rethinking their reliance on Nvidia chips and exploring financing options beyond Nvidia. ⏱️ Huang's resignation was announced just 14 days after last month's New York Times blockbuster exclusive that he was believed to be the target of a Chinese plot, and four days after he admitted an affair . One revelation, two weeks, and the most important CEO in AI is gone. Three forces make this permanent: 🔄 1. Politics swings wildly. This was the seventh straight election in which the White House, Senate or House changed hands. And this time, in truly unthinkable and historic ways. There were a number of " split districts " in 2024 that went for Kamala Harris for president and a Republican for the House. This year, every single one swung to electing a Democrat. We can't find any precedent for this. It's possible we've hit a post-ideological age where people feel very little affiliation to party tribes. How do you explain young men shifting almost 40 points from Republicans to Democrats in two years? 🤖 2. AI concentrates everything. A handful of companies are making historic bets on superhuman intelligence, and propping up the economy while they do it. That puts enormous power and risk in very few hands. One man's affair shook the whole market. Nvidia makes the vital ingredient of AI, and helps finance nearly every big player buying it. But it's not just Nvidia. Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Microsoft or Amazon can rattle the market with one announcement too. ⛓️‍💥 3. Everything is fragile when everything is interconnected. Friday's flight shutdown had nothing to do with AI, spies or elections, but it still shook us all. It appears a contractor was swapping copper wire for fiber. Routers overloaded. Departures stopped nationwide for more than four hours. A total of 18,000+ U.S. flights were canceled over the past three days. Officials said little for hours. Rumors, speculation and gallows humor filled the void. "The aliens have landed," the novelist Stephen King tweeted . "That's the REAL reason for the ground stop. They don't want to start a worldwide panic." The bottom line: The shocks will change. The speed won't. Go deeper : New signs of rising risk.

events.title: Why Democrats may want to make Trump look good
events.summary: DENVER — Democrats' euphoria over their once-in-a-generation wave of midterm victories is giving way to a reality check: They were lucky to have a weakened opposition. And they might be "renting" this year's voters if they don't quickly deliver on their promises. Why it matters: If Democrats want to rack up policy wins ASAP, they'll need to work with President Trump — the guy many of them held up as what's wrong with America. That means giving him a few wins. Zoom in: Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico argued exactly that at a Democratic summit late last week in Denver — What's Next , held by the centrist group Majority Democrats . "If President Trump wants the same plaques and portraits and busts as LBJ, we can help make that a reality," Talarico said. "We should make the final two years of his presidency the most productive of any presidency in American history." Gina Hinojosa, who'll be Texas' first Democratic governor in more than three decades, has said she'll work with Trump on immigration . Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, a frequent Trump target, is pitching the president on rebranding Medicare for All as " TrumpCare " to get it passed. And on CNN's "State of the Union" on Sunday, Mississippi Sen.-elect Scott Colom told Dana Bash he wants to collaborate with Trump to deliver on the president's own past promise to lower grocery prices. Zoom out: Midterm elections are usually a referendum on the sitting president, not a sign that voters are in love with the opposition party. And polls show that Democrats are still unpopular. At the Denver confab, several Democrats acknowledged that. Adam Jentleson , president of the moderate Searchlight Institute, said onstage: "The voters who decided last week's election have not yet fallen in love with us. ... They are on loan to us." Many Democratic leaders believe Congress must prioritize legislation aimed at lowering prices and ending the war in Iran, given the salience of those two issues in this year's elections. Some top Democrats are determined not to repeat the mistakes the party made after the 2022 elections, when they overperformed — and grew complacent. They lost the presidential election two years later. The other side: Merely talking about working with Trump can disillusion parts of the Democratic base. Outside the Denver event, left-wing activists protested the get-together itself. Some accused Democratic leaders of already being too conciliatory toward the Republican president. "I can't believe that Talarico said he'd work with Trump," Anna Libey, a volunteer for the progressive Sunrise Movement, told Axios. "I can't believe that he would go back on his campaign messaging immediately." (During his campaign, Talarico consistently signaled his willingness to work across party lines, while also routinely criticizing the president's agenda.) Yes, but: Many Democrats don't really believe Trump will become a serious governing partner overnight, if ever. They just think they ought to be able to say they tried to work with him. If and when Trump vetoes the priority bills of a Democratic-led Congress — as he's already threatened to do — many in the party figure it'd boost their argument that he's still to blame for high prices and his unpopular war on Iran.

events.title: An executive coach's 5-step plan for navigating a layoff or career pivot
events.summary: Executive coach and author Jovian Zayne George A. Peters, II Executive coach Jovian Zayne thinks companies have gotten "less human-centered…in the last five years." Her new book urges ambitious people in career transition to ask themselves five questions. Zayne also advises to be brutally honest with yourself about your desires. Jovian Zayne didn't think she was overdoing it. She was pregnant with her daughter and pushing hard for a new client when a health scare put her in the hospital. "I don't think I recognized that I was pushing myself as hard as I was because it didn't feel like it," Zayne told Business Insider. "It felt normal." After leaving the hospital, Zayne immediately knew what she had to do. She had to drop the client. Even though she was frustrated with her body back then, she never saw walking away from the client as a failure. Zayne said her faith had a lot to do with that: She trusted God would have the right opportunity waiting for her. "If I'm not well trying to work with this person and this environment, or this client, this is not who I'm meant to be with," she said. That time in her life became part of "Soft Landings for Hard Days: Wisdom, Companionship, and Guidance to Encourage Your Spirit , " released last month. The book began as journal entries and prayers, plus the notes of encouragement she saved when things were at their worst. It's built around five "invitations" (be gentle with yourself, feel your feelings, believe you are worthy, honor the seasons of your life, and appreciate life's goodness), and it works partly like a workbook for those in the middle of transition, such as a layoff or thinking about a professional pivot. Zayne's executive coaching in tech, finance and healthcare shaped the book, too. She thinks companies have gotten "less human-centered, particularly in the last five years." With the constant push for efficiency, she said, it's hard for anyone to feel like the person behind the work counts for much. "I tell leaders now, you will either run into disappointment, dissatisfaction, disease, or depression by ignoring yourself in all of this transition," she said. Jovian Zayne Jovian Zayne The other option, as she sees it, is centering your humanity and then questioning the bigger systems that keep shrinking how people get to show up at work. Since I'm in the middle of a career transition, I wanted to know what that actually looks like. For anyone else in that spot, whether they were laid off, are planning a pivot or just have a feeling it's time to go, here's her advice. Be honest with yourself Zayne said start with questions: 1. "What do I want to do? 2. How do I want to apply the skills that I've gained over time? What are my priorities financially? How do I want to spend my time every day?" According to Zayne, getting an honest answer starts with giving yourself permission to be candid. "So you're not judging your answers, but you're curious about them," she added. Skip that part and you'll end up in what she calls self-abandonment. "So often, we're lying to ourselves, which makes a hard day even harder," she said. "You will not land softly in that." Curate the people around you She also suggests that ambitious people get picky about their circle during a transition. Mentors, sponsors, coaches, and advocates count along with a therapist if you need one. "Curate the people well to hold you honest," she said. Zayne is practicing her own advice right now while on a book tour to promote, "Soft Landings for Hard Days." She's seeing a lot of friends as she travels for the book, but said only a few people have "intimate access" to her right now. A stock image of a man working at a desk. Pressmaster/Getty Images Let go of your timeline If you're entering a new field, Zayne recommends first deciding where you want to show up and how you want to be perceived — then giving yourself time to adjust. It also helps to break a big change into smaller pieces and take it slow. "We have a lot of gripped hands to imaginary timelines, of when something has to happen or how it has to happen," Zayne said. "When we force-feed our life to ourselves, we choke." Zyne knows how this feels. When she wrote her book, which took about six years, she pulled back from people and group chats to sustain her new writing habits. For someone who prides herself on checking in on people, that was tough for Zayne. Her executive coaching business slowed down as well, since she couldn't chase new clients like before. It didn't bother her, however, because in her mind the book was its own business development. Be hard on the systems and soft on yourself And when the workplace itself is the problem, Zayne doesn't want people taking it out on themselves. Instead, direct your critiques on the workplace, the culture, the systems, or the people instead of internalizing them. "Be hard on those systems, be soft on yourself," she said.
