events.title: Should you take a buyout? 9 Big Tech workers share how they made the call.
events.summary: Jay Ongg, Donnetta Kay Hagist, Jonathan Monheit, Fernanda Monteiro, Scott Thurlow, Justin Long, Shawn Mrzena, Mike RothKugel, Bobbie Ziemer, Tyler Le/BI Late last month, some 60,000 Microsoft employees were presented with a choice that could transform the trajectory of their careers: accept a buyout offer or remain at their jobs. Microsoft has said it expects fewer than 5% of eligible employees to accept the voluntary exit offer. The tech giant's move to downsize comes as many companies restructure or shrink their workforces via buyouts or voluntary retirement packages, sometimes citing AI as a rationale. Business Insider spoke to nine people who have previously accepted voluntary exit offers about their decision-making process and their top tips for people grappling with the same choice. They range in age from their 30s to their 60s and mentioned considerations ranging from finances and healthcare coverage to time, family, and identity. We reached out to their former employers for comment. Google and Microsoft declined to comment. Verizon confirmed former employment. Here's what nine people had to say about life after buyouts. Jay Ongg Company: Microsoft Title and years of experience at the time: Principal group engineering manager, spent almost 25 years at Microsoft in various roles. Offer details: Employees who took the Voluntary Retirement Program were offered up to five years of health insurance coverage, with Microsoft paying for the first year; stock vesting; and base pay determined by seniority and tenure, capped at 39 weeks. Jay Ongg suggests that workers debating whether to accept a buyout take stock of their lives and consider the trade-offs. Courtesy of Jay Ongg Because I was there at Microsoft for a long time, it did become a part of my identity. Jay Ongg wasn't thinking about retiring, but when Microsoft offered a voluntary retirement program in the spring, with employees' last day being in July, he began to think more about his future. It was a tough decision to make after more than two decades at Microsoft, where he said he worked on Xbox, Windows Mobile, Teams, and other products. It would mean saying goodbye to a large part of his identity. He decided to take the chance. "It was kind of scary, but I'm actually a pretty optimistic guy," Ongg said. Since then, he's been exercising more, experimenting with large language models to keep flexing his technical skills, and working on a personal finance AI assistant. His advice for workers debating whether to take a buyout is to take stock of your life, goals, and values. Think about yourself and your family. Whatever you decide, you need to feel good about it at the end of the day, he said. "Everything in life is full of tradeoffs. What are you trading off if you take it versus not?" Ongg said. "We all make decisions based on incomplete information, and there's no crime in doing that. We never have complete information." Donnetta Kay Hagist Company: Google Title and years of experience: Core engineering senior program manager, spent more than 5 years at the company and left when she was 36. Offer details: Google buyout for US employees in June 2025 Donnetta Kay Hagist left Google in October 2025. Courtesy of Donnetta Kay Hagist It's a leap of faith, but I have never been happier. My family is thriving now because I left Google. Donnetta Kay Hagist didn't consider Google's voluntary exit offer until she got coffee with a colleague who revealed that he, a respected team leader, was accepting it. Shocked, she called her husband to tell him she, too, wanted to leave. "I believe that things happen for a reason, and this was the push I needed to bet on myself," Hagist said, adding that she wasn't scared to break out of the so-called "golden handcuffs." Given her husband's stable job, finances and healthcare were sorted — they calculated that she wouldn't need to land a new role until the spring. After her last day at Google in October 2025, Hagist spent a lot of time with her daughters, but quickly got nervous about the job market and started applying for new roles. A friend advised her to relax and take a well-deserved solo trip to Switzerland. She went on the vacation; she signed up for a Hyrox and a half-marathon; she spent more time on her relationships. In November, a mechanical services company, The Arcticom Group, reached out about a senior director role. She landed the job. Hagist said those considering a buyout should make sure their basic needs are met, and then ask themselves whether they're OK with their next three years mirroring their previous three years. "If you feel called to do something different, I encourage you to go explore it. The world is so big," she said. Jonathan Monheit Company: Microsoft Title and years of experience: Lead e-discovery program manager, spent more than 12 years at the company and left when he was 58. Offer details: Employees who took the Voluntary Retirement Program were offered up to five years of health insurance coverage, with Microsoft paying for the first year; stock vesting; and base pay determined by seniority and tenure, capped at 39 weeks. Jonathan Monheit had already planned to leave Microsoft. Courtesy of Jonathan Monheit It was hard to imagine a world in which I would say no. For Jonathan Monheit, Microsoft's voluntary retirement offer was a "winner winner, chicken dinner" moment. He and his wife already had plans to move from Seattle to Dallas, where they were building a new home. Monheit had gotten permission to work remotely through the end of 2026 and then planned to leave the company. He received Microsoft's buyout offer in the spring and realized he'd essentially be paid the same amount as if he'd worked through December. After his final day on July 2, Monheit and his wife drove to their new home, stopping at national parks throughout the 10-day journey. They spent the next few weeks settling in before jetting off to Singapore, Thailand, and Toronto. Now, around four months after leaving Microsoft, Monheit is starting to get a bit restless. "You're used to having things drive you every day. There are moments when I'm like, 'OK, what do I do now?' But in general, it's been healthy. I sleep better. I eat better," he said. He's started exploring new jobs. Ideally, Monheit said his next move is to become a consultant, helping companies approach e-discovery more efficiently. Fernanda Monteiro Company: Google Title and years of experience: Head of YouTube partner operations in EMEA, spent 17 years at the company and left when she was 41. Offer details: UK voluntary exit package in late 2025 Fernanda Monteiro started her own business after accepting her offer. Courtesy of Fernanda Monteiro There is the grief, because you're letting a big part of yourself go. That hurts; that is painful. But at the same time, there was also a pressure being released. events.title: "No sane person questions whether AI works" — but an AI bubble appears ready to pop.
events.summary: The downfall of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang adds an explosive new risk to an already-strained AI boom, threatening to burst a financial bubble even if the technology ultimately succeeds. Why it matters: History shows that world-changing technology and devastating financial bubbles often go hand in hand. A market reckoning won't stop the AI revolution. But as with the dot-com crash, it could vaporize trillions in investor wealth as expectations come crashing back to earth. The big picture: "No sane person questions whether AI works. And that 'working' status is precisely what makes a bubble possible," veteran technology investor Paul Kedrosky told Axios. The risks have grown as technology companies commit trillions to infrastructure, increasingly relying on debt, investments in one another and complicated financing arrangements to keep the expansion going. Driving the news: Huang's stunning resignation Thursday has shaken confidence in the company at the center of the AI boom — and raised fresh questions about the sustainability of the broader investment frenzy. Nvidia, which named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO, faces a leadership vacuum at a time when the industry is already grappling with financial and political uncertainty. Beyond selling chips, Nvidia has helped finance the massive expansion of computing infrastructure by investing in its customers and providing financial backstops for major projects. A more cautious approach by Huang's successor could undermine confidence in projects that have depended on Nvidia's financial support. What they're saying: RSM chief economist Joe Brusuelas told Axios that Huang's departure could trigger a "wholesale bursting" of the AI bubble. "The turmoil around Jensen Huang matters for the buildout if it makes lenders less confident that Nvidia will back the next round of projects," Columbia Business School professor Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh told Axios. Zoom out: The financial and political vulnerabilities were piling up well before the Nvidia scandal. Spending is outpacing expected returns. AI providers are projected to spend $7 trillion on infrastructure through 2030, while Gartner forecasts no more than $3.6 trillion in related revenue over the same period, according to Axios reporting . Valuation expectations are being reset. Anthropic's newly announced IPO terms imply a valuation well below earlier hopes of as much as $2 trillion. OpenAI also reportedly secured less cash and a lower valuation than it had hoped in a recent funding round. Investors are growing more cautious. Retail traders, who have routinely bought previous AI-related market dips, instead became net sellers of U.S. stocks during the sharp Nov. 5 selloff, according to Vanda Research. Financing is getting harder. The debt-fueled expansion was already showing signs of strain before the latest turmoil. Rising borrowing costs and an avalanche of new bond offerings have made lenders wary. Political opposition is growing. A wave of election victories for AI-skeptical candidates, along with widespread voter support for data center restrictions, threatens to delay construction, increase costs and undermine the assumptions behind some projects. Regulatory risks are mounting. Huang's downfall has intensified bipartisan demands for tighter restrictions on advanced chip exports to China, which increasingly appear likely to pass. The risk: A retreat in AI investment could become self-reinforcing, turning a market correction into a much broader financial reckoning. Falling valuations and tighter credit could make it harder for startups and cloud providers to finance additional data centers, reducing demand for chips, power and other infrastructure. That could put further pressure on the investors, lenders and companies financing the expansion, spreading the consequences well beyond the companies developing AI models. Yes, but: There is considerable evidence that AI itself is a real and potentially transformative technology — and that demand is growing rapidly. Anthropic reported an annualized revenue run rate of $81 billion at the end of October, up from $71 billion a month earlier. OpenAI grew quarterly revenue roughly 50% to $10 billion in the third quarter, according to The Wall Street Journal, even as its adjusted operating losses reached $10.9 billion. Businesses are already using AI to write software, automate tasks and perform work that previously required significant human effort. Tighter U.S. export controls could also benefit American AI developers by limiting Chinese rivals' access to advanced computing power, even as they complicate Nvidia's business prospects. The historical lesson: Some of the greatest technological transformations have been accompanied by speculative investment booms that ended painfully for investors. "I have no doubt that AI will be transformative. That does not preclude a financial bubble," MIT economics professor Ricardo Caballero told Axios. Caballero argues that excessive optimism may even be necessary to marshal the enormous investments required for a new technology to reach its potential. Such booms can leave behind valuable infrastructure and lasting economic gains, as they did in the dot-com boom-bust cycle, even if many investors suffer losses along the way. The bottom line: "AI can deliver enormous value to users while the companies building the infrastructure earn far less than their investors expected," Van Nieuwerburgh said.

events.title: Omaxian takes the Omarchy look down a different Linux backstreet
events.summary: Omaxian OS is only at version 0.1, but it already takes a distinctly unconventional route through the Linux desktop. The brand-new Linux desktop distro describes itself as "the Omarchy desktop on X11 — as a shell for your Debian, or as a whole OS." That's not quite the impression that we came away with, though. Like most distros, Omaxian is available as an ISO file you can install and use. Alternatively, Omaxian Shell can be installed on an existing Debian-family distro without replacing the underlying operating system. The OS release is codenamed "Trans-Siberian Shaman," and the GitHub project repository shows work going back just a few weeks. No LLM coding assistant is credited on the project page, but we looked inside some of the test scripts, and as well as being verbose and hard to read, they also credit "Grok Bot." Omarchy itself is of course built with LLM assistance, and as we reported last month , so is the new Daemonarchy FreeBSD-based desktop project. Omaxian is styled after Omarchy, and it includes some of the same tools – and optional support for LLMs – but it's not based on the same tech. Instead of Arch, it's based on Devuan 6, the current version of the systemd-free fork of Debian. Omaxian eschews Hyprland, and indeed Wayland altogether: it opts for an X11 tiling window manager – in this case, i3 . i3 first appeared in 2009, so it's been around much longer than Hyprland. Omaxian's configuration also understands familiar keystrokes such as Alt+F4 to close a window. For us, that's a significant usability win. The window manager isn't running on top of X.org. Omaxian uses the 2025 fork, the new XLibre X11 server . This is a controversial project led by a controversial developer , which will be enough for some people to want to avoid Omaxian as a whole. The latest release of GhostBSD uses XLibre too, though. Way back in 2021, The Register reported on Omarchy creator David Heinemeier Hansson's company banning political discussions, and things have only got more vexed since. Just as DHH has attracted some notoriety for his now right-wing views, his Linux is similarly opinionated. If the associations surrounding Omarchy and XLibre put you off, Omaxian's combination of the two probably won't win you over. The flipside is that if you don't care about the political views, but are interested in the idea of a tiling environment set up for power users who embrace LLM coding assistance, then you might like Omaxian. The full distro trades Arch, Wayland, and systemd for a Devuan base, X11, and sysvinit, with APT handling conventional packages. Flatpaks and AppImages are available too. We tried Omaxian in VirtualBox, but we experienced frequent display corruption. We must give it this: the interface is slightly easier to navigate than Hyprland. One touch that we did like is that if you get tired of the tiling stuff and want to switch back to something more conventional, then Xfce is also installed in the background. Xfce provides Omaxian with a file manager and other accessories, but you can just choose Xfce from the login screen and find yourself back in a simple, familiar, classic desktop environment. Omaxian is not the sort of environment we're looking for. This vulture isn't a developer and doesn't use LLMs for anything at all. However, lots of people are looking for something like that, as demonstrated by Omarchy's sponsorship . But it's bold, colorful, and significantly different from the mainstream, and that is the sort of thing we do like to see. ®

events.title: USS Roosevelt arrives in Middle East: Is the US-Iran war about to resume?
events.summary: The aircraft carrier joins two others operating in the US Central Command area of responsibility. The United States has deployed a third aircraft carrier to the Middle East as diplomatic efforts to permanently end the US-Israel war on Iran and reopen the Strait of Hormuz remain stalled. On Monday, a US official told Al Jazeera that the USS Theodore Roosevelt had arrived in the Middle East. The aircraft carrier joins two others operating in the US Central Command (CENTCOM) area of responsibility. list 1 of 3 Will Iraq’s oil smuggling crackdown disarm militias without a conflict? list 2 of 3 Iraqi armed group denies involvement in oil smuggling, calls probe a ‘lie’ list 3 of 3 US and rivals spar over next UN boss as race lurches towards deadline The US and Iran entered into a two-week ceasefire in April and later announced a broader memorandum of understanding in June, which collapsed in early July. Since then, mediators from Pakistan and Qatar have been trying to prevent a return to the full-scale exchange of attacks between the US and Iran that also badly affected the broader Gulf region in March. Last week, US President Donald Trump stated that further military strikes against Iran are “quite unlikely” and said the military component of the war was “effectively over” following discussions with Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani. But he noted the US military remains “locked and loaded” if conditions change. Does the deployment of another aircraft carrier to the region mean the US-Israel war on Iran is going to resume? What is the USS Theodore Roosevelt? Named after the 26th US president, Theodore Roosevelt, the vessel is a nuclear-powered aircraft carrier. Commissioned by the US Navy in 1986, the ship carries more than 5,000 personnel and a full air wing of more than 60 aircraft, including F-18s, the twin-engine, supersonic, all-weather multi-role fighter planes. According to the US Navy, the warship is tasked with “conducting carrier air warfare operations and assisting in the planning, control, coordination and integration of air wing squadrons in support of carrier air warfare”. Besides combat operations, the carrier also replenishes ships at sea and rescues people, including refugees, at sea. The USS Theodore Roosevelt has performed combat and humanitarian missions since it was commissioned. During the 1990-91 Gulf War, it was deployed to the Mediterranean and the Red Sea for combat operations. In 2003, it also supported US strikes during the Iraq War. It was also deployed in the Asia Pacific region from 2020-21 for military exercises with India, Japan, Australia, South Korea and Malaysia. In October, a US official told Al Jazeera that the USS Theodore Roosevelt had left its San Diego base in September, bound for the Middle East. According to another official, it arrived in the Middle East on November 15 . But the Pentagon and CENTCOM, which oversees military operations in the region, have not formally confirmed the carrier’s arrival. What is the state of US deployment in the region? The arrival of the USS Theodore Roosevelt in the Middle East brings the total number of US aircraft carrier strike groups operating in the region to three. The USS George Washington and the USS George HW Bush are the other two aircraft carriers currently deployed there. Last month, a US official told Al Jazeera that the Makin Island Amphibious Ready Group (ARG), carrying more than 2,000 Marines, had also followed the USS Theodore Roosevelt to the Middle East. The Wall Street Journal reported that the strike group and naval deployments could involve an additional 9,000 to 10,000 US soldiers in total, including sailors and Marines assigned to the carrier strike group and other ships. However, the US military is yet to confirm these deployments. The US has had troops and military assets stationed at bases in the Middle East for decades. Of these, eight are permanent bases, located in Bahrain, Egypt, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. As of mid-2025, there were 40,000 to 50,000 US soldiers stationed in and around the Middle East, including personnel at large, permanent bases and smaller forward sites across the region. According to open-source intelligence analysts and military flight-tracking data, the US has deployed more than 120 aircraft to the region since early February, before the war on Iran began. That is the biggest surge in US airpower in the Middle East since the Iraq War. Reported deployments include E-3 Sentry Airborne Warning and Control System (AWACS) aircraft, F-35 stealth strike fighters and F-22 air superiority jets, alongside F-15s and F-16s. In March, the Pentagon also ordered additional US forces to the Gulf. The reinforcements consisted of three distinct formations. The first was the Tripoli ARG, centred around the America-class assault ship USS Tripoli and the 31st Marine Expeditionary Unit (MEU).

events.title: Jordan bans Telegram over national security concerns
events.summary: Authorities say measure is part of ongoing efforts to reduce cybercrime and strengthen digital security. Jordanian authorities have banned the Telegram messaging app, saying the move aims to curb the dissemination of illegal content and what they describe as “extremist material”. The Public Security Directorate (PSD) announced the measure in a statement published on Monday amid a security crackdown after nine people were killed in an attack on a Greek Orthodox church last month. list 1 of 3 Jordan’s King Abdullah promises to confront ‘terrorists’ after Karak attack list 2 of 3 Security ⁠officer killed in stabbing attack in Jordan’s capital list 3 of 3 Jordan sentences three men to death over deadly church attack in Karak The PSD urged citizens to “exercise caution when using social media applications, to avoid interacting with accounts, links, or entities of unknown origin, and to report any unlawful practices or content through official channels”. The church shooting took place in the village of Hammoud in the west-central governorate of Karak. On Sunday, three men were sentenced to death by hanging over the attack. The incident prompted Jordan to carry out air strikes on neighbouring Syria that Amman said killed 20 members of the ISIL (ISIS) armed group linked to the church attack. Meanwhile, a security officer was killed and another wounded this month in Amman in what authorities described as another “terrorist attack”. Telegram, founded by Russian entrepreneur Pavel Durov in 2013, is believed to be used by groups such as ISIL. In July, Russia issued an arrest warrant for Durov, accusing him of aiding “terrorism”. The 42-year-old is currently believed to be in Dubai in the United Arab Emirates and faces up to life in a Russian prison if found guilty. He is also being investigated in several other countries. Telegram supports end-to-end encrypted chats, but not all conversations are encrypted. The messaging app is popular in the Middle East and North Africa. The region accounts for about 8 percent of global users.

events.title: Most UAE salaries flat but top-tier roles to see rises
events.summary: A majority of UAE organisations are expected to keep salaries flat or offer modest increases next year amid economic uncertainty driven by the Iran war, according to a new report. A total of 77 per cent of organisations plan to hold salary ranges steady (42 per cent), or award rises of 1 per cent to 5 per cent (35 per cent), a Cooper Fitch survey found. Midsized firms – those with 251 to 1,000 employees – are expected to keep salaries flat, while large organisations will offer pay rises in 2027, it said. The survey covered more than 1,091 organisations in the Gulf region, representing over 450,000 employees, with questions focusing on recruitment activity, workforce headcounts, and salary trends for 2026 and projections for 2027. Information technology has the highest share of respondents planning salary increases, at 63 per cent, followed by telecoms with 60 per cent, and heavy industry and manufacturing at 59 per cent. Other sectors, including banking, financial services and insurance; and retail, e-commerce and luxury goods, are also expected to raise salaries next year. Salaries in government and the public sector are the most likely to remain unchanged, according to 70 per cent of those organisations. Economic uncertainty has continued across the Gulf region since the start of the Iran war in February. The Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global oil supplies, remains technically shut, disrupting trade and other activities. The International Monetary Fund projects the UAE 's economy will contract by 3.9 per cent this year before rebounding at a 7.7 per cent growth rate in 2027, conditional on the normalisation of shipping routes and the reopening of the strait. The projections by the Washington-based lender in October reflect a downgrade of 7 percentage points for 2026 and an upgrade of 2.4 percentage points for 2027 compared to the fund's April forecast. Companies are also planning to expand their workforce next year, with 42 per cent of respondents expecting to increase their headcount as the economy rebounds from the effects of the war. A staffing increase of 1 per cent to 5 per cent is the most common rate, selected by 24 per cent of respondents, while 32 per cent expect no change. Only 7 per cent anticipate reductions of 10 per cent or more next year, compared with 16 per cent in 2026. Real estate, construction and architecture are most positive about increasing staff numbers followed by retail, e-commerce and luxury goods, and banking, financial services and insurance. Talent outlook Most UAE respondents believe the local market has sufficient talent to meet their organisation’s hiring needs for 2027, while 25 per cent report insufficient talent and 11 per cent are unsure. Views vary by department, with 55 per cent of technology respondents reporting insufficient talent, compared with 16 per cent in human resources. Among the sectors shown, aviation, defence and aerospace has the highest share citing insufficient talent at 60 per cent, followed by information technology and hospitality (40 per cent each), and real estate and construction at 33 per cent. Government and public sector respondents are the most likely to report sufficient talent, at 91 per cent. The survey also that found sales and business development roles were the most difficult to fill, followed by technical and engineering roles and those requiring AI, data and technology skills. or this year’s report, Fitch Insights surveyed business leaders responsible for key decisions across more than 1,091 organisations in the Gulf region, representing over 450,000 employees. The survey comprised of twenty questions focusing on recruitment activity, workforce headcounts, and salary trends for 2026 and projections for 2027. Hiring stabilises LinkedIn, in a separate report on Monday, said hiring in the UAE was stabilising after war-related disruption earlier this year. Hiring fell to 40 per cent below 2025 levels in April, but by August the decline had narrowed to 18 per cent, and 15 out of 17 major industries posted monthly growth, it said. “The sharpest phase of the downturn appears to have passed, although hiring activity remains below 2025,” it added. AI is rapidly changing what employers need, LinkedIn found, with demand for artificial intelligence engineering jobs rising 232.4 per cent year-on-year in August. “The UAE is committed to developing national capabilities while attracting the world’s best talent, creating an agile workforce that can translate technological change into higher productivity, new industries and sustainable opportunities in the UAE,” Dr Thani Al Zeyoudi, Minister of Foreign Trade of the UAE, said.

events.title: ‘NATO will collapse’: Russia stalls Ukraine talks, seeks to divide Europe
events.summary: Russia has proposed nonaggression pacts with individual nations, which could shatter collective defence against Moscow. Kyiv, Ukraine – A Russian drone struck a small house in the northern Ukrainian town of Hlukhiv, burying a nine-year-old boy and his grandmother under the debris. Two Ukrainian police officers arrived on Saturday to dig them out, apply a tourniquet to the woman’s bleeding arm and take them away in their car. But a second drone struck their vehicle, killing one of the officers, Mykola Savchenko, who covered the boy with his body, the Ministry of Internal Affairs said. Such double-tap attacks are Ukraine’s daily reality as the war grinds on to its fifth anniversary. They’re also a metaphor for Russia’s latest attempts to target both Ukraine and those Kyiv has long hoped would help it survive Moscow’s onslaught – NATO and Europe. On the surface, Russia is engaged in United States-mediated diplomacy. But Russian diplomats who met with US negotiators in Abu Dhabi for trilateral talks involving Moscow, Kyiv and Washington last week presented demands that go far beyond any peace settlement. Moscow hasn’t agreed to Kyiv’s proposal to freeze the war along the current front lines as Ukraine lacks Western missile interceptors to shoot down Russian missiles and jet drones. Instead, the Kremlin has shifted the focus of talks from a ceasefire and peace to demands that, if accepted, could dismantle Europe’s post-Cold War security architecture, analysts said. Russia wants NATO to withdraw its troops from Central and Eastern Europe and ban the bloc’s further expansion, according to leaked documents obtained by The New York Times, The Economist and several Ukrainian media outlets. Moscow also wants to ink nonaggression pacts with individual European nations, something that may sound alluring to Russia’s neighbours, such as Estonia or Finland. “Agreements of this kind could be reached, among other things, with individual NATO member states, which would then receive, for instance, additional individual security guarantees” from Moscow, Russian negotiator Alexey Drobinin said at a news conference after the Abu Dhabi talks. But a string of such agreements could in effect negate NATO’s cornerstone principle to regard any armed attack against one member state as an attack against all of its 32 members. “NATO will collapse, and European nations will [individually] be face to face with Russia,” said Boris Bondarev, a former Russian diplomat who left his Ministry of Foreign Affairs job in protest against Moscow’s 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine. “Europe will surrender to Russia without firing a single shot in its defence, without losing a single soldier or spending a single shell,” he told Al Jazeera. “Such individual deals are an absolutely blatant attempt to demolish Europe’s unity, which has already been bursting at the seams, and to undermine NATO’s unity,” said Bondarev, also the author of Time to Win the War, a book that tracks the potential steps needed to reach a peace agreement. Any nonaggression pacts would most likely include conditions that bar a signatory nation from participating in a future conflict between Russia and another European nation, he said, destroying any potential for collective defence against Moscow. Russia’s demands were presented to US special envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff but not to European leaders. “Russians want to talk to Americans. They don’t want to talk to Europe,” Maria Kucherenko, executive director at the Strategic Intelligence Institute, a think tank in Kyiv, told Al Jazeera. To Kucherenko, who has for years scrutinised Moscow’s negotiating tactics, the “maximalist” demands continue the Kremlin’s habit of asking for everything. Russia’s “demands will be maximalist, the way they used to be, and they will be deceptive about the subsequence of steps [towards a peace deal] in their interests. They’ll put politics ahead of security, the way they’ve done all these years,” she said. Kushner, a real estate developer and son-in-law of US President Donald Trump, used the word “very” abundantly to describe the talks. “These deals are very hard and complex, and this one is very emotional, very complex. It’s a very hot war,” Kushner said at a news conference. To Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Russia’s demands sound otherworldly. Russian President Vladimir Putin “lives in a different reality”, Zelenskyy wrote on X on Wednesday, adding, “I can draw a picture for him too where I fully occupy Russia. But it’s not true.” “We are all very cautious with this topic because nobody really understands 100 percent what they want,” Zelenskyy said at a news conference hours later. A top Ukrainian negotiator decried the “difficulty” of the Abu Dhabi talks. “This round of talks was one of the most difficult ones.

events.title: Coders have to learn a new skill: Socializing
events.summary: Getty Images; Tyler Le/BI Michael Irwin's latest project relied more on his woodworking and people skills than his deep knowledge of coding. The principal software engineer for Docker, a platform that helps developers adopt models, tools and agents securely, handmade a wooden base to serve as a gaming controller, attached red, blue, and green buttons with wires, and took it to a conference last week. It corresponded to a game coded by AI, and Irwin used the gimmick to draw people to his booth where he engaged them in talks about AI agents. The game is a frill that Irwin wouldn't have taken the time to make before AI accelerated coding. "It's been a dream of mine for a long time, and it's just now more accessible than it's ever been," he says. Gone are the days when software engineers spent most of their time in solitude, coding remotely and rarely attending meetings. Their remit has expanded beyond the keyboard, and the boundaries of technical work have blurred. Companies, including Amazon , increasingly expect engineers to connect personally with customers. People outside engineering teams at many companies have taken up generating code and using AI at work; a fifth of OpenAI's Codex users were non-developers as of June. Bosses expect developers to manage teams of agents and communicate complex technical work in simple terms, all while acting as designers, architects, and big picture conceptual thinkers rather than cogs in a coding machine. "The micro level is mostly able to be passed off," Irwin says. "It takes a different mindset." "This new way of working, it might not suit the typical engineer personality," says Sam Dhar, an engineer at Galileo, an AI startup Cisco acquired earlier this year. But it relies on the expertise and judgement that engineers have always had to build over their careers. Still, there's pressure for developers to make that mindset shift in a condensed timeline or risk being laid off and replaced by someone who can charm their way through an interview rather than ace a take-home coding test . Hit swiftly and broadly by automation, developers are a bellwether for white-collar work. They sit at the frontier of AI's transformation of work, which will either swallow jobs or create new ones, depending on who you ask. "It's only happening to engineering first," Dhar says. "It's potentially going to manifest in a way where all work is done in some respects with AI, where the accountability still resides with the humans who are reviewing and fixing and asking the right questions." Reports of the coding apocalypse are greatly exaggerated, so far. More people work in the field than ever: About 1.9 million people worked in software development, testing, and quality assurance in the US as of last year, up from about 1.5 million in 2020, according to the US Bureau of Labor Statistics. The bureau projects the industry will grow by 10% over the next decade. A developer in 2020 would hardly recognize the demands of the job today. Vibe coding forever changed software engineering last year. Big companies like Microsoft said Google AI had written large swaths of their latest code, and engineers began spending more time reviewing lines of AI-generated code than they did typing it. Experienced developers finished projects faster, and companies scaled back on hiring junior engineers . 2026, the father of vibe coding said, would be the year of " agentic engineering ." Amazon Web Service recently used agents to generate 100% of the code for a new emulator tool. Software engineers have moved away from writing code and on to concepts. They still need deep technical expertise to evaluate AI's work, but they also need business sense. "You have to really understand a lot more about why we're doing whatever it is we're doing, and ask a lot of the right questions," says Paul Elliott, vice president of product and engineering at software testing company Chromatic. That requires more conversations across the company. For all the left-brain, right-brain debate and stereotypes of developers working remotely with headphones on, engineers are making the leap to become more forward-facing. "It's definitely a trainable skill," Elliott says. Marc Brooker, vice president and distinguished engineer at Amazon Web Services, says engineers on his team now spend more time with customers and prospects, talking to decision-makers and developers at other companies. Training for these scenarios is less formal and more often involves shadowing calls with engineers who have more public-facing experience. "The outcome of that is so that the engineers can go back to their teams and their organizations and turn what they learned into really great product decisions, really great technical decisions," Brooker says. Dylan Wight, founding software engineer at Flagler Health, an AI-native operating system for musculoskeletal care, says that his days now consist of reviewing code issues raised by agents and determining if they're practical problems or oversensitive flags. Wight also has multiple meetings weekly with the system's users in the healthcare industry, which he welcomes. He has a side "that's more entrepreneurial and likes talking to users and understanding their needs," he says. "If people wanted to just think about code, I think it would get harder, because that part is mostly done." The wall between engineer and product manager is breaking down. Product managers previously owned many of those client conversations, volleying between business needs and the technical expertise of developer teams. Now, AI companies increasingly use the term " member of technical staff " to describe their workers. Anthropic released a report about its workforce last month, showing that technical workers spent 16% more time in meetings now compared to a year ago. At the same time, more workers are shipping code, and engineers are gaining a stronger presence: The ratio of engineers to product managers has jumped to 17 to one. "Engineers are definitely taking on more product level autonomy, but product managers are also taking on more technical work," says Frank Fusco, CEO of software company Silicon Society. "I think the definitions of those jobs are changing." Forward-deployed engineers , who work inside another company's systems, have become increasingly popular in the AI era, as they work with clients on solutions, combining technical knowledge with that problem-solving ethos. Companies increasingly demand technical candidates who can work in the office, a shift after years of allowing them to work independently and remotely. Michelle Volberg, CEO of software recruiting company Twill, says that last year about half of the roles her company worked to fill were remote. Now, some 95% of jobs require hybrid or full-time in-office work . events.title: Half of the women in Trump's Cabinet have left the White House. Here are the ones that remain.
events.summary: President Donald Trump speaks during a Cabinet meeting in the White House in May 2026. Win McNamee/Getty Images One-third of Trump's original Cabinet and Cabinet-level appointments — eight out of 24 — were women. Five out of those eight women have since left the Trump administration. Karoline Leavitt, who was the youngest-ever White House press secretary, also departed in August. At the beginning of his second non-consecutive term, President Donald Trump named women to several historic appointments in his administration — from the first female White House chief of staff to the youngest-ever press secretary. At a 2025 White House event for Women's History Month, Trump said he was "thrilled to say that we have more women in our Cabinet than any Republican president in the history of our country." At the time, one-third of Trump's original Cabinet and Cabinet-level appointments — eight out of 24 — were women. However, five have since left their roles. In April, the president fired Attorney General Pam Bondi weeks after firing Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem . Labor Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer resigned in April following investigations into alleged misconduct, and Trump's director of national intelligence, Tulsi Gabbard, resigned in May. In November, Susie Wiles resigned as chief of staff, a Cabinet-level post, following sweeping Republican losses in the 2026 midterm elections . Stephen Miller took her place. Trump and Noem in 2025. BRENDAN SMIALOWSKI/AFP via Getty Images Other high-profile women in Trump's cabinet circle have also departed in recent months. Karoline Leavitt left her role as White House press secretary in August, citing her desire to spend more time with her family after having her second child. Katie Zacharia held the role for five days in October before she left. Trump asked Dana White , the president of the Ultimate Fighting Championship, in November to step in, but he declined. When reached for comment about the departures, White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers told Business Insider that Trump has "assembled the greatest Administration in history" and selected each member based on "their ability to deliver for the American people." "Unlike the identity-politics-obsessed Democrats, the President judges individuals on merit and qualifications, not immutable characteristics," she said. "That's common sense and what makes this country great." Meet the most powerful women remaining in Trump's Cabinet. Linda McMahon, secretary of education Linda McMahon. Win McNamee/Getty Images When nominating Linda McMahon for education secretary, Trump wrote on Truth Social that "We will send Education BACK TO THE STATES, and Linda will spearhead that effort." McMahon, the former CEO of WWE, served as the head of the Small Business Administration during Trump's first term before stepping down to chair the pro-Trump super PAC America First Action. She also served on the Connecticut Board of Education for one year. In March 2025, Trump signed an executive order directing McMahon to begin dismantling the Department of Education . In a radio interview with WABC 770 AM's "Cats & Cosby," McMahon said Trump was "dead serious about the fact that he wants me to fire myself." Kelly Loeffler, administrator of the Small Business Administration Kelly Loeffler. JEFF KOWALSKY/AFP via Getty Images Kelly Loeffler, a millionaire businesswoman and former CEO of the bitcoin company Bakkt, previously served as a senator from Georgia. "Kelly will bring her experience in business and Washington to reduce red tape, and unleash opportunity for our Small Businesses to grow, innovate, and thrive," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "She will focus on ensuring that SBA is accountable to Taxpayers by cracking down on waste, fraud, and regulatory overreach." As head of the Small Business Administration, Loeffler has visited Los Angeles to assess post-wildfire recovery efforts for small businesses and announced that the SBA would move six of its offices out of "sanctuary cities" that refuse ICE detention requests and relocate them to "municipalities who share this Administration's commitment to secure borders and safe communities." Brooke Rollins, secretary of agriculture Brooke Rollins. Alex Wong/Getty Images In Trump's first White House administration, Brooke Rollins served as director of the Domestic Policy Council, assistant to the president for strategic initiatives, and director of the Office of American Innovation. She went on to serve as the president and CEO of the America First Policy Institute, a conservative think tank. "Brooke's commitment to support the American Farmer, defense of American Food Self-Sufficiency, and the restoration of Agriculture-dependent American Small Towns is second to none," Trump said in a statement announcing her nomination. Upon taking office, Rollins' main focus as agriculture secretary was lowering egg prices, which rose 237% from January 2021 to January 2025. She has since worked with HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to introduce new dietary guidelines emphasizing the consumption of meat, full fats, and whole foods. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: ‘The currency competition is now a software competition’: Why Japan’s banks think digital currencies give the yen a boost
events.summary: Currencies such as the Japanese yen or the euro have tried and failed to loosen the U.S. dollar’s grip on world trade , unable to outweigh the U.S.’s deep and open financial markets. But now, Japanese bankers think that the rise of digital currencies could give the yen a new path to worldwide use. “The currency competition is now a software competition,” Tomoya Hasebe, global head of digital and innovation at Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation (SMBC), said at a roundtable organized by FinCity Tokyo in Singapore on Nov. 16. “Currency dominance is increasingly determined not only by central bank policy or regulatory policy, but by which currency is easiest to use as code.” The yen is the world’s third most-used currency, after the U.S. dollar and the euro. Japan was the first country among G7 economies to roll out a comprehensive framework to regulate stablecoins. Yet yen-pegged stablecoins have barely enjoyed much usage, with U.S. dollar-denominated stablecoins accounting for more than 97% of the market . The country’s three megabanks— Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group, Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group, and the Mizuho Financial Group—are planning to change that with a jointly-issued yen-backed stablecoin set to begin transactions next March . The new stablecoin is meant to streamline cross-border payments and boost the appeal of the yen for global business. Several Asian economies are rolling out their own stablecoins to cater to firms seeking alternatives to the U.S. dollar. Hong Kong, for example, issued its first two Hong Kong dollar-backed stablecoin issuer licenses in April , to HSBC and Anchorpoint Financial, a joint venture by Standard Chartered Bank, HKT, and Web3 firm Animoca Brands.  “The majority of global trade is still in USD, but there is certainly a group of firms around the world that want to not use U.S. dollars for trade,” said Tim Way, senior director of global banking at digital asset infrastructure firm Fireblocks. “It’s an opportunity for Asia to stand up and have more trade in Asia running in Asian currencies.” Startups are entering a financial ecosystem that’s long been dominated by incumbents. JPYC, a Japanese startup, launched the country’s first yen-pegged stablecoin in October 2025. “More private enterprises and start-ups are starting to enter the stablecoin area,” Makoto Shibata, the head of Finolab, a Japanese fintech accelerator, said. Yet, it remains to be seen if yen-backed stablecoins—whether by on-chain start-ups or trad-fi institutions—will be able to gain traction. Unlike U.S. dollar stablecoins that generate returns from high-yielding treasury bills, yen-pegged stablecoins operate on razor-thin margins. Since JPYC was founded in 2019, it has faced steep growth bottlenecks , as users frequently redeem the token for traditional fiat, rather than hold it in their digital wallets.  This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: MAGA figures hope Jensen Huang's spy scandal finally breaks Trump's embrace of Big Tech
events.summary: Prominent conservative thinkers and MAGA figures are seizing on former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy to pull President Trump away from his alliance with the tech right. Why it matters: The Nvidia scandal highlights some of the political weaknesses for Trump in allowing himself to be defined by his connections to an increasingly unpopular group of companies. Right-wing players are hoping the bombshell revelations about Huang's affairs will chip away at the president's embrace of the tech industry and offer an opening for anti-tech voices in his administration. What they're saying : They view the midterm elections as proof that people across the political spectrum hate AI, data centers and view Silicon Valley as too powerful. President Trump's perception of China "has always been entirely commercial and transactional. His view was, 'we're getting screwed. I'm going to get a better deal,'" Oren Cass, founder of conservative think tank American Compass, said. Cass, who has warned about Nvidia risks for more than a year, said the allegations of espionage are the strongest evidence yet that China is not a commercial partner but an adversary that is going to "subvert the American political process in ways that end up humiliating the President." MAGA figure Steve Bannon, meanwhile, said in a text he has called Jensen Huang "a CCP 'Agent of Influence' a thousand times." and that it's an OPEN SECRET." "We need to actually cut OFF ALL THE CHIPS NOW," Bannon added as Congress warms up to legislation aimed at that. Reality check: Amid daily revelations about Huang's affairs and the negative consequences for the AI boom and U.S. economy, Trump has created some distance. He backtracked on a suggestion that Jensen could go on a trip to China later this month. Other than that, he has kept it friendly. The president earlier this week called him "honorable" and on Thursday, following Jensen's resignation, the president said he "has done a fantastic job" and called him a "Legend." On Thursday, he said in an interview with Stephen Smith that Jensen is "a tremendous talent" who's done "incredible" and "brilliant" work at Nvidia. What we're watching: Supporters of Jensen Huang are lobbying the White House to support his reinstatement as CEO, according to the Financial Times. What's next: Conservatives are hoping the scandal changes who gets a seat at the table for the remainder of Trump's presidency as 2028 and mounting AI unpopularity approaches.

events.title: Anthropic employees could soon be a lot richer. 4 financial advisors share how they can manage the tax bill.
events.summary: Some Anthropic workers are about to become super wealthy. Here's how they can manage their new tax bills. Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto via Getty Images This year is minting many single-stock millionaires through IPOs from SpaceX and Anthropic. Now, workers face the challenge of diversifying portfolios and paying high taxes. Financial advisors walked through strategies to help: from psychological tricks to buying carwashes. Some Silicon Valley employees are about to see their financial circumstances switch from well-off to extremely wealthy . The year already saw the largest IPO ever, SpaceX, a record that could be broken later this month by Anthropic. For some employees, the windfalls could be life-changing but tied to a single company. Eric Franklin, a former Amazon employee who co-founded Prospero Wealth, a wealth advisory business focused on tech workers, said his firm has talked with several Anthropic employees who are "looking at $100 to $200 million outcomes." With wealth will come taxes, especially as employees try to diversify away from their biggest holdings: their employer. "If you think about the average Anthropic person or SpaceX person , their balance is their 401(k), maybe they've been doing their backdoor Roth IRA, and then they own Anthropic or SpaceX," said Thomas Kopelman, cofounder of AllStreet Wealth, who has managed the wealth of roughly 10 SpaceX employees. Selling those shares to diversify their investments could trigger enormous tax bills, especially for early employees who received shares at a fraction of their current value. In California, where profits from stock sales are taxed like regular income, those capital gains can face up to a 37.1% tax. Business Insider spoke with four financial advisors about the strategies tech workers can use to diversify their fortunes while minimizing their tax bills. Their advice ranged from simple psychological tricks to sophisticated investment strategies — and even buying car washes or shipping-container businesses. But the advisors agreed that before cashing out, employees should figure out how much money they actually need and build a plan around it. "You've won the game; you have all the wealth that you possibly could need," Koppelman said. "What do you want your lifestyle to look like and how much should we lock in day one?" From there, advisors can help a tech worker create a plan to minimize their tax costs and diversify their wealth. Timing is important to consider — employees and other insiders are usually restricted from selling their stock right when a company goes public. "It's almost never: 'Oh, well, let's use this one single product and boom, you're done," Franklin said, instead choosing different strategies for different timelines. Here are some of the tools tech workers are using to save on taxes as they look to stop being all in on their employers, from the simplest to the most complex. The case for keeping it simple The simplest option is to change your mindset. If the only thing certain in life is death and taxes, you might as well come to terms with both. "The real challenge when you have these positions is you look at the value that's on your statement, and you think that's all your money," said Alex Shahidi, co-CIO of Evoke Advisors, a $28 billion AUM wealth advisory firm. "But in reality, there's a tax liability that's not written on your statement." Sophisticated strategies to try to defer and minimize those taxes introduce complexity which, "oftentimes creates unpleasant surprises in the future," he said. One approach for someone prioritizing simplicity, he said, is to sell some one year, some the next year, spreading it out over tax years. They could also focus on building a diversified portfolio, including assets such as gold, commodities, or other equities, to reduce their dependence on their employer's stock. One "completely psychological" technique is to wait until the stock appreciates enough to cover the expected tax bill and then sell it. "Then the market paid the tax for you," Shahidi said. "It actually works. Even very smart people are like, 'I just feel better about that.'" Tax strategy du jour: Tax-loss harvesting The first obvious tool for any tax-aware investor is direct indexing . Instead of holding an index fund that tracks, for example, the S&P 500, investors buy individual stocks that roughly mirror that index's performance. This allows them to roughly achieve the same returns as the index while using losses to offset gains in a process known as tax-loss harvesting. With smaller positions, this is usually where Prospero Wealth's Franklin will start. "That's a place where they can feel like they're getting something beyond what they would generally do themselves," he said. "It's something that's easy to explain." For wealthier clients, advisors may recommend direct indexing "on steroids," Franklin said, or long-short indexing, which introduces leverage and short selling to increase tax losses or to try to outperform an index intentionally. Long-short strategies have higher fees and can often be riskier than direct indexing. "The bigger the portfolio, the more long-short makes sense," Kopelman said. Borrowing against your holdings A popular way to access your stock value without immediately selling and paying taxes is to borrow against your shares. Investors could take out a loan against their shares, but rates aren't fixed and therefore create a lot of risk. Instead, advisors said there are other ways to borrow, with their help. Franklin gave the example of a client at a recently IPO'd tech company who decided to pledge a third of their position, $8 million, to a bank in exchange for instant liquidity of up to 90% of the shares' value. "You get the cash immediately, and then you can immediately diversify that and start doing tax-loss harvesting," Franklin said. This will allow you to generate much higher tax losses than you would if you were just investing with whatever cash you have on hand. Franklin's client was using what's called a variable pre-paid forward, a contract that allows you to delay selling your stock for 3 to 5 years while getting the money now. Of course, there's a risk that the stock price will have gone down in that time, and you could lose money when you repay it. Single-stock exchanges: classic but complicated A classic way to diversify a single stock is to use an exchange fund. An exchange fund allows investors to pool their appreciated shares with other investors' holdings, giving them exposure to a more diversified portfolio without immediately triggering capital gains taxes. The main caveat is that it comes with a seven-year lockup, fees, and sometimes a waitlist, depending on which stock you have. "You almost never can get into them by the position size that you want," Kopelman said. "It's an option, but it's one that I've never had a client do." events.title: Bryan Johnson made a meal delivery service so you can eat like him. Nutritionists have notes.
events.summary: Bryan Johnson is trying to live forever. His latest venture is making it easier for everyone else to follow his longevity diet. Courtesy of Bryan Johnson/Tovala Longevity entrepreneur Bryan Johnson is partnering with a meal delivery service for longevity. The meals are high-protein, high-fiber, and avoid dairy, gluten, and preservatives. Dietitians said it's a good start for healthy eating, but watch the sodium and add a side salad. Bryan Johnson has spent years trying to engineer his way out of aging — measuring his body constantly and spending millions of dollars on a wellness regimen and strict diet. Now, he says he wants to bring his notoriously rigorous Blueprint protocol to the comfort of your home without doing any of that. Johnson is partnering with Tovala, a meal-delivery company, to design meals inspired by his eating philosophy. For roughly $14 per plate, subscribers can get salmon and kale salad, high-fiber snacks, or Johnson's signature " super veggie " — delivered chilled and raw, to be cooked in a Tovala smart oven. If you're wondering how packaged foods could translate Johnson's rigorous wellness regime into benefits for real people, so was he. "We didn't really know what we were getting ourselves into," Johnson told Business Insider. "That put us down the path of testing everything I ate, and looking at all the materials I cook my food in." There were plenty of setbacks along the way, from finding high levels of lead in a supply of lentils to finding workarounds to microplastic-laden packaging, he said. The result "basically solved the problem for someone who says yes to health but doesn't want to put forward a lot of effort, Johnson said. I asked two dietitians to weigh in on whether we can actually eat our way to a longer life via delivery. A Blueprint meal at the push of a button Johnson spends more than 12 hours a day on a strict longevity routine . He said he understands that most of us can't afford that kind of approach. "It's overwhelming, because everywhere you turn there are toxins in your food, you hear conflicting opinions from doctors," he said. The goal of the new venture, in partnership with meal delivery service Tovala, is to bridge the gap between an optimal longevity diet and what actually works in real life for most people (or at least for those who can afford to pay $14 per plate of food). That means combining rigorous standards of Johnson's Blueprint protocol: emphasizing protein and fiber, tightly regulating calorie counts, and scrupulously avoiding more than 100 ingredients on the protocol's "banned" list, such as dairy and refined sugar. Then the real challenge: how to make something like that taste good. "We are threading a pretty fine needle," said Tovala founder and CEO David Rabie, himself a longevity enthusiast, but more moderate than Johnson. David Rabie said he founded the meal company Tovala out of his interest in healthy eating. Courtesy of David Rabie One concession: Johnson doesn't eat animal proteins, but some of the meals contain chicken or fish in hopes of appealing to a more moderate approach to longevity too, Rabie said. "What Bryan does is commendable and so hard for 99.9% of the population to follow with that kind of rigor, where I think some balance can help people eat better most of the time," Rabie said. What dietitians recommend for longevity meals It seems too good to be true that the perfect meal plan for longevity is only a subscription away, so I asked dietitians how the meals stack up to the science of healthy eating. Melissa Hooper, a registered dietitian and founder of Bite-Size Nutrition, said the meals seem fairly balanced and very convenient. However, she cautioned that the Tovala meals are high in sodium, which acts as a preservative in most packaged foods. Too much of it can raise blood pressure , so the American Heart Association recommends limiting sodium intake to 2,300 milligrams per day. The Tovala meals range between 300 mg sodium per serving to 1,000 mg per serving, so consumers may want to adjust the rest of their daily sodium intake accordingly, Hooper told Business Insider. "These could be a lifeline to get something healthy on the table, but people need to have the information to make the best decision for themselves," she told Business Insider. Laurel Santiago, a licensed dietitian-nutritionist and founder of the Integrative Center for Nutrition, said she was impressed by the meals' nutritional content and attention to detail. "I think they nailed a good balance," she told Business Insider. Getting enough protein is key to helping prevent frailty as we age: check. Adequate fiber helps support healthy digestion and ward off chronic illnesses like cancer: check. And nutrients like omega-3 fatty acids help protect brain and heart health as we age. Adding a side salad with olive oil dressing can help round out your daily nutritional intake. fcafotodigital/Getty Images Ingredients like fish, nuts and seeds, and plenty of veggies align with some of the world's healthiest eating plans, like the Mediterranean diet . Both dietitians said they'd supplement the meal delivery with extra veggies — Santiago said she'd add more legumes and fermented foods like yogurt and sauerkraut. The bottom line is that meal delivery can be a tool for healthy eating, especially as a replacement for more processed foods, but it shouldn't be the only thing you rely on. If we want to extend our lifespans, it comes down to decisions we make over and over throughout the day, for weeks, months, and years, so consistency is key. "People do best when they have choices," Santiago said. "Adherence to something that's easy, tasty, and healthier is important." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: 28 Zero-Day Findings in Under Two Days. Is Robotics Security Keeping Pace?
events.summary: This article is brought to you by VicOne . VicOne identified an initial set of 28 zero-day findings in less than two days using AI-assisted research across software and tools supporting the Physical AI ecosystem. These include projects developed or maintained by Google, NVIDIA, and Meta, among others. Based on initial validation, all 28 findings are classified as zero-day vulnerabilities. The count may change following vendor and vulnerability-authority review, and some findings do not yet have CVE tracking numbers. Many of these tools help teams train, simulate, test, and operate robots. Weaknesses in them could influence the models teams build, the test results they trust, and the instructions sent to robots. These findings create two demands for robotics teams: responding as AI helps uncover weaknesses faster , and assessing how each one could affect robot safety and operations . What AI changes about vulnerability discovery Vulnerability discovery involves examining code, tracing how systems communicate, and testing whether a suspected weakness can actually be exploited. AI can accelerate parts of this work, helping researchers analyze more software in less time. Attackers could use similar capabilities. When the weakness is a zero-day — previously unknown and without an available fix — faster discovery can leave teams with little time to respond. While that exposure does not necessarily mean an attack has occurred, teams still need to determine whether they use the affected software and what an attacker could access or change. Where the findings sit across the robot lifecycle VicOne’s findings span three stages of the robotics lifecycle: development and training, simulation and validation, and deployment and runtime. Weaknesses at each stage could affect what a robot learns, how it is tested, and how it is controlled. Figure 1. In this research set, 75% of findings involved development, training, simulation, or validation tools, highlighting risks that can arise before a robot is deployed. VicOne The following scenarios show how a compromised component could influence the robot at each stage. Development and training: Hidden changes can reach the finished robot A team downloads a pretrained model to adapt for its robot. Loading a malicious file could give an attacker access to the training system, allowing changes to training data or the model itself. A manipulated model could behave normally during routine testing but respond incorrectly to a particular object, scene, or command after deployment. The risk can enter through a tool the team trusts, before anyone attacks the robot directly. Simulation and validation: A passing test could give false confidence Importing a compromised scene or robot model could give an attacker access to the simulation environment. With sufficient control, the attacker could alter simulated sensor readings, physical conditions, or test results. A robot could then appear to pass tests that should have exposed unsafe behavior, leading the team to approve it for real-world use on the basis of misleading evidence. Deployment and runtime: Operators could lose visibility or control An attacker could exploit weaknesses to change files that influence motion planning or send malicious map data that crashes the operator’s monitoring display. Compromising a remote-operation computer could also put the instructions sent to the robot at risk. Depending on the system and its safeguards, these weaknesses could alter robot movement or leave operators unable to see what is happening and respond promptly. These are potential consequences and not demonstrated outcomes for every finding. Actual effects depend on the attacker’s access, the system’s design, and whether other safeguards prevent the changes from reaching physical behavior. In a separate demonstration, VicOne researchers provide a concrete example of a weakness affecting a protective function. The researchers exploited a vulnerability to prevent a robot’s remote-stop command from working. The case shows why teams need to test whether safeguards remain effective when the software supporting them is compromised. Video 1. VicOne researchers demonstrate a vulnerability that prevents a robot’s remote-stop command from working. VicOne A published patch still needs to be proven safe AI can shorten the search for weaknesses, but a robotics team still needs to determine whether a fix is safe to deploy. Even after a software maintainer releases a patch, teams must identify affected systems, check compatibility, and verify that the update preserves intended behavior. An earlier successful test remains useful evidence. However, a newly discovered weakness may reveal conditions that test never examined. Three questions can help teams respond: Where do we use the affected software? Include training computers, simulation environments, and deployed robots. What could the weakness change? Assess whether it could affect models, test results, operator visibility, or robot behavior. How do we verify protection? Confirm that the fix addresses the weakness and that the updated system still operates as intended. When immediate updating is impractical, teams may need temporary safeguards, such as restricting access to an affected service, while a validated fix is prepared. From discovery to safer deployment As details from the 28 findings become available through coordinated disclosure, the next step is for robotics manufacturers is to connect each finding to its potential effect on development, deployment, and robot behavior. That work also requires understanding how threats could affect robot behavior and how to protect systems already in operation. VicOne Radeis helps teams identify potential zero-day vulnerabilities, assess AI model and system security, and use simulation to evaluate how these risks could affect robot behavior before deployment. VicOne Rthena supports threat detection and responses within approved policies during operation. Figure 2. Cybersecurity strengthens robot safety evidence throughout the lifecycle. VicOne helps teams test safety limits against manipulation before deployment and monitor the conditions behind safe behavior in operation. VicOne Faster vulnerability discovery matters when teams can turn findings into action: identify what needs attention, verify that safeguards still hold, and confirm that a fix does not introduce new risks. That is how cybersecurity strengthens robot safety as systems continue to change. For a deeper look how cybersecurity can affect robot safety, download our white paper, “ Why Robot Safety Depends on Cybersecurity: Protecting the Information That Safety Decisions Rely On .”

events.title: Chicago Is $55 Billion in Debt, With No End in Sight. It’s a Threat to City Services.
events.summary: Illustration by Matt Rota for ProPublica. Animation by Henrike Lendowski for ProPublica. When the city of Chicago eventually finishes its spending plan for 2027, $3.9 billion will come right off the top.  Taxpayers will have nothing to show for it. Not a single cent of that money will be used to fill a pothole, pick up a can of garbage, pay a firefighter to respond to an emergency or address lead poisoning in children.  Strapped into a straitjacket made up of the city’s debt, there is nothing Chicago’s mayor or City Council can do about it, forced to spend billions every year simply to stay current on the $55 billion it owes to banks and its pension funds.  No other big city will pay more toward its debt this year or next, according to an analysis by WTTW News and ProPublica. This year, $3.6 billion out of a $16.6 billion budget was consumed by debt. New York City, with a population three times the size of Chicago’s and a budget more than seven times as big, has $47 billion in debt backed by tax revenues. Los Angeles, which has approximately 1 million more residents than Chicago but a smaller budget, has $1 billion in debt set to be paid back with taxes, records show. According to all four of the major Wall Street credit-rating agencies, New York’s and Los Angeles’ fiscal health make them much better choices for investors. Chicago’s history of questionable borrowing and budgeting — it chose to either ignore or short its pension payments for years — has undermined its credibility.  Its credit rating now sits just two or three levels above junk status, making the cost of borrowing even more onerous. And the city’s chief financial officer, tasked with managing city debt and relationships with credit agencies, resigned last week in stunning fashion , saying she no longer could continue in the role because it would compromise her “integrity and professional obligations.” She had come from Fitch Ratings, a credit agency, and had been on the job for only three months. Chicago’s Pension Systems Are Less than 50% Funded The city is an outlier among other large cities, where most pensions are at least 75% funded. Note: Most cities have multiple pension funds. This chart displays the range between the pension fund with the least funding and the most funding within each city. Percentages are rounded to the nearest whole number. Source: 2025 city budgets and pension reports (data as of September 2026) Lucas Waldron/ProPublica Options for a financial rescue are limited or unpalatable. Pension obligations, locked in by law and political realities, remain untouchable. There is little public or political appetite to raise property taxes or cut city jobs, particularly among the ranks of police, the city’s largest workforce. A windfall from the city’s still-under-construction casino grows more unlikely than ever.  The office of Mayor Brandon Johnson, who is finishing up his first term in office, blames “reckless financing methods” from past administrations for the city’s financial bind.  “Savings and efficiencies alone cannot solve the city’s persistent structural gap,” the city’s Office of Budget and Management wrote to WTTW and ProPublica in response to questions for this story. In searching for revenue streams, Johnson has sought to impose new taxes on the city’s biggest corporations — an effort that has met stiff resistance. Tackling the pension crisis, the city since 2023 has paid an additional $1 billion into its four pension funds above what is required by state law, records show, an infusion that the city touts as a stabilizing force.  But, like his predecessors, Johnson continues to rely on borrowing. Since taking office in 2023, Johnson has added $1.9 billion to the city’s debt obligations, according to city data. That borrowing has “advanced desperately needed investment in economic development and affordable housing in historically underserved communities on the South and West sides,” according to Johnson’s spokesperson. It also has been used to keep the city functioning. In 2026, for example, Chicago borrowed $166 million to pay firefighters what they were owed for working without a contract — and annual raises — for four years. Officials acknowledged they failed to set enough cash aside annually to cover those widely anticipated costs. The city borrowed an additional $267 million to cover the soaring cost of lawsuits alleging Chicago police officers committed a wide range of misconduct.  In some cases, the Johnson administration has negotiated agreements with its lenders that allow the city to pay only interest for several years, backloading its debt burden. Chicago’s Debt Payments Were the Largest Category of the City’s Budget in 2026 Note: The aviation budget funds the operation of Chicago’s airports, O’Hare International and Midway International. Source: 2026 Chicago city budget Lucas Waldron/ProPublica With so much of the city budget dedicated to debt and pensions — and more cordoned off by federal and state laws that mandate spending for specific purposes, such as transportation —  Chicago officials get to decide how to spend just one-third of its annual budget, records show.  The result for residents: Restaurant inspections are lagging. Complaints about crumbling sidewalks and injuries from those hazards pile up, without timely repairs. The city’s Public Health Department doesn’t have enough caseworkers to handle the intensive intervention needed for children suffering from lead poisoning.   The budget pressures are unrelenting. In August, Johnson announced another borrowing plan to fix a budget shortfall that emerged midyear. He blamed the City Council for overestimating the impact of new revenue streams while his council foes accused him of continuing a pattern of questionable borrowing habits.  Amid the finger-pointing, Johnson acknowledged the bind facing his administration and the city as a whole. “We cannot continue to budget by searching for loose change in the couch,” he said. “We cannot continue to budget by searching for loose change in the couch.” Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson Watching the annual struggles of city officials to climb out of its money pit leaves many residents feeling more than a little uneasy about what comes next. “It is the feeling that people get when they max out their credit card and they’re barely paying the minimum,” said Alderperson Andre Vasquez, who represents the 40th Ward and speaks often of growing up in a family that struggled to pay the rent every month. “You’re behind on your utilities. So you get mail every month, letting you know you’re behind.  “And at some point, you’re not even gonna open the envelope anymore, because the feeling of dread, even trying to see it, is a challenging one. That’s how people in Chicago feel.” Unhealthy Fallout When Johnson ran for mayor in 2023, he repeatedly emphasized his commitment to invest in  the city’s neighborho

events.title: More Americans see DC as safe, poll finds
events.summary: More Americans now say Washington, DC, is safe than have said so in 36 years, a statistic that the White House will likely view as a testament to President Donald Trump’s federal crime crackdown in the nation’s capital. Sixty-four percent of US adults currently view DC as a safe place, according to Gallup, a 12-point increase since 2023. That’s been driven by Republicans: In 2023, 77% of Democrats and only 29% of Republicans said DC was safe; today 70% of Democrats and 63% of Republicans say so. The poll was taken before a recent shooting in DC’s Logan Circle made national headlines. Crime has generally been on the decline in DC, though at least one study found that Trump’s National Guard deployment had minimal effect on violent crime. Another city seeing its highest perceived safety rating since 1990: New York City. — Morgan Chalfant
