events.title: Democrats plan probes into Africa minerals deals
events.summary: Democrats plan to use their incoming majorities to investigate possible corruption in the Trump administration’s critical minerals deals in Africa, after months of what they said was administration stonewalling of their inquiries about the negotiations. Democrats have a mandate to “open formal investigations and commission public reports to map which individuals and companies are receiving lucrative critical-minerals deals,” Rep. Jonathan Jackson, D-Ill., told Semafor. Jackson, along with Reps. Linda Sánchez, D-Calif., and Jared Huffman, D-Calif., led an August letter to four agencies pressing them on the pacts, which Jackson said were struck in near-total secrecy. The administration’s response “dodged almost all of the questions we asked,” he said. Sánchez called the response “little more than something AI would write,” accusing the Republican majority of refusing “to conduct any oversight” of Trump’s trade deals. “That changes in January,” she said. Democrats are also targeting a reported State Department threat to withhold HIV aid to push Zambia into a minerals deal back in March. Using lifesaving aid “to extract unrelated economic concessions is what Russia, Iran, or [China] have traditionally done,” said Rep. Jimmy Panetta, D-Calif., who has separately pressed Secretary of State Marco Rubio for details on the new global health agreements the US has signed with 36 countries . A State Department spokesperson said “our health assistance is not conditional on any commercial agreements,” adding that the health pacts contain nothing related to critical minerals. “As the president has said, he’s willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans,” White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said. “If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people.” — Adrian Elimian

events.title: Avoid this Black Friday scam - how to check it's a real deal
events.summary: Published 16 November 2026, 00:50 GMT This month's Black Friday and the tax return deadline at the end of January are both opportunities for fraudsters to scam you. That's because people are more likely to expect emails, texts and other correspondence at this time of year. Fraudsters will use the dates to impersonate genuine organisations and retailers by pushing victims towards fake websites to steal personal information. Here's how to spot a scam and how you can avoid being caught out. Is it really HMRC? Here's how to tell If you are self-employed or have more than one source of income you will need to file a tax return by the end of January. Fraudsters seize on this deadline to blitz people with messages that look like they are official and from the UK's tax authority, HMRC. Any such calls or messages should be ignored, but you can also check whether an email , external , text message , external or phone call , external claiming to be from HMRC is genuine. "Reporting scams helps us shut them down and protect others," adds Lucy Pike, HMRC's chief security officer. New figures from HMRC, shared with the BBC, show that it received 95,340 reports of suspected scams in the year to the end of October. There were 900 reports of one specific scam which used emails containing a malicious attachment which directed customers to a fake gov.uk webpage designed to steal personal and financial information. To avoid being caught out, HMRC says: it never contacts people by email, text or phone to tell them they are due a refund or ask them to claim one it never asks for personal or financial information by email or text message it never leaves threatening voicemails about legal action or arrest Is it a real deal? Here's how to check In the run-up to Black Friday you may be looking around for discounts, but fraudsters will impersonate genuine retailers to steal personal details or take payment for a product that will never be delivered. Kirsty Adams, a fraud and scams expert at High Street bank Barclays, says make sure you pause before you buy. "When you're scrolling on the sofa and a countdown timer starts ticking, or a deal pops up in your feed from an account that looks just like a brand you trust, it's easy to get swept up and pay before you've had a chance to check. "No deal is worth rushing for. So take a moment before you buy." The bank also advises doing these four things: Pause and check , rather than being blinded by a countdown timer Pay safely using a credit or debit card via a trusted payment service, not a bank transfer to a stranger Open an official website or app yourself rather than clicking on links in emails, ads or social posts Talk to a friend, family or your bank if you think something does not feel right, and calling your bank straight away if you think you've been scammed Doing these things now will help you save money at Christmas Published 7 days ago Don't fall for this - how to protect yourself from AI scams Published 19 October Watch our pick of standout clips from across the BBC 0:39 ‘That win is a statement’: Tuchel on defeating Spain. 00:00:39, play video ‘That win is a statement’: Tuchel on defeating Spain 1:17 'It changed everything': Fire survivor speaks out. 00:01:17, play video 'It changed everything': Fire survivor speaks out 0:59 What are people emergency stockpiling? Here's how to check In the run-up to Black Friday you may be looking around for discounts, but fraudsters will impersonate genuine retailers to steal personal details or take payment for a product that will never be delivered. Kirsty Adams, a fraud and scams expert at High Street bank Barclays, says make sure you pause before you buy. "When you're scrolling on the sofa and a countdown timer starts ticking, or a deal pops up in your feed from an account that looks just like a brand you trust, it's easy to get swept up and pay before you've had a chance to check. "No deal is worth rushing for. So take a moment before you buy." The bank also advises doing these four things: Pause and check , rather than being blinded by a countdown timer Pay safely using a credit or debit card via a trusted payment service, not a bank transfer to a stranger Open an official website or app yourself rather than clicking on links in emails, ads or social posts Talk to a friend, family or your bank if you think something does not feel right, and calling your bank straight away if you think you've been scammed Doing these things now will help you save money at Christmas Published 7 days ago Don't fall for this - how to protect yourself from AI scams Published 19 October Watch our pick of standout clips from across the BBC 0:39 ‘That win is a statement’: Tuchel on defeating Spain. 00:00:39, play video ‘That win is a statement’: Tuchel on defeating Spain 1:17 'It changed everything': Fire survivor speaks out. 00:01:17, play video 'It changed everything': Fire survivor speaks out 0:59 What are people emergency stockpiling? events.title: Pro-tech initiative adds Biden, Fetterman advisers
events.summary: The tech association Chamber of Progress is expanding an initiative launched last year to improve the relationship between the tech industry and Democrats, adding a former adviser to former President Joe Biden and former aide to Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., as senior advisers. Steve Benjamin, Biden’s former director of the White House Office of Public Engagement, is joining the Blue Horizon Project, along with former Fetterman chief of staff Krysta Juris, according to an announcement shared first with Semafor. The group is trying to steer the incoming Democrat-controlled Congress away from heavily regulating and investigating the tech industry; a poll it commissioned from Morning Consult found 84% of voters want Democrats to focus on fighting inflation rather than regulating AI and technology. “Tech and Democrats had a long honeymoon in the Obama era. There was a divorce in the Biden era, and now Democrats have to craft a relationship that’s somewhere in between,” Adam Kovacevich, CEO of Chamber of Progress, told Semafor. The group is among a handful trying to influence Democrats as they take power and weigh policy positions ahead of 2028. Who Decides, an outfit founded by unsuccessful New York congressional candidate Alex Bores that is calling for more stringent AI regulation, is already organizing across battleground states.

events.title: Democrats debate who gets oversight of AI
events.summary: Democrats are debating who will have a piece of investigating and overseeing AI and chip export controls next Congress in the wake of the controversy enveloping Nvidia. Incoming House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Rep. Greg Meeks, D-N.Y., is floating creating a subpanel on chips and AI, and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has said Meeks and incoming Intelligence Committee Chair Rep. Jim Himes, D-Conn., are taking the lead on the Nvidia fallout. But other committees have jurisdiction and also want to lead on AI — including the House Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, or Science, Space and Technology Committees. “It seems like every chairman … or chairwoman is wanting a piece of the pie with AI now,” grumbled one congressional aide, who questioned how that would work logistically, “considering it’s going to be spread out over — how many different committees?” One solution to settle the jurisdictional issues would be to set up a select panel overseeing AI, though a key committee chair has already registered his opposition to that idea. It’s also possible that multiple committees will pursue their own investigative efforts within their jurisdictions anyway, regardless of the turf wars that creates. — Nicholas Wu and Ashley Gold

events.title: Antimicrobial resistance could kill 39 million people over 25 years: WHO
events.summary: UN’s health agency says growing resistance to antibiotics and other medicines are threatening the ‘future of modern medicine’. The World Health Organization (WHO) has warned that growing antimicrobial resistance could cause 39 million deaths over the next 25 years as it threatens to make routine surgery and childbirth life-threatening. Senior officials from the United Nations health agency said on Monday progress in prevention, diagnosis and the appropriate use of antibiotics remained too slow to meet global targets. list 1 of 3 Kenya discharges last Ebola patient, awaits disease-free status list 2 of 3 ‘Horrific crime’: Gaza doctor killed as Israel expands war on healthcare list 3 of 3 With every rainfall, Gaza risks losing access to power and healthcare “Antibiotic resistance – but broadly, we are talking about antimicrobial resistance, or AMR – is widespread and threatening the future of modern medicine,” Jean-Pierre Nyemazi, acting director of the WHO’s AMR department, told a virtual conference of the 6th Annual Global Media Forum on AMR. “Unlike COVID-19, which was very visible, drug-resistant infections have been taking people’s lives for years without us noticing it and raising the alarm as we should,” he said. In 2021 alone, it was directly responsible for more than one million deaths and linked to about 4.7 million others, according to WHO figures. An investigation into the progress of the fight against antimicrobial resistance in 183 countries this year revealed that nearly nine in 10 countries had a national action plan against the phenomenon. In 2017, the figure was just about four in 10. Pravasha Prakash, an AMR technical officer with the global health agency, said only 42 countries – less than one in five – had a plan that was financed, implemented and monitored. “Countries are moving forward in every step, but progress still needs to be speeded up to reach the 2030 targets,” she added. The latest global surveillance data show that, in 2023, one in every six laboratory-confirmed bacterial infections flagged to the WHO was resistant to antibiotics used to treat it. Sylvia Bertagnolo, head of surveillance for AMR at the WHO, said, “Without testing, clinicians must treat without knowing the cause of infection or which antibiotic will work.” The WHO announced the release of two new tools designed to help countries strengthen diagnostic capabilities. The first defines the tests that should be available at every level of the healthcare system, from primary care centres to referral hospitals. The second compiles 73 laboratory procedures, from sample collection to the identification of pathogens and antibiotic susceptibility testing. The agency added that infection prevention, vaccination, improved access to water and sanitation, and the appropriate use of antimicrobials are the main levers to combat the issue.

events.title: Three of the Financial Sins That Left Chicago $55 Billion in Debt — and Counting
events.summary: Matt Rota for ProPublica Chicago’s finances have long been strained by soaring pension expenses, spiraling personnel costs and a massive amount of debt. Budget deficits and financial crises now arrive with regularity, as city leaders face crucial decisions on how to dig out of this financial mess.  The track record of decision-making within City Hall suggests that avoiding hard choices for expediency leads to trouble.  The city must spend billions every year from its main account — known as its corporate fund — to keep current on the $55 billion it owes to banks and its pension funds. The debt consists of $19 billion in loan payments that must be repaid by revenue from property and sales taxes as well as $36 billion to ensure former employees get retirement benefits. The city also borrows money to make improvements to its water and sewer systems and to fund operations at its airports, but that debt is repaid with fees, not money from the corporate fund.  Here are three of the big decisions Chicago officials have made over the years that dug the city into such a massive financial hole. Pension Holiday Snowballs Into Peril In 2000, the city’s pensions were 85% funded, which meant the funds could easily pay benefits to employees as they retired, records show. But a series of decisions in both Chicago and the Illinois capital of Springfield unraveled that strong position, leading to the current mountain of $36.4 billion in pension debt. First, the twin blows of the “dot-com” bubble bursting in 2000 and the Great Recession in 2007 wiped out nearly $16 billion from those funds.  Around the same time came a self-inflicted blow. In 2005, the state legislature, at the request of then Chicago Mayor Richard M. Daley, passed legislation allowing the city to contribute less every year than what was actually needed to pay retirees. As a result, in 2006 and 2007, Daley was able to stop making annual contributions to four pension funds for police officers, firefighters, laborers and municipal employees. He received near-unanimous support from the Chicago City Council. Daley, who was mayor from 1989 through 2011, declined to comment for this story. Former Chicago Mayor Richard M. Daley in 2006 Julio Cortez/AP Daley’s “pension holiday” meant the city could balance its budget without a politically perilous property tax hike. But that maneuver laid the foundation of the current pension crisis facing the city.   In 2010, having seen the financial fallout from the pension legislation, state legislators passed a law that banned city officials from taking another pension holiday by setting a firm schedule for the city to pay back its skipped payments — no excuses allowed. Two of Chicago’s pension funds must be funded at a 90% level by 2055, with the other two hitting that mark by 2058, according to state law. This requirement caused a spike in the city’s annual payments. Trying to ease Chicago’s snowballing pension burdens, lawmakers passed a new measure reducing the retirement benefits offered to state employees who began work on or after January 1, 2011. But that revised law touched off a new set of problems. The well-intentioned effort to reduce costs actually reduced pension benefits too drastically. Under federal law, public sector pension funds must pay workers no less than what they would have earned if they paid into Social Security. In 2021 and 2025, lawmakers agreed to change the law and ensure that first responders — police and firefighters — in Illinois are paid at least the minimum required by law.  Fixing those funds will cost Chicago an additional $11 billion to get to the 90% funded level required by state law over the next three decades, according to city projections. Gov. JB Pritzker signed the legislation over the objections of city officials. Long-Term Lease, Long-Lasting Regrets Facing big deficits in 2008 in the wake of the Great Recession, Daley and the City Council found what they thought was a creative solution to the city’s financial woes.  They would lease the city’s parking meters to a conglomerate of investment funds for 75 years in return for $1.5 billion up front. That massive influx of cash meant no one had to make any hard decisions to fill the city’s budget gap and avoid a politically unpopular property tax increase. A Chicago resident feeds a new parking meter in 2009. The city privatized its parking meters in a $1.1 billion, 75-year deal as a way to get a cash infusion. Charles Rex Arbogast/AP But the deal ended up a loser both politically and financially. The new owners of the meters immediately jacked up the cost to park, infuriating residents. In a matter of months, members of the City Council began regretting their votes, and Daley announced he would not run for reelection. By 2025, the city’s meters generated $2.2 billion in revenue for the investors, with another 58 years still left on the lease. The city considered buying the parking meters back this year, but Mayor Brandon Johnson told reporters “the final purchase price was far too high.” The city would have had to borrow billions to finance the $3.2 billion purchase.  Elected officials across the political spectrum agree that the city would have been much better off raising property taxes instead of leasing the parking meters in 2008. But even as the gap between the city’s revenues and its expenses continues to widen, property tax hikes remain the third rail of Chicago politics. Chicagoans’ property taxes last jumped in 2021, when former Mayor Lori Lightfoot raised them by $93.9 million and passed a budget that automatically hiked property taxes to keep pace with inflation. Johnson campaigned against those automatic property tax increases, forcing Lightfoot to drop a proposal to hike taxes by $42.7 million in 2023, just months before she lost her bid for reelection. The automatic property tax hike was eliminated, even though it could have prevented the city’s credit rating from being downgraded repeatedly and significantly reduced the annual budget gaps. In a postscript to the parking meter debacle, Chicago Parking Meters LLC sold the meters contract earlier this year to an investment firm, triggering a one-time payment to the city of $75 million. The City Council and Johnson then battled over how best to use that money for pension costs, creating a temporary hole in the 2027 city budget. The Financial Toll of Police Misconduct The 2014 police murder of 17-year-old Laquan McDonald changed nearly every aspect of City Hall politics around policing. Despite decades of scandals, misconduct and brutality, the Police Department had managed to fend off reform. But that ended with McDonald’s death, even as city leaders continued to fear a backlash from residents concerned about crime rates and a politically powerful police union. events.title: AI is reshaping banking jobs – but its ability to drive profits remains unclear
events.summary: Banks are expanding AI across operations, customer service and compliance while shifting some employees toward higher-value work. Barclays plans 5,000 job cuts in 2026, while recruiters and analysts say demand is moving toward AI, software engineering and data skills. Lenders can point to efficiency gains and business value, but analysts say separately identifiable AI-driven revenue remains difficult to isolate. Banks' third-quarter results have brought their use of artificial intelligence into sharper focus, as lenders automate routine work, reshape hiring and test whether productivity gains can translate into revenue growth. This earnings season, Barclays unveiled layoffs in certain functions where AI is being deployed; while UniCredit and Santander said technology was freeing employees for higher-value work and improving processes. It comes as U.S. giants such as JPMorgan Chase and Goldman Sachs make similar changes in staffing and workflows. But as banks pursue efficiency savings, strategists say evidence that AI is generating material, demonstrable revenue gains from it remains harder to pin down. UniCredit CEO Andrea Orcel called AI an "opportunity to accelerate" that was allowing a shift toward more commercial, higher-value work and greater client engagement. Orcel said the Italian lender — which reported its best-ever quarterly profit of 3.3 billion euros — is using the technology to "get us to the next level." Orcel called AI "a lever that we didn't anticipate we would have, and working extremely well," on CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Nov. 9. Santander said AI initiatives generated 194 million euros in business value in the first nine months of 2026. AI is now being embedded in "all the processes that we are conducting at the bank," said Chief Financial Officer José García Cantera. "AI basically helps, at least for now, decrease low value-added processes, and the company employees can then focus on more value-added processes — this affects both revenue and costs," Cantera told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Oct. 28. "It's difficult to just to say how much comes from AI, but clearly AI is improving the quality of our services to clients, is helping us in asset quality, in cost management, and is having clearly a very positive impact." Dutch lender ABN AMRO is using AI to support anti-money-laundering checks and expanding its partnership with Infosys to modernize its technology, while preserving human judgement, CEO Marguerite Bérard said in the bank's third-quarter results on Nov. 11. "These improvements make the bank easier to run and scale, and help colleagues spend more time on activities that create value for clients," she said. Some lenders announced big headcount reductions during the third quarter, which are "partly, but not solely, due to AI," said Andrew Stimpson, managing director and head of European banks research at KBW. "The cuts have tended to come from back-office and support functions rather than the front office," Stimpson told CNBC via email. Barclays said it plans to cut 5,000 jobs — about 5% of its workforce — in 2026. Roughly 60% of the reductions will affect support functions, including developer roles, the British lender said in its third-quarter earnings update, though it sought to emphasize that AI is not responsible for all the cuts. The Financial Times reported on Oct. 7 that HSBC could cut around half of management and specialist roles, and as many as 70% of financial adviser roles, in its U.K. wealth business as AI reshapes how it serves clients. Goldman Sachs said it intends to "constrain headcount growth" and cut a limited number of jobs. JPMorgan managers have been told to avoid hiring as the bank deploys AI across its businesses, CFO Jeremy Barnum told analysts in the lender's third-quarter earnings call. Revenue growth remains a bigger test A KBW study published in September examined AI use across European banks. Customer service — including chatbots and sorting customer requests — was the most frequently cited use case, followed by behind-the-scenes functions such as operations, identity checks and preventing financial crime. Cost savings remain the most commonly cited goal: just under half of the use cases KBW tracked were aimed at cutting costs or improving efficiency. The report found banks are increasingly exploring ways to grow revenue, while noting AI is not yet seen as a major driver of profits. Wealth management and advisory are emerging as key tests of whether AI can boost bank revenues, rather than only lower costs, analysts say. Banks seem "fairly aligned" that they can do this in wealth management, where AI could enable advisors "to serve a larger number of clients as AI makes onboarding and reporting much more efficient," said Stimpson. Sophia Whitbread, an analyst at Ninety One, said the evidence is still strongest for AI improving service, engagement and employee productivity, rather than demonstrably generating revenue.

events.title: We don't need no education platform evolution. Hey, Redmond, leave those kids alone
events.summary: "Give me the child until he is seven, and I will give you the man." This saying about the importance of influence in early education is variously attributed either to St Ignatius of Loyola, founder of the Jesuits, or Aristotle, depending on whether you wanted to entrust your very young son to Catholic priests or ancient Greeks. Fortunately for both groups, perhaps, neither of them ever said that, even though both certainly believed it. Another group that certainly believes it is the cadre of tech company policy makers, which goes a long way to explain the cultural and legislative backlash to what happens to young people online. The least pernicious and longest established example of the catch 'em young principle is the educational discount for hardware and software. Apple has been the highest profile company to do this, with hardware discounts and aggressively positioned complete service packages for educational institutions, often integrated with funding authorities. If you grow up using a package or platform, it becomes your first tech language and you're likely to become a lifetime customer. Microsoft has also played this long game, seasoned where it can with curriculum integration. Its latest wheeze, described by the company as educational platform evolution is a response to institutions' changing needs, with clearer pathways to adopting and enabling new technologies. Yada, as we say, yada. The evolved platform removes email and Teams from the free student tier, while imposing the requirement for Windows hardware to qualify, along with comprehensive restructuring of higher tiers and storage not necessarily to the advantage of the educators. This is the same sort of evolution to evolving needs as the British Empire brought to natives of other lands. Hello, India. Greetings, Africa. Whassup, America! These warships packed with gun-toting Brits are here to evolve your changing needs in local resource management. Microsoft has realized what Imperial Great Britain adopted as its primary principle. If you can get your future, ahem, customers over a barrel, then not only can you imprint your brand on their minds, you can take their money. You have to come up with some balderdash to cover it, whether it's about civilization and progress or enabling educators to… oh God, these poor fingers can't even type this stuff. Missing completely is the idea that educators' evolving needs may not include spending even more money on basic necessary services when budgets are stretched tight. Moreover, while existing uses of the old tier can stay on it until the end of next year, new sign-ups have to be on the Enhanced Speedy plans. Keen students of history, especially those in the former colonial lands of Eastern North America, may care to refresh their memories of events some 250 years ago. It is quite natural, when being bent over a barrel ceases to be an amusing pastime, to seek a less barrel-shaped position. In this case, the pressure to find alternatives has many elements. As well as the cost, support for Macs and Chromebooks becomes problematic. Both platforms are heavily represented in education at various levels, with the Macbook Neo thundering onto the battlefield with colors flying. Add to that the pressure towards digital sovereignty in Microsoft's own colonial outposts, the accelerants for an Old World version of the Boston Tea Party are only building. We even have a Boston of our very own . It's very nice. Microsoft isn't threatening anyone with guns and rapine, not yet anyway, and the whipping away of free student access to email and Teams only feels like extortion because of the misery it is causing across the sector. It is perfectly legal for Microsoft to cause as much suffering coated in balderdash as it likes. It is also perfectly legal to return the favor by actively seeking a sector-wide migration strategy. There are pioneers to learn from, especially huge multi-state, multi-supply chain organizations like Airbus and the various European governmental entities that are some way down that path already. This growing pool of expertise may be the most important factor in being able to react to Microsoft's efforts to turn education into a science fair experiment in high velocity frog boiling — one where the frog most definitely feels the heat — that and the growing distaste for the antics of American big tech. It's not just the forcing of unwanted technology that makes the barrel increasingly unbearable, nor using that as an excuse to charge more, it's what the companies are actually trying to do in Europe. Google Chromebooks are nice. Google wolves invading your villages because the company illegally erased their ecosystem are not nice. You thought those Wi-Fi snooping Maps cars were bad? The Microsoft educational platform "evolution" is foolhardy, counterproductive, and hugely tone deaf. It will not make it new lifetime customers, it will increase the speed at which its already hostile constituency grows resentment and appetite for radical action. Colonies revolt when the time is right, and empires are lost when arrogance and under-estimation of the situation combine with mismanagement and strategic blindness. The US midterms showed how that storm is blowing in. To choose this time to provoke an entire global sector is functional illiteracy writ large. Perhaps Microsoft should get an education. ®

events.title: ‘Standing on one leg’: IMF chief warns about global economy as AI circular financing hits $1 trillion
events.summary: The global economy is "standing on one leg" — artificial intelligence, IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said. "If this leg wobbles, that can lead to financial stability troubles," Georgieva warned. Circular financing among AI companies has grown to just over $1 trillion, with about two-thirds of it funded by debt, Georgieva said. The global economy is "on the AI leg," International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said Monday, warning that the overdependence on the sector risks the world's financial stability. Georgieva flagged that a "sudden drop in investment confidence and withdrawal from the AI field" could weaken economic growth, speaking with CNBC's JP Ong on the sidelines of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations' summit in the Philippines. "We have a world economy that is standing on one leg on the AI leg. If this leg wobbles, that can lead to financial stability troubles," Georgieva warned. Circular financing among AI companies — where money invested in an AI company ultimately flows back to the investor through purchase orders — has grown to a little over $1 trillion, two-thirds of it funded by debt, the IMF estimates. "It's not a huge size, but it is a rapid increase," Georgieva said. Nvidia Corp , which has seen more than $1 trillion wiped out of its market value over the past month, is at the center of these circular financial deals. The fallout from the chipmaker's former CEO Jensen Huang's extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy, has led to a sell-off in global AI-linked stocks and put the spotlight on the company's role as a key financier of the AI infrastructure buildout. UBS analyst Tim Arcuri estimated in a recent note that an Nvidia financing pullback could easily remove $50 billion or more out of the system, at a time when rising interest rates have already made corporate borrowing more expensive. Georgieva's warning comes as the AI build-out has been a critical engine of growth for the global economy, propping up trade and investment. The IMF raised its 2026 global growth forecast to 3.1% in October as major economies lean on AI investment to power growth otherwise curtailed by the energy crunch caused by the Iran war. The institution estimated that about 40% of the world's workforce will be affected by AI. Capital Economics suggested that as much as 80% of the recent expansion in global exports was concentrated in AI-related goods. Investors' frenzy for AI reflects expectations running ahead of what the technology has proven to deliver, Georgieva said. "We tend to rush ahead," as valuations climb, she said, therefore "some corrections" become necessary. IMF in October had warned that a short-term disappointment could set off a disorderly correction across asset classes: in its worst case scenario, if AI fails to live up to the market's lofty expectations, U.S. equity prices could fall 20% in 2026 and global output end up 1.1% below its baseline estimate by 2028. Global equites, including U.S. chipmakers, have been seeing a bruising sell-off over the past few weeks, with investor appetite for the AI trade facing a fresh test this week ahead of earnings from Nvidia and Anthropic's blockbuster listing. Georgieva on Monday characterized the recent market swings as "orderly," and unlikely to spiral into anything that could undermine the world economy, while urging caution. "We have to be watchful."

events.title: Mubadala and Centerbridge to acquire UK's Canaccord Wealth
events.summary: Abu Dhabi sovereign wealth fund Mubadala Investment Company and US-based Centerbridge Partners have agreed to acquire UK-based Canaccord Wealth in an all-cash transaction. The transaction , which involves Canaccord Genuity’s wealth management business in the UK and Crown Dependencies, gives the business an enterprise value of approximately £1.17 billion ($1.54 billion), Mubadala said in a statement on Monday. Canaccord Wealth provides investment management and financial planning services to private clients, with £43.4 billion in assets under management and administration as of June 30. “We see significant opportunity in a market where growing wealth and increasing financial complexity are driving demand for expert advice,” said Yasir Badri, executive director of financial services at Mubadala. The transaction is expected to close in the first half of 2027, subject to closing conditions and regulatory approvals. Once completed, Mubadala and Centerbridge will jointly own Canaccord Wealth, with the existing management team retaining a “meaningful” ownership interest. “The UK wealth management sector continues to benefit from powerful structural tailwinds, as demand for high quality, personalised financial advice grows alongside increasing complexity in clients’ financial needs,” said Ben Langworthy, senior managing director and head of Europe at Centerbridge. Canaccord Wealth's assets under management and revenue have nearly tripled over the past decade, the statement said. The investment by Mubadala and Centerbridge will support the business’s next phase of growth, it added. Mubadala, which invests on behalf of the Abu Dhabi government, has been steadily expanding its global investment portfolio with a focus on sectors including renewables, mobility, advanced technology, artificial intelligence and life science. Last year, it reported a 17 per cent annual rise in assets to $385 billion, with its portfolio spanning six continents across asset classes. Last month, Mubadala's chief financial officer said it planned to maintain its annual investment with a focus on Asia. “Last year, we invested about $39 billion, which is roughly 10 per cent of our portfolio, and our aim is to continue doing that through all cycles. Every year, we want to deploy that same amount,” Carlos Obeid told the Milken Institute Asia Summit in Singapore. In September, Mubadala announced a significant minority investment in Chinese coffee chain Luckin Coffee alongside its controlling shareholder, Centurium Capital, in a deal worth about $1 billion.

events.title: I moved to Sweden for my wife. I've faced challenges running my US business from here, but life in Sweden is exceptional.
events.summary: When Pat Ahern left the US for Sweden, he had to figure out what it meant for his business. Courtesy of Pat Ahern Pat Ahern moved to Sweden from the US after falling in love during a semester abroad. His wife was building a career in law, and Sweden felt like a better option for her than the US. Ahern has had to learn how to run his business from a new country. It's come with challenges. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Pat Ahern, 33, who moved from Colorado to Stockholm in 2021. The following has been edited for length and clarity. When I did a semester abroad in Sweden in 2014, I told myself I wasn't going to get into a relationship . Then I met Evelina. She was studying law, and we crossed paths at a pub crawl. I was drawn to her compassion, curiosity, sense of humor, and love for nature. We started dating shortly after meeting, and went long-distance when I went back to the US. In 2015, she got an opportunity to study abroad for about a year in Colorado . The business I'd been trying to start in New York was crashing and burning, so I made a fresh start in Colorado to be with her. This story is part of Business Insider's ongoing series, Trailing Spouses. We want to speak to people who have moved countries to support their partner's career. Please fill out this form to share your experience with us. We won't publish any part of your submission without contacting you first. We got to spend more time together over the next few years and wanted to build our life, but as Evelina had a law degree from Sweden, the US didn't seem like a realistic path. Seven years after we met, in 2021, I moved to Sweden , having applied for a residence permit. Evelina and I got married in 2022. In the grand scheme of things, I think I made a pretty small sacrifice by coming over to Sweden . It would've been a pretty massive sacrifice for her if we chose to live in the US. How I run my company from Sweden In order to take my digital marketing agency overseas, I set up a separate business entity in Sweden. I had to pass anti-money-laundering checks to set up a bank account. After seven to eight months, I was legally able to pay myself from the Swedish entity. Thankfully, I'd planned for that and set money aside. Sweden is eight hours ahead of Colorado, where the majority of my team and clients are based, so I mostly have meetings in the latter half of my day. At first, I worked into the evening, typically wrapping up around 8 p.m. When I had my son in 2024, I had to make adjustments. Three days per week, I work until between 8 p.m. and 10 p.m. On Tuesdays, I work from the climbing gym I'm a member of near my son's preschool so I can pick him up, spend the evening with him, and put him to bed. I also take Fridays off so we can go on day trips. Working across time zones has made it more challenging to grab a beer with a friend or go rock climbing after work, but I'm trying to see the positives. I can use the earlier hours of my day to have a more leisurely morning or for deep, focused work. Most weekday mornings, I get my son ready for pre-school and have breakfast with him. Then, I start my day around 10 a.m. I'm taxed more in Sweden, but it feels worth it Sweden is exceptional. I pay more taxes than I would in the US, but feel I'm benefiting. When my son was born, the hospital bill was somewhere around $100. In the US, it would have likely cost several thousand dollars. Plus, parents get to share 480 days of parental leave. The biggest challenge is that Sweden is not a fun place to be in winter. Compared to my experience with Colorado winters , it's colder, windier, and it gets dark far earlier in the day. Traditional Swedish food has grown on me over the years, but I crave good bagels, breakfast burritos, and pizza. Ahern has made friends in Sweden through his wife and his climbing gym. Courtesy of Pat Ahern. Living in Sweden makes it harder for us to see my friends or family in the US. Thankfully, my wife's friends and their partners in Sweden are now my friends, too, and I've met great people through my climbing gym. Most people I've met here have no issues communicating in English, but I'm still trying to learn Swedish. Our son is 2 years old. In the future, flipping back and forth between Sweden and the US may be hard, but I'd still love for our family to have a place to call home in both countries someday. events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Travellers face delays and cancellations at Sydney Airport due to cloud and wind activity Airlines are working to minimise disruptions to passengers. ( ABC News: Billy Cooper ) Airline travellers have experienced major delays at Sydney Airport due to severe weather conditions, with 104 flight cancellations recorded so far. Wind and cloud activity had impacted flights to and from Sydney Airport, with the bulk of cancellations affecting domestic routes. In a statement, an Airservices Australia spokesperson confirmed the delays, recommending passengers check with their airline for flight updates. "Aircraft delays are being experienced in Sydney today with factors including cloud and wind affecting air traffic operations," they said. "Airservices is working with industry to safely manage air traffic demand throughout the day." Wind and cloud activity had impacted flights to and from Sydney Airport. ( ABC News: Billy Cooper ) There was also Virgin Australia ground crew industrial action related to pay and working conditions that took place on Monday. A Virgin Australia spokesperson said there were a number of "contingencies in place" to ensure the industrial action did not impact operations or passengers' travel. The airline was working to minimise the weather-related disruption to guests. Qantas has also experienced disruptions and cancellations across their network. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) A Qantas spokesperson said the adverse weather had resulted in a ground delay program being put in place by Airservices Australia, affecting all airlines. "[This] has caused disruptions and cancellations across our network. A small number of services were cancelled overnight in preparation for the ground delay program," the spokesperson said. "Customers were contacted directly and re-accommodated on alternate flights within 24 hours of their original booking." The airline was working to up-gauge some aircraft to increase capacity and recover cancelled flights. Toula Vorinos's Virgin flight to Melbourne was due to depart Sydney at 10am this morning before it was cancelled. At 8pm she was still waiting at the airport, and had managed to secure a seat on a Jetstar flight leaving at 9:15pm. "We got a notification when we got off the boat on the way to the airport ... and we've been waiting since literally 7:20 this morning," she said. Toula Vorinos's flight was due to leave Sydney at 10am but was cancelled. ( ABC News: Nabil Al-Nashar ) Brownwyn Jackson from the Sunshine Coast was struggling to get accommodation near the airport after the cancellation of her connecting flight to Hobart. "So, have been trying for the past two hours to get another flight that didn't happen, so now trying to get accommodation and an alternative flight tomorrow [Tuesday] hopefully," she said. "I've got accommodation in Hobart booked for a week, so it's quite a waste of money as well, plus the extra night tonight, so very frustrating." Ms Jackson said she received no notice about the disruption, and found out from another passenger when she went to check-in. Barbara Evans is staying in Sydney until she gets a flight home to Launceston. ( ABC News: Nabil Al-Nashar ) Barbara Evans got notified that her evening flight to Launceston was not going ahead while at the airport. She had arrived three hours prior to departure, and has since been trying to work on alternatives to get home. "I can't get down there even via Melbourne tonight. I can't do it on Jetstar tomorrow, I can't do it direct on Virgin tomorrow," she said. "I could do it by going to the Gold Coast and then the Gold Coast to Adelaide … it's totally crazy. Aidan Osmani told the ABC it was "frustrating" after his flight to Brisbane for a work trip was cancelled, and his rescheduled flight was going to the Gold Coast. He had been waiting at the airport for more than an hour-and-a-half. "It is what it is, and just have to be patient and wait," he said.

events.title: Ahmad Tibi elected deputy speaker of Israel’s Knesset
events.summary: Leader of alliance representing Palestinian citizens of Israel says his election is a ‘rightful achievement’ for the Joint List. An Arab member of Israel’s parliament, Ahmad Tibi, the chairman of the Joint List alliance, has been elected deputy speaker of the Knesset. “This is a rightful achievement for the Joint List, which secured 11 seats” in the October 27 elections, Tibi told Al Jazeera on Monday. He added that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir “attempted to prevent my election, but they failed despite their reckless incitement. The Joint List will be represented in all committees.” Tibi, who was elected by his fellow Knesset members on Monday, is the leader of the Ta’al party, which is part of the Joint List. The groups representing Palestinian citizens of Israel – the Joint List and the United Arab List (Ra’am) – made historic electoral gains in last month’s elections, securing a cumulative 19 seats in the 120-member parliament. The bloc endorsed Gadi Eisenkot after President Isaac Herzog tasked him this month with forming the next government . Palestinian-led parties are now focused on using their increased representation to address discrimination and other issues facing their community. Tibi on Sunday called for a criminal investigation into Netanyahu and his aides, accusing them of engaging in “Mafia-style conduct” after an investigative media report accused them of interference in the parliamentary elections. According to Israel’s Channel 12 broadcaster, Netanyahu’s chief of staff, Ido Norden, contacted the police commissioner’s office before the Knesset elections, alleging that three activists from the Ra’am party in southern Israel were carrying large sums of cash and vouchers intended to sway voters. Police relied on information from an intelligence source who was a former employee of the prime minister’s office to arrest the activists after raiding their homes without valid search or arrest warrants, the report said. “No one is above the law, not even Netanyahu,” Tibi said on X. Tibi was first elected to the Knesset in 1999 and previously served as its deputy speaker from 2006 to 2022. Several Arabs have served as deputy speakers of the Knesset. Mansour Abbas, the leader of Ra’am, held the position between 2020 and 2022. Mohammad Barakeh, a former leader of the Hadash party, was appointed in 2003. Other appointed Arab deputy speakers include Abdulmalik Dehamshe, a former Ra’am lawmaker, and Nawaf Massalha, the first Muslim to be appointed to the Knesset in 1988.

events.title: ASEAN to remain supply chain priority for US firms even as Trump’s tariffs face pushback
events.summary: US goods imports from ASEAN increased from US$185.8 billion in 2018 to US$453.6 billion (S$583.8 billion) in 2025. US firms are keeping ASEAN, especially Singapore, as a key supply chain base. They are diversifying away from China to reduce tariff, geopolitical and disruption risks. US imports from ASEAN rose from US$185.8 billion in 2018 to US$453.6 billion in 2025, up about 144%, according to the Office of the United States Trade Representative. Experts say tariff fights may continue, but companies are still strengthening traceability, audits and origin records. Smaller firms may return to China if South-east Asia loses its tariff advantage. SINGAPORE – The fate of US President Donald Trump’s trade tariffs may remain in limb o for the next two years after his party lost the majority in both houses of Congress, but American manufacturers reliant on Asian imports are not waiting for a resolution. Instead, they are busy bolstering supply chains painstakingly built over recent years to avoid getting blindsided by disruptions from protectionist measures or geopolitical tensions. And as US manufacturers seek to move sourcing of industrial components and supplies to more reliable, trustworthy and quality-conscious exporters, they are increasingly ending up in South-east Asia, including Singapore. US goods imports from ASEAN increased from US$185.8 billion in 2018 to US$453.6 billion (S$583.8 billion) in 2025, representing an increase of about 144%, according to the Office of the United States Trade Representative. When the US-China trade war started in earnest around 2018, large corporations and multinational companies pivoted from a just-in-time strategy to supply-chain resilience. A couple of years later, Covid-19 pandemic disruptions intensified the trend. In more recent years, however, smaller and mid-sized US manufacturers have turned to the just-in-case strategy, as trade disruptions turned into chaos amid Trump’s new and harsher tariffs, geopolitical conflicts and unending uncertainty over costs and pricing power. “Our clients aren’t unwinding diversification,” said Joseph Jurken, founder and managing director of US supply chain management firm The ABC Group. “They’re making it origin-defensible” to withstand US Customs scrutiny on tariff avoidance. US consultant Baker McKenzie believes the Democratic Party will use its congressional majority to try to undo certain tariffs. However, enacting legislation impervious to a presidential veto will require Republican support. While congressional committees may hold oversight hearings on how tariffs drive up consumer prices, trade enforcement and tariffs targeting unfair trade and China will continue to enjoy bipartisan support, it noted. “A Democratic-led Congress will likely push for tighter technology export restrictions, particularly regarding advanced semiconductors and artificial intelligence, alongside broader limits on US investment in China,” Baker McKenzie said in a post-midterm commentary. In an interview with The Straits Times, Jurken said his firm is gradually adding to its offering qualified suppliers across South-east Asia, including Singapore, for clients looking to diversify outside of China. He added that India is becoming an increasingly important ex-China market. The ABC Group is a Milwaukee-based supply chain management firm that runs sourcing, quality control and supplier management in Asia for mid-market US manufacturers. It manages more than US$350 million in supply chain spend across six Asian markets. In the past few years in Singapore alone, ABC has helped insulate the supply chains of several clients from China-specific risks and disruptions in areas such as precision watch movements, complex injection mouldings, food and beverage processing, and high-end LED lighting. Jurken said: “With competition between the US and China intensifying around AI and robotics , markets like Singapore provide advanced manufacturing capabilities along with a way to reduce exposure to geopolitical risk in a single country.” However, for more price-conscious clients looking for low-end manufacturing products, Vietnam, Thailand and India remain in focus, he added. In Malaysia, factories in Johor with links to Singapore are also getting a lot of attention. While Jurken launched ABC only in 2021, he has been in the business of helping American companies navigate Asia for more than three decades. He said that cracks in the decades-old sourcing and supply management models had always been there. Tariffs and other trade distortions from 2018 onwards made them impossible to ignore. “The tariffs helped us broaden our market reach. It was the impetus for American firms to listen to why they should have a China-plus-one initiative,” he added. In fact, even before the US-China trade war began, ABC had started looking for alternative suppliers across South-east Asia.

events.title: China confirms Xi-Trump-Putin historic summit. What will be on the agenda?
events.summary: The talks are expected to focus on issues including nuclear non-proliferation, the Middle East war, trade policies and, possibly, the Ukraine war. The three-way summit among the three nations is unprecedented. "The ability to bring Putin and Trump to the table, a first-among-equals scenario, will deliver much of the political benefit" for Beijing: analyst. China confirmed Monday that President Xi Jinping will meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump in Shenzhen on Thursday, setting up the first-ever gathering of the three leaders. That confirmation from a spokesperson at China's Foreign Ministry follows announcements from Moscow and the White House. The Wall Street Journal had reported last month that Putin had proposed a three-way sit-down in an attempt to negotiate an end to the four-year war in Ukraine. While the summit among the three nations, on the sidelines of the APEC meeting in Shenzhen, is unprecedented, the leaders have held bilateral meetings over the years. Xi has met with Trump three times since October last year and more than 40 times with Putin since becoming president in 2013. Trump and Putin have met in person on several occasions, including a visit to Alaska by the Russian leader in August 2025. "For Xi, just the ability to bring Putin and Trump to the table, a first among equals scenario, will deliver much of the political benefit even before the discussions begin," said Peter Alexander, Shanghai-based managing director at Z-Ben Advisors. Trump has departed Washington, D.C. for a four-day trip to Asia that also includes a stop in the Philippines. The main hurdle to the first-of-its-kind summit now appears to be "a disagreement over the agenda," said Neo Wang, chief China strategist at Evercore ISI. The White House signaled the U.S. intention to prioritize talks over nuclear non-proliferation and the Middle East war, while downplaying the prospects of engaging in talks over Ukraine — a topic high on Moscow's agenda. "He [Trump] will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world , whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," Olivia Wales, a White House spokeswoman, told reporters on a briefing call . The president will raise the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran in the meeting but is not expected to bring up Russia's war in Ukraine, the official said. China has no interest in engaging in nuclear disarmament talks until it achieves parity with the U.S. in about 10 years, said David Roche, strategist at Quantum Strategy. Putin's position on the war appears unwavering, with the Russian president telling U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff in a meeting in Moscow last week that Europe should "figure out" whether "they want peace or war." The meeting came a day after an earlier round of talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine wrapped up in Abu Dhabi. Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov said last week the talks in Shenzhen would continue the diplomatic efforts aimed at reaching a negotiated settlement to the Ukraine war, according to state-controlled local media Russia Today. The summit will likely yield little concrete result, but presents an "almost 100% photo op" that lifts China's status and power at the top table, said Roche, while Trump's political standing slides. Nvidia and the chip-smuggling issues involving a suspected Chinese spy will stay off the agenda, as Trump steers clear of thorny issues where he is unlikely to claim success. China and Russia could turn more aggressive with their military ambitions over the next two years if they perceive Trump as politically weakened, Brookings Institution senior fellow Robert Kagan told CNBC earlier this month, following the dramatic defeat of Trump's Republican Party in the midterm election. China did not specify what will be discussed at the three leaders' meeting in Monday's statement. "Xi may be inclined to do Putin a favor by showing up, given close strategic ties," said Wang. But a joint statement on Ukraine territory, security arrangements or sanctions against Russia appears unlikely, he said, as it would leave Beijing "more exposed to political scrutiny and accountability." A U.S.-China trade truce set to expire in January is likely to be on the table, with analysts largely expecting an extension despite signs of growing friction in the bilateral relationship. Aside from an immediate extension, leaders may also look to assess "whether a more durable framework for a rebalancing of U.S.–China trade relations can be established," said Carlos Casanova, senior economist for Asia at UBP. U.S. trade deficit with China remains substantial, with Beijing's exports to Washington recording double-digit growth for most of this year, from last year's low base. Narrowing that deficit will be central to Washington's call for a more balanced trade, Casanova said.

events.title: Indonesian rupiah falls to record low as Fed bets boost dollar
events.summary: The rupiah dropped as much as 0.4% to 18,271 per US dollar on Nov 16. The Indonesian rupiah hit a record low of 18,271 per US dollar as a stronger dollar and higher Fed rate bets hit the currency. Investor worries grew over President Prabowo Subianto’s policy uncertainty, key policymaker exits, and MSCI’s warning of a possible market downgrade. Bank Indonesia said it will stay in markets to support stability, and it is expected to keep its policy rate unchanged on Nov 18. The Indonesian rupiah fell to a fresh record low, pressured by a stronger dollar amid hawkish US Federal Reserve expectations, lingering worries over domestic political stability and a potential market downgrade. The rupiah dropped as much as 0.4% to 18,271 per US dollar on Nov 16 . The currency has weakened about 9% in 2026 to underperform regional peers. Investors have soured on the nation’s assets in 2026 due to concerns over President Prabowo Subianto’s policy uncertainty, the exits of several key policymakers and MSCI’s warning that it could downgrade Indonesia’s equity market to standalone status. Most recently, the resignation of Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka compounded those worries, while growing bets on Fed interest rate hikes boosted the dollar and further pressured the rupiah. Bank Indonesia (BI) has said that it will remain present in the markets to maintain the rupiah stability. It regularly intervened in the currency’s spot market as well as offshore and onshore non-deliverable forwards. The central bank has also been buying government bonds in the secondary market to stem volatility. The central bank is expected to keep its policy rate unchanged on Nov 18 as the rupiah’s decline reflects tighter global financial conditions and bets on faster Fed rate hikes, according to Jeffrey Zhang, an emerging market strategist at Credit Agricole CIB. “We expect BI would judge the recent rupiah move to be in line with fundamentals, and don’t expect it to deviate from the current monetary policy stance,” he said. events.title: DWP glitch threatens my partner’s leave to remain
events.summary: Government department admits it is making a mistake that affects his immigration status but says it can’t put it right The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) is knowingly paying me too much local housing allowance because of a system glitch and it could have serious implications for my partner’s immigration status. I am entitled to shared accommodation allowance as I am under 35 and claim universal credit. However, the DWP is paying me the higher one-bedroom rate for couples. Although we co-habit, my partner is an international student subject to immigration control and is not entitled to public funds. The DWP knows this, but insists a “recognised system defect” means it’s unable to implement the correct calculation. It told me that, until a technical solution is introduced, the system will continue calculating at the higher rate, and staff have been told not to correct accounts manually. It claims I will not be required to refund overpayments, but I’m more concerned about the wider implications for him. Your concerns are understandable. For the past 18 months, you have been receiving the higher rate (now £790 a month) because your partner lives with you, instead of the £586 to which you are entitled. That’s an overpayment of more than £3,600 and counting. If someone subject to immigration control benefits from public funds to which they are not entitled, the Home Office could curtail their leave to remain. You have been trying from the outset to correct the calculation. Your efforts were undermined by a tribunal last year which ruled your partner’s living arrangements entitled you to the higher rate. You appealed and in April another tribunal agreed a mistake had been made. It ordered your allowance be recalculated. When the DWP failed to do this, you involved your MP. That’s when you learned from the DWP of this extraordinary defect that prevents claims such as yours being automatically recalculated. Even more extraordinary was the “operational guidance” preventing staff from making the changes themselves. I submitted a freedom of information request asking how many claimants are affected and how much has been erroneously paid, but was told the information would be too expensive to collate. Almost certainly not as expensive as the sums being expended on ineligible recipients who do not wish to receive them. I asked the Home Office whether the issue might compromise the status of people in your partner’s situation, but it referred me back to the DWP. Despite having insisted it cannot manually override the system, the DWP did just that when I questioned it. It says: “We are aware of this issue, which involves an extremely small number of people. We will correct PJ’s case so she receives the right amount, and are working to ensure customers do not experience a similar issue.” I was assured that no one will be asked to refund the overpayments. events.title: Qantas strands Christmas Island students on mainland after cancellations
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Qantas cancellations leave remote island residents stranded on mainland Qantas operates the only air services between Christmas Island, the Cocos (Keeling) Islands and the Australian mainland. ( ABC News: Billy Cooper ) An ongoing series of Qantas cancellations have left residents on Christmas Island and the Cocos (Keeling) Islands outraged. Twenty-five students from Christmas Island are among those stranded by the cancellations. Qantas says delays have been unavoidable for safety reasons. A group of school students are among residents left stranded on the Australian mainland after several weeks of Qantas flight cancellations to the country's most remote inhabited territories. Residents of Christmas Island and the Cocos (Keeling) Islands are reliant on the national carrier for their sole freight and transport link with Western Australia. But the delays have outraged residents of both islands, with some accusing Qantas of neglecting the critical route. A group of 25 Christmas Island students were part of those affected by the most recent disruptions, and have been stranded in Perth for two days. They were participating in a school camp on the Cocos (Keeling) Islands, but found themselves diverted 2,700 kilometres away to Perth during the return journey. "Our kids weren't packed to go to the mainland," Christmas Islander Avin McKnight said. His son, Callum, is now staying with a relative. "They had no phones because part of school camp regulations was they weren't able to take their phones," Mr McKnight said. A spokesperson from the Department of Education said Qantas was providing accommodation for students and accompanying staff, while some had opted to stay with family. The students are expected to board a recovery flight home tomorrow. Avin McKnight's son Callum (right) has been stuck in Perth. ( Supplied: Avin McKnight ) Two days of flights to and from Perth were grounded last week due to forecast low-lying cloud, Qantas said. Another landed in Cocos only, skipping its layover in Christmas Island to return to the mainland. In the month prior, about half of flights were delayed or rescheduled for various reasons. A Qantas spokesperson said recent weather had proven a challenge. "The monsoon season is the most challenging time for flying from the mainland to the Indian Ocean Territories," the spokesperson said. "We thank customers for their patience; however, we will always prioritise safety over schedule." It adds to existing tensions between islanders and Qantas, which slashed baggage allowances and increased prices earlier this year. Mr McKnight, a Christmas Island resident of 30 years, said the problem had grown worse since Qantas took over the flights contract from Virgin Australia last year. "Everyone's just really had a real kick in the guts this weekend and it's just not good enough for that airline," he said. Hundreds of islanders gathered on both islands to protest about luggage cuts and price increases in September. ( Supplied: Khaliesha Amin ) Other residents took to social media to voice complaints over lost bookings, accommodation and hire cars. Christmas islander Mark Stein said three consecutive cancellations had forced him to push a specialist medical appointment. "[Qantas] should really remove the spirit of Australia from the side of the plane, because the Australian spirit is to try and give something a crack." Christmas Island relies on twice weekly flights for access to the mainland. ( Supplied: Chris Bray Photography ) Last week, a Productivity Commission interim report counted Christmas and Cocos (Keeling) Islands as two communities most impacted by skyrocketing regional airfares . Skyrocketing regional airfares hurting patients Fears FIFO specialists will soon need to pass rising flight costs onto vulnerable country patients. It urged the federal government to reform subsidy arrangements like those in place on the Indian Ocean Territories to ensure they provide better value for money. Indian Ocean Territories administrator Farzian Zainal said she was urgently seeking a meeting with Qantas. "Reliable air services are essential for our community and I understand the consequences extend well beyond travel inconvenience," she said. "It is important that the community has confidence in the air services it relies on, and that these concerns are heard and appropriately addressed.

The Department for Infrastructure and Transport's checks were prompted by a call from the Transport Minister's chief of staff on September 11 shortly after he met with the lawyer preparing the court claim. The opposition has used a parliamentary committee to question whether "critical information" was left out in that call between the minister's office and the department. The company, Career Boss Australia, had its contract to supply workers on the South Road upgrade suspended on October 18, after it was revealed in the media to be the subject of a civil claim alleging bikie Jamie Brown and another man had attempted to coerce the transfer of company shares. The Supreme Court claim was lodged on October 12 by businessman Robert Cammarano, who is claiming full ownership of Career Boss Australia. Robert Cammarano outside an Adelaide court. ( ABC News ) Five weeks before the court case was publicised, Mr Cammarano's lawyer, Scott Jelbert, met with Transport Minister Joe Szakacs's chief of staff Daniel Wills and Child Protection Minister Alice Rolls. At the September 11 meeting, according to accounts from both Mr Jelbert and the government, Mr Jelbert raised matters regarding the Torrens to Darlington (T2D) project, the Career Boss contract, Jamie Brown, the impending court action and a car wash in Malvern. The car wash, which Mr Cammarano claims to part-own, was destroyed in March after three firebombings. The ABC is not suggesting the destruction of the car wash is linked to any of the parties listed in the civil case, only that it was raised by Mr Jelbert at the September 11 meeting. Straight after the meeting, Mr Wills called Transport Department executive Paula Norman. Ms Norman said Mr Wills asked her to check with the private sector consortium leading the project, the T2D Alliance, whether "Jamie Brown had been a shareholder and whether Career Boss had raised any contractual issues with the T2D Alliance". Paula Norman appeared before a parliamentary committee. ( ABC News ) Ms Norman said Mr Wills did not pass on any mention of firebombings. "The advice that I got was to check for a shareholding related to Jamie Brown who was a bikie … and had any of these allegations or contractual issues been raised directly to the Alliance," she told parliament's budget and finance committee on Monday. Ms Norman said she phoned the general manager of the T2D Alliance, Stephen Shaddock, to investigate these two things and heard back on September 14. "He advised me that Jamie Brown was not a shareholder and, more importantly, that there were no contractual issues raised by Career Boss directly with the Alliance," Ms Norman said. Opposition questions information chain During the hearing, Liberal Party MLC Heidi Girolamo suggested to Ms Norman that Mr Wills and Ms Rolls did not pass on "pretty critical information" about firebombings that "may have changed the way you approached things going forward". Ms Norman replied that she was responsible for checking whether contractual issues with Career Boss Australia had been raised with the Alliance. "Career Boss Australia, if they had those allegations or any issues relating to the contract, should have raised it directly with the Alliance," she said.

events.title: What Is Acoustic Micro Imaging? A Quick Guide To This Inspection Process
events.summary: We all know how important inspection is for advanced packaging. Not only are these processes critical for ensuring higher yield, but they’re also integral for maintaining device reliability. As the industry pushes for smaller features and tighter spacing, even the smallest defects can pose major challenges. For instance, delaminations and air gaps can be detrimental in a market that demands increasingly complex devices. Such defects will lead to electrical or mechanical failures down the road. One technology that’s mitigating these issues is acoustic micro imaging (AMI). AMI is a high-frequency ultrasound technology, and it’s being used by the industry as an inspection method. How AMI works At the core of AMI technology is a transducer, or a device that turns energy from one form to another. It starts with a pulse of electrical energy, then converts it to mechanical energy, or a high-frequency ultrasound wave. Because ultrasound doesn’t travel through air, this allows inspectors to obtain clear images of gaps and delaminations in the device that could otherwise be difficult to see. However, the transducers used for AMI are not all the same. Each transducer handles a specific frequency, and they’re chosen based on the sample that needs to be inspected. By moving the transducer across the sample, the inspector can generate multiple images that can then be analyzed by the AMI software. Through this analysis, the inspector can choose to accept or reject parts based on the number of defects the package is found to have. So, how do these defects typically present themselves? The biggest difference between ideal and defective samples is that some defective samples will have very clear air gaps. However, another common defect is thinning of the attach material on solder pads. When this material is too thin, any stress that would be put on the device could lead to delamination. An uneven solder or thermal interface material (TIM) layer may also indicate a larger problem with the build process. When to use AMI – inspection, destructive testing, and X-rays With the ability to gather so much information without damaging the device, why would anyone choose to perform a destructive test to identify a defect, rather than simply use AMI inspection to check for them? One reason is for R&D purposes. Oftentimes, companies want to ensure that a process is fully developed before integrating it into their production cycle, and a destructive test can confirm proof of concept for AMI. An example of this in action is a standard capacitor inspection. New capacitor companies will often require a destructive test to confirm the presence of voids or delaminations found by the AMI software. Once the destructive proof of concept has been completed, the company can then integrate the software into their inspection process. There are some key differences between AMI and its transmission technology counterpart, which is more comparable to X-ray. Whereas AMI is an ultrasound technology, transmission scanning uses both a sending and receiving transducer positioned above and below the sample. Both transmission technology and X-ray create composite images, unlike AMI, which inspects layer-by-layer. Ultrasound and X-ray are complementary technologies. There are some things AMI can do that X-ray can’t, and vice versa. For certain applications, both technologies may be recommended. For example, composite images are preferable for inspecting spherical objects like ball grid arrays. The challenges and future of AMI Although AMI technology has tangible benefits, keeping up with the industry’s rapid pace is a hurdle that AMI must continually overcome. As applications become more complex, AMI software needs to quickly adapt to changing components. For instance, instead of scanning a single flip chip, AMI software could now be required to inspect multi-die stacks. One way this mounting complexity is being addressed is through machine learning algorithms. For example, some wafers have via patterns that look similar or identical to delamination, and humans have typically been responsible for distinguishing them. However, through advancements in machine learning, AMI software can now identify via patterns and exclude those from the defect count. As machine learning becomes more robust, it will open new doors for inspecting increasingly complicated devices. In addition, customer requirements for higher resolution and better throughput are also driving new developments for AMI software. To meet these rising demands, Nordson Test & Inspection developed its automated SpinSAM tool that can inspect four 300mm wafers at a time. Traditionally, acoustic microscopy systems move the transducer in a raster pattern, which is a small grid made up of individual pixels. This approach allows inspectors to collect data at every XY point, but it also requires decelerating to turn the transducer at the end of each line, thereby reducing throughput. Some acoustic microscopes address the need for better throughput by skipping lines and interpolating data points, or by using multiple transducers and stitching images together – both of which have their own drawbacks. In contrast, SpinSAM spins the wafer to move the transducer and the wafer continuously, allowing inspectors to scan each pixel faster, allowing for better throughput without image stitching distortion.
