events.title: Are AI Agents The New Semiconductor IP?
events.summary: Key Takeaways: AI agents could make customized design workflows faster and less expensive to develop. Multi-agent systems introduce new challenges for orchestration, verification, and tool integration. Consumption-based pricing could reshape EDA business models, but trust and proprietary data remain obstacles. AI agents are emerging as a new category of reusable design capability, but with a twist. Rather than providing tightly defined design blocks, agents can be used to explore different options, integrate them, and use those changes to improve designs. At the leading edge, soft IP developers have been customizing their code for large customers for more than a decade to boost performance and/or reduce power. But that customization is typically narrow and costly, and optimizations for one design may not directly transfer to derivative chips — especially multi-die assemblies at the leading edge. Agents, in contrast, can be used to customize different functions with little or no human intervention, and they can self-optimize for different workloads and use cases, and some agents can even adjust for aging hardware. And they can do all of this much faster than a human, even though an experienced engineering team is needed to verify those results and recommendations. “We have in-house specialized AI agents to do different things, to do spec analysis, RTL generation for design, for formal and functional verification, and then CDC linking, and place-and-route,” said William Wang, CEO of ChipAgents . “We provide our optimized agents to a customer, and sometimes a customer builds their own AI agent. But there are some similarities with the IP business. Sometimes we’re specifically building an agent for one customer for a particular flow, which is similar to what happens in the IP business. What’s different is that we can do it in a very short amount of time. With IP, you need 10 months. Our cycle is much shorter because AI agents are very easy to customize. In some cases we can give solutions to the customer the same day.” Those solutions still need to be verified and debugged. But the ability to sort through many different options quickly is an attractive formula, especially with rapid evolution of AI. “I draw parallels to the early 2000s gigahertz wars, where all of a sudden everything was multicore,” said Mo Faisal, CEO of Movellus . “Now we’ve gone from,’ Everything is going to be a GPU,’ to ‘Oh, no, it’s CPUs and GPUs, and this is a one-to-one ratio.’ So effectively we’re going through the same architectural churn that we go through every 10 to 15 years.” The business of agents Business models still need to solidify around agents. but they also need to be flexible enough to evolve at the same pace as the technology. “If you look at how the EDA industry has evolved, we’re not selling perpetual licenses anymore,” said Rob Knoth, senior group director of Strategy & New Ventures at Cadence . “We moved to time-based licenses many years ago. Now we see similar things as agents roll around. They’re hitting up the tool usage even more because they want to find answers quickly, and they’re trying lots of experiments. So putting together more of a consumption-based model is really good because customers know how to use that.” This isn’t a simple transition, though. While the promise of agents is significant, their adoption in chip design will take time. In addition, security and permissions aren’t always well-defined. “There are some things where you’d really rather sell an agent than sell the software,” said Wally Rhines, CEO of Silvaco . “People are trying to figure out if anybody in EDA is actually pricing based upon tokens rather than traditional pricing models. It doesn’t seem like anyone is, but their customers are all talking about it. I’m very much open to selling an agent that will automate [manufacturing equipment] calibration, then jump back to my store of synthetic simulated data against the physical data. We don’t get to see the physical data, but we do know how many tokens our agents consumed. It’s a way that EDA can sell a product, get the benefit, and no one ever sees the underlying data that companies want to keep proprietary.” Divide and conquer, but with caveats One of the big changes with the shift from generative AI to agentic AI is the need for orchestration, and this has broad business implications. Orchestration is basically a blueprint that defines how tasks are assigned, how agents access tools and data, and how that work is coordinated. But it’s especially challenging if multiple agents execute at the same time and their actions overlap. “What’s different about traditional AI and agentic AI is the coordination of multiple agents that are working in parallel, but doing different types of work,” said Robbie Williamson, vice president of customer engineering for cloud AI at Arm . “It’s not like there’s a unique workload that we haven’t seen before. It’s more about how do you coordinate all of these at the CPU level, and have enough bandwidth, memory, etc., to do all of this at scale. Instead of an individual making a request and driving AI, we have computers that can do it much faster. The transition that we see when we talk to hyperscalers is now about what they need from the CPU. With training, that wasn’t as important because you’re just batching the job and waiting for it to come back.” That creates a new hierarchy in the design flow. “What has happened with this multi-agent workflow is that, in an organization, you’re trying to design a chip,” said Prith Banerjee, senior vice president of innovation at Synopsys . “When they’re having a problem with the PPA, some engineers say they know exactly what changes to make to lower the power. They’ll do clock gating. But when you clock gate power, then it changes something else. It increases the area. So some area will come in — and this is exactly what happens in the real world with coordination when multiple people come together to design a system. The human manager is coordinating the activities of the human agents in the world of a multi-agent framework. We have agents for EDA tools and agents for the CAE (computer-aided engineering) tools. events.title: ‘Strangers gave me £2,409’: the online community helping people in debt
events.summary: People come together online to support one another with small voluntary donations to ease financial worries F or some time people struggling with debt have used social media to document what they owe, swap advice and hold themselves accountable as they try to pay it off. Some have built large audiences around their repayment journeys, using views and engagement to generate income through creator payment schemes, livestream gifts and donations from followers towards their debts. Now the idea is being taken a step further: rather than one person building an audience to help clear their own debt, strangers are creating communities to help pay off one another’s. One UK group, the Ripple Effect Project, has grown to nearly 7,000 members on Facebook since launching in September. It aims to bring people together to help those struggling with debt and financial difficulties through small, voluntary donations. Members can put themselves forward for support without having to contribute. Every week one is randomly selected by an online raffle system, their identity and evidence of their debt are privately verified, and then a fundraiser is opened. It lasts for a week and donations are voluntary. A recent fundraiser gained £2,409 from 1,347 donations. Before donations opened, members were told that the recipient had recently graduated and given birth, and wasn’t entitled to maternity pay because she had been a student. She had an operation approaching and was struggling to keep up with her car finance payments. She chose to remain anonymous but agreed to share her circumstances with the group. “The money raised has made such an impact on my overall mental wellbeing, relieving a lot of stress,” she says, adding that she feels privileged to receive “that kind of support from strangers”. Recipients do not have to make an appeal themselves. Once selected, they complete a private form outlining their circumstances and what they are comfortable sharing with other members. The group’s founder then writes a short description explaining their situation and what the money will help with, which the recipient approves before it is shared. The founder also manages the fundraiser and posts updates and reminders. Hope Imogen* got the idea after seeing a US community called Dollar by Dollar Relief on TikTok . Unable to find a British equivalent, she decided to start one herself. “The idea behind the Ripple Effect is that lots of people giving a little, can add up to something significant,” she says. The idea may feel redolent of the social media age, but collective financial support is nothing new. Peter Tutton, the director of policy, research and public affairs at the debt charity StepChange, sees parallels with other communities with a long history of supporting one another, including pardner schemes , and describes the principle as one of “social solidarity”. Pardner, a savings system with deep roots in Caribbean communities, including Britain’s Jamaican community, involves an established group making agreed contributions and taking turns to receive the pooled sum. The Ripple Effect community differs in that changing groups of online strangers make voluntary donations to a randomly selected recipient. Emma*, 48, joined the Ripple Effect Project despite not being in debt herself. Her daughter had left an abusive relationship with significant debts and Emma’s family was able to help, making her think about people without that support. She has donated to all of the fundraisers so far and intends to continue. “I think giving without expecting anything back is something we have forgotten about,” she says. Hope Imogen is exploring whether the group could become a community interest company. “This has started as clearing debt and that’s really important, it remains at the heart of the project, but I don’t think that should limit where it can go,” she says. Social-media fundraising involving chance has attracted regulatory attention. Gambling Commission research published in August examined individual-led lotteries and raffles promoted through social media. The Ripple Effect’s model is different, according to Richard Williams, a partner at Keystone Law, who specialises in gambling law. He says it does not constitute a lottery under the Gambling Act 2005 because no payment is required to participate. Of the Ripple Effect’s model, he says: “If it’s free to participate it isn’t regulated gambling.” How widespread this could become is unclear. In the US, Dollar by Dollar Relief has grown to more than 43,000 Facebook members. As with the Ripple Effect, people are randomly selected and others encouraged to make voluntary contributions, with one recipient selected for every 10,000 members. Selection is restricted to US residents. In Britain, a TikTok account called Debt Help UK is attempting to build a similar community based on small voluntary contributions, but there are few other examples.

events.title: European football body’s plan to go global leaves Fifa on tenterhooks
events.summary: Findings of ‘feasibility study’ into quest for world domination loom with Europe’s wealthiest certain to benefit whatever the outcome I t will be one of the most eagerly anticipated documents in football circles, assuming its contents are ever fully revealed. In September the increasingly powerful European Football Clubs body announced a “feasibility study” into exactly how it can become established on a more global scale, morphing into an organisation that represents clubs all over the world. The study’s findings could, some leading figures in the sport’s governance believe, define football’s long-term future. It has the potential to transform a landscape destabilised by the scandals surrounding Fifa and Gianni Infantino . Once considered a lobby group representing clubs’ interests in the face of domineering governing bodies, EFC has mushroomed into a behemoth with almost 1,000 members that has the potential to supplant them. “Now is the time to create World Football Clubs,” the EFC chair, Nasser Al-Khelaïfi, told delegates at its general assembly in Copenhagen seven weeks ago. The desire to expand exists in plain sight and is perfectly natural, some with a close interest in the process point out, given players and domestic leagues already have their own global representative bodies. However, others warn of “a takeover by stealth” and fear it is merely a fig leaf for the tightening of top European clubs’ influence over the game’s shape. Sources familiar with EFC’s intentions say it is examining how to enter the international football market as a competition organiser, floating the idea of organising more effective tournaments in different formats. That is the role of Fifa or continental organisations such as Uefa and Concacaf but, should leading clubs find a way to forge events of their own, they could reap financial and commercial benefits far beyond those on offer through the confederations. The prospect has some of the established powers on high alert. “You’re starting to see one of the major unspoken fault lines in football open up,” one source says of EFC’s relationship with Uefa, which has become structurally closer in recent years, but is still conducted with an air of high mutual caution. “Friends close, enemies closer” is one characterisation of that relationship. It particularly appears the case now that, amid the wreckage of Infantino’s doomed Fifa Forward Enterprise proposal , all parties find themselves jostling for leverage. Beyond a dramatic increase in funding for the member associations, many senior figures in football have remarked that the biggest long-term consequence of FFE’s failure will be to increase the power of the biggest European clubs. While the former development is already in motion, with Fifa announcing last month that it will hand over an additional $2.7bn (£2.05bn) from its reserves over the next four years, increasing their total investment to $6.35bn (£4.83bn), the latter will not be far behind. That is because EFC’s study is not alone in harbouring huge implications for football’s shape. As revealed in September, a joint venture between EFC and Fifa to run the commercial side of global club competitions like the Club World Cup has been in the works for some time, with the fallout from FFE emerging as the catalyst required to push it through. Multiple sources say the joint venture, similar to the agreement under which Uefa and the EFC have operated European club competitions since 2008 that was formalised with the creation of commercial entity UC3 last year, is ready to proceed pending approval from Infantino. One source with knowledge of the discussions claims that Infantino had been holding up the deal until the FFE scandal broke in July, since when negotiations have accelerated. An announcement could even be made at next month’s Fifa Council meeting in Doha, although waiting until after March’s presidential election at the governing body seems more likely. The joint venture’s contents have caused particular concern within Uefa, whose hierarchy are believed to have made clear their wish that a deal between EFC and Fifa is not rushed through in the current climate. While Uefa have continued to attack Infantino forcibly and are on the verge of backing a candidate to stand against him in next year’s election, EFC has been largely silent since an explosive letter sent to Fifa’s secretary general, Mattias Grafström, by its chief executive, Charlie Marshall, on 31 July. Back then EFC strongly condemned FFE, with the Guardian revealing the body threatened to boycott future Club World Cups (CWC) and withdraw its endorsement of the international match calendar. The sell-off plan was formally dropped the following day.

events.title: Abu Dhabi’s Al Ain Asset Management and Emaar team up for Dh8 billion projects
events.summary: Abu Dhabi’s Al Ain Asset Management is teaming up with Emaar Hospitality to launch five property projects worth Dh8 billion ($2.17 billion) in Abu Dhabi amid continued demand for property in the emirate. The first project, consisting of 452 apartment units and some penthouses, will be built on Al Maryah Island , according to its group chief executive. Timelines and locations of other projects were not disclosed. The five projects will be built in an area spanning 4.7 million square feet, with Al Maryah Island project to be built in one million square feet. The starting price for a one-bedroom home will be Dh3.7 million and “sales will begin very soon,” Rabih Karam told The National. “It’s a standalone project in one of the most strategic areas of Al Maryah Island, directly connected to the mall, ADGM and Cleveland Clinic,” he said. The launch of the new projects comes as demand for property remains strong in the emirate, despite Iran-war-driven uncertainty. A total of 38,483 property transactions worth Dh171.26 billion were registered in Abu Dhabi in the first nine months of 2026, marking a 76.1 per cent increase in value and a 32.8 per cent rise in volume on an annual basis, according to data from the Abu Dhabi Real Estate Centre. A growing number of companies are setting up their base at the ADGM, boosting demand for property in and around the international financial centre, including Reem Island. Reem Island recorded the highest transaction value at Dh29.86 billion during the period, followed by Al Hudayriyat Island (Dh28.62 billion), Al Saadiyat Island (Dh18.69 billion), Yas Island (Dh13.4 billion) and Zayed City (Dh5.36 billion), ADREC data shows. Assets under management at ADGM grew 54 per cent annually in the first six months of 2026, with 49,027 professionals now based at Al Maryah Island and Reem Island, an increase of 34 per cent on the same period last year. “Demand has been amazing in Abu Dhabi. We are witnessing it in our other projects that we are selling currently," Mr Karam said. The company sold two mansions for Dh350 million each in one of its developments on Saadiyat Island this summer, he added. He, however, did not say who bought these villas, but he said, “these are profile of people that they can choose to be any place in the world, and they are choosing to be in UAE and in Abu Dhabi”. The privately owned company is chaired by Sheikh Hamdan bin Zayed. The latest partnership with Emaar follows the launch of Address Beach Resort and Residences in Dubai in JBR by the two companies in 2016, Mr Karam said. The collaboration has since expanded with the launch of Vida Residences Saadiyat Island, which introduced the Vida brand to Abu Dhabi for the first time. The company did not disclose how it planned to fund the new developments. Emaar is looking forward to introducing more of its hospitality brands to Abu Dhabi, Mohamed Alabbar, founder and managing director of Emaar, said in a statement on Monday.

events.title: Russia is letting conscripts dodge army service by joining its drone forces for 1 year
events.summary: Russia also offers large sign-up bonuses for men willing to fight in Ukraine. Contributor/Getty Images A top Moscow official said men in the capital can join Russia's drone forces to avoid conscription. A one-year special contract with the Unmanned Systems Forces would count as their service, he said. Russian men aged 18 to 30 are eligible for a year of mandatory military service, usually in the army. Russia is allowing men in Moscow to skip their standard one-year military conscription by signing a contract with the country's drone force, which the Kremlin seeks to expand quickly. State media outlet TASS cited the capital's military commissar, Maj. Gen. Maxim Loktev, saying that Moscow was piloting the alternative program. Russia requires male citizens aged 18 to 30 to serve a year of military service, which can be deferred or exempted in some cases. Most draftees are sent to the Russian armed forces, though some go to alternatives such as the emergencies ministry or national guard. Loktev said the new program would count a special one-year contract with Russia's Unmanned Systems Forces as fulfillment of compulsory service . Fully established in November 2025, the service branch is Russia's dedicated force for air, land, and sea drone warfare. "Selection is underway for positions as drone operators, engineers, and technicians, with priority given to candidates with experience in IT, electronics, radio engineering, and aeromodelling," Loktev told TASS. There have been concerns in the country, however, about one-year military contracts being renewed indefinitely while the war in Ukraine lasts. Russia's defense ministry did not immediately respond to a comment request sent outside regular business hours. Such contracts might not be what they seem The Kremlin drafts roughly 250,000 to 300,000 conscripts a year, and has pledged that these men would not be sent to the front lines of Ukraine. But some conscripts have been posted to Russian regions close to Ukraine, subject to drone attacks or sabotage. Similar conditions are promised to those who sign up for the Unmanned Systems Forces. Russia has tried recruiting for this branch from universities and colleges, telling students that they would only be posted to rear areas of the war. Opposition media in Russia, however, has repeatedly raised concerns that the country's special one-year military contracts are subject to involuntary renewal. One anti-war lawyer, Artem Klyga, in April posted what he described as a letter from a top military official in the branch, which said that once a soldier's contract was up, his commander was legally given the right, but was not obligated, to discharge him. The letter posted by Klyga has been cited frequently by Russian opposition media. Russia's defense ministry publicly issued instructions in April for commanders to abide by contract terms, but the framework for discharge remains murky since federal law still gives them discretion over a soldier's release. There have also been reports that some who signed such contracts were sent to infantry assault units . The BBC's Russian service reported in June that three students were killed in frontline combat after signing up for the Unmanned Systems Forces. Despite all of this, Russia's Unmanned Systems Forces appears to be recruiting steadily. Ukrainian officials have estimated that it grew from about 10,000 to 20,000 members in November 2025 to over 100,000 troops by April 2026. Russia plans to expand the branch to 210,000 servicemen by 2030, they said. Kyiv has its own Unmanned Systems Forces , established in 2024, comprising elite drone units that work alongside the drone squads of Ukraine's regular armed forces. Led by Maj. Robert "Magyar" Brovdi, it's been credited with about a third of Ukraine's verified drone hits. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Burnham pledges early intervention and ‘benefits backstop’ to tackle youth jobs crisis
events.summary: Prime minister promises ‘root-and-branch rethink’ of support for young people as Milburn report advises sweeping changes to some benefits Andy Burnham: The crisis facing Britain’s young people is politicians’ fault. To fix it, we need a generational response Andy Burnham has pledged to intervene as early as childhood to tackle youth unemployment before a watershed review, promising “a root-and-branch rethink of how we support childhood in the modern world”. Burnham said the government would intervene at all the stages of life in which young people fell behind, and “long before they find themselves out of work and reliant on the state”, including providing more opportunities for vocational training in schools. Writing in the Guardian, the prime minister said ministers’ response to Alan Milburn’s long-awaited review into the crisis of youth unemployment in the UK would not be “a traditional … reform” but “societal and generational”. He promised to reduce the number of Neets – 18- to 24-year-olds not in employment, education or training – which topped a million this year for the first time in more than a decade. Hoping to head off opposition from leftwing MPs in his own party, who rebelled to block Starmer’s welfare changes last summer , Burnham said the government would “invest in our young people and give them a proper chance to get on”, but said the support “will have to come with responsibilities”. “If we give young people genuine opportunities to learn, train and work, we should expect them to take them where they can. Benefits must become the backstop, not the starting point,” said Burnham. Milburn’s long-awaited report on youth unemployment will promise almost half a million job and education opportunities within a decade, but will also advise sweeping changes to the benefits system for under-25s . Some young people will lose their personal independence payments and the right to claim the health element of universal credit, and instead will get a new youth allowance paid at the standard rate of universal credit. The report will also recommend cutting national insurance payments by businesses for employees aged between 21 and 24 for a five-year period, starting in retail and hospitality. The move could cost as much as £5bn, according to the Resolution Foundation thinktank. The government has also announced it will expand a taxpayer-funded scheme aimed at helping young people into work to under-25s who have been claiming benefits for a year. Eligible 18- to 24-year-olds will be “guaranteed” a fully funded, six-month job matched to their skills after 12 months on universal credit. The Liberal Democrats said the six-month offering was worth “very little” without a job at the end of it. Before the publication of the report, Milburn said the government would have to be “candid with people”, that it would take 10 years for the benefits bill to come down, and investment would have to be made upfront. Addressing critics calling for the benefits bill to be immediately slashed, the former health secretary told the BBC’s Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg programme: “There’s no such thing as a free lunch. If you are going to will the ends, you’ve got to will the means. I don’t think there’s a single person in this country who believes that it’s tolerable to have one million young people, aged 16 to 24, who are not in education, employment, or training.” Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, acknowledged that Milburn’s review would have an “element of compulsion” for Neets and there would be people who would receive less in benefits than currently. He said the UK had to become more like countries that had dealt with youth unemployment more successfully, such as the Netherlands, where the youth desk would “literally knock on your door” and offer options of training or work. But he denied that Milburn was proposing a ban on young people claiming health-related benefits. “That’s not what he’s saying. He’s saying if you have a long-term disability, that means you can never work,” he said. “You will actually get more than you will now. He’s saying that if you have extra costs, there will be a benefit you can apply to for extra costs. He’s also saying there should be a local fund for short-term needs, and for other people, he’s saying there should be more support to get into work. Change was necessary, he added, because the number of young people claiming personal independence payments (Pip) had doubled since the start of the decade, while the number of young people on the health element of universal credit had increased by 80%. Burnham hit out at the Conservatives and Reform, who have called for deep and immediate cuts to welfare, with Kemi Badenoch vowing to slash the bill by £36.1bn by 2030 if the party wins the next general election.

events.title: Andy Burnham to say Brexit ‘has not worked’ and he will sign new deal with EU
events.summary: PM to meet European leaders at summit this week aiming to secure agreements that ‘could raise GDP by 0.4%’ Andy Burnham will say on Monday that Brexit “has not worked” and that he will sign a new deal with the EU. It is the latest in a string of comments by the prime minister criticising Brexit, after he told the Welsh Labour conference on Saturday that the UK has “lost more than we gained” through leaving the EU. Burnham is due to meet European leaders at a summit this week and secure agreements that he says could raise GDP by 0.4% – about £17bn – including on food and farming, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme. Speaking at the lord mayor’s banquet in the City of London, Burnham is expected to argue that Boris Johnson’s promise to take back control was not delivered, and that the country was left with a needlessly hard Brexit that created barriers for businesses and damaged its economic potential. “It’s like the Emperor’s New Clothes – where no one is prepared to say the obvious truth. Well, I say it as I see it. And to be frank, the emperor has nothing on,” Burnham will say. “The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we gained.” Burnham is to say he will sign an agreement with the EU, so long as it: Is consistent with the Labour manifesto and the government’s red lines. It improves the Brexit deal and brings it closer to what people thought they were voting for in 2016. And it passes the so-called “ Makerfield test” by delivering real, tangible improvements in people’s everyday lives. “This is a win-win,” Burnham is expected to say. “It illustrates our new approach. Not adversarial. No longer burning bridges – but being constructive and positive, showing that we can come together to confront shared challenges.” However, the EU relations minister, Hamish Falconer, told the BBC on Sunday that the UK could have a “voice in the room” under a new deal with the bloc, but no vote on EU food policies. He added there could well be an “exit clause” in case a future UK government reversed the closer alignment, explaining that the EU was “worried” about the possibility of a future Reform or Conservative government undoing the agreement. The exit clause, previously nicknamed the “Farage clause” , is designed to guard against any the cost of potentially reversing any reset on Friday should the UK’s political landscape change. The cost of infrastructure at the borders has largely been paid for by private companies, including Eurotunnel, but French staff the food checks there, at Calais port and at Boulogne-sur-Mer, where all fish checks take place. Meanwhile, Johnson, the former Conservative prime minister who resigned over Partygate in 2022, has said Britain would “absolutely” vote for Brexit again if Burnham forced another vote on the issue. He told the Telegraph: “It is madness to escalate the Brexit issue as your political priority. He will impale himself and his party on this point, and he needs to move off it because he won’t win – because the reality is that people are not fools.”

events.title: Helsing backer Plural raises $1.1B to fund Europe’s next moonshots
events.summary: Operator-led VC firm Plural has raised €1 billion ($1.1 billion) in new capital, joining a growing cohort of larger European funds that also includes Mundi Ventures’ Kembara and EQT-managed Scaleup Europe Fund . Despite its size, Plural’s fundraise isn’t (only) for a growth fund: two thirds will go to its third early-stage fund, and one third to a new “opportunities” fund making select follow-on investments, TechCrunch learned from Plural partners Khaled Helioui and Carina Namih. The two buckets are fixed, but the check size is not. Plural is “still very committed to being an early stage fund,” Namih said. But Helioui added that some of the early-stage “moonshots” it plans to back may require “raising a couple hundred million” to get off the ground. “Moonshot” is an appropriate term to describe some of Plural’s portfolio highlights, such as Proxima Fusion and The Exploration Company — and its new fund will be looking for equally promising opportunities in energy, AI infrastructure, defense, health, and more. Many of these are capital-intensive, but this is no longer stopping European entrepreneurs, especially second-time founders, and companies like Daniel Ek’s Helsing are “not isolated cases,” said Helioui, who backed the startup’s seed round alongside two Plural partners. “If you’ve built and scaled a company, chances are, you’re more likely to be driven and passionate about having an impact on Europe’s ability to defend itself, procure its own energy, or own its operations and manufacturing, rather than just another app,” he said. With bigger pockets, Plural will be able to keep up longer with the larger and larger rounds its portfolio companies have gone on to raise. It also made an effort to raise more of this capital from Europe, Namih said. While Europe’s institutional LPs were, for a long time, more likely to back banker types than founders hoping to displace those bankers , the current shift towards Europe’s sovereignty and resilience creates tailwinds for Plural, whose office in Tallinn played a key role in its decision to invest in defense tech — including in a missile company, Hypersonica . “The reality is today still, you have a different level of conversation and a different sense of appreciation of the urgency and the criticality of these topics depending on how far from the border to Russia you are,” said Helioui. Two of Plural’s six partners are Estonians, and Skype alumni: Wise cofounder Taavet Hinrikus and Teleport’s Sten Tamkivi. However, there is more to Plural than Tallinn; the fund also has offices in London, where Helioui, Namih and Ian Hogarth are based; and in Paris, where it hired former Uber executive Pierre-Dimitri Gore-Coty as a full-time partner in October 2025. According to a press release, each partner will lead a small number of new investments a year. These companies will then get access to Plural’s growing portfolio support, which already ranges from hiring and communications to finance, Helioui said. That’s another indicator that VC firms in Europe are increasingly starting to look like their U.S. peers. events.title: Small regional town fights back against proposed AI data centre
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Small regional Victorian town fights back against proposed AI data centre Dozens of people travelled from the Ballarat region to protest the proposal of a data centre in Miners Rest. ( Supplied: 60_harvests_left/Instagram ) Thousands of Victorians protested against data centres on Saturday including dozens from the small town of Miners Rest. Miners Rest, north of Ballarat, is home to just under 4,000 people and is the proposed location for a data centre to be constructed by Resi Ventures. Protesters are calling for a statewide moratorium on the construction of AI data centres. The small regional town of Miners Rest, north of Ballarat, is home to just under 4,000 people. Locals say their quiet country life might be about to change after developer Resi Ventures announced to the Australian Stock Exchange in June its intention to build an AI data centre at the town's old quarry. Volunteer firefighter and First Nations man Jedd Willis said the proposal on a 67 hectare plot of land in his town had been overwhelming. "There been a complete lack of care for country which disturbs me as a First Nations person," Mr Willis said. "[The site] has a very valuable resource for water and for firefighting." Jedd Willis (left) says he often uses water from the proposed site to fill firefighting tankers. ( Supplied: 60_harvests_left/Instagram ) Mr Willis, who is a CFA volunteer, said firefighters would often use the water at the proposed site for fighting bushfires. "Along that, the concerns around the lack of water availability across the state as a whole, let alone just this region and with the upcoming fire season being forecasted to be quite treacherous is concerning." On Saturday, dozens of Miners Rest locals joined thousands from across the state at the steps of the state library in Melbourne to protest against the rise of AI data centres in Victoria. As of September this year, there were 50 data centres operating across Victoria with another 18 in the pipeline. Protesters called for a statewide moratorium on their construction. Chris Phillips says the data centre proposed for Miners Rest could be up to 350 metres long. ( Supplied: 60_harvests_left/Instagram ) Secretary for the No Data Centre Miners Rest group, Chris Phillips said the developer had not been open about its plans. He said locals learned about this proposal through the media, rather than consultation with the community. "The benefit to the community would be very little." Mr Phillips said one of his concerns was whether the company would be making use of an aquifer at the site. "There's an aquifer [at the site] that goes many hundreds of kilometres underground and people draw water out of that to grow food like, potato farmers," he said. 'Nervously watching' upcoming election Miners Rest locals say they are concerned about the light and noise pollution the proposed data centre may emit. ( Supplied: 60_harvests_left/Instagram ) Mr Phillips said locals were also concerned about the noise pollution that could come from the centre. "It's going to have a noise transmission of 63 to 65 decibels, which will be heard up to 1 kilometre away, over a constant 24 hours," he said. He said he would be anxiously watching the upcoming election and hoped politicians were listening to the local community. "I think if [politicians] don't listen to people they're going to get a very, very rude shock come this election," he said. "We are very nervously watching and we've had commitments from various political parties but we are also very nervous as to what could happen once the party is elected we could be steam rolled." Locals say there has been no consultation from the developer regarding the proposed data centre. ( Supplied: 60_harvests_left/Instagram ) In a statement Ripon MP, Martha Haylett said Miners Rest families deserved to be consulted before decisions were made that could fundamentally change their local area. "There has been no planning approval, no permits issued, and no meaningful consultation with the community," Ms Haylett said. "A project of this scale and significance cannot be imposed on a community without proper scrutiny, transparency, and engagement." The City of Ballarat said in a statement it had not received any planning applications for the proposal. "While Council officers have had early conversations with the developer, no formal applications have been lodged," it said. "All planning applications are subject to a thorough assessment process." The ABC has contacted Resi Ventures for comment.

events.title: AIX investors urged to register claims before creditors' meeting in December
events.summary: Investors in AIX Investment Group's liquidated unit have been urged to register their claims by December 4, as its liquidators plan to hold the first creditors' meeting four days later. AIX Secure SPV, the Cayman-registered issuer of fixed-income notes linked to Dubai-based AIX Investment Group, was placed into liquidation on October 30 by the Grand Court of the Cayman Islands. The court appointed Angela Barkhouse of Kroll (Cayman) and Michael Byrne of Kroll Middle East Consultancy in the Dubai International Financial Centre as joint official liquidators. Claims must be filed online through the liquidation website, said law firm ALBM Excello Law, whose clients were among the creditors who supported the winding-up petition, in a statement on Monday. The firm is helping AIX investors file claims, appoint proxies and put forward members for the liquidation committee. “Many AIX investors are based in the UAE, and the liquidators have been authorised by the Cayman Islands Court to pursue proceedings before the DIFC Courts and the Dubai courts,” said Sujith Mathew, partner at ALBM Excello Law. “We will continue to monitor developments and keep investors informed as the liquidation progresses.” What went wrong AIX Secure SPV, which was registered in the Cayman Islands on December 9, 2022, was established to issue debt notes to raise funds for investment activities, either directly or through affiliated entities. However, investors alleged that AIX Secure SPV failed to make interest payments when due and filed claims against them. According to the Financial Times , investors have filed claims seeking to recover about $10 million, including two individual claims for almost $2 million and $8 million. The company reportedly suspended payments to thousands of investors after promising annual returns of up to 30 per cent. AIX on its website said that “a period of exceptional geopolitical uncertainty and significant volatility across global financial markets has affected valuations and investment realisation cycles within a limited part of AIX’s product offering”. Last month, the UAE's Capital Market Authority said it was reviewing AIX Financial Consultations' activities after receiving information that the company had delayed or even missed payouts. Without disclosing the details of the information it received or the nature of the review, the CMA said it would keep the matter confidential to ensure a thorough, fair and impartial assessment. Following the Cayman Islands ruling, AIX said it had written to its investors directly, explaining why it was proposing a restructuring rather than a forced sale of assets in the current market conditions. “AIX intends to apply to the court for a stay of the order within the period permitted, and will ask the court to consider in full the alternative to liquidation presented to investors in October,” it said on November 4. Steps for investors The liquidators have “determined that AIX Secure SPV should be treated as insolvent, so the liquidation committee must have between three and five creditors”, the latest statement said. While late claims will still be accepted, those creditors may be shut out of the meeting. “A claim admitted for voting is not yet admitted for payment; the liquidators will assess claims for distribution later,” it added. The liquidators have also asked investors not to visit their offices. According to the letter to creditors, nominations for the liquidation committee close on November 26. Submission of claim information for voting, notice of attendance and proxy forms are due by December 4. The creditors’ meeting will be held virtually on December 8. The committee will advise the liquidators on strategy and approve the basis of their fees.

We call it Who, Me? , we print one every Monday, and you're reading this week's instalment! Today, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Axl" who once worked at a petrol station (aka a gas station for US readers). One Friday afternoon, in the shadow of a holiday weekend, the PC that drove the station's pumps and point of sale stopped working, leaving it unable to operate. Axl called the manufacturer and got the very unwelcome news that a technician could visit on Tuesday at the earliest. As the petrol station was in a spot that would attract a few weekend tourists, the potential losses were substantial, and Axl felt he needed to act. He knew the main computer lived inside a large metal box affixed to a wall, an arrangement that meant electronics and flammable vapors were always kept well apart. The machine's power switch was accessible, so Axl turned it off and on again – and watched the machine come back to life, before shutting itself down five minutes later. That behavior was a strong hint that something was overheating but confirming that theory was not easy because the metal case included a lock (see previous remarks about preventing fires) and Axl didn't have they key. Axl inspected the hinges on the box, found they were held on with screws and was able to remove the lid and access the PC. "Aside from the considerable amount of dust and hair inside, I could see that the CPU fan was not turning," he wrote. "Either it had failed or was not receiving the control signal to cool." The service station had an office out the back. Axl liberated a desk fan, pointed it at the PC, and watched it come alive again. An hour later, the PC was still working, so Axl decided he needed a fix that would last the weekend. "I drove to a local electrical shop and purchased a high speed bathroom extraction fan which I rigged up inside the case, then closed it up best I could with tape and cardboard," he told The Register . That rickety rig kept fuel flowing for three days. "On Tuesday afternoon, the support engineer arrived and I explained how I kept us in business over the weekend," Axl wrote. "He just shrugged his shoulders, smiled and changed the failed fan. I didn't even get the 'It's our kit, leave it alone' lecture." He did get the satisfaction of a job well done. "No one died from an exploding petrol station and the tourists were happy they could go home," he wrote. Have you made a risky fix in a dangerous place? events.title: Labour hire syndicates have 'little fear of consequence', watchdog says
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts NSW anti-slavery commissioner criticises policing of labour hire syndicates exploiting migrants Topic: Business and Industry Regulation The Coffs Coast in NSW is Australia's largest blueberry-growing region. ( ABC Coffs Coast: Claudia Jambor ) The NSW anti-slavery commissioner has released a report into labour hire firms, alleging a slew of illegal practices including extortion, blackmail and more. The report comes only a week after the government responded to 31 recommendations made by the Parliamentary Inquiry into Modern Slavery, which recommended urgent reform to the industry. James Cockayne has referred multiple allegations to NSW Police and the AFP. The New South Wales anti-slavery commissioner says he has seen no sign of proactive, intelligence-led policing of labour hire syndicates accused of exploiting migrant workers in regional NSW. James Cockayne made the comments in his formal response to a parliamentary inquiry into the modern slavery risks faced by temporary migrant workers, which handed down its final report in August. His response, tabled in parliament today, includes allegations that labour hire syndicates in the Riverina and on the Mid North Coast have underpaid workers and been involved in identity theft, money laundering and tax fraud. These cases have been referred to state and federal police. In a statement, NSW Police directed the ABC to the Australian Federal Police, which has also been contacted for comment. Dr Cockayne said the state government was not doing enough to combat issues in the labour hire industry, which supplied migrant workers to farms across the state. "For years, we pretended not to see the elephant in the room. The Committee changed that. Now the task is to move that elephant out of our homes and communities, and out of our supply -chains," Dr Cockayne said in a statement. James Cockayne has released a report on modern slavery. ( ABC News: Abbey Haberecht ) Dr Cockayne said multiple sources told him workers were moved off farms just before surprise inspections. He also reported unverified allegations that some had been moved out of the region involuntarily, for weeks or longer. The report said policing remained reactive, with fewer than 10 per cent of trafficking and modern slavery reports to the AFP reaching prosecution, according to Australian Institute of Criminology figures cited in the report. Only about 1 to 4 per cent end in a trial, guilty plea or conviction. The labour hire industry has been under intense scrutiny from advocates and government agencies for many months. In August, a Four Corners investigation highlighted how migrant workers had been exploited by labour hire firms , with some fruit pickers saying they were treated like "animals". During the same week, the NSW Parliamentary Inquiry into Modern Slavery released its final report , detailing "harrowing stories of mistreatment" faced by workers and making 31 recommendations to the government. The report highlighted exploitation in the Coffs Harbour and Nambucca Valley regions on the Mid North Coast, asking for an investigation into allegations of systemic labour exploitation. In its response on November 9, the state government said it was working with state and federal agencies on a range of measures and had improved information sharing. Meanwhile, agencies have worked together to carry out surprise inspections on farms, while unions and migrant support groups ramped up their presence in affected regions. Migrant workers have seen increased assistance and resources from support organisations in recent months. ( ABC News: Lucy Cooper ) Dr Cockayne recommended police step up proactive investigations into labour hire syndicates and publish their national protocol for combating human trafficking and slavery. He also called for a plan to move high-risk industries away from exploitative labour hire, including support for worker-run cooperatives. He said major buyers need to do due diligence on supply chains to ensure they were not contributing to modern slavery. "Until licensing is in place, responsibility falls squarely on business," Dr Cockayne said. "The biggest players in these supply chains have the most weight with which to leverage the system. "They can afford to use it — and probably should, given big business may soon face criminal penalties for failure to prevent modern slavery in its supply chain. "This is not only about doing the right thing. Responsible businesses are being undercut by operators who cheat workers and dodge tax. Acting now protects workers, and fair competition too.

events.title: Gas starts flowing from Jackdaw after government green light
events.summary: The Jackdaw platform is located 150 miles east of Aberdeen Gas has begun flowing from the Jackdaw gas field, with the UK energy secretary saying it will help to heat millions of homes and businesses this winter. Ministers last month announced the Jackdaw field, which lies 150 miles east of Aberdeen, had been approved after years of uncertainty and a court case. It has now been announced that it has begun producing gas which will start flowing into Britain, according to its operator Adura. The UK government approved production from the gas field in the North Sea last month, amid intense debate about the project's environmental and economic impact. Miliband says he won't resign if government approves Rosebank oil field Published 25 minutes ago Burnham defends Jackdaw decision as Badenoch urges PM to overturn ban on new oil and gas licences Published 21 October Jackdaw is operated by Adura under a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian state energy firm Equinor. A decision is yet to be taken on whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, which is located off the coast of Shetland in the North Atlantic. Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said: "Last month, I gave Jackdaw the green light and today its gas will start flowing into Britain, thanks to the hard work of the skilled North Sea workers. "It means homegrown gas from this project will help to heat millions of British homes and businesses this winter and beyond, in a boost for our energy security. "It also will help minimise the UK's use of imported higher emission gas as we continue our transition to renewables and nuclear." Claire Mueller, Jackdaw project director at Adura, said the gas field was "now helping to power Britain". She added: "At a time of considerable uncertainty around the world, Jackdaw will provide secure energy from our own waters to heat British homes and power our economy, while reducing our reliance on imports with higher emissions. "Jackdaw also demonstrates what can be achieved when Britain makes pragmatic, evidence-led decisions about the energy it needs, while properly accounting for our climate responsibilities." Mueller said the decision was a "positive step towards restoring confidence in the North Sea". She added that Adura was "proud to be producing the oil and gas our country will continue to need for decades". Why is the Jackdaw gas field approval so controversial? Adura has said Jackdaw will provide about 6% of UK gas production, enough to power 1.4 million homes. After imports are included, that amounts to about 2% of total UK demand. The gas will be pumped to the existing Shearwater platform for processing – known as a tie-back in industry terms – before being piped to the St Fergus gas terminal in Aberdeenshire. The UK government said that over its expected 11-year lifespan, Jackdaw would support the UK's gas supply, protect hundreds of jobs and add £2.9bn to the economy. The timeline of Jackdaw and Rosebank The decision to green-light Jackdaw drew criticism from some Labour backbenchers and environmentalists, while Conservatives called on the government to also approve the Rosebank oil field. Both projects were approved for development by the previous Tory government in 2022 and 2023 respectively but these decisions were struck down by the Scottish courts after a challenge from environmental campaigners. This followed a Supreme Court ruling that developers had to account for the climate impact caused by burning fossil fuels in their planning applications. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged to stick to the UK's net zero target despite giving the green light to Jackdaw. He previously said the decision would "significantly strengthen our energy security by increasing domestic gas production by about 6% and support the UK's energy supply for more than a decade". A decision on the larger Rosebank oil project is yet to be made. Protesters gathered outside the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero in Westminster on Wednesday morning The co-leader of the Scottish Greens, Ross Greer, described the Jackdaw approval as "climate vandalism". He said: "It is a devastating betrayal of our children's future and it won't even lower energy bills in the here and now." Environmental campaigners argue that this summer's heatwaves demonstrate the need to tackle climate change by rejecting both Jackdaw and Rosebank. Areeba Hamid, the co-executive director of Greenpeace, said approving Jackdaw was "the wrong decision" in terms of lowering energy bills, providing energy security, and addressing climate change. Oxfam said the government had "drilled straight through the UK's climate commitments" and accused the prime minister of sending "the wrong signal as the impacts of climate change intensify". The charity says the government must commit to not approving any new oil and gas licences, including the proposals for Rosebank.

events.title: India feels less threatened by AI than the US, official says
events.summary: Indians see AI as less of a threat than people in the US because fewer workers hold the “cognitive and office-oriented jobs” that the technology could replace, one of the country’s top tech officials said. Young Indians are drawn to technology and see AI as a way to raise productivity, reduce poverty, and help India become a developed country within two decades, S Krishnan, secretary of India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. The gains, he predicts, could touch sectors such as agriculture, education, healthcare, and government. Krishnan told Semafor Deputy Editor-in-Chief Shelly Banjo that AI tools could help advise farmers with the expertise that’s only available to the largest companies, or screen chest X-rays for tuberculosis to enhance the productivity of the stressed healthcare sector. With around 6 million people in IT and related services, Krishnan said India has the workforce that can diffuse the technology throughout the economy. But the constraint, shared in many countries, is that “AI compute is still in short supply and expensive.” Krishnan said India and the US were “pretty close” to a trade deal, with one or two issues left to resolve. “We’d prefer to have it by yesterday, but, yes, as quickly as we can,” he said. Asked about a potential bilateral visit between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and US President Donald Trump, which hasn’t happened in Trump’s second term, he said: “Well, I think they still share a very good relationship.” — J.D. Hey, Redmond, leave those kids alone 4 hours ago Microsoft lifts Indian cloud prices by 15 percent, cuts costs in China 14 hours ago Another Linux kernel developer steps back from some duties due to overload 2 days ago Microsoft has issued version 4.0 of its very own Azure Linux, which it built atop Fedora for the first time and now suggests is ready to run mainstream workloads. Redmond’s history with Linux is long and tangled. Former CEO Steve Ballmer infamously labelled the project a cancer but by 2015 Microsoft had quietly adapted the OS to power some switches in its Azure Cloud. Microsoft then built some of its own Azure services on containers and created a lightweight Linux for them to run in. In 2020, Microsoft released that Linux as CBL-Mariner, largely so that developers who used services like Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) that relied on the OS could access the platform they were building for. In 2022, CBL-Mariner became Azure Linux 2.0, another container-centric lightweight release. Version 3.0 followed in 2024, now billed as ready for “broad Azure usage” with Azure Kubernetes Service. In June 2026, Microsoft announced version 4.0 and billed it as suitable for Azure Virtual Machines, VM Scale Sets, and container images. The big change that made that repositioning possible was basing the OS on Fedora rather than Microsoft’s own Common Base Linux. Microsoft also tuned the Linux kernel – version 6.18 LTS – by adding Hyper-V guest drivers and other features that make it behave well in Azure. It also natively supports tools like Microsoft Defender for Cloud, Azure Monitor, and the Azure CLI, which Microsoft reckons committed Azure users already employ and therefore want to apply to their cloudy Linux workloads. Or as Redmond puts it: “the familiarity of [the] RPM package ecosystem, while adding Azure-native security, compliance, and operational capabilities.” All of those changes add up to an OS that Microsoft says is worth a look “Whether you're running web applications, databases, or GPU-accelerated AI/ML workloads.” Redmond makes that recommendation in part because Azure Linux comes with “no additional OS licensing cost.” Other commercial Linux distributions will cost users money, meaning Microsoft can now make an argument that SUSE and RHEL subscriptions might be superfluous for both AKS users and those who use Azure to host other applications on Linux. events.title: Thrift shop asks shoppers to nominate a charity
events.summary: Julie Rindam (front) and Jeanette Worthington (back) plan to be transparent with donors by having a book in the shop which will evidence where money is going. Shoppers and donors at a new charity shop will be able to help decide which organisations benefit from the money it raises. Twisted Sisters Thrift Store, in Tunstall opened last week, and is inviting customers to nominate causes they would like to support, with a different charity set to receive donations each month. Owner Julie Rindam said the idea came after the closure of a charity shop; she had run for eight years. "The pastor is retiring and it was either another empty shop or I took it on." Rindam said many of the shop's regular donors wanted to continue supporting charitable causes, leading to the idea of allowing the community to decide where the money goes. "All my donators still wanted to drop off to us, so we thought, well, how about a different charity every month?" she said. "We ask all the donators who they'd like us to donate to, so every month it will be a different charity benefiting." Rather than supporting a single organisation, the shop plans to keep a record of suggestions, being completely transparent with customers and donors before selecting a charity at the end of each month. "Everyone who drops off, we ask and we keep a book and every month we'll pick a different charity to benefit from, whether that's City Dogs Home, Cancer Research, Diabetes or other charities," Rindam said. The owner hopes that the store will also be a centre for the community. Shop manager Jeanette Worthington said the approach was designed to ensure local people remained involved in how the money was distributed. As well as raising money for charity, the store also aims to act as a community hub, offering free food, sanitary products, contraception and school uniforms when available. Worthington said supporting local people was just as important as supporting charities. "People know they can come here, it's a safe space," she said. "We will help anybody if we have the time and if we can't do it, we'll say come back at such and such a time." Janet Smart had been a regular donater to the shop before it was taken over by the new team. Regular customer and donor Janet Smart said the shop had become a valuable part of the community. "When I'm decluttering everything, it comes to here because I know they don't charge a lot. People haven't got much money today," she said. "You meet such nice people in here as well." She added that the social side of the shop was equally important. "I think for people on their own, it's nice to be able to come in somewhere and people chat with them." Jack Spencer is managing to find clothes and items that he wouldn't be able to find in more mainstream stores. Shopper Jack Spencer said the store offered affordable options for people who might otherwise struggle to buy certain items. "It feels a lot more personal, a lot more out there. You go in, you don't know what you're going to walk into, it changes constantly," he said. "You might find something that you could have been looking for, but you just couldn't afford it." For Rindam and Worthington, the hope is that both the charities and the local community will benefit. events.title: CNMC Goldmine shares plunge as gold falls below US$4,000
events.summary: SINGAPORE – Shares of CNMC Goldmine Holdings plunged on Nov 16, extending recent losses as gold prices dipped below US$4,000 an ounce following a sell-off in the precious metal. The mainboard-listed mining stock sank nearly 11% to 85 cents at the midday trading break on Nov 16, bringing its losses to about 20.56% over the past five trading sessions and almost 30% over the past month. About 5.5 million shares changed hands during the morning trading session on Nov 16. Spot gold, meanwhile, fell 0.24% to US$3,872 an ounce, as signs that the US Federal Reserve could raise rates weighed on sentiment. This came ahead of remarks by Fed chair Kevin Warsh at a Nov 16 US conference that could offer further clues on the direction of interest rates. Gold has fallen nearly 6% since the start of the year, as elevated US Treasury yields and a stronger greenback dampened demand for the precious metal. Hashim Osman, a research analyst at Phillip Securities Research, attributed CNMC’s share price decline to growing expectations of further US interest rate hikes. This follows stronger-than-expected inflation data last week and consensus among Fed officials that inflation remains too high. “In this environment, the key differentiator among miners is their ability to limit margin erosion as gold prices ease,” he said. Elevated fuel costs remain a concern for investors, particularly for miners investing in exploration and development, he added. CNMC’s net profit rose 17.8% to US$18.6 million (S$23.9 million) for the six months ended June 30, 2026, from US$15.8 million a year earlier. The Singapore-headquartered gold and base metals producer, which operates in Kelantan, Malaysia, generated US$65.2 million in revenue for the first half of 2026, up 23.4% from a year earlier, driven by higher gold, silver and zinc prices. Revenue from gold produced at its flagship Sokor mine’s carbon-in-leach plant rose 32% to US$49.8 million, even as production fell 6% to 11,105 ounces. Including gold produced from lead concentrate at its flotation plant, which is used primarily to recover base metals, the company generated total revenue of US$56.7 million from gold in the first half of 2026, a 27.4% increase from a year earlier. Still, CNMC’s all-in production cost is about US$2,000 per ounce, so margins would still be intact even if gold retreats further.

events.title: Weakening UK electric vehicle targets would hurt car industry, ministers told
events.summary: Exclusive: Experts say watering down ZEV mandate would slow market and hamper efforts to reduce cost of living Moves to weaken the UK’s targets on electric vehicles would hurt the car industry as well as consumers, campaigners and experts have said before a key intervention from government advisers expected this week. The climate change committee (CCC) will write to ministers on Wednesday about the effects of changing the zero emissions vehicle (ZEV) mandate on the cost of living and the UK’s net zero targets. The current mandate stipulates that 80% of new car sales will have to be electric from 2030, and 100% from 2035, but it has been reported that Labour is poised to reduce those targets. Campaigners said the evidence to be examined by the CCC all pointed to consumers losing out from any weakening of the targets. The CCC has kept its deliberations under wraps, but its chair, Nigel Topping, has a long history of advocacy for electric vehicles. He was involved in the automotive sector in various roles for two decades, and has frequently urged carmakers to move faster to electric vehicles, which are more efficient and cheaper to run than their fossil-fuelled counterparts while producing less air pollution and carbon dioxide. He has also long been a champion of UK innovation and engineering, and believes the UK’s target of net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050 is spurring economic growth and creating jobs. He has said: “Our leadership in decarbonisation is driving industrial leadership, which is driving competitiveness and growth.” If the CCC letter is critical of proposals to weaken the ZEV mandate, ministers will face an uphill task to justify such a decision. Doing so would hamper efforts to reduce the cost of living, because it would slow the market for electric cars, which are much cheaper to run , analysts and campaigners say. Filling up a petrol-fuelled car can currently cost more than £100, while an electric vehicle can be fully charged for less than £10. The head of politics at Greenpeace UK, Ami McCarthy, said: “Watering down the current sales targets for EVs would be like driving with the handbrake on. The UK has an upbeat story to tell on electrification but the car industry keeps trying to drag it backwards. “The prime minister was absolutely right in his speech [to the Cop31 UN climate summit on Thursday] when he said we need industry to play their part. Aligning our sales targets with the EU would only slow us down.” Carmakers say the UK’s current targets are too onerous and that they are having to heavily discount vehicles in order to sell enough to meet them. The chief executive of the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders, Mike Hawes, said manufacturers were investing billions in ZEV but that demand remained below the targets. “Regulation mustn’t undermine UK competitiveness or hold back the transition,” he said. “Government must act now, with fundamental change to the targets, backed by ongoing and increased support for consumers, including incentives, affordable charging, and tackling disincentives.”.” One expert, however, pointed out that the UK was exceeding its current sales target by a significant margin, whereas if manufacturers were struggling, the target would be barely met. “That shows it’s nonsense to say they’re discounting heavily,” they said. “EVs are so clearly the future, it is hard to understand why the car industry is not embracing them.” Most of the UK’s cars are sold for export, and sales of EVs are growing strongly in the EU, a major market for manufacturers . Given that Chinese competitors face EU tariffs, the UK could seize an advantage over its rivals if it pushed harder for EVs, the analyst said. Sales of battery-only electric vehicles rose by half last month compared with the same month last year. McCarthy said sales in the UK were strong and benefitting households. “It’s great to see minister Katie White celebrating the fact that an electric vehicle is sold every 52 seconds in the UK,” they said. “While the EU seems to be dropping into second gear, the UK has an opportunity to ensure British companies and consumers reap the rewards. Leading from the front isn’t just good for UK industry. It will help lower the cost of living, increase energy security and reach our climate goals.” A government spokesperson said: “We remain committed to the phase out of all new cars relying solely on petrol and diesel engines by 2030, and to 100% of new car and van sales being zero emission by 2035, and our legally binding net zero targets. “Our consultation on the mandate will not change this and will ensure we are taking a pragmatic and balanced approach to the ZEV transition.” Electric, hybrid and low-emission cars

events.title: I went back to India when my H-1B was rejected. Now I have 2 public companies and am a judge on 'Shark Tank India'.
events.summary: Kunal Bahl's H-1B rejection kickstarted his entrepreneurial journey in India. Kunal Bahl Kunal Bahl's entrepreneurial ambitions in the US were crushed when his H-1B visa was rejected in 2007. He chose to return to India, where he cofounded a company with his high school friend. He's since taken two companies public, invested in over 300 startups, and is a judge on "Shark Tank India". This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Kunal Bahl, the 43-year-old cofounder of the Indian digital commerce holding company AceVector Limited and investment firm Titan Capital. It has been edited for length and clarity. Entrepreneurship was always on the cards for me. An H-1B rejection just fast-tracked it. I grew up in New Delhi, and then I went to the University of Pennsylvania in the US for a program that blended an engineering and business degree. While I was in college, a bunch of big things happened in the tech sphere: Google went public, and Facebook became viral. By 2006, which is when I graduated, it was all the rage. The internet economy was taking off. I had a lot of business ideas, but it became clear that I could not start a company because of my visa status. I was on an F-1 visa , and I first needed to find an employer who could sponsor my H-1B, then lay out a pathway into Silicon Valley. From there, I'd try to start my own company. I interned at Microsoft during my junior year and returned in October 2006 in a full-time role after graduating. Then my H-1B visa petition was rejected While waiting for my H-1B visa selection, I was counting down the days until my Optional Practical Training , a temporary yearlong work authorization after graduation, would expire. I remember vividly that, in June or July of 2007, I got an email that said my H-1B petition had been rejected. For a moment, I didn't understand. It was unfathomable to me that, if I worked at a company like Microsoft, my H-1B visa would not be approved. I checked with the Microsoft team. Looking at their faces, I gathered that there was a finality to the rejection . The company was very nice about the situation, suggesting that I work in the Microsoft India office and try again for the H-1B after a year. At no point had I considered moving back to India . But I gathered myself up and decided that if I go back to my country, I'd work for myself, not for Microsoft. No time wasted starting my company I no longer had the baggage of having to figure out this H-1B situation. I felt liberated because I didn't have to worry about visas or green cards. So I called up my best friend from high school, Rohit Bansal, who was working in a financial institution at the time. We used to sit next to each other in class and talk about starting a business together. I asked if he wanted to do something together. He said, "Great, let's do it." Our company was incorporated on September 12, 2007, a few days before I touched down in India. Building a startup in India in 2007 was a challenge India has a hot startup ecosystem now. That cannot be said of the India of 2007. The country had very few internet users and smartphones, and digital payments were few and far between. Things were pretty dull, to be honest. I was not returning to the promised land or a burgeoning startup ecosystem. Even launching a startup was frowned upon. People would ask, "You guys have a good education, so why didn't you get a job? Does nobody want to hire you?" We started as a physical coupon book business, because Indians love a good value. But getting funding was a challenge. Angel investors weren't common then. We had both saved up a bit from our year working corporate jobs and pooled our savings — about $60,000 in total. That became our seed capital. We stayed with our families for food and accommodation, and worked out of a small office in the basement of a residential building in Delhi's furniture market. We had neighbors complain about people going in and out of the building late, because Rohit and I would work 20 hours a day to get our business off the ground. Our company pivoted from being an online couponing platform like Groupon to one of India's first e-commerce platforms, called Snapdeal. Now we have two publicly listed companies that we spun off from the original coupon book business. We wanted to give back to the startup ecosystem in India, as well. In 2011, once we had built up some capital, we started investing in early-stage startups and formed Titan Capital . Over the last 15 years, we've invested in more than 320 startups, many of which have gone public. I'm now also a judge on Shark Tank India. The India of today is full of opportunity In hindsight, my not getting the H-1B visa was serendipitous, though it hurt at the time. It was part of a larger plan: I had to return to India and help the next generation of founders. It was easy for me to pack up my bags and come back because I wasn't married and didn't have children. And I know it's far more difficult for those who have dependents living with them in the US, like children or parents. So I do empathize with workers facing immigration struggles in the US. That said, India has changed drastically since the time we started our company. India now has a billion internet users. There's ubiquitous smartphone penetration. There are so many coworking spaces for startup founders. There is a high talent density. There is a robust funding ecosystem. The startup tech scene is front of mind for the government. There is no better time to come back to India. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: 'Break-in and rising costs could kill my business'
events.summary: Gordon Kidd says he is struggling with business-related costs and a recent break-in has not helped The owner of a cycle shop says he is considering closing the business after a break-in and soaring costs. Gordon Kidd, who runs Shifnal Cycles, estimates that a burglary last month cost him about £20,000 after three customer bikes and a frame were stolen and the subsequent repairs to his shop. Along with rising bills and a "lack of government support", the former armed forces veteran said the business in Shifnal may not be viable if financial pressures continue. A government spokesperson said that, from next year, businesses such as cycle shops would see their business rates either frozen, reduced or cut to zero, with half of the high-street retailers paying no rates. West Mercia Police said it had received a report of a burglary on 31 October, and an investigation was ongoing. "They stole customers' bikes, which, for me, as a shop owner, is my biggest fear," said Kidd, who was concerned the burglary could affect his reputation. "That might put them [customers] off from using my shop, and that kills a shop." He added: "I've got to do what's financially viable for the business. "I've got to look at another avenue now, and I've got to look at a more cost-effective way of doing it." Burglars stole three cycles and a frame and damaged the shop in the raid Alongside coping with the impact of the burglary, Kidd called on the government to do more to help small businesses. "I don't know how the government expects small businesses to operate and make a living," he said. "We just break even with the repairs side of things, and it's tough." He said the break-in "had not helped whatsoever". "A lot of people probably think that bike shops make a lot of money when we really don't," he said. Kidd, who not only sells cycles but also repairs and services them, told the BBC that the break-in had made him feel angry that his safe space had been invaded. He suffers post-traumatic stress disorder and said the business was "like therapy". "Working on bikes calms me down; it helps me keep in control of my PTSD and my mental health in general." A government spokesperson said: "Corporation tax remains capped, and there are generous tax reliefs offered for hiring young people. "We are also making the business environment work better through our £4.3bn business rates support package, small business plan and action on late payments.
