events.title: Taiwan deputy minister on Jensen Huang scandal: ‘We feel sad’
events.summary: The scandal surrounding former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has sparked a wave of sadness in his native Taiwan, the island’s deputy digital minister said Sunday. Huang had a close relationship with Taiwanese tech companies, meeting with them every year, Isabel Hou said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & the World. “The relationship is very personal,” she told Semafor Editor-in-Chief Ben Smith. “The supply chain leaders, I think, were concerned about how this kind of trust can be replaced. It will be tough.” Those ties went beyond business: Hou referenced a New York Times article in which Huang’s longtime hairstylist admitted he was too upset to sleep , drank a bottle of red wine, and prayed for the former chip CEO after his resignation. “We feel sad,” she added. The Nvidia ordeal has fueled calls in Washington for tighter chip export controls, given Huang’s years of lobbying to sell chips to China, and the revelation that he had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman whom US officials suspect spying for Beijing. US authorities are probing whether Megaspeed, the company the woman formerly led, smuggled Nvidia chips to China. Singapore-based Megaspeed has denied the allegations. US lawmakers from both parties have pushed for tougher export restrictions, and Democrats have opened an inquiry into the Trump administration’s approval of Nvidia’s H200 chip sales to China. Taipei has been aligning its export control policy with the US. Hou said Taiwanese don’t want frontier chips going to China, where they could end up in military equipment aimed at the island. Reading a line prepared by her staff, she called for a policy that’s “precise, predictable, and coordinated with partners.” China, once the destination for the vast majority of Taiwan’s outbound investment, now draws less than 1%, Hou said, as companies expand elsewhere, many in the US. In AI especially, Taiwan needs “trusted partners.” — J.D. Capelouto

events.title: US official says government needs to make a better case for AI
events.summary: The US government has a responsibility to explain AI’s benefits to the public after the midterm elections showed widespread antagonism to the technology, a top State Department official said Sunday. Jacob Helberg, the undersecretary for economic affairs, said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & the World that the election, in which many voters were opposed to AI and data centers, should be seen as an “opportunity.” “The onus really is on everyone serving in government at all levels, local, state, and federal, to do a better job of communicating to the public the opportunity and the upside of this great technology,” Helberg told Semafor Editor-in-Chief Ben Smith. Helberg pointed to data showing that AI has helped prop up the US economy through investment and productivity gains. He said AI hasn’t caused mass job losses, and “we haven’t seen any evidence at all that super intelligence has had an inflationary effect,” using the Trump administration’s preferred alternative term for AI. Competitor obsession Helberg, who has spearheaded the Pax Silica effort with US allies to secure global supply chains for critical industries, also said US global tech policy shouldn’t “obsess” over China. “Great companies don’t try to succeed by obsessing over their competitors,” he said. “One of the temptations in policy roles is you spend so much time studying what competitors do that it almost becomes easy to over-obsess on them.” While Pax Silica is building a bloc of US-allied nations to reduce their dependence on China, Helberg said the effort is intended to be “an America-centric initiative, not a China-centric initiative.” — J.D. events.title: Goldman Sachs predicts ‘sizeable surplus’ for oil market in 2027
events.summary: The Paris-based International Energy Agency said last week the global oil market is set swing to a surplus for the first time since the US-Iran war began. Goldman Sachs says the oil market will face a “sizeable surplus” in 2027, with crude supply minus demand at 2 million barrels a day. It expects Brent to average US$88 a barrel in 2027, then fall to US$78 by year-end as the “risk premium” fades. China’s weak fuel demand may limit prices, and Goldman says its total oil demand likely peaked in 2025. SINGAPORE – The oil market faces a “sizeable surplus” in 2027 that will drag prices lower even as supply risks remain, Goldman Sachs Group said. Crude production minus so-called end-use demand will reach two million barrels a day in 2027, despite accounting for supply disruptions half that size, analysts including Daan Struyven said in a Nov 15 note outlining their base case. Brent futures are expected to average US$88 a barrel in 2027 , easing to US$78 by the year-end “as the risk premium gradually normalises”, they said. The worldwide crude market has been rocked in 2026 by the US-Iran war, which initially choked off regional production before suppliers tapped alternative export routes and restored flows through the Strait of Hormuz. The Paris-based International Energy Agency said last week the global oil market is set to swing to a surplus for the first time since the conflict began. “For 2027, we again expect a contest between high supply disruption risk and increasing market adaptation,” they said. “Under our base case, Middle East supply rises above its 2025 average on ongoing adaptation through ship-to-ship transfers and pipeline additions, while supply growth elsewhere stalls.” China – typically the world’s largest crude importer – is unlikely to prop up prices, with “persistent weakness” in road-fuel usage to scar demand by 400,000 barrels a day, according to the Goldman analysts. All in, “we estimate that China’s total oil demand peaked in 2025”, they added. Brent traded below US$95 a barrel on Nov 16 after dropping more than 1%. The benchmark peaked in 2026 above US$126 a barrel in April, hitting the highest intra-day price since 2022. Year to date, it has averaged about US$91. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Coles investigates cyber attack but provides little detail
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Supermarket group Coles investigates cybersecurity incident but provides little detail Coles advised customers to remain vigilant after disclosing a cybersecurity incident. ( ABC News: Patrick Stone ) Coles says it is investigating a cybersecurity incident but provided little further detail to customers or investors. The supermarket group is looking into a small number of customers experiencing issues with Liquorland click-and-collect. Coles says it will provide updates on the investigation "as appropriate". Supermarket group Coles is investigating a cybersecurity incident, but has provided little detail on what occurred. Coles disclosed the cyber attack in a statement to the stock exchange on Monday morning, saying it is currently not aware of any data being accessed or stolen as a result of the incident. "Based on the findings of our investigation to date, we have not identified any evidence that customer, team or supplier data has been compromised or removed from Coles' systems," the statement read. On its website, Coles Group listed gift cards as working as normal, "no indication" of an impact on Flybuys accounts and no issues identified with Coles Plus, Coles Plus Delivery or QuiteLike subscriptions. However, the retailer said it was looking into a small number of customers experiencing issues with Liquorland click-and-collect, which it was investigating. It said it was working with global cybersecurity experts to "contain and secure the Coles IT environment". Coles says no action needed by customers Coles told investors and customers on Monday morning that it was business as usual for its operations. "Operations continue and customers are able to shop as normal with Coles in stores and online," the company website said. The supermarket group said customers do not need to take any action at this time but advised caution. Woolworths probes reports of drained digital gift cards Woolworths has acknowledged an issue affecting a number of customer e-gift cards and is investigating, with replacement cards among the possible next steps for affected customers. "We advise everyone to take basic online precautions and recommend remaining vigilant to suspicious links, attempts to solicit personal information from you — including by email, phone, text, or post — and potential scam activity," Coles said. "We recommend you regularly update your password with a strong, unique password for your account and not reusing the same password across multiple services." It urged similar caution from suppliers. "We apologise for any concern this may cause our customers and key stakeholders at a time of increasing cyber incidents in Australia and around the world," the company said. In recent weeks, European supermarkets have been hit by IT incidents affecting fridge and freezer temperatures , which were believed to be cyber attacks. Over the weekend, customers of Coles' major rival Woolworths reported digital gift cards being drained by unauthorised transactions . Woolworths told ABC News it was investigating. A number of major Australian corporations have been rocked by cyber attacks and data breaches this year, including Origin Energy . The hacking incident in July left about 900,000 current and former Origin customers' data exposed. Coles said further updates would be provided "as appropriate".

events.title: Czechs gather in big numbers to reject government's plan to overhaul funding of public media
events.summary: Hundreds of thousands of people rallied in Prague against the Czech government's plan to overhaul funding for public broadcasters PRAGUE -- Hundreds of thousands of people rallied in Prague on Sunday against a plan by the government of Czech billionaire Andrej Babiš to overhaul funding for public broadcasters that many say will erode media independence and democracy. The massive protest took place at the capital's Letná Park, where huge crowds gathered during the 1989 Velvet Revolution, which ended more than 40 years of communist rule in the country. The rally, just two days before the anniversary of the 1989 protests, drew an estimated 350,000 people, said Mikuláš Minář, the lead organizer from the Million Moments for Democracy group. They demanded that the government withdraw its plan and expressed concern that Babiš and his coalition partners pose a threat to democracy. “We do witness here something extraordinary today,” Minář said. “It's just a beginning.” Under the plan, the country’s public radio and television broadcasters would be financed from the state budget, replacing the existing system of regular fees paid by individuals, households and businesses. The broadcasters would receive about 15% less money than they do now, which could lead to layoffs, limited production and program cancellations. Critics say the overhaul would give the three-party coalition the means to take control of the media, similar to what populist governments did in Slovakia under Prime Minister Robert Fico and in Hungary, before former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán was ousted from power in April. “We refuse the Slovak scenario,” one protest banner read. “Hands off the media,” said another. One of the protesters, singer Šarka Dumišincová, said that for her “the media represent freedom. And the fact that someone here is trying to control that freedom is unacceptable to me. That’s why I’m here today.” The ruling coalition unexpectedly moved ahead with the plan in the lower house of Parliament on Oct. 24. Its lawmakers limited the opposition's speaking time before voting at 4:36 a.m. to advance the bill through the first of three parliamentary readings. Thousands took to the streets the following day to protest the rushed process, and public media employees went on strike on Nov. 3. The strike was backed by labor unions, universities, students, churches, artists, athletes and international media organizations, among others. “We are here to stand up against the rule by force in the style of 4:36,” Minář said Sunday, referring to the time the bill cleared its first reading. Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech Authorities investigate 'credible' unknown device threat at Illinois plant Microsoft apologizes for email disruption, says AI agents not responsible Media freedom and the rule of law in the Czech Republic were debated Wednesday in the European Parliament. EU Justice Commissioner Michael McGrath said national legislation must ensure that funding for public service iis based on transparent and objective criteria and guarantees "adequate, sustainable and predictable financial resources.” Babiš vowed to press ahead with the plan despite the protests and denied that it would affect media freedom. He returned to power in the Czech Republic after his ANO, or YES, movement, won the country’s election last year and formed a coalition with two small political groups — the anti-migrant and pro-Russian party Freedom and Direct Democracy, and the right-wing Motorists for Themselves. Babiš has opposed some key European Union policies on environment and migration and rejected financial aid for Ukraine and guarantees for EU loans to help it fight the Russian invasion . His government has been under fire from NATO allies for failing to spend enough on defense. Protesters also condemned its defense policy and demanded the resignation of the Freedom party leader, parliamentary Speaker Tomio Okamura, and Defense Minister Jaromír Zůna. The party is in charge of the ministry. "While (Russia's President Vladimir) Putin threatens Europe, the pro-Russian (party) is systematically undermining the state’s defensive capability and endangering national security,” Minář, the main protest organizer, said. Associated Press video journalist Stanislav Hodina contributed to this report. events.title: DBS, JPMorgan launch US-Singapore tokenised deposit service for institutions
events.summary: The solution connects blockchain-based accounts on DBS Token Services and the Blockchain Deposit Account network by JPMorgan’s digital payments unit, Kinexys. DBS and JPMorgan Chase launched a cross-border tokenised deposit service for institutions, allowing 24/7 US dollar transfers between the US and Singapore. Ant International is the first client, using it for global treasury and liquidity management, as firms seek faster payment tools for digital businesses. The move follows wider tokenised money trials and standards work, including a DBS-Citi weekend transfer completed in minutes and Project Bloom under the Monetary Authority of Singapore. SINGAPORE – DBS Bank and JPMorgan Chase on Nov 16 announced the launch of its cross-border tokenised deposit solution, which allows institutions to make 24/7 US dollar transfers between the US and Singapore. The solution connects blockchain-based accounts on DBS Token Services and the Blockchain Deposit Account network by JPMorgan’s digital payments unit Kinexys. Ant International, the global arm of Chinese fintech company Ant, is the first client to use the solution for its global treasury and liquidity management. The announcement comes as financial institutions seek faster liquidity management tools to support digital industries 24/7 such as e-commerce and digital services. For example, a DBS report released on Oct 28 showed that 88% of 422 business leaders surveyed in 11 markets were already deploying or piloting tokenised money use cases. Tokenised money is becoming increasingly mainstream among large corporations seeking access to a wider range of markets and greater liquidity, added the report. Meanwhile, outbound cross-border payment volume in Asia is projected to nearly double to US$24 trillion (S$30.92 trillion) by 2033, from US$13.5 trillion in 2025, based on a report by conference platform Money20/20 and market research provider FXC intelligence. “Tokenised money is moving rapidly from experimentation to delivering live tangible value for clients,” said Rachel Chew, chief operating officer and co-head of digital assets, global transaction services at DBS, Singapore’s largest lender. Over a weekend in September, DBS and Citi announced their successful trial of a US dollar payment between Singapore and the US, using tokenised deposits via the Swift Digital Ledger. The transfer was completed in minutes, faster than regular cross-border settlements that can take up to two business days due to weekend closures and time-zone differences. The launch of the cross-border tokenised deposit service follows an interoperability framework by DBS and Kinexys released in November 2025. More broadly, the two banks are also co-leading a token interoperability work group under Project Bloom, an industry initiative led by the Monetary Authority of Singapore to enable the safe, seamless and scalable use of tokenised money. events.title: Coles investigates cyber-attack and apologises to customers
events.summary: Supermarket giant says no customer, team or supplier data compromised but recommends updating passwords as a precaution Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Australia’s second-largest retailer has been targeted in a cyber-attack, though it is still too early to tell whether any of its data has been stolen or compromised. Coles revealed the threat on Monday morning, saying it was investigating with support from the Australian Cyber Security Centre and global security experts. “Coles Group Limited is currently investigating a cyber security incident,” the company said in a statement to the stock exchange. “We have not identified any evidence that customer, team or supplier data has been compromised or removed from Coles’ systems. “Operations continue and customers are able to shop as normal with Coles in stores and online.” Coles apologised to its customers for any concerns they might have at “a time of increasing cyber incidents in Australia and around the world”. “We have security measures in place to protect customer and supplier accounts and are continuing to closely monitor our system,” it said. “We recommend you regularly update your password with a strong, unique password for your account and not reuse the same password across multiple services.” Coles also warned customers to be cautious if they received unexpected emails or SMS messages purporting to be from the retailer, and not to click any links. In a separate and unrelated incident, Woolworths said it was aware of reports from customers who purchased compromised e-gift cards. The ABC first reported on Monday some customers had lost hundreds of dollars after buying the company’s Everyday WISH gift cards through its rewards website or app, only to find the sums loaded on to them had been spent by someone else. Some customers told the national broadcaster they had lost up to $500, with transactions showing up at stores in different states to where they purchased the cards. “We are aware of reports of an issue affecting a number of customer e-gift cards and are looking into the matter as a priority,” a Woolworths spokesperson said in a statement. “We recognise the concern this has caused affected customers and we apologise to customers impacted. We encourage any customer who notices a transaction they don’t recognise to contact our Gift Card Support team.” The company says it is working through all reported issues and will look into replacing affected e-gift cards. – Additional reporting by Nick Visser

events.title: China’s slowdown deepens in October as industrial output, retail sales, investment miss estimates
events.summary: Retail sales rose 0.4% from a year ago in October, disappointing analysts' forecast for a 0.8% rise. Industrial output expanded 4.8% from a year earlier, sharply slowing from 5.5% in September, the highest level in five months. For the first ten months of this year, fixed-asset investments, including property and infrastructure, shrank 8.1%, deepening a collapse unprecedented outside the Covid-19 period. China's economic slowdown worsened in October with retail sales, investment and industrial output all missing economists' estimates, as analysts warn a growing reliance on external demand leaves growth more exposed to shocks abroad. Monday's data showed the investment slump deepened and retail sales again lagged industrial output, as consumer spending languished with the property market downturn eroding household wealth for a fifth year. Retail sales, a gauge of consumption, rose 0.4% from a year ago in October, disappointing analysts' forecast for a 0.8% rise, slowing from a six-month high of 1.1% in September. Industrial output expanded 4.8% from a year earlier last month, missing analysts' estimates for 5.3% growth and sharply slowing from 5.5% in September, the highest level in five months. For the first ten months of this year, fixed-asset investments, including property and infrastructure, shrank 8.1%, deepening a collapse plaguing the economy this year that's unprecedented outside the Covid-19 period. That figure marked a significant deterioration compared to analysts' expectations for a 7% decline. The economic malaise also weighed on the labor market. Unemployment inched lower to 5.1% in October, while the jobless rate for those aged between 16 and 24, excluding students, hovered near the highest level in a year, standing at 18% in September. Growth in the world's second-largest economy bounced off three-year lows in the third quarter, expanding 4.5% from a year earlier. Goldman Sachs expects China's economy to slow to 4.6% this year , from 5% expansion in 2025, before easing further to 4.5% in 2027. The Wall Street bank expects the low inflation to extend into next year, with consumer inflation ticking lower to 0.8% this year, 0.5 in 2027. It cited soft domestic demand, abundant aggregate supply, easing commodity-price momentum and potential artificial intelligence disruption risks. Despite the moderation, the projected growth rate still puts the economy on track to achieve Beijing's ambition of doubling 2020 per capita income by 2035, Goldman Sachs said in a note Monday. Subdued consumer inflation and roaring exports paint a picture of an economy increasingly dominant in global markets but struggling to generate prosperity at home. Consumer inflation ticked down to 0.7% in October, its first deceleration after two straight months of increases, while exports surged by a more-than-expected 35.2% . China is on track to surpass last year's record $1.2 trillion trade surplus despite growing trade tensions, with the gap reaching the $1 trillion threshold by October — the fastest it has ever reached that mark. The strong export momentum has largely been driven by global demand for AI-related technology and equipment. Any signs of pullback in the industry could weigh on China's exports, analysts warn. "The market was already worried" about a slowdown in the AI capital-spending cycle even before the Nvidia scandal that put flows of restricted chips to China under renewed scrutiny, said Zhiwei Zhang, president and chief economist at Pinpoint Asset Management. "Now the risk has become even more serious," Zhang said, forecasting further downside risk for global economic growth next year. The increasingly lopsided growth came as major trading partners have ramped up calls for the economy to rebalance. Headwinds on China's export engine could intensify next year, with further trade restrictions from the European Union posing a critical downside risk, Citi Research analysts said. "More EU trade measures targeting China look plausible to us, potentially adding to tensions ahead," the bank said, though Beijing is likely to be open to negotiating "reasonable, practical concessions," such as import pledges, sector-specific deals and value-added tax rebate cuts. — CNBC's Evelyn Cheng contributed to this report.

events.title: Thai GDP growth rebounds as AI drives investments, exports
events.summary: The pickup showed the growing impact of the global AI investment cycle on Thailand, where electronics exports and private investment have surged. BANGKOK – Thailand shed its place as South-east Asia’s slowest-growing major economy in the third quarter, with the artificial intelligence boom powering exports while masking persistent weakness in household spending and tourism. Gross domestic product in the three months through September rose 2.9% from a year earlier, the National Economic and Social Development Council said on Nov 16. That was below the 3.1% median estimate in a Bloomberg survey. Second-quarter growth was restated at 2.4% from 1.9%. The pickup partly reflected a favourable comparison with a year earlier, when US tariffs and a border conflict with Cambodia disrupted trade. But it also showed the growing impact of the global AI investment cycle on Thailand, where electronics exports and private investment have surged. Investment growth accelerated to 11.8% in the third quarter, while exports jumped 18.3%, the council said. Household consumption ticked up just 2.5%, while government spending shrank 1.6%. The economic data put Thailand ahead of the Philippines, which expanded 2.1% in the quarter. The country still trailed most regional peers, with Vietnam growing almost 10% and Indonesia, Singapore and Malaysia all expanding more than 5%. Growth above 3% has become unusual for Thailand, an ageing tiger economy constrained by high household debt and limited fiscal room. The country last grew more than 3% in a quarter in early 2025 and has not recorded annual growth above that level since 2018. The stronger performance comes during a period of unusual political stability. Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul leads one of Thailand’s strongest governing coalitions in decades, giving his administration more room to pursue investment and economic policies even with a no-confidence vote looming next month and street protests simmering. Thailand has also attracted a surge in investment tied to AI, data centres and advanced electronics, while foreign investors have returned to its bonds and stocks. BLOOMBERG

events.title: China’s economy misses forecasts with across-the-board slowdown
events.summary: The People’s Bank of China has signalled caution about cutting interest rates when borrowing demand is already weak. China’s growth weakened across the board in October as consumption and industrial output undershot expectations while investment unexpectedly worsened, in a sign Beijing’s latest stimulus measures have yet to feed through to the economy. Retail sales rose 0.4% from a year ago, far worse than the consensus forecast of 0.8% by economists polled by Bloomberg. That compares with an increase of 1.1% in September. Fixed-asset investment fell 8.1% in the first 10 months of 2026 from the same period in 2025 , lower than the 7% decline expected by economists. Investment dropped 7.2% in the January-September period. Industrial output grew 4.8% in October from a year ago, missing expectations for a 5.3% increase and slowing from September. The figures pointed to a downbeat picture of an economy that’s losing momentum, after Beijing stepped up efforts to bolster growth in late September. Officials rolled out a moderate stimulus package including mortgage subsidies and greater public borrowing quota, while accelerating measures to shore up investment. Separate data on Nov 16 showed residential prices continued to fall in October, extending a slump that has dragged on economic growth for more than five years. Property investment plunged 21.6% in the first 10 months of 2026 from a year earlier, compared with a 20.6% decline in January-September. The economy was “overall stable” and “extended a trend of renewing growth engines and improving its structure,” the National Bureau of Statistics said in a statement. The agency highlighted challenges faced by the economy, include an uncertain global environment, imbalances between supply and demand, as well as difficulties in some businesses’ operation. Despite indications that growth has come under pressure, the urban surveyed jobless rate unexpectedly slipped to 5.1% in October from 5.2% in September. Many economists see the official unemployment gauge as an incomplete reflection of the labour market because it excludes migrant workers who returned to the countryside after losing work. The economy rebounded in the third quarter, with growth reaching the lower end of Beijing’s annual target of 4.5% to 5%. But the recovery remained heavily reliant on overseas demand, with net exports contributing almost 40% of the increase in gross domestic product – the most for any quarter since the start of 2025. That dependence is becoming a bigger risk as questions mount over the sustainability of the global artificial intelligence investment boom, which has powered demand for Chinese electronics and other manufactured goods. A slowdown in exports would increase pressure on domestic consumption and investment to pick up the slack. The October figures will be closely scrutinised by top officials ahead of the Central Economic Work Conference, usually held in the first half of December. The gathering will offer clues on Beijing’s economic priorities for 2027 and the scale of any additional support. Policymakers may lean more heavily on fiscal measures if the economy loses further momentum. The People’s Bank of China has signalled caution about cutting interest rates when borrowing demand is already weak. BLOOMBERG

events.title: A new generation of media will shape the 2028 Democratic primary
events.summary: The Scoop Last week, while shouting out supporters at the Muslim Public Affairs Council gala in Washington, DC, Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed singled out a figure in the crowd for special thanks: the founder of Zeteo, Mehdi Hasan, whose posts and videos pushed back against claims that progressives had underperformed more moderate candidates. Three days later, Mississippi Sen.-elect Scott Colom told the anti-Trump digital outlet MeidasTouch that the network had given him a key boost at a moment when few people believed Mississippi would be in play for a Democratic candidate. “Thank you for giving me the opportunity very early on, when nobody thought Mississippi would be on the radar, to tell my story, tell my message,” Colom said. The first two years of President Donald Trump’s return to power were a waking nightmare for the Democratic Party. But in Trump’s shadow, oppositional media on the left has seen a period of extraordinary growth. Creators like Aaron Parnas, Keith Edwards, and Jack Cocchiarella gained millions of followers railing against Trump on YouTube. Independent media companies like The Bulwark, Crooked Media, and Zeteo gained millions of combined subscriptions on Substack, which grew from a platform largely favored by right-leaning or “heterodox” publishers to one dominated by left-leaning new media outlets and voices. Scarred by Trump’s 2024 podcast tours, Democratic donors are pouring money into the independent media space, and Democratic candidates have new media figures on speed dial. And now this ascendant new media ecosystem is positioning itself to help pick the next Democratic presidential nominee — or at least weed out a few of the duds. Progressive outlets are aiming to serve as a check on traditional media that they feel wants to knock out left-wing candidates, while moderate forces are starting up their own media to try and counter a zealous left flank that has shouted down moderates online. “That’s going to be the war more than anything: the attention fight… How can I, with the least amount of friction, get these people to start sharing clips?” Cocchiarella told Semafor. The Left While many legacy outlets that had experienced ratings and subscriptions growth during Trump’s first term have seen little to no meaningful gains in his second go-around, independent media outlets critical of Trump, the mainstream media, and Democratic Party leadership saw huge gains. Since the beginning of Trump’s presidency, Zeteo has added almost 2 million YouTube subscribers. The Bernie Sanders-ite outlet More Perfect Union has added 3 million. Hasan Piker, the leftist Twitch streamer who became a midterm campaign fixation, has gained millions of followers on YouTube and increased viewership of his stream. Now, both MPU and Zeteo are hoping to bring different issues — or candidates — to the front of the Democratic presidential primary debate. Over the last two years, Zeteo has provided early coverage and political air cover for left-wing and socialist candidates, particularly those that have expressed aggressive criticism of Israel. In an interview on Thursday, Hasan pointed to the company’s early interviews with then-New York City mayoral candidate Zohran Mamdani and El-Sayed as examples; both were able to gain exposure to like-minded voters while other outlets were skeptical of their candidacies. “From Zohran Mamdani’s race, to AOC’s rise, to Abdul El-Sayed’s victory, I think it’s been very clear — I’m not saying they wouldn’t have happened without us; that’s a little bit too arrogant and not accurate — but certainly they were aided and abetted and strengthened and bolstered by the fact that we exist,” he said. Hasan said potential 2028 candidates clearly have taken notice. Before the midterm elections, Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., said in a candid rare interview on Zeteo that he was considering running in 2028 , an admission he hadn’t made on-camera anywhere else. Hasan said although his political views are clear, multiple likely candidates who do not necessarily share Zeteo’s progressive, Israel-critical stance had nonetheless been in touch in recent days about appearing on the outlet’s show. “Democratic presidential [hopefuls] and their teams have reached out to us, not the other way around, even people we’ve criticized,” Hasan said, noting that he’s angling for an interview with Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, a pro-Israel Democrat. Other outlets are more interested in highlighting specific issues, but could end up tipping the conversation in favor of certain candidates that they choose to spotlight. More Perfect Union, the viral video channel founded by Sanders advisor Faiz Shakir, has not outright endorsed candidates in races, but its story selection and tone have bolstered candidates on the left. During the midterms, the organization published a video on then-Maine Senate candidate Graham Platner titled It was less investigatory (the piece did not uncover the various scandals that later led to Platner’s decision to drop out), and more complimentary; it gave space for Platner to explain his view on various media controversies, and showed working class Platner supporters who were unbothered by the unfolding scandals. Over the last few months, More Perfect Union has interviewed Sanders and Reps. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. In an email, More Perfect Union Editor-in-Chief Josh Miller-Lewis told Semafor that although the organization had not finalized its 2028 plans yet, it was hoping to host multiple events with candidates. The organization also hopes to grow its More Perfect University program, which hosted town halls where candidates faced college student questioners. But primarily, Miller-Lewis said, it plans to create content that would “put candidates in conversation with working class audiences and force substantive policy discussions that are often lacking in election coverage,” citing videos the organization made with Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz during the 2024 election and El-Sayed during the 2026 Senate race. “Our goal will be to create spaces where our working class audience has the opportunity to challenge candidates in substantive, solutions driven conversations, candidates can outline the big ideas they’ll prioritize if elected and show viewers how candidates engage with the voters they need to persuade to win,” Miller-Lewis wrote. Beyond highlighting more ideologically aligned candidates, left-wing outlets also plan to highlight shortcomings of centrist and moderate candidates. Ryan Grim, a founder of the foreign policy-centric Drop Site News, noted that the investigative outlet will be expanding its domestic coverage to focus on spotlighting how three powerful interest groups hope to influence the Democratic presidential primary. “Crypto and AI, and to some extent AIPAC, are gonna wanna participate, which is wonderful, and we’re a big democracy, but we’re gonna make sure that the public knows who they’re support

events.title: Tug of war continues over mysterious foreign barge
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts So-called Indonesian ghost barge rusts, months after running aground in Torres Strait The barge is almost as long as the island it washed up on. ( Supplied ) An Indonesian barge that ran aground on a rocky island in the Torres Strait will remain there until the tides are high enough for it to be salvaged. A marine expert has come up with a plan to do so, but he has not heard back from the barge owner's insurers. The salvage operation relies on 3.7-metre tides, which are due to occur between December and March. A 100-metre barge remains grounded on a rocky islet, 10 months after it mysteriously drifted through international waters and crashed in Australia's far north. Far North Queensland marine services specialist Vance Wallin has a plan to salvage the Indonesian barge. But first, he needs the green light from an overseas insurance company and almost 4-metre tides in the Torres Strait. "You only get those tides in the wet season and, unfortunately, you get cyclones in the same period," he said. "You've got to make sure … the conditions are good enough to get in there and do it." Nelly 112's hull was intact in March, but it is expected some compartments may now have been breached. ( Supplied ) Nelly 112 was not carrying any people or cargo when it washed up on Athikho Poji, near Badu Island, in late January, after going adrift in bad weather in Indonesia. Mr Wallin's company, Carpentaria Marine Service, put forward a salvage plan, but he said the barge owner had handed responsibility for the boat to an insurance company. "To date, they haven't come to the party on agreeing with us on that salvage," he said. Mr Wallin, whose company has performed about 60 to 70 salvages and wreck removals, said it would take two or three days to remove the barge from its position "high on the rocks". "We need about a 3.7-metre tide to look at a salvage attempt," he said. "With a fair bit of ballasting, we think we'll be able to get it off." He said there would be tides high enough to perform the salvage in January, February and March. The barge, Nelly 112, washed up on the small island in January. ( Supplied ) However, Mr Wallin's proposal hinges on selling the barge to a buyer in Papua New Guinea, who has agreed to pay the entire salvage cost so the barge can be towed there to be used as a floating dock. "I believe they need to make a decision in the next couple of months," Mr Wallin said. Edmund Tamwoy has also expressed interest in taking on the barge for his Indigenous-owned Badu Island quarry business, but has not had success in contacting its owners. Mr Tamwoy regularly spots the abandoned barge on his run to collect recycling waste from nearby Mabuiag Island. "It's just getting rusty, of course," he said. He estimated it would cost about $200,000 to remove the barge from the island, a price he said he was prepared to pay. "Giving the opportunity locally to someone I think is the best outcome for everyone else, even for the owner," he said. However, Mr Wallin argued the cost of registering the Indonesian-flagged barge in Australia would be "uneconomical" and exceed the barge's value. A spokesperson for Maritime Safety Queensland said it had not set a deadline for the barge's removal. The regulator, which has the power to take possession of abandoned or derelict boats, has remained in contact with the barge owner to monitor progress on a salvage plan.

events.title: Intel sued by investors after PC sales slump hits share price
events.summary: Published 16 November 2026, 03:04 GMT Intel, the US chip giant, is being sued by its shareholders who accuse the firm of hiding the severity of a slump in its personal computer (PC) sales that caused its share price to plunge almost 29% in one day. Billions of dollars was knocked off the value of the company after it forecast disappointing revenues ahead of its latest earnings report. The BBC has contacted Intel for comment. In October, Intel firm announced its computer hardware sales had dropped sharply in the three months that ended in September. That report undermined earlier suggestions from the chipmaker that demand had been improving, sending Intel shares plunging, according to the lawsuit. The lawsuit, filed by legal firm Robbins Geller Rudman & Dowd on behalf of owners of Intel common shares between 23 July and 29 October this year, was filed against the chipmaker, its chief executive Tan Lip-Bu and other company leaders. Intel has poured huge investments into manufacturing to meet the enormous demand for AI computing power. As more semiconductors are channelled towards data centres, chips for PCs and other electronics have become more expensive. Intel boss Tan had told analysts that the industry was facing an "unprecedented memory crunch", resulting in a shortage of chip supplies for PCs. "We need to address these challenges with urgency," Tan said in October. Intel shares have fallen sharply in the past month by 37.5%, though its share price is still up by 51% overall this year. events.title: Asian shares fall before Nvidia earnings, Anthropic IPO test tech rally
events.summary: Asian shares fell on Nov 16 after a whiplash week capped by the shock exit of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO. Asian shares fell as Nvidia earnings and Anthropic’s IPO are set to test the AI rally. Nvidia’s market value has dropped from US$5.8 trillion to US$3.9 trillion after Jensen Huang’s shock exit. US inflation data kept rate worries alive. Fed funds futures now fully price a quarter-point hike next month, while odds of a 50-basis-point move have fallen to 6%. Markets also watched key global events. Trump may meet Xi and Putin in Shenzhen, while US Treasuries, the dollar and oil moved as investors awaited Fed minutes and more policy signals. SYDNEY – Asian shares fell on Nov 16 after a whiplash week capped by the shock exit of Jensen Huang as Nvidia chief executive, with the chipmaker’s earnings and Anthropic’s IPO this week set to test whether the AI-fuelled bull market still has further to run. Also later in the week, US President Donald Trump is set to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen to discuss nuclear arms reduction and the US-Israeli war with Iran. The minutes of the US Federal Reserve’s October policy meeting are due on Nov 18, while a parade of Fed speakers will also be on the bill this week. Markets will be alert for any hint of policymakers being receptive to the idea of an outsize 50-basis-point interest rate hike in December. In Asia on Nov 16, Japan’s Nikkei fell 0.6%, while South Korea slipped 0.2%. MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan eased 0.1%. S&P 500 futures edged up 0.3%, while Nasdaq futures bounced 0.5%. Nvidia, the poster child of a four-year US bull market, has seen its market value tumble from about US$5.8 trillion (S$7.47 trillion) in early October to US$3.9 trillion as at Nov 13, LSEG data showed, as investors rushed for the exit after Huang’s departure. Analysts expect earnings growth of 90% on revenue of US$109 billion in Nvidia’s fiscal third quarter when its earnings are due on Nov 17, LSEG data showed, with all eyes on whether the chipmaker will stick to its bullish outlook for 2027 under new management. “Options markets imply an earnings day move of approximately plus or minus 7%, yet I question whether the quarterly numbers will carry their usual significance,” said Chris Weston, head of research at foreign exchange brokerage Pepperstone. “Nvidia may well deliver another exceptional beat and raise at tomorrow’s earnings, but investors are increasingly trying to value a business in financial years 2028 and 2029 potentially without the individual who architected its competitive advantage.” The Financial Times reported that Huang has discussed with confidants the possibility of returning as CEO. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said Nvidia needs to “go outside the company” for a new CEO. Just two days after Nvidia’s earnings, trading in Claude chatbot creator Anthropic is scheduled to begin, setting up a real-time barometer for sentiment on the AI trade. The firm’s initial public offering has drawn more institutional interest than SpaceX, people familiar with the matter told Reuters. Data on Nov 13 showed US producer prices rose in October a touch less than markets had expected, though there were signs that inflation pressure was broadening. Together with a hotter than forecast consumer price index report, the figures on Nov 13 led analysts to estimate a 0.3% rise in core personal consumption expenditure (PCE) for October, which would be the third successive monthly increase at that pace. The PCE index is the Fed’s preferred gauge of inflation when considering whether to change its policy interest rate. Fed funds futures imply a quarter-point rate hike in December is essentially locked in, while odds for a 50-basis-point move lengthened to 6% from 12% a day earlier. A total tightening of 90 basis points is priced in by late 2027. In San Francisco on Nov 16, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh is set to tell a public forum that artificial intelligence will reshape the US economy, but how the region’s new tech boom evolves, and on what timetable, is a wild card for central bankers. In government debt, US Treasuries were steady after rate hike expectations prompted their biggest weekly fall since April 2025, when the trigger was Trump’s so-called Liberation Day tariffs . Two-year yields were little changed at 4.8652% after surging 35 basis points (bps) last week. Ten-year yields were flat at 5.1433%, having jumped 29 bps to be back above the psychologically important 5% level. The US dollar lifted with yield support, rising 1.1% last week against major peers to its highest since April 2025. The dollar index was steady at 103.42 on Nov 16. In commodities, oil prices were mostly steady after two weeks of decline.

events.title: Nvidia earnings and Anthropic IPO lead crucial week for AI bulls
events.summary: Nvidia earnings and Anthropic 's public debut are set to lead a blockbuster week on Wall Street as questions mount over the AI bull market that has powered US equities to record highs for the past four years. The two events will cap what has been a turbulent period in a sector rocked by disappointing earnings reports, investor anxiety over rising AI financing and expenditure , the Democrats' stunning sweep in the midterm elections , and Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang 's affair with a woman suspected by US authorities of having links to Chinese intelligence. “I think both events have the potential to be positive catalysts for the AI trade, which has otherwise been hitting a lot of bumps in the road over the course of the last two weeks,” said Art Hogan, chief market strategist at B Riley Wealth. Nvidia accounts for about 90 per cent of the market for the most advanced chips that run and train AI models. It and Anthropic are at the core of AI. Nvidia is expected to post third-quarter revenue growth of 91.3 per cent to $109 billion, with earnings increasing to $2.47 a share when it reports on Tuesday. Fourth-quarter guidance is expected to show earnings growth of 69.5 per cent to $2.75 a share, with revenue up 84.4 per cent to $125 billion. Shares in the company are down about 14 per cent for the year so far. Nvidia's quarterly reports are highly scrutinised and investors expect the company to not merely meet, but overwhelm expectations. But the company's leadership vacuum is expected to generate as much interest this week, as are questions over the possible diversion of Nvidia chips to China, which have turned Mr Huang's extramarital affair into a political firestorm. Nvidia's board of directors told CNBC on Friday that it is in the process of selecting a search company to find a new chief executive. Chief financial officer Colette Kress has filled the role in an interim basis. Vijay Valecha, chief investment officer at Century Financial, said investors should look past Mr Huang's resignation as they pore through this weeks' numbers. “If the financial results remain strong, the market may look past the leadership change,” Mr Valecha wrote in a note. Attention will quickly turn towards Mr Huang's rival Dario Amodei , whose company Anthropic will begin trading on the Nasdaq market on Thursday under the symbol “ANT”, joining SpaceX as among the major AI IPOs this year. OpenAI is expected to stage its IPO next year. Anthropic said in an updated S-1 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission that it will offer 825 million shares priced between $70 and $78, giving it a market valuation of $1.3 trillion to $1.45 trillion. Earlier estimates put the company's valuation as high as $2 trillion, but those have dipped alongside a broader AI slide on Wall Street. Its amended filing also showed how connected the companies powering the AI build are. Google, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft and TSMC have agreed to buy $26 billion of non-voting shares at the IPO price in a separate private placement. UAE-based technology firm MGX participated in a $65 billion funding round for Anthropic this year. The Silicon Valley company is one of three frontier model front-runners the company has stakes in, along with OpenAI and xAI. Founded in 2021, Anthropic's Claude chatbot and a deep bench of other AI models and services have quickly gained momentum. The company reported $33.24 billion in revenue for the first nine months of 2026 ending September 30, an about 1,200 per cent increase compared to the same period last year. Its public listing will also beat rival OpenAI, whose IPO has been delayed. Unlike his rivals, Mr Amodei has pushed for stronger AI regulation, drawing opposition from US President Donald Trump's administration. The Pentagon designated the AI company as a “supply chain risk to national security”, with a legal battle being fought. Mr Amodei has been pushing to restrict certain US semiconductors and technology exports to China. The issue deepened into a potential national security crisis last week after Mr Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy who worked at a Singapore-based firm called Megaspeed. Megaspeed is under investigation in the US for allegedly smuggling chips to China, in a charge the company denies. Mr Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick have agreed to testify before Congress to answer questions on the extent to which US national security had been compromised. Anthropic's rivalry extends beyond Nvidia and OpenAI, however. The company also faces competition from Alphabet and Microsoft in AI software, as well as newer Chinese businesses. The rivalling AI buildout has also raised fears of cash burn. Anthropic reported a net loss of more than $104 billion in the nine months ending on September 30, 2026, although most of this reflected non-cash accounting adjustments to the value of its financing instruments. Amazon posted a free cash outflow of $42.4 billion when it reported in October, while Alphabet posted $9.1 billion of negative free cash flow in its fourth-quarter report. Those concerns have caused stocks to swing wildly in recent weeks, amplified by concerns about stricter regulation and a potential data centre moratorium after the midterm elections. US equities have broadly recouped their losses, with the major averages ending last week in positive territory. “I think we're still in early innings of this game, and I think the impact of artificial intelligence is going to be massive. That said, I think there's always going to be volatility in the trade because we find something to scare us about the trade,” Mr Hogan said.

events.title: Energy security has been forgotten in Kurdistan’s political squabbles
events.summary: If a house divided against itself cannot stand, what are the chances for a house triply divided? On November 8, explosive drones slammed into the Khor Mor gasfield in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq, turning out the lights across the semi-autonomous territory. The Kurdish governing parties are at loggerheads ; their debate with Baghdad continues, and the federal government is conflicted about bringing the perpetrators to justice. The strike is far from the first on Khor Mor, which is run by the Pearl Petroleum consortium that includes Sharjah-based Crescent and Dana Gas . Dana Gas said on Saturday that “great damage has hit the Khor Mor gas facility, and at present no quantity of gas can be produced”. The field is the main producer in Kurdistan and was expanded to 750 million cubic feet per day of gas capacity last October. Without it, Kurdistan has very limited alternative production, and its power plants quickly go dark. Electricity generation plunged to 1,000 megawatts from 3,700MW before the attack. A domestic dispute The attack was not directly a result of the US- Iran war , despite early claims that the drones came from Iran. If Iran wanted to target US interests, it would probably have attacked the Sarsang oilfield, run by American company HKN, led by Ross Perot Junior, son of Ross Perot, who ran as an independent candidate in the 1992 presidential election. Indeed, Sarsang was damaged in March and April, early in the war. Cutting off oil is more to Tehran ’s advantage right now in keeping pressure on global markets and the US administration. The Khor Mor attack stems instead from domestic politics . The Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK), which controls the southern part of the region from Sulaymaniyah, has withdrawn from the regional government. It is threatening to set up its own separate administration, reversing the unification reached under American auspices in 2006. Its leader, Bafel Talabani, son of former Iraqi president Jalal Talabani, denied that he was “in Tehran’s pocket” and called this an “old perception”. His party, which has steadily lost ground to the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), based in Erbil, fears exclusion from its share of the oil industry. Mr Talabani said in October 2024 that “I will never hand over gas to them”. The US is not going to step in to resolve the squabble this time, special envoy Tom Barrack saying, “This is an Iraqi issue; this is not an American decision.” Three sides, no solution The Kurdistan–federal struggle has not gone away either, despite the deal finally reached in March to resume exporting the region’s oil through the pipeline to Turkey, this time under Baghdad’s authority. There are complaints of unauthorised exports from Kurdistan through Iran, and of the region not producing the amounts required. The blockade of the Strait of Hormuz has made the Kurdistan region’s pipeline to Turkey even more important. It now moves about 500,000 barrels per day, including 200,000 bpd trucked from southern Iraq. The importance of the Kurdish line could diminish if Baghdad fulfills its plans to reconstruct the direct route from Kirkuk. Pro-Iranian forces in federal Iraq are certainly behind the drones – and, before that, rockets – launched at Khor Mor. They have also been implicated in attacks on oil infrastructure in Saudi Arabia; these are more clearly linked to the US-Iran war and the conflict of Riyadh with Tehran’s allies in Yemen. The US withdrew its air defences from Kurdistan in September, and the regional government complains that Baghdad has not authorised promised anti-drone systems. Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi , who took office in May, is locked in his own struggle with some of the militias, moving lately against lucrative oil smuggling activities run from the town of Jurf Al Sakhar, a base for Kataib Hezbollah. It is widely suspected the central government knows very well the culprits for the attacks on Kurdish oilfields, but cannot arrest them, or only detains some lackeys. The Kurdistan region has no immediate solutions to the loss of its main gasfield. Pearl is developing the large Chemchemal field, with hopes of some output next year. In August, it began sending some Khor Mor gas to the federally governed Taza power plant in Kirkuk province, but the Kurdistan Regional Government complained this was in breach of its contract and not in accordance with the region’s priorities. HKN was awarded Miran, another big field, last May. But its sour gas, with a high concentration of toxic, corrosive hydrogen sulphide, will take years to develop. It has already suffered years of commercial deadlock since discovery in 2009. These and other sizeable resources are all in the PUK-controlled zone. This contrasts with oil, concentrated in the KDP zone, with nature’s usual whims to foster trouble. In the absence of major progress on new developments in Kurdistan, Baghdad has taken the chance to lure away investment. After a historic policy of blacklisting companies that worked in the region, it has welcomed first Crescent and, more recently, HKN into oil and gas projects. Two of the other leading operators in Kurdistan, Shamaran of Canada and the UK’s Gulf Keystone, are in the process of merging and entering HKN’s Hamrin field. The Kurdistan region could greatly improve its strategic position by seizing opportunities. It holds almost the only big gas fields in Iraq that are not associated with oil, and so can be developed flexibly. If it had even one more major gas supplier, it would not be so exposed to the violent blackmail of Khor Mor. Beyond gas dependence Its Runaki initiative has been a worthy effort to ensure people pay their bills and rely on centralised electricity and not on the costly and dirty diesel generators that blight the streets of the rest of Iraq. If it rehabilitated its hydroelectric plants, and advanced large-scale solar power, it would further ease reliance on gas. It could develop a larger power surplus and send gas or electricity to the rest of Iraq. That would be a bargaining chip in further debates over oil. It would also give Baghdad more reason to safeguard Kurdish energy sites if another drone caused blackouts in Kirkuk or even Baghdad. A gas link to Turkey has long been in the works, and the Turks have extended their grid up to the border. A bidirectional connection would further boost Kurdish energy resilience to sabotage. Independent gas exports to Turkey, long a dream, now look checkmated by the oil pipeline negotiations. But the Kurdistan region, if still divided, could at least make itself part of a trilateral trade.

events.title: Japan's economy unexpectedly contracts in third-quarter as elevated energy costs bite
events.summary: A Reuters poll of economists had estimated the economy to grow at 0.3%. While Japan's exports beat expectations for two of the three months in the quarter, net exports weighed on the economy as elevated energy prices increased import values. The data comes amid expectations that the Bank of Japan could raise rates once more at its December meeting. Japan's economy unexpectedly contracted in the third quarter, shrinking at an annualized 0.1% compared to the previous quarter, as elevated energy prices weighed on consumption and net exports. A Reuters poll of economists had estimated the economy to grow at 0.3% in the three months to September, while GDP had expanded at 1.4% in the previous quarter. Japan's exports beat expectations for two of the three months in the quarter, but net exports weighed on the economy due to higher costs of energy imports, cutting 0.6 percentage point from the country's growth. Energy subsidies for households had reportedly expired in September, exposing consumers to higher energy prices brought about by the Iran war. The GDP data could complicate Japan's policy normalization path, though there's still a 75.6% chance of the Bank of Japan raising rates by 25 basis points in December, according to LSEG. "Today's GDP data is hardly a green light for the BOJ to hike in December," according to Krishna Bhimavarapu, APAC economist at State Street Investment Management. He pointed out that real final sales of domestic product fell 2.1% annualized, which is the largest decline outside the Covid-19 pandemic and the first quarter of 2022. "[This] looks to be a loss of momentum," he added. That metric is a measure of Real final sales of domestic product refer to GDP growth, net of private inventories , and indicate underlying demand. Marcel Thieliant, head of Asia Pacific at Capital Economics, still expects the BOJ to go ahead with the rate hike. "It looks increasingly likely that the Bank will have to tighten policy more aggressively than we've been anticipating as inflation is about to surge." The BOJ had declared that its 2% underlying inflation target had been met for the first time in 13 years at its meeting last month. Core inflation in September also hit its highest level this year at 2.1%, overshooting analysts' expectations. On an year-on-year basis Japan's economy grew 1.1%, its strongest growth since the second quarter of 2025. Theliant noted that this was owed to a lower base in the third quarter of 2025. Following the data release, the Nikkei 225 fell 0.62%, while the yield on the benchmark 10-year Japanese Government Bonds was at 2.885%. The yen weakened marginally against the dollar, trading at 159.76.

events.title: HK stock exchange launches first dim sum bond index to boost renminbi debt market
events.summary: Hong Kong is the world’s largest offshore renminbi market. The Hong Kong stock exchange has launched its first bond index, as the city seeks to boost liquidity and trading in the world’s largest offshore renminbi market. The offshore renminbi bond index will track dim sum bonds listed on the exchange or settled through the Central Moneymarkets Unit – a clearing house for debt securities in the city, according to a press release from Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing. The launch follows Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee’s September policy address, which outlined the offshore renminbi bond index as a reference for market trends. The government’s five-year plan unveiled that month also pledged to promote regular dim sum bond issuance, support building an offshore renminbi yield curve and broaden the usage of the notes as collateral. The Chinese authorities have sought to help cement Hong Kong’s position as the main offshore renminbi hub , tapping growing investor enthusiasm for China’s currency as a cheaper path for debt financing. Bloomberg Index Services will serve as index administrator and calculation agent, according to the press release. Bloomberg LP, the parent of Bloomberg News, offers index products for various asset classes through Bloomberg Index Services. Momentum in the dim sum bond market has accelerated notably in 2026. Sovereign and corporate issuers have sold around 1.2 trillion yuan (S$231 billion) of offshore renminbi-denominated bonds so far in 2026, a record for the period and already surpassing the full-year issuance in 2025, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. events.title: $180 million Van Gogh tests the art market and collector confidence
events.summary: Total sales at Sotheby's, Christie's and Phillips are expected to be around $2.4 billion, which would equal last year's total, according to ArtTactic. Sotheby's alone is expected to pull in over $1.1 billion, with a single collection from The Blaquier-Arrieta Collection estimated at $450 million. The collection includes the two big headliners of the week: Vincent van Gogh's landscape "Châtaigniers en fleurs," (Chestnut Trees in Flower) estimated at $180 million and Paul Cézanne's "Arlequin," estimated at $120 million. A version of this article appeared in CNBC's Inside Wealth newsletter, a weekly guide to the high-net-worth investor and consumer. Sign up to receive future editions straight to your inbox. The art auctions in New York next week could top $2 billion, as a treasure trove of masterpieces comes to the market for the first time in decades. Total sales at Sotheby's, Christie's and Phillips are expected to be around $2.4 billion, which would equal last year's total, according to ArtTactic. Sotheby's alone is expected to pull in over $1.1 billion, with a single collection from The Blaquier-Arrieta Collection estimated at $450 million. The collection includes the two big headliners of the week: Vincent van Gogh's landscape "Châtaigniers en fleurs," (Chestnut Trees in Flower) estimated at $180 million and Paul Cézanne's "Arlequin," estimated at $120 million. Neither has been seen in public for a half a century. Sotheby's CEO Charles Stewart said demand is strong in the art market, especially for the highest quality blue-chip works, as rising stocks markets and private wealth boost the confidence of collectors. "There's been enormous wealth creation and a lot of confidence in markets," Stewart said. "It's a global phenomenon. We're seeing recovery and greater interest across Asia and something really exciting happening from the Middle East across to Singapore and Europe and the U.S." Christie's star of the week is Wassily Kandinsky's "Betonte Ecken," estimated at $60 million to $80 million. Christie's CEO Bonnie Brennan describes the market is "confident but discerning, rewarding truly exceptional works." She said recent gyrations in the stock market and fears of an AI bubble aren't likely to deter serious collectors. "At the very highest end of our market, collectors tend to take a much longer-term view," Brennan said. "They understand that the opportunity to acquire a masterpiece may come only once in a generation, and that can be far more important than what the stock market has done in any particular week. In uncertain moments, the very best can actually become even more compelling." The art market has continued to rebound this year after declines in 2023 and 2024, with auction sales in the first half up 70% over last year, to $6.8 billion, according to Bank of America. Drew Watson, head of art services at Bank of America, said blue-chip art is outperforming, with Impressionist & Modern sales up 133% in the first half. "Our outlook for the art market this November is cautiously optimistic," Watson said. "Improving liquidity, combined with an unusually strong concentration of fresh-to-market private collections, creates a favorable backdrop for the marquee sales." events.title: It’s important to find your strengths to leverage, a career coach says
events.summary: How compatible are you with your job? Can our MBTI help us find one that is? In this episode, career coach and co-founder of Strengths School Jason Ho sits down with hosts Kai Wen and Sue-Ann to talk about what to look out for when trying to figure out what career suits you. While personality tests can serve as a useful guide to point us in the right direction, what you are interested in, might not be what you are good at. events.title: Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says
events.summary: The Nvidia scandal has sent shockwaves through Silicon Valley as well as the political establishment Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year, the company says. Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well as with one of his employees. Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and the scandal at Nvidia has raised questions about the possibility that high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions. The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business. Megaspeed said it was aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence". It added that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation". Alice Huang stepped down from her role as director of Megaspeed near the end of 2023, according to Washington-based security analysis group C4ADS but it said she was still "practically in control" of the company. Alice Huang - who is of no relation to Nvidia's former boss - had been investigated by Singapore authorities in February 2025 as part of the country's probe into Megaspeed and other companies. Also on Sunday, US Congressman John Moolenaar said that Jensen Huang had agreed to testify before the House Select Committee on China, which he chairs, as well as the Foreign Affairs and the Intelligence committees. The committees had threatened to issue subpoenas to Jensen Huang if he did not comply with their requests to testify. Moolenaar told CBS, BBC's US partner, that none were ultimately issued. Jensen Huang's testimony is expected to take place behind close doors, with the dates still being finalised. Moolenaar said: "That's going to be a very important meeting to understand to what degree privileged information was accessed, and to what degree this potential alleged Chinese spy influenced Nvidia's philosophy and may have had an influence on some of our policies with respect to AI and export controls." Separately, a group of tech leaders including Space X's Elon Musk, have been trying to rally support to have Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia's chief executive. A representative forJensen Huang declined to comment on a report in the Financial Times suggesting that he was discussing a comeback to the firm he co-founded. The BBC understands that the likelihood of him being reinstated is very low while the company's internal investigations are ongoing. The move would also face scrutiny from Washington, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent calling for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company. For the moment, Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress is leading the firm and will present the company's results on Tuesday, 17 November. On Friday, Bessent blamed the US Commerce Department, led by fellow cabinet colleague Howard Lutnick, for failing to properly oversee the export of high-end chips. Bessent told CNBC that several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months... but Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process". The so-called entity list restricts US trade with overseas firms and individuals. Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips. Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Jensen Huang. Megaspeed is suspected of giving backdoor access to Nvidia chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand. Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation? Nvidia has been banned from selling its advanced semiconductors to China. While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls. Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations. Megaspeed said it "designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes". It said this includes "US export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate". China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.

events.title: Japan’s economy unexpectedly shrinks as inflation squeezes households
events.summary: The first contraction in four quarters underscores the uneven nature of Japan’s economic recovery. Japan’s economy shrank 0.1% in July-September, as households cut spending because of higher living costs, poor weather and weaker demand for cars and air conditioners. Capital spending rose 1.6% on labour-saving technology and AI projects, but net external demand cut 0.6 percentage point from growth as imports jumped. Economists said the dip is unlikely to stop the Bank of Japan’s rate rises, as inflation stays high and growth is expected to remain modest but resilient. TOKYO – Japan’s economy unexpectedly contracted an annualised 0.1% in the July to September quarter, government data showed on Nov 16 , reflecting weak consumer spending as households grappled with higher living costs. The first contraction in four quarters underscores the uneven nature of Japan’s economic recovery, with households remaining vulnerable to persistent inflation despite rising wages. Still, policymakers are unlikely to view the weakness as a brake on Japan’s moderate recovery, with resilient corporate activity, rising real wages and robust demand for AI-related investment underpinning growth. “While growth was indeed negative this time, there is no need to be overly pessimistic about the result,” said Kento Minami, senior economist at Daiwa Securities. “My impression is that moderate growth is probably continuing.” Minami also said the results are unlikely to derail the Bank of Japan’s (BOJ) tightening path, as the central bank remains focused on inflation risks. He added that firm domestic price pressures and a global backdrop of higher interest rates leave little room for a dovish policy shift. The gross domestic product data compared with a median market forecast of 0.3% annualised growth in a Reuters poll, and followed a revised 1.7% expansion in the previous quarter. The reading translated into a quarterly fall of 0.02%, compared with the median estimate of a 0.1% increase. Private consumption, which accounts for more than half of economic output, fell 0.3%, compared with a market estimate of a 0.2% decline. Household spending was hurt by persistent price pressures and poor weather, including heavy rain and typhoons, during the quarter. Demand for cars and air-conditioners retreated following the temporary boost in the previous quarter from tax and regulatory changes. “Strong wage growth should support consumption, but higher prices linked to Middle East tensions will continue to squeeze household purchasing power,” said Masato Koike, senior economist at Sompo Institute Plus. Capital spending, a key driver of private demand, rose 1.6%, versus a market forecast for a 1.5% increase, backed by investment in labour-saving technologies and artificial intelligence-related projects. Net external demand, or exports minus imports, knocked 0.6 percentage point off growth, compared with a market forecast for a 0.4 percentage point drag on GDP growth. Imports rose sharply as oil and other energy purchases recovered after Japan diversified procurement following disruptions linked to the war in the Middle East. The BOJ will closely scrutinise the latest data as it assesses whether the economy can withstand further interest rate increases. With stubbornly high energy costs and rising import prices from a weak yen adding to inflationary pressures, the BOJ has stepped up its policy tightening in 2026, delivering interest rate hikes in June and September. Many analysts expect the next BOJ rate hike as soon as December. A monthly survey of 37 economists by the Japan Center for Economic Research showed the economy is expected to grow 0.89% in fiscal 2026 and 1.02% in fiscal 2027, suggesting economists see growth remaining modest but resilient. Japan’s longer-term growth challenges remain in focus, with the International Monetary Fund projecting the country will slip to become the world’s sixth-largest economy in nominal dollar terms in 2027 in dollar terms, overtaken by India and Britain. Japan is currently the world’s fourth-largest after Germany. REUTERS
