events.title: Nvidia shares primed for bounce as investors eye report on Jensen Huang comeback
events.summary: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has already been discussing the idea of returning, with backing from several Silicon Valley allies. Nvidia shares rose after the Financial Times said Jensen Huang is discussing a comeback. Investors hope his return would calm worries and restore clarity on supply deals. Huang’s exit followed an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, and his return is still uncertain. Nvidia is down 32% from its October peak and faces wider AI boom worries. Earnings on Nov 17 should show demand trends and may shape the stock’s next move. Nvidia shares may be poised for some relief after the Financial Times reported that former chief executive Jensen Huang is discussing a possible comeback to the chipmaker. A perpetual futures contract on the Hyperliquid blockchain referencing Nvidia’s share price rose more than 3% on the evening of Nov 15. Nasdaq 100 futures advanced nearly 0.9% before paring gains. Nvidia’s stock is coming off its worst week since April 2025, after Huang’s admission of an affair with an alleged Chinese spy and his quick ouster from the company. Huang has already been discussing the idea of returning , with backing from several Silicon Valley allies, according to the Financial Times report. Altimeter Capital Management and Atreides Management are among those that have urged Nvidia’s board to reconsider. “Markets are reacting positively because Jensen Huang remains synonymous with Nvidia,” said Tim Waterer, chief market analyst at KCM Trade. “His track record is exceptional, and the prospect of his return would restore a degree of clarity around future supply commitments – many of which were based on his personal handshake agreements that could otherwise have been at risk.” Prospects for an actual return by Huang remain uncertain. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is urging the company to make a “dramatic” leadership shake - up, and come clean about its compliance with export controls on its prized artifical intelligence chips. Nvidia shares are down 32% from their October all-time high, with the Huang controversy adding to broader concerns over the sustainability of the AI boom. The company is due to report quarterly earnings on Nov 17, which should give investors insight into the outlook for demand. “Markets are desperate after non-stop bad news and are looking for remedies,” said Anna Wu, an investment strategist and founder of Floodlines Research. “Even unconfirmed ones.” BLOOMBERG

The Lockheed/Boeing joint venture United Launch Alliance (ULA) created that rocket, a version of its Vulcan heavy lifter using a six-booster configuration and a Centaur V upper stage optimized to carry payloads into low Earth orbit. Last week, Amazon previewed the launch with a post that noted this mission, code-named LV-01, is the first of 38 planned missions with ULA, and that LV-02 would likely follow within weeks. Amazon put 40 satellites aboard the Sunday mission and said it is “already planning larger configurations for subsequent missions.” Those plans, and the LV-02 launch, are probably on hold after the rocket suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight. The flight began well, with the Vulcan reaching an altitude of 95 miles (150 km) and completing the first phase of its flight. Six minutes into the mission, the main booster and payload fairing both separated as planned, and ULA lit up the Centaur V’s engines for the first planned firings needed to reach low Earth orbit. events.title: Apple launches new app to study how people use AI for health
events.summary: Big AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic have made their bets on offering chatbots that can answer health-related queries with specialized features. Apple is debuting a new study to understand how people use AI for health. But it isn’t quite following other AI startups just yet; it wants to study how clinically grounded answers can help people. The iPhone maker is partnering with healthcare-focused AI company OpenEvidence to launch a new study app. Apple is inviting users in the U.S. over 21, using iPhone 15 or later, and running iOS 26 or later, with Apple Intelligence enabled. The company is aiming to run this study with up to 200,000 participants for more than 12 months. The new app will allow users to ask health-related questions, as they do with ChatGPT or Claude, with answers grounded in clinical data, from sources including The New England Journal of Medicine, Journal of the American Medical Association, and Nature. Apple said that the app will try to give simplified answers to everyday medical questions. Users can rate those answers and provide feedback about the responses; they’ll also be asked to participate in monthly surveys. Participants can share data from HealthKit such as resting heart rate, activity, sleep, or lab results to get more personalized and pointed suggestions from the app. The company said the app can also help prepare participants better for a doctor’s visit, and it will guide users to specific providers for answers related to concerning medical issues. Apple specified that the data will be anonymized before sending it to a secure third-party cloud provider, and it won’t be used to train any kind of AI models. The company said that OpenEvidence deletes the query and response data after 24 hours. “At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding. Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life,” Sumbul Desai, M.D., Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness, said in a statement, adding, “Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey.” The app is available to download starting today for U.S. users. It’s not clear if Apple wants to release AI-powered answering to its Health app or Siri yet. The potential is huge — earlier this year, OpenAI said users were asking over 300 million health-related queries each week . events.title: Apple launches research study to explore the use of AI for health
events.summary: Store Mac iPad iPhone Watch Vision AirPods TV & Home Entertainment Accessories Support Text of this article November 15, 2026 UPDATE Apple launches research study to explore the use of AI for health The Apple Health AI Usage Study, conducted in collaboration with OpenEvidence, will evaluate trust, comprehension, and real-world health AI engagement Apple today announced the launch of the Apple Health AI Usage Study in the United States, a virtual research study and associated app designed to advance the understanding of how people interact with conversational health AI tools. 1 By examining what drives user trust, the quality of responses, comprehension, and everyday health actions, the study aims to inform the responsible design of health AI experiences for Apple and the industry. “At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding. Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life,” said Sumbul Desai, M.D., Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness. “Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey.” The study is conducted in collaboration with OpenEvidence, a leading clinical AI platform widely used by healthcare professionals that generates answers using medical information from established sources such as The New England Journal of Medicine , Journal of the American Medical Association , and Nature . The study brings together medically grounded AI technology developed by OpenEvidence with an Apple-designed research experience. Participants will be able to ask the study app everyday health questions; explore complex medical information communicated with approachable language; and see linked, peer-reviewed clinical citations that ground each response. Participants can also choose to share HealthKit data types — such as resting heart rate, activity, sleep, or lab results — to explore how personal data integration impacts relevance and understanding. Consumer health technologies powered by LLMs may at times offer responses that are incomplete or unclear, which is why research is critical to presenting health information to users with greater clarity. The study will also explore how health AI can potentially help participants better prepare for clinical visits with their own doctors. “Patients and clinicians are both turning to AI, but the tools they use are being built and tested in separate worlds,” said Robert M. Wachter, M.D., UCSF’s professor and chair of the Department of Medicine. “When patients and doctors draw on versions of the same trustworthy tools, patients arrive prepared, conversations improve, and next steps happen seamlessly. Connecting these tools, and rigorously studying what works, is how we’ll get there.” The study is designed from the ground up with privacy protections, transparency, and clinical guardrails, and study data will not be used to train AI models. Participants retain control over whether to share any HealthKit metrics or survey responses, and Apple has implemented security measures to protect the study data it maintains, as well as the confidentiality of participants’ information. The study app features safety guardrails that are intended to detect certain concerning questions and suggest that a participant follow up with a provider or other resources if needed. Study Details and Availability The Apple Health AI Usage Study is open to up to 200,000 eligible participants age 21 and older across the United States. To join, participants must have an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone (iPhone 15 Pro or later) running iOS 26 or later. Download the study app to learn more about the study and choose to enroll. The study app is not meant to diagnose or treat any condition, or replace the advice of medical professionals. Participants should consult a doctor or clinician to address health concerns or verify medical information. events.title: SK Hynix to spend $1.35 billion over five years to support chip suppliers
events.summary: South Korea’s SK Hynix aims to strengthen its supply chain as competition intensifies in the AI chip market. SK Hynix will spend 1.4 trillion won over five years to support domestic chip suppliers and strengthen its supply chain as AI chip competition grows. It will help suppliers through research, testing, mass production and sales, including advance funding and support even if projects fail. A jointly funded 874.6 billion won testing facility, Trinity Fab, will open in May 2027 to cut costs, speed up testing and protect sensitive information. SEOUL – South Korea’s SK Hynix said on Nov 16 that it plans to spend 1.4 trillion won (S$1.35 billion) over the next five years to support domestic suppliers of semiconductor materials, parts and equipment, aiming to strengthen its supply chain as competition intensifies in the artificial intelligence chip market. The chipmaker also outlined plans for a jointly funded 874.6 billion won testing facility at its semiconductor complex in Yongin, south of Seoul, where smaller suppliers will be able to test products under conditions similar to those on commercial chip production lines. SK Hynix said its supplier support programme covers four stages – research and development, testing, mass production and sales. It aims to help smaller companies overcome financing and technology hurdles. The testing facility, named Trinity Fab, is a partnership between SK Hynix, the central government and local governments in South Korea. It is scheduled to open in May 2027. SK Hynix will contribute 443.2 billion won, the central government 373.6 billion won and local governments 57.7 billion won, according to the company. The facility will be housed within the first chip plant at SK Hynix’s Yongin semiconductor cluster, 40km south of Seoul, where the company plans to invest 600 trillion won to build four chip fabrication plants. It will include a 3,305 sq m cleanroom and equipment for processes including lithography, etching, deposition and inspection. Suppliers will be able to evaluate materials and equipment using 30cm wafers before deploying them on production lines. SK Hynix said the shared facility would help small suppliers reduce testing costs and shorten the time needed to bring products to market. It will be run by an independent non-profit foundation to protect intellectual property and commercially sensitive information. Under its research support programme, SK Hynix will provide up to 50% of initial development costs in advance and compensate suppliers for work undertaken even if a project fails to meet its targets. SK Hynix and financial institutions will also provide two trillion won in financing backed by the Korea Trade Insurance Corporation, while other programmes offer low interest loans and technical consulting to suppliers, including smaller sub-contractors. events.title: Intel sued by shareholders following 29% stock plunge
events.summary: In the lawsuit, shareholders said Intel was too slow to disclose information about how slowing PC sales and an inventory glut would weigh on revenue. Intel shareholders sued the chipmaker, saying it hid the impact of weak PC sales and high inventory before a 29% share price plunge. The suit, led by the City of Southfield Fire and Police Retirement System, says Intel delayed warnings while raising US$23 billion in stock in mid-August. Intel blamed supply shortages and an "unprecedented memory crunch" for weaker PCs; the case seeks damages and names Lip-Bu Tan and David Zinsner. Intel has been sued by shareholders who accused the US chipmaker of defrauding them by concealing the impact of a prolonged slowdown in personal computer sales that caused its stock price to plunge nearly 29% in a single day. In a proposed class action filed on Nov 13 in the San Jose, California, federal court, shareholders led by a Michigan pension fund said Intel was too slow to disclose information about how slowing PC sales and an inventory glut would weigh on revenue. The shareholders said Intel’s problems with PC sales and excess inventory outweighed data centre construction and other benefits related to the artificial intelligence boom. They also said Intel had the motive and opportunity to defraud by raising capital in mid-August, halfway through its “disastrous” third quarter, when it sold US$23 billion (S$29.6 billion) of stock at US$95 per share. The sale came as Intel looked to build out its chip contract manufacturing business, a key part of chief executive Tan Lip-Bu’s business strategy. Shares of Intel closed on Nov 13 at US$59.66. Intel did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Nov 15 . Tan told analysts that he was disappointed by manufacturing supply shortages, an “unprecedented memory crunch”, and resulting softness in PCs. “We need to address these challenges with urgency,” Tan added. Like many other large technology companies, Intel has poured money into manufacturing, but supply disruptions have made it harder to benefit from growing demand for data centre chips. Meanwhile, rising memory prices have made PCs more expensive, weighing on demand. The Nov 13 lawsuit, led by the City of Southfield Fire and Police Retirement System, seeks unspecified damages for Intel shareholders between July 23 and Oct 29. Tan and chief financial officer David Zinsner are also defendants. Intel shares are up 62% in 2026 through Nov 13, though they have slid from their recent peak of US$142.35 on June 30. REUTERS

events.title: AI Day Seoul Brings Together Korea’s Industry Leaders, Startups and Developer Communities
events.summary: Over two days at COEX, more than 2,000 attendees converged for AI Day Seoul, bringing together Korea’s industry leaders, startups and developer communities advancing physical AI and AI agents. At the plenary sessions, Deepu Talla, vice president of robotics and edge AI at NVIDIA, said Korea is “punching above its weight,” with Doosan Robotics, Hyundai Motor Group, LG Electronics and SK Group — as well as startups like Real World and Luda Robotics — using NVIDIA platforms to bring general-purpose robotics into the real world. Jonathan Cohen, vice president of applied research at NVIDIA, showed how enterprises can build agents they own and control. Breakout sessions featured speakers from Coupang Intelligent Cloud, Doosan Robotics, LG AI Research, LG Electronics, NAVER Cloud, SK Telecom and Upstage. “It was a genuinely enjoyable time to have candid conversations,” said Hyunho Yang, research engineer for omnimodal foundation models at SK Telecom. “Seeing the passion of fellow AI developers was a real source of inspiration for me.” The Agentic AI 10x Bootcamp Community Day brought together Pseudo Lab, Python Korea, PyTorchKR, HAERAE, Hugging Face KREW, Graph User Group, Womxn Who Code Korea, Dnol (Datayanolja) and other developer communities. Five finalists from the Hangul Day hackathon, co-hosted with Fastcampus, built agents trained on the Korean language and culture with the OpenShell runtime. The winning team, FlyGate, received an NVIDIA DGX Spark system. More than 500 developers also took part in full-day NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute workshops and NVIDIA Certification exams in Korean. Workshops covered deploying and optimizing AI inference at scale, building end-to-end robotics workflows with the NVIDIA Isaac platform and developing secure AI agents. Certification included the new AI Model and Application Development exam. The Physical AI Startup Connect event included pitches from 10 NVIDIA Inception startups: AIM Intelligence, Avikus, GoLe Robotics, MOVIN, Neubility, ROAI, ROBROS, TESOLLO, TwelveLabs and XYZ. The AI for Science Forum brought together the Korea Institute of Science and Technology Information, Korean universities and NVIDIA Research. events.title: 2 planes collide on the ground in Miami, only minor injuries reported
events.summary: Federal aviation safety officials are investigating a minor collision between two planes at a taxiway intersection at Miami International Airport MIAMI -- Federal aviation safety officials on Sunday were investigating a minor collision between two planes at a taxiway intersection at Miami International Airport, where one aircraft's wingtip struck the nose of another, authorities said. Two people reported minor injuries. The accident happened at about 9 p.m. Saturday and involved a Copa Airlines Boeing 737 aircraft with 172 people aboard and a UPS Boeing 767 cargo plane, according to the National Transportation Safety Board and Copa Airlines. The wing of the Copa flight and the nose of the UPS plane collided, the NTSB said. Photos taken at the scene show the UPS plane nose with a horizontal gash on one side and a larger hole in the middle. On audio recorded by ATC.com, a pilot on the UPS plane told air traffic control that he went too far at the intersection and his plane was clipped by the Copa flight. Air traffic control told the UPS pilot that he was supposed to yield to the Copa aircraft. The NTSB said Sunday that preliminary information showed the UPS plane was instructed to give way to the Copa Airlines flight but did not stop. The UPS aircraft had substantial damage, while an assessment of the Copa plane had not been completed, it said. The NTSB said it opened an investigation and expected a preliminary report to be released within 30 days. The Copa plane had just arrived from Panama City and the UPS plane was headed to Bogota, Colombia, officials said. UPS said it was working with authorities to determine what happened. “We cannot speculate on the details of the incident,” UPS said in a statement. “The National Transportation Safety Board is responsible for investigating incidents like this and will control the flow of information.” The mishap came two months after an Amazon cargo plane careened off a runway at Miami International and smashed into a van carrying workers for a company that cleans airplanes, killing five people. events.title: Microsoft lifts Indian cloud prices by 15 percent, cuts costs in China
events.summary: Microsoft has announced massive price rises for commercial cloud services in India and New Zealand, but a substantial reduction in China. The software giant sells its cloudy services in many local currencies, at an equivalent rate to the prices it charges in the USA. As exchange rates shift, so do the prices Microsoft charges around the world. Microsoft last week announced the new charges that will come into effect from January 1, 2027, and the news isn’t pleasant for customers in India, who face an increase of 15.7 percent for cloud services and up to 20 percent for some on-prem offerings. New Zealand customers face a ten percent price hike. Customers in China, where Microsoft relies on a local partner called 21Vianet to deliver its cloud, will see costs fall by up to 8.5 percent. Australian buyers will see costs fall by 4.5 percent. The only nation not in Asia on Microsoft’s list is Norway, where prices will ease 5.9 percent. Sega Japan hits double trouble Sega has just had a rotten week that saw it battle a data leak and an outage. The outage impacted the company’s ALL.Net and Aime services, which connect arcade games across different locations. The services include administrative features for arcade operators, plus services for gamers including pre-payment to play, high score and profile recording, and networked gaming. Sega suspended some ALL.Net and Aime services on November 1 after discovering unauthorized access to servers. At least thirteen games and services were then unavailable until around November 15. The company hasn’t explained what went wrong, but assured customers the incident was not a data breach and that payment information was safe. But data did leak for those who subscribe to some Sega newsletters. Sega uses a third-party outfit called Arara Co. to send some emails, and it leaked email addresses. No other personal data leaked from Arara. Sega has nonetheless warned newsletter recipients to watch out for suspicious messages. Alibaba floats chip unit Chinese tech giant Alibaba last week announced its intention to float its T-Head chip design biz on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange. The filing announcing the spinoff describes T-Head as “a leading provider of full-stack data center chips which enable system-level compute solutions in China,” suggesting Alibaba doesn’t think buyers in the rest of the world are keen to acquire its chips. T-Head going public “allows a more efficient deployment of Alibaba Group’s financial resources,” the filing states, and should also mean the chip design outfit can more easily find third-party customers. India bans export of dead batteries The government of India last week banned the export of “Lithium-Ion battery Black Mass” – a powdery substance created during the process of recycling batteries. “It contains recoverable quantities of critical minerals, including lithium, cobalt, nickel and manganese,” according to the government’s announcement of the ban, which argues the measure “will increase domestic recovery of lithium, cobalt, nickel and other critical minerals, thereby reducing import dependence and the associated foreign exchange outgo. It will also strengthen supply chains for battery manufacturing, electric vehicles, energy storage and clean-energy technologies.” “Further, the measure will advance the circular economy and ‘urban mining’, reducing reliance on primary mining, while supporting environmentally sound recycling of this hazardous material within the country in accordance with applicable environmental regulations.” Japanese giants to investigate orbiting datacenters Five giant Japanese companies – NTT, Mitsubishi Electric, MUFG Bank, the Development Bank of Japan, and telco NTT DOCOMO – last week signed a memorandum of understanding that will see them jointly explore development and operation of a mega-constellation of satellites. The five “will examine the technical and business feasibility of commercializing a diverse range of services enabled by mega-constellations, including communications, Earth observation, satellite-based positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT), and space data centers.” Mitsubishi already works with the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) to jointly develop and manufacture rockets. The two banks regularly back big infrastructure projects, while the two NTT entities have advanced comms expertise. The five companies didn’t set a deadline for delivery of a plan. If they do decide there’s a business opportunity, they’ll likely need to look beyond Japan for launch capacity as JAXA does not currently possess a re-usable launch vehicle and operates at a modest launch cadence compared to private launch operators. ®

events.title: Musk, Uber co-founder join call for Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia
events.summary: Elon Musk and several tech heavyweights are among more than 158,000 signatories of an open letter calling for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia chief. Elon Musk, Travis Kalanick and over 158,000 others want Jensen Huang back as Nvidia chief after his Nov 12 resignation over two extramarital affairs. Supporters say Huang made Nvidia central to AI and ask the board to “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”. Some investors back all options, but US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent wants an outside chief and a “dramatic shake-up” over chip smuggling concerns. SAN FRANCISCO – Tech tycoon Elon Musk and an Uber co-founder are, as at Nov 15, among more than 158,000 signatories of an open letter calling for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia chief. The letter demands that the company’s board members “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”. Huang resigned on Nov 12, ending a 33-year run at the helm of the AI giant he co-founded after revelations he had two extramarital affairs, one with a woman accused of spying for China and another with a subordinate. Alongside the SpaceX chief, the tech heavyweight signatories include Tim Sweeney, founder and chief executive of video game publisher Epic Games, and Garry Tan, president of Y Combinator, San Francisco’s most renowned business incubator. Another signatory, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, wrote that Huang had “erred, yes – to err is to be human – but I do not believe anything he has done rises to the bar of separating him from his company”. More than 7,500 signatories identify themselves as Nvidia employees, equivalent to 18% of the company’s workforce. The support illustrates the unique standing of the leather-jacketed executive, who is seen as a godfather of artificial intelligence within the industry. Under his leadership, Nvidia became a pivotal Silicon Valley investor, financing data centres and start-ups, earning it the nickname “the central bank of AI”. But the company has also faced criticism that it has fuelled a speculative investment bubble. Huang championed open AI models, including Chinese ones, and fought any constraints on the AI race, clashing on these issues with Claude creator Anthropic and its chief Dario Amodei. According to the Financial Times, Huang has discussed a possible return with people close to him, and one of his allies says he is assembling a crisis team of executives to seek White House support. On Nov 13, two major shareholders, investors Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker, urged the board to keep “all options” open. In Washington, however, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent argued on Nov 15 that Nvidia should look “outside” the company for its next chief. “They need a dramatic shake-up,” Bessent said on Fox News, demanding that the company explain whether it had knowingly turned a blind eye to the smuggling of its chips to China. events.title: Indian chip startup Bharat Semi lands $24M seed round as it eyes global AI sensor market
events.summary: Bharat Semi , an Indian semiconductor startup, has raised $24 million in seed funding to develop AI-enabled image sensors, as it seeks to win customers in the United States and elsewhere. The investment comes as the nearly five-year-old, pre-revenue startup says it has secured design wins with U.S. defense technology company General Atomics and India’s Kaynes Semicon. Its image sensors, however, remain under development, with the startup targeting its initial commercial production in 2027. India has committed billions of dollars to build up a domestic semiconductor industry, with a hope to become an alternative manufacturing hub as U.S. companies look to diversify supply chains beyond China. The country, however, has yet to establish itself as a major chip manufacturing hub. Meanwhile, the AI boom is also giving Indian startups such as Bharat Semi an opportunity to develop specialized chips for global markets. The New Delhi-based startup is developing programmable image sensors that combine image capture, processing, and AI capabilities on a single chip, reducing the need to send visual data to separate processors. The move could cut system costs by at least 70% compared with conventional setups that use a separate image sensor, image signal processor, and a system-on-chip, co-founder Vrinda Kapoor (pictured above, right) said in an interview. “Our aim here is to move from sensors to sense-making solutions,” Kapoor told TechCrunch. Kapoor, a South Park Commons fellow who earlier worked in healthcare technology, co-founded Bharat Semi in late 2021 with Vinayak Dalmia (pictured above, left), the startup’s managing director, who previously worked at McKinsey and in private equity. Its chief technology officer, Boyd Fowler, previously held the same role at image-sensor maker OmniVision. Bharat Semi is targeting smart homes, industrial automation, surveillance, and aerospace. Without disclosing specifics, Kapoor pointed to air conditioners that could detect when a room is empty and adjust automatically and drones that could process visual information — even with the absence of more expensive computing hardware elsewhere in the system. The startup’s first-generation sensors are already in prototyping, while its second-generation sensors, which will incorporate more advanced AI capabilities, are expected to reach the prototype stage by mid-2027, Kapoor said. Moreover, the startup plans to get those newer sensors into customers’ hands by the end of 2027. The all-equity seed round was led by Info Edge Group, South Park Commons, and Indus Bridge Ventures, with participation from Valour Capital, Micromax, Gaingels, and individual investors. Bharat Semi, Kapoor said, plans to use the funding to expand its engineering team, complete product development, and bring its sensors to market. Bharat Semi has about 75 employees across India and the U.S., including 10 to 12 in its American operations, which span engineering and business development in Santa Clara. The startup plans to increase its U.S. headcount to around 20 by mid-2027, Kapoor said. It has also begun hiring engineers in Europe. “It’s a story of can we build a global technology company out of India,” Kapoor said. In 2024, Bharat Semi announced plans for a semiconductor fabrication project in India involving a technology partnership with the U.S. Space Force. The initiative, Kapoor said, remains in development and the startup is working to identify domestic partners that would build and operate the facility. The project is separate from Bharat Semi’s image-sensor business, Kapoor added. The startup plans to remain fabless, outsourcing chip manufacturing while focusing on semiconductor design and software. The new funding will not be used to finance the proposed fabrication facility. events.title: Woolworths apologises after customers report drained gift card balances
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Woolworths customers report hundreds of dollars stolen from digital gift cards The gift cards were purchased following a 4 per cent discount promotion through Everyday Gifting. ( Supplied ) Dozens of Woolworths customers say their digital WISH gift cards have been drained. Woolworths has acknowledged an issue affecting a number of e-gift cards and is investigating. Customers who contacted the ABC say they purchased their cards after a 4 per cent promotional offer on Everyday Gifting. Dozens of Woolworths customers say they have lost hundreds of dollars after discovering their digital gift cards were drained by transactions they did not authorise. The ABC has been contacted by customers across Australia who say their Everyday WISH gift cards, purchased through the Everyday Rewards website or app, were spent by someone else. Some customers have reported losing up to $500, with transactions appearing at stores in different states from where the cards were purchased. Woolworths has acknowledged an issue affecting "a number of" customer e-gift cards, apologising to those affected and saying it is investigating the reports as a priority. Complaints first appeared on Australian bargain-sharing website OzBargain last week, with similar reports subsequently emerging across Facebook and Reddit. All of the customers who contacted the ABC appear to have purchased their gift cards during a promotional offer through Everyday Gifting that advertised a 4 per cent discount. Everyday WISH gift cards can be redeemed in store and online at participating Woolworths Group retailers and partners, including Big W, BWS, Dan Murphy's and Cellarmasters. The complaints reported to the ABC so far involve Everyday WISH cards purchased digitally through the Everyday Rewards website or app. ( Supplied ) Deborah Kellie, from Brisbane, said she lost $500 after purchasing an Everyday WISH card last Monday. "I have been an Everyday Rewards customer for ages, and I usually buy my rewards cards through the RACQ," she said. But Ms Kellie said a promotional email from Everyday Gifting advertised a "great deal", offering an extra 1 per cent discount on WISH gift cards compared with RACQ. "So I thought I've got to go shopping next week, I'll get one from them [Everyday Gifting] instead." Two days later, she discovered the entire balance had been spent at a Big W store in Doncaster, Victoria, despite never having used the card or shared its details. In Sydney, Michael Bennett said he had also switched from buying the WISH gift card through the NRMA app after seeing the 4 per cent discount offer in the Everyday Rewards app. He said he purchased a $400 WISH gift card through the app on November 9. But when he attempted to use it at a Woolworths store in Hornsby on November 14, the card had disappeared from his digital wallet. Deborah Kellie says her gift card was drained in another state two days after she purchased it. ( Supplied ) After checking the balance through a link in his email, he discovered the money had been spent. The transaction history showed $400 had been spent at a Big W store in Pagewood, in Sydney's east, on November 12. Mr Bennett said he had not shared the gift card details, his mobile phone had remained in his possession, and his Everyday Rewards account was protected by a complex password and two-factor authentication. He also said the gift card had never been physically printed. "Woolworths warn customers to treat gift cards like cash," Mr Bennett said. Suspecting a cybersecurity breach, Ms Kellie said she cancelled her Visa card as a precaution. She said she made three attempts to contact Woolworths customer service, but was unable to speak to anyone despite waiting for more than an hour on the phone the first two times. On her third attempt, Ms Kellie said an automated message advised the company was receiving an increasing number of calls before disconnecting her. She subsequently emailed Woolworths screenshots and details of the transactions and lodged a report with cybersecurity authorities. The report has since been referred to Queensland Police for assessment in correspondence seen by the ABC. Following ABC enquiries, a Woolworths spokesperson advised customers who notice an unrecognised transaction to contact its Gift Card Support team at giftcard@customerservice.woolworths.com.au . Customers can also log into the Everyday Gifting website and register their details on the homepage. "Our team will work directly with customers to determine the appropriate next steps, including issuing replacement e-gift cards for customers impacted," the spokesperson said.

events.title: What to know about summer jobs, from where to find them to thinking 'strategically'
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts What to consider before hunting for a summer job There's an influx of hospitality, retail and tourism jobs over summer, economist Blair Chapman says. ( ABC News: Sam Ikin ) If you're looking for a few extra hours of work or desperately trying to save before university begins, a summer job could be the right fit for you. These seasonal roles can simply be about earning extra cash, but it could help you discover what you love (or hate) doing for work. It could even help with starting a new career. Ben Walker was 16 when he got a casual job at his local supermarket in Sale, in regional Victoria. Ben Walker's first casual job led to ongoing part-time work. ( Supplied: Ben Walker ) The 21-year-old says that led to the part-time job that now supports him while studying game design at university. In the beginning, Ben says he learnt a lot from interactions with people outside of school and cricket. "The people skills, I think, are massive," he says. Why summer is a good time to get a job There is an influx of roles in hospitality, retail and tourism ahead of Christmas and summer, says Blair Chapman, the chief economist at employment service Seek. "In Australia we get the double dose of Christmas and summer," he says. Retail picks up from early November (because of Black Friday sales), and online shopping has led to an increase in warehouse or "pick-packer roles" too, Dr Chapman says. And given cost-of-living pressures and airfare prices, more Australians are likely to holiday closer to home this summer, he says. "That sort of domestic-driven tourism might pick up because people can't afford to go overseas." Dr Chapman says there is also "a bit of an evolution" in who is looking for summer jobs. "There's a cost-of-living crunch and people are looking for that second job to help supplement their income," he says. What are the benefits (other than pay)? Grozdana Manalo says her first job as a barista began a "love affair" with coffee and helped her build confidence and communication skills. Why a job 'that's just a job' works for these people The dos and don'ts of job hunting while still employed The steps first home buyers can take while saving for their deposit "It also showed me just how hard and long some people work and made me really appreciate being a uni student," she says. She's now a career services manager at the University of Sydney's Business School. "Summer jobs can also help students discover what they enjoy, and just as importantly, what they don't," Ms Manalo says. Seasonal and casual roles can also help young people develop professional skills, she says. "Teamwork, communication, problem solving and time management — all important skills no matter what job or career you pick in the future." Thinking strategically when applying for jobs Irma Mooi-Reci is a professor of sociology at the University of Melbourne and the CEO of a company specialising in workforce data and skill gaps. She would like young people to think "more strategically" about summer employment. "Is it because you want to pay your bills? Is it because you want to have that experience or get a reference? Or is it because you want to get that first permanent job?" she asks. Economic report dubs 2026 'year of AI' A new economic report by consultancy firm Deloitte says the AI "winners" will be organisations that combine human and machine strengths, with recruiters saying human judgement will still be key. It's worth looking for a job that complements your career goals and whether an employer will see the experience as relevant, Professor Mooi-Reci says. "Find something that you like doing, that you feel passionate about and learn as much as possible." Professor Mooi-Reci says young people can become overwhelmed by information and fearmongering about the job market, the value of their degree and artificial intelligence. "Don't be afraid, but think strategically," she adds. How to find a summer job (and avoid exploitation) If you're after seasonal work, Ms Manalo recommends looking for roles advertised on social media and job boards, or simply walking into local businesses and asking if there are positions available. She says there are also "hidden job markets", which is why so many positions are filled before they're advertised. "This is all about leveraging your personal networks and making it known that you're looking for work," she says. If you're young or have never been employed before, understanding workplace rights and responsibilities is very important, Ms Manalo says.

events.title: South Korea’s instant ramen giants take their spicy rivalry global
events.summary: For nearly four decades, NongShim has dominated South Korea’s instant noodle market with its signature Shin Ramyun. NongShim is fighting Samyang overseas with a 200 billion won Busan export plant for Shin Ramyun, which will lift export capacity by 70% and support global growth. Samyang’s Buldak has become a viral hit, lifting overseas sales above 80% of revenue and helping it overtake NongShim in some markets, including China and Europe. Both firms are expanding fast as the global instant-noodle market grows, and NongShim wants to double global noodle sales by 2030 and enter the stir-fried noodle market next year. SEOUL – For nearly four decades, NongShim has dominated South Korea’s instant noodle market with its signature Shin Ramyun. But when South Korean ramen became a global phenomenon, it was a rival that captured the world’s appetite – and investors’ imagination. Samyang Foods did it with its Buldak, which became a viral sensation with global fans filming themselves eating the intensely spicy noodles on social media. The craze pushed Samyang’s overseas sales above 80% of revenue – compared with NongShim’s 37% – and lifted its market value to nearly four times that of its rival. Now NongShim is spending heavily to rebuild investor confidence. At the heart of the push is a 200 billion won (S$190 million) factory for NongShim’s iconic Shin Ramyun in the port city of Busan, the company’s first dedicated export plant and home to what the company calls the world’s fastest instant-noodle production lines. The facility will boost NongShim’s domestic export capacity by 70% as it seeks to regain ground lost to Samyang overseas. “We may have been somewhat slow in responding to global demand early on because our products were so deeply loved at home for so long,” said Ji Songha, NongShim’s head of global marketing. A decades-old domestic rivalry between two of South Korea’s biggest food makers is intensifying overseas. NongShim and Samyang, both based in Seoul, are racing to capitalise on a K-food boom that has pushed Korean noodles into mainstream supermarkets from the US to Europe, just as the global instant noodle market is projected to grow about 23% to US$63.3 billion (S$81.5 billion) by 2030. NongShim’s new six-storey complex, which opened in October, is designed to produce 600 packets a minute on each line – twice the speed of conventional setups. Inside, raw dough takes barely seven minutes to become a shelf-ready packet of Shin Ramyun. Guided by artificial intelligence sensors and automated mixers, the noodles are rolled, flash-fried and boxed at blinding speed. The factory will nearly double NongShim’s annual domestic export capacity to 1.2 billion packets, and raise its total global capacity to 6.2 billion across Korea and four factories in the US and China. Production from Busan will initially be directed to Japan, Europe, Australia, India and South-east Asia. NongShim aims to double global noodle sales to 5.4 trillion won by 2030, which would lift overseas sale to more than 60% of revenue. Such growth would also elevate it to the global top five instant noodle makers alongside Nissin Foods Holdings and Maggi-maker Nestle. NongShim’s push puts it head-to-head with Samyang. The Buldak maker is rapidly gaining ground in overseas markets where NongShim dominated, having already overtaken it in key markets like China and Europe. It is on track to become the third-largest instant noodle seller in the US in 2026 – right behind NongShim, according to Euromonitor International. Samyang is also accelerating its global expansion, and announced last week it would invest more than 131 billion won in a new Vietnamese production line. Its first overseas plant in China is set to open in January. For NongShim, the test will be whether the new capacity translates into faster sales growth and improved profitability. The company’s valuation could get a lift from a rebound in US sales and increased output from the Busan facility, according to Hanwha Investment & Securities analyst Han Yujung. NongShim’s push for overseas growth has a promising early start – sales of Shin Ramyun abroad jumped 36% in the first half of 2026. Still, Samyang commands a valuation premium over NongShim, its stock is trading at 13.4-times forward-earnings versus the latter’s 11.4 – meaning investors are paying more per won of projected profit in anticipation of faster growth. NongShim is also borrowing from its rival’s playbook. To court Gen Z shoppers abroad, it has leaned into pop culture – launching limited-edition Shin Ramyun tied to Netflix’s K-Pop Demon Hunters and setting up booths at fan conventions globally. It also plans to roll out a new stir-fried Shin Ramyun in 2027, entering the soupless-noodle category that propelled Buldak’s global success. “We cannot yet claim that we are outperforming Samyang in many international markets,” Ji, NongShim’s marketing head, said. “But we are studying and benchmarking what Samyang has done well.

events.title: Dems' Denver victory party previews 2028 battles
events.summary: DENVER — Thousands of Democrats gathered here this weekend for a giddy postelection summit, reveling in their party's historic midterm victories and touting the center-left strategy they say powered them. But some progressives saw the event as a lavish, out-of-touch affair bankrolled by billionaires — exactly what Democrats just campaigned against. "I'm all for celebration, but perhaps a fancy retreat does not exactly meet the tenor of the moment," said Josh Orton, president of the liberal group Demand Justice and a veteran of Bernie Sanders' 2020 campaign. Why it matters: The competing views of What's Next, the buzzy confab held by the influential centrist organization Majority Democrats, offer an early glimpse of the ideological battles over health care, money in politics and other issues that will define the party's 2028 presidential primary. Zoom in: Democrats in the Mile High City were practically vibrating with happiness, still not quite able to believe they'd won back both chambers of Congress and flipped deep-red states such as Mississippi and South Carolina. "The vibes are excellent," Delaware Rep. Sarah McBride, a member of the Majority Democrats, said in an interview. "The last high-water mark, we were all in our houses on Zooms," she added, referring to the 2020 presidential election. "This is the first time there's been an undeniable capacity to celebrate widespread wins in the last decade." Free drinks flowed. Political operatives sported bomber jackets embroidered with the phrase "Majority Democrats." Speakers were immortalized in rock concert–style posters on the walls. For a brief moment in Denver's Mission Ballroom, the often-in-disarray Democratic Party looked united. Several presidential hopefuls downplayed the party's divides in speeches. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro said onstage that ordinary people don't give "a damn" about "where we fall on some imaginary political spectrum." Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin quipped in her address that elected officials who were fighting over progressives vs. moderates had "missed the plot." The other side: But others in the party weren't interested in all the kumbaya. Young protesters sneaked into the event and heckled House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), shouting "You're a f**king traitor!" while calling for Medicare for All and impeachment. Some audience members were palpably annoyed, yelling "Shut up!" Another flashpoint emerged over high-dollar donors and super PACs. Majority Democrats — which is largely funded by a billionaire couple and describes itself as an alternative to both the "activist left" and a "gerontocratic establishment" — is already in the crosshairs of the Lever, a progressive publication. Majority Democrats' funding has been the focus of reporting by the Lever. The group tussled with the news site over the Denver event, initially denying it press passes and later blocking one of its journalists from interviewing an elected official. David Sirota, founder of the Lever, said the group's actions were "Trump-like attempts at retribution." But there was a silver lining for the outlet: The back-and-forth generated the single biggest influx of new subscribers in its history, he said. What they're saying: "What's Next was an overwhelming success: It brought together 3,500 Democrats from across the political spectrum to talk about what worked this cycle and where we go next," said Majority Democrats spokesperson Vidhya Jeyadev. "This cycle, we won seats that had been written off for a generation and proved there is no one way to be a Democrat." The intrigue: Some potential 2028 candidates in Denver tried to portray themselves as unifiers who can bridge the party's divides. New Jersey Sen. Andy Kim, who declined to rule out a 2028 bid, said, "I understand" where the protesters were coming from. "People are furious," he added.

events.title: Trump blames Biden for airline ground stop
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Trump breaks silence after airline ground stop to blame Biden administration Donald Trump says the Biden administration was "a disaster" for the Federal Aviation Administration. ( Reuters: Aaron Schwartz ) Donald Trump has made his first public comments on the weekend's air travel issues, blaming the Biden administration for leaving "a broken system". He has also called on Congress for more funding to upgrade America's outdated air traffic control systems. Thousands more US flights have been cancelled, with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy warning travel disruptions would continue for another day. The Trump administration says the air travel havoc triggered by a no-take-off order on Friday could drag on for another day, pushing back its timetable for a return to normal. Nearly 2,000 more flights were cancelled on Sunday and questions remained over how such chaos could unfold in the world's largest economy, a country that prides itself on its technological prowess. Stranded passengers wandered through chaotic US airports for a third day. Officials have blamed Friday's flight chaos on faulty work to upgrade air traffic control communication cables. US says wires to blame for grounded flights The US government has blamed a nationwide aviation shutdown which has disrupted more than 20,000 flights on a program to replace copper wires with new fibre ones. On Sunday, US President Donald Trump ended uncharacteristic days of silence on the ground stop, but only to blame his predecessor, Joe Biden, for the debacle. Mr Trump insisted he inherited a mess from the Biden administration and said Congress, which his party controlled for two years, must approve funds to upgrade America's outdated air traffic control system. "The Biden administration was an FAA disaster," Mr Trump said, referring to the Federal Aviation Administration. "Everything they touched turned bad. Big money spent unwisely, making an old and broken system worse than when they began." FAA chief Bryan Bedford said on Saturday that air travel for millions of Americans stranded at airports would return to normal by the close of business on Sunday. Sean Duffy has also blamed prior administrations for dated systems. ( Reuters: Eric Lee ) But Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Sunday morning that it would take longer to get planes, crews and travellers to where they needed to be. "So, in the airspace, we're going to see things come back to normal today, but probably fully normal tomorrow," Mr Duffy told America's ABC News. "We had airplanes and crews out of position because of Friday, so it takes a little bit of time to do that." Mr Duffy also flatly rejected calls for his resignation over the travel chaos, insisting he inherited woefully outdated air traffic control infrastructure such as, he said, radar equipment dating back to the 1960s. "So when we do work and things go wrong, of course I'm the secretary. But I also have to acknowledge what was delivered to me," Mr Duffy said in an interview on CNN. As of Sunday afternoon, more than 1,880 flights within, into or out of the United States had been cancelled, according to the travel monitor site FlightAware. The Trump administration has blamed Friday's nationwide ground stoppage — meaning no planes could take off — on a botched replacement of old copper wire communication lines. What we know about why US flights were grounded Aviation authorities cited "extraordinary circumstances and reasons of safety", with the White House blaming outdated air traffic control technology for a communications outage. Friday's disruption was only the second time such a ground stop had been issued in US airspace, among the busiest in the world, since the 9/11 attacks. Mr Duffy has appealed for $US50 billion ($74 billion) in funds to upgrade and modernise the air traffic control system, and called for Congress, which controls the purse strings of the US government, to "meet this moment". But Democrats quickly pounced to say Congress under Trump's Republicans could already have done this.

events.title: Some Dems' 2028 strategy: Make America Nice Again
events.summary: Some Democrats weighing 2028 campaigns for president believe the midterms proved that Americans have soured on Trump-style, scorched-earth political warfare and want a brand of politics that's nicer and more optimistic. Others aren't so sure. Why it matters: Democrats' midterm blowout has prompted a debate over the lessons of 2026 — whether voters in the 2028 primary will want their own ruthless fighter after two more years of President Trump, or will be itching for a more unifying figure. Zoom in: That divide was reflected in several potential 2028 contenders' comments around the midterms. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg told his supporters that the end of the Trump era "means a politics where we can check the news and actually feel our blood pressure come down a little." In his reelection victory speech, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro told supporters that "you declared that you could not be more ready for an end of this ruthless chaos and cruelty." In California, Gov. Gavin Newsom — who led the successful ballot measure to create more Democratic House seats in response to Trump's redistricting push in red states — boasted that California "fought fire with fire." Newsom mocked Democrats who he said would have responded by merely writing op-eds in the New York Times. "Donald Trump is not screwing around, nor are we," Newsom said at a preelection rally, adding that he was proud of leading the "most un-Trump state in America." The big picture: The midterm results provided an argument for each side. Several key victories for Democrats in red states came from candidates preaching decency, or voters recoiling from vicious Republican attacks. In Kansas, Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton said one of his campaign's big ideas was "decency" — and that he wanted to become the "best friend" of Sen. Jerry Moran (R-Kan.). In Ohio, Gov.-elect Amy Acton told her supporters that "basic decency is on the ballot" after her opponent and Vice President Vance defended an attack ad featuring Acton's mother, from whom Acton had been estranged since childhood after accusing her stepfather of sexual abuse. Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico, a seminarian and the first Democrat to be elected statewide in three decades, said that "love my neighbor" informed his approach to politics. In Denver last week at a gathering of Democratic leaders, Talarico pressed the point: "It's been 10 years of this kind of politics — politics as blood sport, politics as trolling and owning and name-calling, politics as professional wrestling. It tears families apart. It ends friendships, and it leaves us all feeling terrible all of the time." The other side: Other Democrats who won key races embraced something like Newsom's edgier approach by pledging to fight fire with fire, and to not unilaterally disarm against Republicans. Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed said on the campaign trail that when his opponents go low, he doesn't take the higher ground. He prefers to take them "to the mud and choke them out." He added that too many Democrats "tell you they're fighting, only to show up with a strongly worded letter." Reality check: Hamilton, Acton and Talarico had unifying messages, but they and their allies also ran tens of millions of dollars in negative ads against their Republican opponents. In 2008, Barack Obama also had a larger theme of change and unity but ran a campaign that unapologetically attacked his opponents.

events.title: Vance may wait until late spring to reveal 2028 plans
events.summary: Vice President Vance won't make a final decision on whether to run for president in 2028 until after the new year — and may wait until late spring to announce his intentions publicly, two sources with knowledge of his plans tell Axios. Why it matters: Vance remains the early favorite to succeed President Trump as the GOP's presidential nominee, but the party's midterm losses have complicated his political future and could reshape the 2028 field. People familiar with Vance's thinking say he's genuinely undecided about running, and that his decision-making timeline was in place before the midterms. Advisers caution that the timing could change, however. Vance is still discussing a potential bid with his family, including his wife, Usha, following the birth of their fourth child, the sources said. The big picture: Vance allies say the midterm losses haven't changed his standing as the early 2028 GOP front-runner, citing his donor network, political infrastructure and name recognition. Vance co-founded the secretive Rockbridge Network , which could anchor his presidential fundraising operation. The group met in Houston after the midterms. As Republican National Committee finance chair, Vance has cultivated relationships with major contributors. He also has ties to technology donors Peter Thiel, David Sacks and Elon Musk — the world's richest person and the GOP's biggest financier. Vance campaigned nationwide for the midterms, building relationships with GOP activists and officials who could prove valuable in 2028. Behind the scenes: Vance's closest political advisers believe he should run in 2028 and that he's likely to do so, according to a person close to the vice president. But the GOP's midterm losses have given Republicans who want to move on from the Trump administration an opening to argue for a different direction in 2028. Vance likely will have to answer for the Trump administration's record in 2028, potentially complicating his presidential ambitions. Vance privately opposed the Iran war, and some Republicans interpreted his post-midterm criticism of the conflict as an effort to distance himself from Trump's decision to attack Iran. The intrigue: Republicans close to Vance see Trump's continued presence as another reason to delay announcing his 2028 plans. Vance is wary that launching a campaign too early could shift attention away from Trump and risk alienating him. Trump said that "a lot of people didn't like [Vance's] comments" about the Iran war, but added that he wasn't among them and insisted their relationship wasn't affected. Zoom in: While Vance weighs a presidential campaign, a few other Republicans are doing so as well — namely Texas Sen. Ted Cruz, who's been among the most active Republicans preparing for a potential 2028 run. Cruz's team has held meetings about a possible run, according to people familiar with his operation. But many Republicans, including some Cruz allies, doubt he could seriously challenge Vance, particularly if Trump endorses the vice president. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is viewed by some Republicans as a potentially more formidable rival to Vance. Rubio has attracted support from influential GOP figures, including megadonor Ken Griffin . But Rubio repeatedly has said he would support Vance if the VP were to run, and Rubio's workload as secretary of state and national security adviser has left him without Vance's ready-made political operation. Other potential Republican contenders include former Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin, Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp and Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis. DeSantis has been particularly outspoken , calling the GOP's midterm losses a near "extinction-level event" and pointing to Florida's Republican victories as a model for rebuilding the party. What they're saying: A Vance spokesperson declined to comment.

events.title: UK will have 'voice' but no vote on EU food rules in Brexit reset
events.summary: The UK will have a "voice in the room" but no vote on European Union food policies as part of a so-called "Brexit reset" to reduce red tape, EU relations minister Hamish Falconer has told the BBC. Prime Minister Andy Burnham hopes to agree a deal at a summit on Friday but critics have said a reset will make the UK "a rule taker" but not a rule maker. Falconer said the UK will be involved in a process to shape the rules and said the deal could help bring down prices for shoppers. The reset would not involve any upfront payments, Falconer added, but made it clear there could well be an "exit clause" in case a future UK government reversed the closer alignment. Falconer said it was "reasonable" to consider what would happen if a future Conservative or Reform government wanted to undo the new arrangements. "The EU is worried about that and you can see why," he said. The BBC understands that the clause is a result of EU concerns about the possible cost of having to rebuild facilities for border food safety checks which were put in place following Brexit. The reset means they will be dismantled. In September, the Conservative Party said it was "raising the alarm" over the government's planned reset, saying it would leave British consumers and businesses "dangerously exposed, with no input on how regulations are made or power to reject them". Both the Conservatives and Reform have said they would undo the planned reset if they were in power. Minister for EU relations Hamish Falconer The prime minister has said he believes there is a "win-win" deal to be had with the EU. Speaking at a Marks & Spencer food court in central London, Falconer said the deal would help bring down costs for firms importing food. "This will mean less cost for supermarkets, and I hope that less cost then turns into cheaper produce on the shelves," he said. He said currently "pages and pages" of form-filling meant some suppliers had given up exporting to the EU and some products, such as Lincolnshire sausages, meant they were almost impossible to export at all. Some M&S trucks require over 300 pages of documents for food exports, from export health certificates, phytosanitary certificates, visits from vets and border check paperwork. Some exports are rejected for having the wrong colour of ink on forms, or an inaccurate Latin name for cooked meats. "The amount of paperwork you would need to do, the amount of uncertainty - you have to have it in the right pen colour, if it's not black, it might be refused," Falconer said. "If you're selling Cox apples from Kent, they have to wait a day before they go into the European Union." The reset could also mean "tearing up" checks that were introduced on goods flowing from Great Britain to Northern Ireland, following Brexit, he said, as well as separate "Not for EU" labelling. Falconer said the impact of the reset deal for food would be an additional £5bn. The whole deal to be signed on Friday is calculated to add 0.4% to UK GDP. This wider agreement includes aligning emissions trading rules, and agreeing to a youth mobility scheme, as well as the reset on food trading. Some British sausages have faced barriers to being exported to the EU Tom Bradshaw, president of the National Farmers' Union, welcomed reduced border inspections and paperwork but said that for the NFU it was "a moment of opportunity and risk" with farmers waiting to see what carve-outs and transitional arrangements would be included. Trade volumes in food exports to the EU had "fallen significantly - by over a third" since 2019, he said. But the UK should take a "pragmatic" approach to implementing any new rules. He raised pesticides and precision breeding - or gene edited crops - as areas where he hoped some compromise would be found. UK firms are, for example, developing tomatoes engineered to contain extra vitamin D. Historically the EU has had much stricter rules on gene-editing, but this year relaxed regulations. Falconer said people would have to "wait and see the detail" in this area. He said there were bound to be compromises and trade-offs in any deal but that where the UK had advantages the government wanted to make sure "those aren't lost under the deal". Crisp flavourings a contentious area Another contentious area has been crisp flavourings, with concerns raised that stricter EU rules on certain ingredients might limit the sale of some popular snack flavours in the UK. "I want to take this opportunity to absolutely stamp down on misinformation about smoky bacon crisps," Falconer said. Post-Brexit the UK had stayed "pretty closely aligned" to European food safety standards, he said. Two leading snack brands had already adapted their recipes to accommodate EU rules, an example of the kind of alignment that would happen whether or not there was a reset of UK-EU relations. "The truth is, almost every business in this country that wants to export food or drink will be aligning with EU rules because it's our biggest market.

events.title: Is bad news for Jensen Huang also bad news for the AI industry?
events.summary: We didn’t see this coming. Or at least, I didn’t — a week ago, when I wrote about Nvidia’s board opening an investigation into then-CEO Jensen Huang, I assumed his job was safe. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Rebecca Bellan, Tim De Chant, and I discussed how Huang’s ouster went down and what it means for the larger AI economy. While Tim said he saw it coming (albeit not this quickly), Rebecca said, “I didn’t think it was going to happen at all.” “Jensen is Nvidia, right?” she added. “And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia.” Similarly, I marveled at how quickly Huang’s support seemed to crumble, with more scandals seeming to emerge every day. (At the same time, there are many who’d still like to see him return .) And we also took a moment to wonder what will happen to Nvidia’s investments in the larger AI ecosystem. Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity; you can listen to the whole episode here . Tim De Chant: I figured this was coming. I didn’t think it would happen this quickly. I thought there would be at least a few days. Rebecca Bellan: I didn’t think it was going to happen at all. I mean, Jensen is Nvidia, right? And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia. And we’ve got nothing but the last few years of data to show us that billionaires can do whatever the hell they want. So it was surprising to me — it almost restored my faith in humanity, that he resigned. But someone said to me, “If this were Elon, nothing would happen.” He would not be resigning. Nothing would be going down Anthony Ha: Which is interesting, because I would have said, as of a week ago, or even just a few days ago, that Jensen is in the same category as Elon. I mean, no one is quite as special as Elon is, but it’s a big, incredibly successful company. Like you said — in a lot of ways, the entire AI economy is built on top of Nvidia. And for most people, Jensen Huang is Nvidia. He’s the biggest shareholder. He has family members who work at the company, and probably most importantly, there was no succession plan in place. So this was not something that they were prepared for at all. Rebecca: I think we should actually take a step back, because we just launched into this conversation assuming — rightly so — that our listeners will know what the heck we’re talking about. But for those who somehow don’t, Jensen resigned on Thursday, after it came out he was having an affair with a former executive at an Nvidia customer called Megaspeed, who’s alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence. And then there was another reported affair with an Nvidia executive. So he’s resigned. Nvidia CFO Collette Kress is jumping in as the interim CEO. She’s a longtime board member. I think it’s always interesting when a CFO steps in to be a CEO. It just means we’re going to manage expenses right now, like that’s the key. Anthony: I think a big part of the message is: This is not necessarily someone you should expect to be in this role for the long term. No disrespect to her, but it feels like a caretaker appointment while they figure things out. Just to get into that backstory a little bit more, what has been really remarkable to me has been this sense that a lot of what ultimately brought Huang down, [that] stuff was at least known in intelligence circles for a while. Apparently, this report that [raises] questions, concerns about his relationship with Alice Huang is something that was circulating a year ago, or close to a year ago. And then suddenly, everything really accelerated, Starting over the weekend, with Jensen Huang admitting to having an affair, the board saying it was investigating, but that it still had a lot of faith in him. And then this week, this other affair being reported on, and it just felt like there was all this bad news coming fairly quickly. But also, it wasn’t this thing that no one had known before. I guess a lot of the general public hadn’t known. So it’s this combined feeling of, “Wow, the ground kind of shifted so quickly under him,” even though the worst stuff, the possibility that somehow national security might have been threatened, is something that actually has been known by the government for nearly a year, if not more. Rebecca: That’s exactly right. Trump was given some warnings about Huang’s affair with someone who has ties to Chinese intelligence, potentially, and it seemed like he didn’t really mind. I think what’s important here, though, is to note that Jensen Huang has been an advocate for loosening chip exports to China. And so this is where the crux of it is. Can anyone trust him as the CEO of this company when he’s advocating for loosening chip exports to China? Which a lot of people believe is a national security issue, because that means it will give Chinese AI companies access to our powerful chips, which will help them improve their AI, which could threaten America. I mean, there’s two sides of this coin.

events.title: SNL gathers all the tech tycoons for a lesson in dating and spycraft
events.summary: While awkward, creepy tech executives have become a recurring theme on Saturday Night Live, this week’s episode gave the cast a chance to show off all their impressions at once. In a single sketch, we got James Austin Johnson as Peter Thiel, Ben Marshall as Sam Altman, Jane Wickline as Dario Amodei, Jeremy Culhane as Elon Musk, Andrew Dismukes as Mark Zuckerberg — and eventually, the recently departed Bowen Yang joined the fun as Jensen Huang. Huang’s ouster from Nvidia (after admitting to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy) could have serious implications for the tech industry ; it also provided a hook for some obvious jokes about rich nerds being easy marks for women (or men) who are out of their league. In the sketch, a CIA agent played by host John Mulaney (hilarious as ever, if not entirely confident about how to pronounce “Palantir” or “Nvidia”) attempts to painstakingly explain why these execs should be suspicious when someone attractive suddenly seems interested in them romantically. For Altman and Thiel’s sake, he added, “I hope this is obvious: Even though you’re gay, you can still be tricked by a spy.” Johnson’s version of Thiel pushed back, insisting that tech tycoons deserve more respect, given all they’ve done for the country. “Name one time technology has let us down,” he said, giving Mulaney a chance to remind viewers about flights being halted all across the United States on Friday night. “Okay, name one more time,” the fictional Thiel said, leading to an obligatory mention of Microsoft Outlook going down on Thursday . When asked for a third example, Mulaney said, “No, I’m done naming times.” “Look, I get it,” he said. “I can’t imagine how disorienting this has been for you, to go from being bug-eyed weirdos to being gods. I mean, never in the history of our species have people as pale and as strange as you a) survived, and b) been given all the world’s wealth and power.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission .
