events.title: FBI raids and a recycling firm: how a promising US mayor wound up at the center of a bribery scandal
events.summary: As Oakland residents watch ex-mayor Sheng Thao stand trial, the scandal has come to symbolise wider frustrations T wo years ago, residents of Oakland, California , woke up to a shocking scene: their mayor’s home was being raided by the FBI. Agents were seen carrying dozens of boxes from the hilltop home of Sheng Thao, the city’s 38-year-old leader, as part of an investigation constituents would later learn alleged her participation in a pay-to-play scheme with the city’s recycling contractor. It was a stunning moment for Thao, who was elected to lead the Bay Area city in 2022 and was once seen as a promising young mayor in a city that has long grappled with economic inequality and a reputation for violent crime. Her story of growing up in a refugee family and overcoming domestic violence and homelessness to become the first person of Hmong descent to run a major US city resonated with readers confronting questions about equity and representation that came to the fore during the Covid-19 pandemic, and made her the subject of glowing media profiles . As mayor, Thao revived the city’s Ceasefire violence-reduction strategy and brought in a much-needed infusion of revenue through the sale of the Oakland Coliseum sports complex. But her tenure was far from smooth. At the time of the raid she was already facing a heated recall campaign grounded in her perceived failure to address the city’s mounting public safety and homelessness crises – one that would see her ousted from office in November 2024. Two months later, Thao was indicted on federal corruption charges, and eventually replaced by longtime progressive congresswoman Barbara Lee in a special election. Now, Oakland is anxiously watching the final chapter in this political drama unfold as Thao and three co-defendents stand trial over the alleged bribery scheme. Having just concluded its fifth week of hearings, the case is rich with soap-opera-esque plot points, from an alleged beating at a recycling company’s headquarters to text threads in which co-defendants celebrated the plot that would make them “$100 million dollars richer” and touted that “money buys everything”. Proceedings are expected to conclude later this month, with Thao facing six federal counts in total. If found guilty, she could face up to 20 years in prison. To the frustration of other witnesses , Thao, who has a constitutional right not to testify, has yet to take the stand. The saga has left residents disappointed and reopened longstanding frustrations about a city that has everything it needs to thrive – a prime location on the bay, a diverse population, a burgeoning arts and culture scene, and a growing economy – but a government that struggles to deliver basic services or answer for its shortcomings. “When the news [of the FBI raids] broke, there was a wide range of feelings from the community,” said Stephanie Tran, president of the Oakland Chinatown chamber of commerce, of the fall from grace of a mayor who offered representation to Oakland’s sizeable Asian-American community. “Many were, quite honestly, just disappointed, even sad,” she said, that an Asian woman in such a high position of power was now associated with this controversy. The bribery, conspiracy and fraud charges against Thao rest on claims that during her 2022 campaign, David and Andy Duong – a father and son whose family runs California Waste Solutions, the company that provides Oakland’s recycling services – paid for negative mailers attacking her rivals and promised her romantic partner, Andre Jones, a $300,000 no-show job. In exchange, prosecutors allege, Thao promised to extend the company’s multi-million-dollar city contract, appoint the Duongs’ preferred people to important municipal positions, and buy shipping containers converted into homes for unhoused people from a company the Duongs ran with a business partner. All four defendants have pleaded not guilty, with their lawyers denying the existence of any bribery scheme. Thao’s legal team did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment. Darwin BondGraham, news editor at local non-profit media outlet The Oaklandside, said the courthouse has been frequented by members of Oakland’s political class. But when it comes to everyday Oaklanders, many just want the mess behind them. “The trial is accounting for things that happened when Oakland bottomed out during the first few years of the pandemic,” BondGraham said. “I think people moved on.” What many want is simple: a City Hall that fixes the potholes, answers 911 calls and acts with accountability. But in Oakland – which has faced recurring budget deficits for decades, leading to substantial staffing shortages and hundreds of millions in deferred maintenance – these basic services are not a given. Those are the sorts of core concerns that pushed Emily Wasserman, a mother of two living in the city’s Laurel neighborhood, toward local advocacy. In 2024, Wasserman was ready for change.

events.title: Megaspeed says Alice Huang left last year as it launches internal investigation
events.summary: Megaspeed, the AI infrastructure company linked to the scandal that toppled Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang , has said Alice Huang left the business more than a year ago. “Ms Alice Huang officially left Megaspeed effective August 30, 2025, and currently has no role with the company,” it said in a statement on Sunday. The company said it “conducts legitimate and lawful business” and had “retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation”, including a review of its compliance with US export controls. It said media reports against it were not supported by verifiable evidence. Megaspeed is suspected of helping Chinese companies get around US restrictions by buying Nvidia’s advanced chips for data centres in South-East Asia and routing them to China. Singapore authorities have said servers containing advanced AI chips were shipped to Malaysia and may have been delivered elsewhere, contrary to declarations made in Singapore. Singapore police said their investigation is continuing. Alice Huang, a businesswoman whom US investigators accuse of spying for China, was at the centre of the scandal that led to Mr Huang’s resignation on Thursday. Mr Huang had admitted he had been “unfaithful” to his wife after reports of their relationship, and Nvidia’s board opened an inquiry into whether he was the target of a foreign intelligence operation. China has denied the spying allegations. Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, has taken over as interim chief executive while the board searches for a permanent successor. The fall-out has intensified scrutiny in Washington of how advanced chips reach China, with politicians from both main parties calling for tighter export controls . Nvidia reports quarterly results on Tuesday, its first since Mr Huang’s departure.

events.title: Why would anyone want a smart fridge? | Dave Schilling
events.summary: Why would anyone want a smart fridge? After a hack in France, internet-enabled appliances are looking even less appealing – especially before the holidays We are deep into the holiday season now, past Halloween and a mere two weeks away from American Thanksgiving . I’ve already given up taking care of my body, surrendering fully to gluttony, vices, and going to bed at 7pm because it’s pitch black outside. I’ve begun to hibernate like a slothful bear, my blanket and pillow never too far from my grasp. The only thing closer to my hands than my bedsheets is a slice of cold pizza. I just want to eat in peace, thank you very much. Grocery retailers are keen to take advantage of holiday-related binge eating, developing and releasing ever-more-depraved festive novelty foods to subdue us into carb-induced slumber. In the UK, Marks & Spencer is expected to unleash hoards of weird, miniature packages of comical junk, affectionately known as “ picky bits ”, to prevent your digestive system from ever idling into park. “Ham and Barber’s Cheddar Crumpets”. “Twelve Mini Chicken Kyivs”. “British Melton Mowbray pork pie”. These dishes either sound like a thing a tertiary character orders in a Harry Potter novel or the last meal of a 60s British gangster. In America, we have Trader Joe’s . There’s no fun name like “picky bits” for the plastic tubs of slop they sell in the refrigerator section. Instead, we turn to our spouses and partners and mumble: “Pick me up some of that crap.” Toffee-flavored cheddar cheese. Pumpkin spice yogurt dip. An advent calendar … for dogs. I don’t begrudge anyone for cramming their shopping carts with intentionally whimsical perishable food products for depressed people. Overeating is a better use of your hibernation time than drunk-driving into an Arby’s at 2am. This is a holiday rite of passage: the junk food gauntlet. It’s as crucial to the festive season as a decorated tree and a surplus of good cheer. But what if I told you that with the press of a button, the entire picky bits industrial complex could collapse before we even have a chance to open our canine advent calendars? In France last month, supermarket refrigerators across the country were shut off remotely by Iranian terrorists . Other European countries have been hit with similar attacks, which occasionally lead to food having to be thrown out. My entire body goes numb thinking about what it would do to US and British citizens if their supermarkets were similarly affected during the holidays. Can I muddle through another family get-together without a large, rapidly-warming bowl of chicken uncured bacon ranch dip to soothe my anxiety? Doubtful. The chaos would be unprecedented. It’d be like Judge Dredd, Blade Runner and The Purge rolled into one, but with worse catering. You might be wondering how someone even hacks a fridge. Well, industrial fridges like the ones hacked in France are operated remotely via computer. It makes some sense that large-scale operations like grocery stores need to have the ability to make temperature changes quickly, without a bunch of fumbling around with knobs and buttons. But internet-connected fridges are available to consumers, too. Refrigerators from brands such as LG and Samsung allow regular people to change the temperature of their fridge from a smartphone app. My house is not nearly big enough to require me to adjust the settings on my appliances from another room. I only have six rooms (counting the bathrooms, with which I am very familiar during the holidays). Once again, technology aims to solve a problem that doesn’t exist. All we’re doing is trying to get closer to the God-level control of everything at the push of a button. The issue with that is: if we are God to our machines, then the devil also exists, and he knows how to code. Maybe there are a few useful applications of this technology for those of us who are supremely lazy. Some fridges have cameras and AI capabilities that tell you what food is inside, so that you might maintain a clean, tidy food storage system – one that tells you when your groceries are about to go bad. As though your actual human eyes and hands don’t work. That old broccoli is in there. Do I need a computer to tell me what my poisoned nose already can sense? Yup, that’s rotten food. Confirmed. Until there’s a robot that can take the food out for me, move it to the compost bin, and hose down the interior, I’ll pass on the smart fridge. I’ve already pointed out that computers have overwhelmed our cars , but this feels far more ominous. I need my holiday trash. I need my 2,000-calorie tandoori chicken bites. I can’t function without uncured ham and swiss cheese pockets. This is existential. It goes beyond mere sustenance. This is my emotional support during trying times. If black-hat hackers can shut off my fridge and spoil my food, I might start picking my hair out or nibbling on one of my less crucial digits.

events.title: Bad jobs or benefits? Milburn should force employers to help the young | Richard Partington
events.summary: Bad jobs or benefits? Milburn should force employers to help the young Long-awaited final report will call for benefit cuts but lack of entry-level jobs is also driving the crisis ‘I’m scared about my future’: young people on the stress and desperation of jobseeking A generation is being sold short. Almost a million young people are not in education, employment or training (Neet). Austerity and the Covid pandemic cast a lengthy shadow, AI is upending the jobs market, and the cost of living is soaring – all under the microscope of the social media age. On Tuesday, Alan Milburn’s final report on young people and work will bring Britain to a fork in the road: either continue on this path of state and market failure or sharply change direction. It will be a big test for Andy Burnham’s government. Milburn will call for controversial benefit cuts for under-25s in exchange for a legal guarantee of a job or training. Alongside changes to education and health, his plan will take a decade to implement. Behind his argument is a principle Labour has struggled with – that restricting benefits to encourage work is a good idea. The system clearly is not working. Milburn makes the case eloquently – pointing out that for every £1 spent on job support £25 goes on benefits. But there are also important caveats: change will count for nothing unless employers play their part; half of all Neets are not on benefits, and bad jobs and a lack of entry-level opportunities are far bigger drivers of Britain’s youth jobs crisis than the generosity of the benefits system. Last week, the Bank of England deputy governor Clare Lombardelli told me Britain’s young people were bearing the brunt of a “low-gear economy” , with employers freezing recruitment amid the war in the Middle East. Unemployment among the under-25s has risen at the fastest rate since the 2008 financial crisis to reach its highest level relative to the total for all ages since the early 1990s. Young people now make up about 40% of all unemployment. All of this compounds a drop in entry-level jobs over the past two decades. The Saturday job died long ago, while to make matters worse, those positions at the start of the career ladder are most at risk of automation or replacement by AI. Perhaps unsurprisingly, the places in Britain with the fewest job vacancies have the highest Neet rates. Highlighting stark regional divisions, young jobseekers in Rotherham face a sixfold gap in opportunity relative to their peers in the Cotswolds. The preferred fixes called for by employers are tax cuts, looser regulations, and holding back rises in the youth minimum wage. But while policy costs are unquestionably a factor to consider, and the state could do more to help young people get ready for work, the problems go much deeper. When Milburn’s report comes out, corporate Britain will be out in force to show willing. Amazon, Marks & Spencer, Shell and Pret a Manger are among those who have already spotted the PR opportunity to showcase their efforts. But most are doing nowhere near enough. Of course it costs time and money to run youth outreach programmes, work experience schemes and to help recruits who need support to get up to speed – especially in tough economic times. But the consequences from not doing so are becoming increasingly clear. Almost half of jobseekers under 25 surveyed by the organisation Youth Employment UK think employers were unsupportive. Stories of the applications black holes and the catch-22 of companies demanding experience – even for entry-level roles – are all too commonplace. In Britain’s youth jobs crisis, issues with the quality of work on offer and opportunities for progression also play a part. Low paid, insecure jobs are rife – most notably in places with the highest Neet rates. Over the past quarter of a century in-work poverty has increased. Among working households, the relative poverty rate is almost a fifth (18%) compared with 13% in the mid-1990s. Figures this month show people’s job satisfaction has dropped to the lowest level recorded by the British Social Attitudes survey. Among young people it is particularly gloomy: separate figures show most believe that not everyone can go as far as their talent and hard work will take them. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Young people are more likely to find insecure work , only to end up jobless again within weeks. More than one in 10 are on zero-hours contracts. For many that flexibility is welcome and can be launchpad to a career – a point seized on by employers’ groups. But despite the gig economy boom of the past 25 years, Britain’s Neet rate has only fallen below 10% once. Countless studies show badly paid and insecure work is linked to poor mental wellbeing . Across all types of jobs, almost 1 million people in Britain suffer from work-related stress, depression or anxiety .

events.title: UAE engineering firm Kent heads for record order book despite Iran war
events.summary: Kent, the Dubai-based energy engineering company owned by Saudi Arabia's Nesma & Partners , expects to end the year with a record order backlog as Gulf producers press ahead with major projects despite months of disruption caused by the Iran war. The company is on track to meet its revenue target of about $1.5 billion this year and deliver on earnings, chief executive John Gilley told The National in an interview in Abu Dhabi. The war involving the US, Israel and Iran, which began in late February, has disrupted energy shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and damaged critical infrastructure across the Gulf. But it has also generated a wave of work for engineering contractors with a deep presence in the region, from repairing damaged plants to building export routes that avoid the strait. Rystad Energy estimates the cost of restoring energy infrastructure damaged in the conflict could reach $58 billion. Kent is helping energy producers in Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE assess damage to plants after the attacks. While some repairs are relatively minor, others require extensive planning before operations can resume. "We're very proud of the fact that we'll probably hit budget this year at a time when supply chains have been massively disrupted," Mr Gilley said. Kent's order backlog was nearly $3 billion by the end of 2025, much of it concentrated in Gulf countries, and was expected to reach a record by December. Its contracts with Adnoc Gas are progressing, including a $1.1 billion deal to expand the Asab and Buhasa gas processing plants under Adnoc Gas's $5 billion Rich Gas Development project . Supply chain bottlenecks have slowed progress, but Kent still aims to deliver on schedule, Mr Gilley said. New urgency for bypass pipelines Gulf producers are accelerating projects that allow them to export crude without passing through the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi Aramco has started work to expand its East-West pipeline to the Red Sea, while Adnoc is fast-tracking a new West-East pipeline to Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman. Mr Gilley said he did not see a major change in strategy from oil companies, but the war has transformed how such projects are viewed. "In the past, when these types of projects, which really don't add any production, are talked about, they're always on a slow burn," he said. "Now the risk rating and the benefit for the project have increased exponentially, so they're much more likely to go ahead." Kent does not expect to significantly increase capital spending next year, relying instead on its 5,000 to 6,000 engineers worldwide, including teams across five offices in India. Iraq emerges as major market Iraq is becoming a "very, very large" market for Kent as international oil companies expand their involvement in the country's energy sector. The company has a major framework agreement with Basrah Gas Company, works with BP at the Rumaila oilfield and with China's Sinopec, and has secured a new contract with BP at Kirkuk. Mr Gilley expects ExxonMobil , and potentially Chevron, to return to Iraq, creating opportunities for contractors at major fields, including Majnoon. LNG a key growth area Mr Gilley expects liquefied natural gas to remain a major growth area over the next decade, and Kent is pursuing opportunities linked to Mozambique's LNG developments. However, volatile prices complicate the long-term supply agreements needed to finance projects costing billions of dollars, he said, and contractors rarely share in the upside when commodity prices rise. "When the prices of gas and oil reduce, our customers ask us to reduce our rates," he said. "But they never get us to increase our rates when they make such profits." Kent is also expanding into data centre engineering, advising operators on grid optimisation and renewable electricity supplies. Mr Gilley said the business was "absolutely flying". "The world is addicted to two things: energy and data," he added. "The problem with increased demand for data is the increased demand for power. As an offering, we can do both." Kent has reduced its carbon intensity by 43 per cent, exceeding a 30 per cent reduction target set for 2027, and aims to achieve net zero by 2040. That does not mean retreating from hydrocarbons, particularly in the Gulf, where production costs and emissions intensity are relatively low. "We'll continue to proudly produce fossil fuels," Mr Gilley said.

events.title: Minister backs legal right to job support for young people
events.summary: Watch: Pat McFadden refuses to rule out that some young people might lose benefits The work and pensions secretary has backed the idea that the government should legally guarantee young people help to get into employment. Pat McFadden told the BBC that job support should be given a "legislative underpinning", adding the level of assistance on offer was currently "vague". McFadden also confirmed that some current benefit claimants would see their current entitlement to benefits reduced when they are reassessed. But his Conservative counterpart Helen Whately said the idea of legally guaranteeing support "doesn't make sense" and ministers should focus instead on reducing taxes paid by employers. It comes ahead of a long-awaited review by former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn, which will recommend on Tuesday that under-25s should be guaranteed job placements or training to help them find permanent work. His report is also expected to say that under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of UK-wide universal credit - or personal independence payment (Pip), the main disability benefit in England and Wales. Some could be eligible for a new "additional cost allowance" to cover day-to-day costs related to health conditions, under the plans. Speaking to Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Milburn said the government should divert money away from the benefits system to boost work support, adding he wanted to see "billions" extra spent on help over the next decade. However, the idea of reducing the entitlement of existing benefit claimants could prove controversial among Labour MPs, who scuppered a previous benefits-cutting plan under Sir Keir Starmer last year. Milburn said the reduced entitlement for some should be accompanied by a new "duty on government" to provide jobs support to young people, such as apprenticeships, college places, job coaching, or a job. He added that the temporary nature of previous job support schemes, including the Kickstart programme during the Covid pandemic, meant that they had been less effective as reducing long-term joblessness. How the new guarantee would work in practice is not yet clear, with McFadden adding it would have to be "carefully" drafted. Although local councils have some specific legal duties, including in the areas of child protection and homelessness, duties on central government currently tend to be much broader, such as operating a "comprehensive" health service. Watch: Helen Whately says legal guarantee of work or training for under-25s 'doesn't make sense' Asked on the same programme whether he agreed with the idea of a guarantee, McFadden said: "I do think we need some legislative underpinning to this." He added that the offer of support "needs to be more firm," adding: "People need more certainty about what they are entitled to." He confirmed that the government planned to move younger claimants onto a new benefits system when they undergo scheduled reassessment, and some of them would not receive "what they would get today". Other claimants, such as those with long-term disabilities, would receive an increased amount, he added. Also speaking to Kuenssberg, shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said her party backed moves to reduce welfare spending. But she criticised the proposed legal guarantee of work support, arguing it might "sound a nice thing to do," but ministers would be better off reducing taxes and regulations on businesses to help youngsters find "real jobs". She added it was "absurd" the government had increased taxes for employers in order to "subsidise things that look like jobs". She added: "Just stop doing the taxing. Elsewhere in his interview, former health secretary Milburn said: a sustainable reduction in welfare spending cannot be achieved in two or three years, warning that "crude cuts" to the benefits system would create other additional costs for government GPs should not be responsible for signing sick notes declaring people unable to work ministers should "look very carefully" at Labour's manifesto commitment to phase out the reduced minimum wage for those aged 18-21, adding that moves towards this had "imposed a lot of cost" on firms It comes as the government announced it will further widen eligibly for its scheme that offers jobless under-25s subsidised six-month job roles on the minimum wage. From next April, eligible claimants will be offered a role after 12 months of unsuccessfully looking for work, rather 18 currently. It is the second time that eligibility for the scheme has been widened, after the maximum age was increased from 21 to 24 earlier this year . How have you been affected by the issues raised in this story? Tell us about your experience. events.title: ‘Nobody else is going to save us’: the direct action group taking on the UK’s banks, bailiffs and water firms
events.summary: Community union Acorn is helping people fight unfair bills, AI decision-making and housing injustices as cost of living crisis deepens Y asmin didn’t expect to find herself sitting across a negotiating table from executives at one of Britain’s biggest water companies. But her growing frustration with her water bills had led her to launch a national campaign. The 34-year-old single mother from Manchester had endured unexplained charges and a nine-month wait for a water meter. She went to the community union Acorn to propose a campaign that would in time force four large water companies into negotiations. United Utilities eventually apologised for its handling of her case and credited £250 to her account. It is the latest in a series of direct actions by Acorn targeting the cost of living crisis, from challenging councils over bailiffs to confronting banks over housing policies. Rather than wait for government intervention, members say they are taking matters into their own hands and forcing powerful institutions to negotiate directly with them. “Joining the union has given me so much confidence,” Yasmin said. “Because nobody else is going to save us. We can only save ourselves, right? And save each other.” Founded in Bristol in 2014, Acorn began by organising renters against rogue landlords and evictions, before expanding into wider campaigns on cost of living. Its members propose, debate and vote on campaigns at branch level, with issues of wider significance referred to regional or national committees made up of elected members. National campaigns can also be proposed at conferences and put to a membership vote. On 20 August, Acorn staged nine protests as part of its national Dignity Not Debt campaign, forcing Yorkshire Water, Severn Trent, United Utilities and Dŵr Cymru Welsh Water into negotiations and securing concessions. Acorn state that Yorkshire Water agreed to stop sending bailiffs after vulnerable customers, while Dŵr Cymru pledged not to use artificial intelligence to make debt-collection decisions or contact vulnerable people. Dŵr Cymru confirmed discussions with Acorn. United Utilities committed to avoiding AI in customer dealings and establishing a direct route for Acorn members to resolve complaints, according to the group. The company confirmed talks and said it would review individual cases. Severn Trent agreed to explore writing off debts accumulated since September 2021 and widening access to discounted bills for low-income households, with the company confirming it had incorporated Acorn’s suggestions into its existing plans. Andy Burnham’s government has offered a £100 payment to help 20 million households with soaring energy bills, but the prime minister has since said his first budget did not go far enough. Acorn members are testing whether collective action can achieve what politicians say they cannot. In Bristol, members have spent two years campaigning against the city council’s use of bailiffs to recover unpaid council tax and other debts. After negotiations produced what they considered an inadequate offer, they voted to escalate their campaign, disrupting a full council meeting and prompting its cancellation. The council’s leader, Tony Dyer, criticised the disruption, saying it had interrupted an update on a cyber-attack affecting schools and prevented debate on furniture poverty. Sam Kidel, Acorn’s south-west area organiser, said the council had previously promised to protect people who received council tax reductions from bailiff action, but campaigners wanted those protections extended to other low-income and vulnerable residents. “There’s people getting a £30 parking fine and then it’ll get sent to the wrong address, or the person doesn’t open the letters because they’ve got mental health issues,” he said. “And then they end up getting bailiffs sent and the bailiffs add hundreds of pounds of fees on top.” Kidel said the organisation’s experience showed why members were unwilling to rely solely on politicians to tackle rising living costs. “We don’t feel like our democracy is working. If it was working, we wouldn’t be constantly being pushed into debt by energy bills, by rising council tax, by rising rents,” he said. “So we’re not going to wait around for politicians to sort that out.” He pointed to a previous national campaign against TSB, in which Acorn targeted 32 bank branches over mortgage conditions restricting the length of tenancies landlords could offer. Within days, he said, the bank entered negotiations and agreed to change the policy, a change TSB confirmed it had made in 2024, attributing it to a product review. In Leeds, Usman Akhtar, 26, the chair of Acorn’s local branch, helped organise a blockade of a Yorkshire Water facility near Bradford. Growing up in a cold, mouldy flat with his brother and single mother had drawn him into housing activism. But conversations with residents revealed how often housing insecurity was compounded by utility debts.

events.title: ‘Shameless venality’: how a flurry of lawsuits has thwarted Trump’s self-enrichment schemes
events.summary: Courts have issued stinging rebukes to president’s ‘blatant’ financial ploys as pro-democracy groups defend ‘government of laws, not of men’ pillar Donald Trump’s legal and political ploys to increase his wealth and boost Republican electoral prospects have fueled lawsuits by non-partisan groups, prompting federal judges to issue stinging rejections to some of the president’s schemes. Several lawsuits were filed in 2026 against Trump’s schemes to benefit his bottom line by reducing potential tax liabilities, boosting his Truth Social platform financially by offering big investors early access to his posts, and helping Republicans by using federal funds to pay for highly partisan ads touting Trump’s record in the run-up to the midterm elections, in which Republicans suffered a heavy defeat. The major lawsuits against Trump’s financial ploys have been the handiwork of several nonpartisan groups including Democracy Defenders Fund and the Campaign Legal Center. In response, judges in Florida and New York used strong language to condemn and help nullify some of Trump’s financial stratagems. Florida judge Kathleen Williams castigated a Trump scheme backed by the justice department to settle a $10bn lawsuit he filed against the Internal Revenue Service over an old leak of his tax information to the New York Times. Williams ruled that the Trump backed deal to set up a $1.8bn slush fund to pay alleged victims of political persecutions under Joe Biden and giving him immunity from IRS audits before May 2026 was “premised on deception” and a “fraud against the court”. In a separate legal blow to Trump in the closing weeks of the campaign, the president was rebuked by a federal judge in New York, for channeling $20m of public funds to run ads touting his administration’s achievements. The ads were widely attacked as campaign ads and propaganda. Former judges and ex-DoJ lawyers say that he Trump moves to boost his bottom line and political drives with backing from DoJ lawyers exemplify various kinds of Trump “corruption”. Stacey Young, a former DoJ lawyer who set up Justice Connection last year as a network to defend the justice department workforce and the rule of law, told the Guardian: “The justice department’s leadership believes it has one chief client: President Trump. They have allowed him to use the department to protect his financial interests, punish his enemies, and reward his friends. “Thanks to the efforts of some of the country’s best litigators, the people of the United States are pushing back and standing up for the ideal that we remain a government of laws, not of men.” Further, retired federal appeals court judge J Michael Luttig said: “The courts have recently begun to strike down Trump’s countless schemes of blatant and shameless venality and corruption in the forms of self-enrichment, bribery, and extortion. That is the through-line of these three cases and the numerous other cases to come.” For Luttig, the court rebuffs are part of a broader trend of federal courts also rejecting as unconstitutional major presidential initiatives including tariffs and birthright citizenship. Luttig’s analysis was underscored by a July lawsuit filed by Democracy Defenders Fund and a coalition of 35 ex-judges, including Luttig, to kill a key piece of Trump’s proposed settlement of his $10bn lawsuit against the IRS by establishing a $1.8bn fund to pay alleged victims of political persecution that could have helped some January 6 Capitol rioters. The DoJ dropped the slush-fund idea after Williams ruling and some political blowback by Congress. But despite Williams’s legal objections and sharp criticism from Democratic senators, including Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, a provision is still in effect providing immunity to Trump, his family and the Trump Organization from investigations and prosecutions of past tax matters by the IRS as compensation over a leak of his tax returns. In her ruling, Williams charged that the plaintiffs initiated the lawsuit “for an improper purpose – to gain the imprimatur of judicial legitimacy for a ‘settlement’ that had no viable basis in law or fact”. Williams’s scathing opinion in mid-July noted that Trump was on both sides of the issue and that the court itself was perhaps “the victim of fraud”. Williams concluded that the plaintiffs had acted in bad faith by “collusively filing a lawsuit with claims subject to multiple dispositive defenses solely to provide cover for a collusive settlement”. Citing language from an earlier ruling, Williams said “this case is part of Mr Trump’s pattern of misusing the courts to serve political purposes”. In summary, Williams wrote, acidly, that the plaintiffs “pursued this lawsuit in bad faith for the improper purpose of dishonestly advancing a political narrative”. Trump’s lawyers in late July said they would appeal the Williams order.

events.title: How Nvidia's scandal knocked thousands off your 401(k)
events.summary: Nvidia's near-30% stock plunge in the last month is a drag on the retirement savings of millions of Americans, many who may not realize just how much their investments are tied to the scandal-engulfed chip giant. Why it matters: Nvidia's enormous weight in popular index funds means even those who have never purchased a single share of the company could feel the pain of its corporate upheaval in their 401(k)s. The resignation of CEO Jensen Huang after he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy may have cost an average Baby Boomer thousands of dollars, according to an Axios analysis of outside estimates. By the numbers: Index funds held nearly half of the assets in large private-sector 401(k) plans in 2023, according to the Investment Company Institute. Those funds include investments tracking the S&P 500, and Nvidia accounts for roughly 8% of that index, according to Tom Graff, chief investment officer at financial planning firm Facet. That exposure rises to around 14% in growth-style index funds and can reach 25% to 30% in some technology and semiconductor funds commonly found in retirement plans, Graff said. Zoom in : For an investor with $100,000 in an S&P 500 fund, a 30% drop in Nvidia shares would knock about $2,400 off the value of that investment given an 8% S&P holding, assuming other stocks in the fund stayed flat. For a growth-style tech fund with 25% exposure to Nvidia, that decline would amount to $7,500 in lost value. An average Baby Boomer holds about $260,000 in their 401(k), according to Fidelity . A tech-style exposure applied to that amount of holdings would equate to about a $20,000 reduction. Yes, but: Remember, a drop in your investment's value doesn't mean you've actually lost that cash — unless you sell your holdings. Zoom out: The potential fallout extends beyond Nvidia itself. About 40% of the S&P 500 is tied to the AI buildout, for which Nvidia is central, providing much of the financing and infrastructure needed to fuel the tech boom. If Nvidia's troubles slow the pace of AI data center investment, the damage could spread to other stocks held in Americans' retirement portfolios, analyst Bob Iaccino notes to Axios via message. "A lot of people are starting to realize just how much Nvidia exposure they have in funds they thought were diversified," Graff told Axios. "You don't want too much of your retirement riding on whether Nvidia has a successful transition to new leadership or not," he added. Reality check: While Nvidia has come to define the AI trade, its competitors have also emerged as potential beneficiaries of the stock's decline. "The mindset has flipped very quickly to 'who might benefit from this?'" Steve Sosnick of Interactive Brokers told Axios. Chip-company AMD's stock went on a run, rising by more than 30% in a five-day stretch last week, contributing to a broader run in the semiconductor sector. Nvidia makes up a sizable portion of many semiconductor indices and ETFs, showing how rotation can keep bull runs alive even as single stocks falter. Hyperscalers with their own chip ambitions , which at times have looked competitive with Nvidia, have also beaten the growth of the S&P 500 index over the last five days. Reality check: For those who are direct shareholders, the widely held financial advice would always tell you not to lock in losses as a stock drops. It's very unclear what the investigation will unveil. Nvidia is set to report earnings on Tuesday, giving shareholders more insight into its latest quarterly performance. The bottom line: Americans don't need to own Nvidia shares directly to have their retirement savings tied to the company's successes, or failures.

events.title: Space data centers could end stargazing as we know it
events.summary: Sprawling networks of space data centers could make it nearly impossible for humans to stargaze. That's just one of the many risks that come with placing tens of thousands of AI computers into orbit, according to a new report. Why it matters: Most Americans don't want data centers built near them, but putting them in space brings a new set of problems. Threat level: "Companies and policymakers should proceed with great caution," top academic researchers warn in a report for the Innovation for Cool Earth Forum, an annual event hosted by the Japanese government. If space data centers proliferate, the "most visible points of light in the sky during much of the night in much of the world could be satellites, not stars," the report said, mirroring astronomers ' worries. If the U.S. military adopts the technology, the data centers could become potential targets during future space conflicts . Thousands of orbital data centers whipping around the Earth at 17,000 miles per hour mean a growing "risk of collisions" and dangerous space debris . Space data centers are solar-powered, but the vast number of rocket launches needed to put them in orbit generate greenhouse gases and black carbon emissions . What they're saying: Columbia University's David Sandalow, the report's lead author, told Axios there are still "unknown unknowns" about space data center impacts. "If this is going to happen, it should happen slowly and with care," Sandalow said. "Not just launching lots and lots of these things and, kind of, seeing what happens. ... There's big risks." By the numbers: Despite those concerns, investors and tech innovators are all in on space data centers. In 2025, around $197 million in investments were tied to orbital data centers, per market research firm Quilty Space. That figure has swelled to $1.11 billion so far this year. SpaceX has applied for a constellation of 1 million data center satellites, according to the Secure World Foundation . Starcloud and Blue Origin's Project Sunrise have ambitions for 88,000 and 51,600 satellites, respectively. Yes, but: Caleb Henry, Quilty Space's director of research, said that companies may be filing for more satellites than they will likely field. "They don't want to have to bump the number higher up later on," he said in an interview. "We're at a point where people are tallying paper filings as if they are substantive and real," Henry said, "and we just don't know that yet." The bottom line: Researchers warned that governments and companies need to wait until space data center "risks and impacts are better understood and well managed" before putting them in orbit.

events.title: Gen Z shatters America's political orthodoxies
events.summary: Young Americans are challenging beliefs their parents and grandparents once considered sacred — from socialism and Israel to Christianity . Why it matters: Neither party can count on old political loyalties to win over a generation increasingly willing to break with the past. Socialism: 35 years after the Soviet Union collapsed, some 57% of Americans ages 18–34 view socialism positively, compared with 43% for capitalism, according to a September 2026 Gallup poll . Among Americans 55 and older, 65% view capitalism positively, compared with 34% for socialism. Israel: Decades after Israel fought wars against neighboring Arab states, some 53% of Americans ages 18–34 sympathize more with Palestinians, compared with 23% who sympathize more with Israelis, according to Gallup's February 2026 survey . Christianity: After centuries as the overwhelming religious identity of Americans, only 54% of Americans ages 18–29 now identify as Christian, compared with 76% of those 65 and older, according to nonpartisan Public Religion Research Institute's 2025 Census of American Religion , released in April 2026. Between the lines : The return of forces that voters haven't felt in generations can scramble their priorities all over again. After decades of relatively low inflation, prices surged during the COVID era, with annual inflation hitting 9.1% in June 2022 — its highest rate since 1981. In 2024, young voters who ranked the economy and jobs as their top issue favored Trump by 24 points , according to CIRCLE's analysis of AP VoteCast. Two years later, 78% of financially struggling young students backed Democratic House candidates, compared with 16% for Republicans, according to a November 5 CIRCLE analysis . State of play: Young voters showed both parties how quickly their support can shift between elections in last week's midterms. Some 66% of voters ages 18–29 backed Democratic House candidates, compared with 31% for Republicans, according to Tufts University's CIRCLE , citing preliminary NORC data. That 35-point Democratic advantage compares with a 14-point margin in the 2024 House election, according to separate Edison Research exit polling. Trump's 2024 gains among young voters , especially men, now look less like a lasting GOP realignment and more like a warning about how quickly younger Americans can change course. Zoom in: Socialism's fading stigma reached the ballot box in America's two largest cities. Democratic socialists now stand poised to lead New York and Los Angeles after Nithya Raman defeated Karen Bass in Tuesday's mayoral election, joining New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Both built campaigns around affordable housing and inequality, tapping into younger Americans' financial frustrations. The bottom line: Young Americans aren't necessarily embracing socialism because they've rejected their grandparents' Cold War beliefs, PRRI CEO Melissa Deckman told Axios. They're questioning capitalism because their own economic experiences have left them disillusioned. "What they're seeing isn't working, and the American dream is increasingly out of reach for them," said Deckman, author of " The Politics of Gen Z ."

events.title: A Cop Was Charged With Causing His Wife’s Miscarriage. Alabama’s Laws Came Down Harder on Pregnant Women Who Used Drugs.
events.summary: Illustration by Shoshana Gordon/ProPublica On the night of Feb. 15, 2022, Robert Maddox Jr., a rookie cop in a small Alabama town, called his colleague in a panic. His wife was about three months pregnant and bleeding heavily. They needed someone to watch their two sleeping children while they went to the hospital. Headland police Officer James “Bo” Knight arrived with his wife. He had been serving as a mentor of sorts to Robert, who had just recently joined the department, and had urged him to reach out if he ever needed help. The situation Knight encountered was a heavy one. Robert had something in a plastic bag that looked to Knight like fetal remains. His wife stood by silently. Robert said he’d be back as soon as possible, that he was taking both his wife and the bag to the hospital.  When the couple returned three hours later, Robert was holding a white container. “They put my fucking baby in a box,” he said. Investigators soon began building a case that it was Robert who caused the miscarriage. About six weeks after she lost the pregnancy, Brittany Maddox reported her husband for assaulting her before and after she went to the hospital. She first went to an abuse-prevention organization, which connected her to the police and helped her get a protective order from the court. She provided the Houston County judge with a description of how Robert choked and beat her in front of their 1- and 2-year-old children just before the miscarriage, as well as pictures taken starting the following week of marks on her neck. She handed over text messages from Robert in which he promised not to hurt her again and begged her to consider how his imprisonment would hurt their family. “Being honest is going to get us both screwed,” he wrote. “The truth is going to give me locked up.” Then, the Headland Police Department colleague who had offered to help Robert stepped forward. Knight gave a sworn statement to investigators in Dothan, the nearby city where the young couple rented an apartment. He recounted how, weeks after the incident, Robert confided in him that he had hit Brittany in the stomach, choked her and pushed her to the ground. “I asked him how many times he has done this,” Knight said in his statement. “He stated many.” According to the statement, Knight asked when he had last hurt her — and Robert responded “the night before you kept my kids.” In Alabama, the legal implications of causing a miscarriage are severe. Politicians and prosecutors have long proclaimed their mission to defend the unborn. The state has gone further than almost every other to embrace “fetal personhood” — the legal concept that embryos and fetuses deserve the same rights and protections as children. The result is that people charged in Alabama with harming a fetus face especially lengthy prison sentences. The authorities came down hard on Robert, at least at first. He was charged with murder. But in the years that followed, Houston County’s criminal justice system would prove lenient for him. Robert was released on bond about five weeks after his arrest and never again saw the inside of a jail or prison cell. His case stands in stark contrast to dozens of other fetal personhood prosecutions in Houston County, which sits in the corner of the state near the borders of Florida and Georgia. Those defendants were pregnant women. They were charged not for actually harming their unborn babies but for potentially endangering them — not by violence but by using drugs.  In all but one of those cases, which date back nearly two decades, their babies survived. Some of the women spent months in jail and even went to prison. A former nurse, who had been battling a meth addiction for years, was arrested in 2018 after she tested positive for drug use while in labor and wound up spending nearly 10 months in prison. Another woman, who also tested positive at the hospital where she gave birth, ended up in jail for four months in 2024 — and said many fellow inmates were women who’d been arrested for using drugs while pregnant.  Courtney Haney at a family member’s home last month in Dothan, Alabama. Her daughter was born healthy, but Haney spent four months in jail for prenatal drug use. A. Wallace for ProPublica Houston County District Attorney Russ Goodman, who took office in January 2023, said in an email that his office has made efforts to help the women by recommending addiction treatment as part of their sentences. He also said some were rearrested and imprisoned for violating probation — or never completed the treatment offered by the court. “During my term it is rare that we would sentence a defendant in these types of cases to a straight prison sentence,” Goodman said, “unless of course there were other extenuating circumstances, such as prior criminal history.”  As for Robert Maddox, Goodman said that the evidence against him was inconclusive, and he questioned the prior district attorney’s decision to seek an indictment. “It pained me as a prosecutor that I was not to be able to seek justice in this case,” he said. Robert declined an interview but said in an email, “I was made out to be someone I wasn’t.” He did not respond when pressed to elaborate. ProPublica later sent him a detailed list of the allegations against him. He replied, “That is not what happened.” In response to a follow-up email, he said his wife had no bruising or marks at the hospital. “If I was abusive and abused her then took her to the hospital they would have saw the marks and not let me leave with her,” he wrote in an email. Lourdes Rivera, president of the advocacy group Pregnancy Justice, said her organization has identified 2,298 cases of women arrested since 2006 on charges related to their pregnancy. Most of those were for drug use and are concentrated in Oklahoma, South Carolina and Alabama. Rivera said the numbers of women prosecuted for pregnancy loss appear to be on the rise compared with the years before the U.S. Supreme Court overturned the right to an abortion. “Law enforcement is using laws that were never intended to apply to pregnancy to investigate, arrest and punish women,” Rivera said. “And it’s only getting worse.” Robert’s promise not to hurt Brittany again after the miscarriage lasted about a week, she said. She would later tell a judge that he began hitting and choking her again, and photos from that time show bruising on her neck and eye. In that time, something shifted.  “I started hating him when I saw my baby dead,” she wrote in response to ProPublica’s questions.  She said it took her several weeks to come forward because she had to work through complicated feelings about the loss of both her pregnancy and a husband she still loved despite the hatred that was building. events.title: LEO gets a birthday bash, 75 years after clocking in
events.summary: Business computing turns 75 this month, and Cambridge's Centre for Computing History is throwing a party for LEO, the machine that helped start it all. The LEO@75 event takes place on Saturday, November 28, from 10am to 5pm, with film screenings, historical displays, and hands-on activities for children. The Register has written about the Centre for Computing History a few times. It's an interactive computer museum just off Coldhams Lane in Cambridge, and back in 2018 it won National Lottery funding to help it "preserve, archive and digitise a range of LEO Computers artefacts, documents and personal memories." Admission supports the museum charity, with student and concession tickets at £10 and family tickets starting at £15. As well as stuff for the grown-ups, including a film screening, it will include events for smaller children (5-7) and a Python coding event for older (12-16) kids. Regular readers might recall our story about the Lyons Electronic Office back in 2021, celebrating its 70th anniversary. The Reg also published an obituary for Mary Coombs, the first female commercial programmer the following year. Coombs started programming LEO in 1952. Both stories offer more on the machine and the people behind it. LEO was an early computer, but from three-quarters of a century away, it's easy to miss just how early. Its design was based on Cambridge University's EDSAC, developed by a team led by the late, great Sir Maurice Wilkes. The Reg mentioned EDSAC in our obituary for Wilkes, and went into more detail for his centenary in 2013 . It also crops up in our Geek's Guide to Cambridge . The design of EDSAC was directly inspired by John von Neumann's famous, and incomplete, "First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC" – which The Reg talked about in 2011 . The draft report was circulated in 1945, based on the proposal for EDVAC, four years before the hardware was delivered. That was also the year John Mauchly and J. Presper Eckert completed its predecessor, ENIAC. In its original form, ENIAC was programmed by setting switches and reconnecting cables; EDVAC, by contrast, was designed to store its instructions in memory. The report set out what's now called the "von Neumann architecture." Wilkes and Douglas Hartree drew on those ideas in developing EDSAC, LEO's immediate forerunner and one of the world's earliest practical stored-program computers. The first working electronic stored-program machine was the Manchester "Baby," the Small-Scale Experimental Machine, which ran its first program in 1948 . EDSAC ran its first program in May 1949 – a few months before the delivery of BINAC, Eckert and Mauchly's first stored-program machine. LEO ran its first commercial application in 1951. That was also the year the US Census Bureau took delivery of Eckert and Mauchly's UNIVAC I . ®

events.title: Protesters drive home message to data centre company
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Rally organiser Magdalene Lippett says the community does not want to see just a "pause" to the Tungkillo data centre plan. ( ABC News: Trent Murphy ) More than 250 people rallied at SA Parliament on Sunday, calling for plans for a data centre in the Adelaide Hills to be scrapped. Quantum DC announced earlier this week it would pause its plans to build a data centre at Tungkillo, following a strong community backlash. The SA government says it is working on developing legislation that will "comprehensively deal with the rollout of data centres". Hundreds of protesters have doubled down on their message to data centre company Quantum DC that its plans for a 1,200-megawatt AI data centre are not welcome in the Adelaide Hills. It comes after the company announced it would pause its plans for the development at Tungkillo earlier this week, after deep frustration, anger and protests from the surrounding community. At least 250 people rallied on the South Australian steps of parliament on Sunday, with various political parties including the SA Liberals, Greens, One Nation and independent federal MP Rebekha Sharkie in support of the protest group. Campaign organiser Magdalene Lippett said the community was hopeful it had won the fight against the development. Local farmer Kym Gladigau said the proposed area was prime land for food production. "The Adelaide Hills is a food production area, that's what it's all about," Mr Gladigau said. Kym Gladigau says there is limited prime agricultural land and the area should not be put at risk of bushfires. ( ABC News: Trent Murphy ) "We're losing farmland at Mt Barker, we've lost it at Virginia. "The risk with this data centre, is that we lose that. "If this thing goes wrong … we cannot afford another big bushfire in the Adelaide Hills, and who is going to tackle it?" Liberal leader Ashton Hurn, who spoke at the rally, agreed the proposed area should be reserved for farming. Ashton Hurn says Tunkillo is prime agricultural land that should be protected. ( ABC News: Trent Murphy ) "We keep hearing that data centres are a part of our future, there are of course economic opportunities, but we also need to make sure the community is brought along for the ride as well." Greens leader Robert Simms said he wanted to see the Tungkillo plans rejected if they reached the government. "That's why Greens are moving a motion calling on the government to reject this proposal," he said. "We're also calling for a statewide moratorium on data centres. We don't want to see South Australia become the test dummy for the nation." An estimated 250 people were at the rally. ( ABC News: Trent Murphy ) Energy Minister Tom Koutsantonis said he was "very disappointed" with the Tungkillo developers, referencing the company's poor method of community engagement. "I mean, they have behaved in a way that has really lit this fire," he said. Mr Koutsantonis said the developers had not approached government at all about the plans. "I'm the energy minister and the treasurer. They've never spoken to me, and you would've thought the first door you'd knock on is the government's," he said. "Data centres are an essential part of our future. There's no world where Australia cannot have data centres. "If we don't have our own data centres, we'll be price takers rather than price setters." Mr Koutsantonis said the government was working on developing legislation that would "comprehensively deal with the roll-out of data centres". "Data centres have got to have almost no impact on the grid for them to operate in South Australia, and until that time is achieved, we won't license them." In response to Sunday's protest, Quantum DC CEO Alby Tomassi said the company respected the right of community members to express their views. events.title: No, thank you: Shukran hack a reminder financial details not essential for fraud
events.summary: The perpetrators of this week's data breach of Landmark Group's loyalty programme Shukran may have gained only basic user information, but that could be enough to commit more damaging fraudulent activity. On Wednesday, the Dubai-based conglomerate said it was investigating a cyber incident involving “unauthorised access” to Shukran, involving customer names, contact details and dates of birth. Shukran's initial assessment on its website remained unchanged on Saturday. Analysts caution that this type of data could be used to create convincing impersonation scams, phishing messages and other forms of social engineering in which a victim is coerced to reveal sensitive information. “The key concern is that a data breach does not need to involve financial information to create opportunities for financial fraud,” Mohamed Emam, a security researcher at Singapore-based cybersecurity firm Group-IB, told The National . “Even when financial information is not compromised, exposed customer names and phone numbers can still be valuable to cybercriminals.” How fast can stolen data be shared? After information has been extracted from a compromised system, it has the potential to travel very quickly through the dark web – in mere minutes with some reports even claiming instantly – including in cybercrime forums, illicit marketplaces and private messaging channels. “Stolen information can circulate rapidly within cybercriminal communities. Depending on the nature of the breach and the attacker's intentions, compromised data may be offered for sale or shared on underground forums within hours of being obtained,” Mr Emam said. “However, not every breach results in immediate publication or sale. In some cases, attackers may retain the information for their own operations or distribute it privately.” Stolen data “can also be combined with information obtained from previous breaches to build more detailed profiles of individuals”, Maher Yamout, a lead security researcher at Kaspersky, told The National . That point is related to what US data privacy firm Cloaked calls the archive and enrichment phase, which typically happens two years after the data was stolen. It is a part of a broader journey for stolen data, according to the New York-based company. The first three phases are the triage window, the first 24 to 72 hours in which data is sorted and tested before hitting a marketplace; the general sale from weeks two through eight, where data is made available for bulk buys; and commodity pricing from the third to the 12th month, where a collection of data pulled from multiple breaches is sold at lower rates. A domino effect is also on the table, because threat actors can weaponise the stolen data on a broader scale, particularly involving the other accounts of victims. An example is a scammer calling and coercing you to reset your bank app password. “In the Shukran incident … [the stolen data] may not sound as serious as passwords or payment card details, but this information is typically sold to other criminal organisations on the dark web for use in future attacks on consumers,” Danny Jenkins, chief executive and co-founder of US cybersecurity company ThreatLocker, told The National . “Containing a breach is essential, but it does not mean the risk to affected customers has gone away. Even if the most sensitive data has been protected, any personal identifiable information can be of value to criminals.” Worst-case scenario That's part of more severe outcomes. Mr Yamout said the worst-case scenario is that seemingly basic personal information becomes the starting point for targeted attacks, with names, phone numbers and dates of birth giving criminals the tools to establish credibility and tailor their approach to individual victims. “This could lead to phishing attacks, identity fraud, account takeover attempts or financial scams if the method of the attack is convincing enough to trick victims into disclosing additional information or security credentials,” he said. If scammers successfully obtain login credentials, verification codes or other authentication information, the consequences could extend to account takeover, unauthorised transactions or identity-related fraud, Mr Emam cautioned. “The severity of the risk depends on what information was actually exposed and whether attackers can combine it with data obtained from other sources,” he said. “The immediate concern is not necessarily what criminals can do with a phone number alone, but what they may convince someone to reveal by using that information to gain their trust.”

events.title: Where was Nvidia’s security team?
events.summary: Outsiders had little reason to notice when Nvidia’s longtime chief security officer and head of product security stepped down in August. Just two and a half months later, CEO Jensen Huang himself left the company over growing questions about his extramarital relationships — starting with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore data center company that U.S. investigators suspect of funneling Nvidia chips to China, then widening to reports about two separate affairs with Nvidia employees. At the time, David Reber, who spent four years as CSO and seven at Nvidia overall, said he was leaving for health reasons. “This wasn’t a pivot I had planned. But I know what needs to come first: family and health,” he wrote on LinkedIn in late August, disclosing that he’d been diagnosed with young-onset Parkinson’s more than two years ago. Reber’s replacement, Saša Zdjelar, previously spent 17 years at ExxonMobil in Houston, leaving as a senior IT manager before spending one year at Salesforce and several years at the cybersecurity company ReversingLabs. Zdjelar didn’t respond to questions Thursday about the transition or what the security team knew. Nothing public connects Reber’s or Zdjelar’s role changes to the Megaspeed matter, but it seems fair to wonder what Nvidia’s security team knew about the government’s scrutiny of Megaspeed and about Huang’s relationships, and whether anyone raised concerns. Reber didn’t respond to questions Thursday. Nvidia also has not answered our related questions. Relationships between a CEO and his employees typically fall to HR, legal and the board, not security. But security specialists say any affair — even one inside the office — can give a foreign intelligence service leverage over an exec who wants it kept quiet. Still, spotting the clues isn’t easy. The way intelligence services collect information, much of it through everyday conversation rather than hacking, makes it especially difficult for security teams to identify risks, according to retired senior intelligence officer Nicholas Eftimiades, who says he has trained more than 1,000 corporate security professionals. Some people inside Nvidia clearly knew parts of the picture. Nvidia’s top lawyer was engaged with the government’s Megaspeed inquiry more than a year ago, The New York Times reported earlier this week . (Nvidia has said it regularly contacts officials.) Reports about Huang’s relationships with employees suggest colleagues also knew of them, even if the behavior is not expressly forbidden by Nvidia’s code of conduct . The Times cited five Nvidia employees who said he was involved with a vice president who reported directly to him; Reuters, citing two people, later reported a second relationship. What’s unclear is whether any of that reached security. Even if it had, Eftimiades, who wrote Chinese Espionage Operations and Tactics in 2020, told TechCrunch that a security team’s resources are often limited. For one thing, they’re often underfunded because, unlike some other cost centers, they don’t drive revenue. It’s astonishingly common for CEOs to answer a security team’s warnings with “not a nickel more than compliance,” he said. Many companies also define security overly narrowly, specialists say. In an opinion piece in The Hill , Don Aviv, CEO of the corporate investigations firm Interfor International, and author Jeremy Hurewitz, wrote, “Too many companies still approach security primarily as a matter of protecting facilities, preventing cyberattacks, and responding to physical threats.” The two argued that “[s]ecurity teams need to pay greater attention to insider threats, including the cultivation of executives and employees by foreign intelligence services, suspicious business relationships, conflicts of interest and attempts to obtain sensitive information through trusted personal contacts.” It would be surprising if Nvidia’s security team didn’t have a more expansive remit than most companies given its scale and business partners, but it’s possible. In fairness, some of it is simply beyond what any team can do. Speaking generally, not about Huang, Eftimiades offered a hypothetical in which a CEO complains that he can’t do something because “I’m fighting a board who doesn’t want to do this.” That tells an intelligence asset who the obstacle is. The service then asks, “Who’s the sticking point here?” and looks for ways into that person’s email and phone. What a rival intelligence service wants is often less technology than policy insight, including who’s pushing to change export rules and who the biggest blocker is. “Intel world tends to be like cancer,” he said. “Once it gets into the body, it looks to spread and looks to reach out.” The playbook isn’t new, Eftimiades added, “particularly for China.” Any executive dealing with the country “will tell you that they’ve been approached.” He said there are also “tons of diplomat stories” of U.S. diplomats walking into a hotel room to find a woman on the bed.

events.title: Beauty advent calendars can cost hundreds but are they value for money?
events.summary: It's easy to see the appeal of a beauty advent calendar. Like many women at this time of year, Julia says she often finds herself tempted to splurge on one - especially a perfume calendar. But she takes quite an unsentimental approach. "I always look at what's in them. If I like enough of the fragrances, I'll buy it," says the 39-year old, who works as a senior commercial manager in engineering. Luxury advent calendars are supposed to offer the thrill of a surprise but, for Julia, it is more important she actually wants the items inside - a thought that is also striking more and more customers in the wake of the scandal over the Skims calendar. Customers likened the contents of Kim Kardashian's Skims calendar to something you would find down the back of a sofa This week, Kim Kardashian's beauty brand offered all of its customers refunds for its $148 (£110) calendar after being widely criticised on social media over the quality of its contents, with some customers likening the hair clips, scrunchies and keychains inside to things you might find down the back of a sofa. Julia says she earns a good salary but is keen to get value for money and doesn't want to waste it on items she won't use. "I spent £160 on a Space NK fragrance calendar last year," she says. "I got some fragrances I'd been wanting for a while for a lot less than recommended retail price, and those I didn't like I managed to sell on for a slight mark-up on what I paid." Julia, 39, says she thinks fragrance calendars are usually good value for money Beauty calendars, which often cost upwards of £100 and sometimes much more, have been around for more than a decade and the marketing has grown ever more sophisticated. High-profile brands will warn that their calendars risk running out, which may boost early demand, while unboxing videos posted by influencers can encourage spending by creating an infectious sense of surprise and delight. And it appears to be working. Ipsos data shows , external around 15% of all advent calendars sold are beauty ones, with people aged 18-34 particularly willing to splash out. But in the face of that tsunami of marketing, customers seem to be getting savvier. "I love beauty, but I rarely buy beauty advent calendars. They are pricey and often only have a few things that I actually want to try or are trending products," says Priya Raj, 30, a fashion journalist. She thinks some are good value but, for her, the advantage is being able to try on a small scale without forking out for a full-size product. "For me, an advent calendar - particularly a beauty one - serves the purpose of allowing me to try out different products, particularly in the lead-up to Christmas, and then I can hopefully snag a bargain in the Boxing Day sales." Priya Raj, 30, a fashion journalist, says the calendars "serve the purpose of allowing me to try out different products" Podcaster Rhea Somaiya, 28, also likes the general idea, but has a healthy scepticism around a lot of them in practice. "I do think some brands take the consumer for granted in that they provide each day with something so menial that people are bombarded with irrelevant and cluttering items. "And when that's the case, they certainly put me off as the excitement to open each window dwindles into irritation rather than joy." Podcaster Rhea Somaiya, 28, is less keen on the calendars and says they leave consumers "bombarded with irrelevant and cluttering items" Jessica Jasper, a marketing consultant, is more positive - she thinks it's worth it. But she also thinks some companies are just jumping on a trend and that "some brands are getting a little carried away with the pricing". So can beauty calendars offer value for both the brands and the customer - an example of a win-win? Or are they mainly designed to make us spend more at Christmas than we need to? "Some brands are getting a little carried away with the pricing," says marketing consultant Jessica Jasper Heather Widdows, a beauty expert and philosophy professor at Warwick University, has pointed out that while you might buy some of the products in an advent calendar individually, it's highly unlikely you'd buy all of them. "Beauty calendars may offer you lots of products for a really good price. They can also be a bit of fun and feel sensuous. "But it is exceptionally unlikely that you would use all the products inside them, so they're probably not worth it." This year, Julia has spent £99 on a John Lewis fragrance calendar which she thinks is good value for money. But it doesn't mean she'll keep everything in it. In fact she's joined a Facebook group where people trade the ones they don't want for ones they do. "The ones I keep are already a lot cheaper per mililitre than if you bought them at retail," she says.
