events.title: New Orleans port sues to get control of tanker that crashed into cruise ship on Mississippi River
events.summary: New Orleans port officials have sued the owner of a tanker that slammed into a cruise ship on the Mississippi River Just hours after a tanker in New Orleans lost its steering and slammed into a docked river cruise boat, the city’s port sued to make sure federal investigators can seize the vessel that is owned by a subsidiary of a Chinese company. All 197 passengers and crew on the American Heritage cruise ship survived Friday as well as the crew on the tanker. Officials said 32 people were brought to the hospital, including two police officers thrown into the Mississippi River when the boat rolled. But none of the injuries were critical and eight remained hospitalized Saturday. The National Transportation Safety Board said the tanker’s voyage data recorder has been recovered. A 16-member team will spend a week in New Orleans investigating the incident. NTSB member John DeLeeuw said the agency expects to release a preliminary report within 24 to 30 days, with the final investigation report expected in 18 to 24 months. The lawsuit, filed by the Board of Commissioners of the Port of New Orleans, said the Atlantic Asphalt tanker caused at least $1 million in damage to its terminal. A judge issued a warrant Friday giving federal officials control of the ship for now. The tanker has been towed away from the site, but it could take weeks to move the cruise ship, which remains turned on its side against a terminal in the Mississippi River, Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham told reporters Saturday. The first step is to make sure the 16,000 gallons (60,500 liters) of fuel on the boat are removed safely, she said. Traffic has been limited on the Mississippi River, but Burnham said boats should be able to move both upstream and downstream soon. The tanker appeared to lose steering, but the exact cause of the crash is not known, Burnham said. The National Transportation Safety Board was sending investigators to New Orleans. The first warning people on board the American Heritage had was the tanker blasting its horn several times as it floated toward the cruise ship, passenger Joe Knab told WDSU-TV. The hit was hard, and the ship immediately started leaning. The crew gathered everyone on the third deck to put on life vests and start getting them off the boat, but it suddenly rolled and sent Knab and about 100 other passengers and crew into the muddy Mississippi River, where the water was 66 degrees Fahrenheit (19 degrees Celsius). Tugboat operators, other cruise ship captains, nearby workers, police and other rescuers rushed to help. Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech Authorities investigate 'credible' unknown device threat at Illinois plant Microsoft apologizes for email disruption, says AI agents not responsible “It’s fine now, but it was a little scary there at the time. I thought I was drowning because I kept bobbing underneath — and the water doesn’t taste very good,” Knab told the television station, still in the jeans he was wearing on the boat, now covered in mud. Knab said he thinks he was in the water about 15 minutes. He laughed and said his 20 years in the Navy likely helped him. “They taught us not to drown,” Knab said. Knab was wearing a shirt from a Hilton hotel where the passengers gathered. The rest of his belongings were in the river. Somehow his cellphone still worked. He hoped to get on a plane soon back to Wichita, Kansas, but he was not sure how Friday’s nationwide ground stop was going to throw another problem at him. Putting the life vests on the passengers as they waited to get off the boat likely saved a number of lives when the boat suddenly turned into the water, New Orleans Harbor Police Chief Melanie Montroll said. “Whether it’s 10 feet of water or 200 feet, having those vests, having that population put those vests on and kind of float upriver while we retrieve them — I think was the best factor of success,” Montroll said. The American Heritage was finishing an eight-day cruise to several Mississippi River destinations. The Atlantic Asphalt is a 520-foot-long (160-meter-long) vessel. It had a final destination in New Orleans, according to MarineTraffic, and was sailing under a flag for the Marshall Islands. The ship is owned by a company called Nave Shipping SA, which is registered in Monrovia, Liberia, according to the International Maritime Organization and was one of the defendants in the lawsuit filed Friday. Nave Shipping is a subsidiary of the China State Shipbuilding Corporation, a sprawling Chinese state-owned conglomerate, according to the live shipping tracker MarineTraffic. China State Shipbuilding Corp. didn’t respond to an emailed request for comment. The tanker involved in the crash specializes in carrying large quantities of asphalt and bitumen, a semi-solid substance that is often used for road construction and roofing, according to MarineTraffic.

events.title: Author Tim Winton says Exmouth wrong place for a port
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Author Tim Winton leads campaign to stop Exmouth port development Tim Winton has been a long-term advocate against plans for a port in the Exmouth Gulf. ( Supplied: BlueMediaExmouth ) A deepwater industrial port in a northern WA tourist town is facing a backlash from locals and conservationists. The Exmouth Chamber of Commerce backs the plan and says it will provide plenty of benefits to the community. If approved, construction of the port is scheduled to begin in early 2029. A proposed deepwater industrial port in northern Western Australia has been described as unnecessary, unjustified and unacceptable by locals and conservationists worried about the impact on marine animals. The Gascoyne Gateway Marine Complex is proposed to be built just outside of Exmouth, 1,230km north of Perth, where it will feature a single jetty wharf, bulk fuel storage, a solar farm, and a seawater desalination plant. The port is proposed to be built 10km south of the township. ( Supplied: Gascoyne Gateway Ltd. ) The port will be designed to service cruise liners, defence and commercial supply vessels. The proposal has caught the attention of conservationist and famous author Tim Winton who has opposed the project. Exmouth local Brinkley Davies also said she was concerned about the port's location so close to town and World Heritage Ningaloo. "It is worrying because it is my front yard, but also the marine ecosystem that is at risk is a major factor," Ms Davies said. Having worked in marine conservation herself, Ms Davies has been involved in the campaign against the port since its initial proposal in 2020. Brinkley Davies believes more people are now aware of the issues with the port. ( ABC Pilbara: Yousuf Shameel ) "It was not widely spoken about then and in the last five or six years, the town has really boomed and there is a lot more people living here and more people standing up for the place," she said. "There are a few key species that really have an importance in this area, one of them is dugongs. "There is a very important seagrass meadows where they are feeding and they also come in here to nurse their calves and rest, and that area is at direct risk of being covered in silt if they are going to dredge." Signs with messages opposing the port have been placed around town. ( ABC Pilbara: Yousuf Shameel ) Fellow Exmouth local Violeta Brosig said she was concerned the port could impact the humpback whales that rely on the Gulf. "My main concern is it is going to be right in the middle of the parts of the humpback highway in Exmouth Gulf," she said. "It needs to be preserved and protected instead of destroyed." However, the Exmouth Chamber of Commerce president David Gillespie said it was an opportunity of a lifetime for locals and there would be flow-on benefits for the community. "There will be upgrades and roads, jobs, " he said. "There's for and against on both sides with businesses that agree to disagree, but I just get back to what the positives are from an economic perspective and what that will do for the town, for increased housing and population." Exmouth Gulf is now the chosen site for the Gascoyne Gateway Marine Complex. ( ABC Pilbara: Yousuf Shameel ) Gascoyne Gateway CEO Daniel Jackson said there had been extensive community consultation and believed the majority of locals and businesses were in favour of the port. "We certainly acknowledge that there's seasonal windows, we're talking a few months of the year in which higher degree of risk mitigation is required to manage interaction between vessels and fauna, as it does now. "There's commercial vessels operating there today that are moving in and out and around fauna in the Gulf." The project is still undergoing approvals, with the WA Environmental Protection Authority currently undertaking public consultation. World renowned author, conservationist and patron of Protect Ningaloo, Tim Winton, said the Exmouth Gulf was the wrong place for a port. "It is one of the world's most important humpback whale nurseries and the idea of building a wharf a kilometre long into the whale refuge and to bring up to 600 vessels a year into the whale nursery just seems fundamentally wrong," Mr Winton said. "We're of the view that this is unnecessary, unjustified and unacceptable in its impacts to the Ningaloo estate." While this proposal could be approved by and started by 2029, the Exmouth Gulf is also being considered for National Heritage Listing, with that decision not expected until 2030. The WA government is also looking to establish a new marine park covering the entire Exmouth Gulf.

events.title: Elon Musk, other tech execs sign petition calling on Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang
events.summary: A petition calling on Nvidia to reinstate the company’s recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang appears to have attracted more than 115,000 signatures as of Saturday afternoon. The petition website said the signers include 5,965 current Nvidia employees, 1,108 former employees, and 63,063 shareholders. Notable supporters include Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan. The petition states that its signers are “concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process” and demands that the board “bring him back while an independent investigation establishes the facts.” It also calls on the board to ensure a fair investigation and provide more information to the public. “Jensen deserves due process, not mob justice,” the petition says. Huang resigned on Thursday , four days after confessing to having an affair with a chip executive suspected by U.S. intelligence to be a Chinese spy. The former CEO has agreed to testify before Congress, while news reports have also suggested that Huang engaged in multiple extramarital affairs . Nvidia appointed CFO Colette Kress as the company’s interim CEO while it searches for a permanent replacement. Nvidia’s stock price fell sharply through the week, while Huang’s departure is also expected to leave a big gap in AI industry funding . events.title: Tens of thousands march in Portuguese cities against surging home prices
events.summary: Tens of thousands of people have marched in Portugal in the biggest protest yet against surging housing prices LISBON, Portugal -- Tens of thousands of people marched through more than 30 cities and towns across Portugal on Saturday in the largest protest yet against soaring housing costs that many say have put buying or renting a home beyond their reach. The housing crisis has fueled weeks of demonstrations. Some activists have camped in central squares in Lisbon and Porto, the country’s two largest cities. Riot police with dogs have dispersed some protests, drawing accusations of heavy-handed tactics. The demonstrations took inspiration from protests that began in neighboring Spain last month over similar housing concerns. They come amid widespread social unrest across Europe this autumn. Marching under the slogan “We won’t let them steal our right to housing,” participants ranged from teenagers to retirees. Drums, music and chants accompanied the Lisbon march as protesters carried large banners and flags. Susana Pacheco, a 35-year-old data analyst who works part-time as an astrologer to help pay her mortgage, said she worried about whether her younger sister could afford to move out of their parents’ home. “I’m really worried about young people,” Pacheco said. “I don’t know how they’re going to be able to pay” for their own home. “Things have become intolerable,” said Ana Encarnação, 42, citing rising living costs and the widening gap between rich and poor. Activists want ceilings placed on rent increases, greater legal protection for tenants against eviction, and more affordable housing. House prices in Portugal have risen much faster than incomes, statistics show. Between 2015 and 2025, Portugal posted the biggest jump in the European Union in the home price-to-income ratio, with an increase of 61%, followed by the Netherlands with 34%, the EU statistical office Eurostat said last week. There is no indication that the rise in housing costs is slowing. Between the first quarter of last year and the first quarter of 2026, housing prices rose by almost 20%, the National Statistics Institute, a government agency, said last month. Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech Authorities investigate 'credible' unknown device threat at Illinois plant Microsoft apologizes for email disruption, says AI agents not responsible Rental prices, too, have climbed significantly, recording a 68% increase since 2020, according to the government. Foreign buyers and investment funds have fueled price rises by buying Portuguese real estate. The country’s mild climate and long coastline have helped it grow popular with digital nomads and other remote workers, as well as retirees. Tourism has also surged, with many city center apartments switched to short-term rentals. The government has responded with measures such as lowering taxes on new construction, restricting short-term rentals and promising to build 145,000 new homes. But it acknowledges that the effects won’t be immediate. Portuguese President António José Seguro, whose role is mostly ceremonial but who wields political influence, convened a Council of State, an advisory body, to discuss the protests earlier this month and met Friday with some of the protesters. events.title: US government says wire replacement caused nationwide grounding of flights
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Travellers in Atlanta wait for news about rescheduled flights. ( Reuters: Elijah Nouvelage ) Flights have resumed in the US after being grounded for about five hours, but airlines are struggling to clear a backlog. Officials are blaming the aviation shutdown on the replacement of old copper wires with new fibre ones. Nearly 29 million passengers are expected to fly on US airlines during the Thanksgiving travel period from November 20–30. The US government has blamed a nationwide aviation shutdown which has disrupted more than 20,000 flights on a program to replace copper wires with new fibre ones. Airlines are struggling to clear a backlog of delayed and cancelled services after a major air traffic control communications failure forced authorities to suspend departures across the country for about five hours on Friday, local time. Flights have since resumed , but airlines are warning it could take days for services to return to normal. The US government says it may have been the fault of a single router installed by a government contractor. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told reporters on Saturday, local time, that contractor L3Harris had been replacing a section of the air traffic control system's old copper wire with new fibre wire, and that work somehow caused the system overload. Mr Duffy said the work caused "intermittent" communications and radar gaps. He said officials were investigating whether contractor "incompetence" or a faulty router was the cause. "Our contractor didn't meet the moment or the equipment didn't meet the moment," Mr Duffy said. L3Harris said it took the issue seriously, and was "supporting the FAA [Federal Aviation Administration] in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the ground stop of our nation's air travel". Race to replace old copper wire system The issue began overloading communications at 17 of the FAA's 22 en route centres across the country, which prompted the authority to halt departures because it could not identify a root cause. Mr Duffy said the new routers started flooding other routers with more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, which sparked communications issues with planes and radar at FAA facilities. The FAA is still trying to understand the root cause of what went wrong. It said communications did not go down but led to instability in data at the centres, and it did not lead to centres going dark. Mr Duffy said the routers being replaced were about 25 years old and were supposed to be replaced in 2006. The FAA spends $US1 billion ($US1.47 billion) annually to maintain its old copper wire system and is racing to replace it with modern fibre-based communications. "We need L3Harris or whoever provided that router to us to do a better job," Mr Duffy said. "Virtually every single institution in America has gone from copper to fibre, from analog to digital." L3Harris noted it has completed more than 70 per cent of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fibre-optic system. The disruption comes less than a week before the Thanksgiving travel rush, with industry group Airlines for America forecasting nearly 29 million passengers will fly on US airlines between November 20 and 30. Almost 10,000 flights were cancelled, including 1,800 on United Airlines. ( Reuters: Eduardo Munoz ) While officials expect operations to return to normal before the holiday rush, Mr Duffy has warned the process will be gradual. What we know about the US flight groundstop Aviation authorities cited "extraordinary circumstances and reasons of safety", with the White House blaming outdated air traffic control technology for a communications outage. Thousands of flights were cancelled or delayed, leaving passengers stranded at airports across the country and forcing airlines to rearrange aircraft and crew schedules. Nearly 10,000 flights were cancelled during the disruption, including more than 2,200 each at Delta Air Lines and American Airlines, and 1,800 at United Airlines, according to flight-tracking website Flightradar24. Some aircraft at major airports were forced to wait more than five hours for a gate, the website reported. US airlines will not be required to compensate stranded passengers because the disruption was caused by failures in the Federal Aviation Administration's systems rather than the carriers themselves. Flights in Europe were also afected by the problems in the US. ( AP Photo: Mike Stewart ) The impact extended beyond the United States, with European aviation authorities asked to suspend US-bound departures during the emergency.

events.title: Got an iPhone Duo? These 9 settings make it easier to use
events.summary: Apple’s new foldable , the iPhone Duo, has proven popular enough that the company can’t keep the device in stock . While the Duo introduces a new way to use an iPhone, getting the most out of this initial version may require adjusting a few settings to make it work better when it comes to everyday tasks, like unlocking the device with Touch ID, navigating the interface, and taking photos. After spending some time with the Duo, we’d recommend making the following adjustments to make the new iPhone a bit easier to use, most notably when it comes to the use of Touch ID. Settings to make it easier to live with Touch ID Unlike modern iPhones, the Duo doesn’t support Face ID. That means you have to adjust to pressing a finger on the side of the device once again to authenticate with apps, unlock the device, and use Apple Pay. But there are a few things you can do to make the switch back to the older technology a bit less painful. Register extra fingerprints: This may seem like an obvious suggestion, but if you’re used to just registering a fingerprint or two with Touch ID, prepare to rethink that strategy with the Duo. Because the device can be held in multiple orientations, flipped both horizontally and vertically, and because of the small size of the Duo’s screen, you may find that a lot of your fingers (and thumbs!) can now reach the Touch ID button. We’d recommend holding the device in your hand and turning it in different ways, then register the fingerprints where you end up holding the device the most — on both hands. Yes, setting up Touch ID can be a bit tedious compared with Face ID, as there are multiple prints to register. Still, it’s a one-time setup, and later on you’ll be glad that you took the time to make more of your fingerprints work. To register a fingerprint, go to Settings > Touch ID & Passcode > Add a Fingerprint. Unlock with Apple Watch: If you’re in the market for the iPhone Duo, there’s a good likelihood that you own other Apple devices, like the Apple Watch. If that’s the case, you’re in luck because you can use your Watch to unlock the Duo without having to bother with Touch ID. This will save you time and frustration in the long run, so get used to wearing your Apple Watch more often, especially when you’re out and about and don’t want to fiddle as much with finger placement. To use the Apple Watch unlock, your watch will need to be passcode-protected and worn near your phone. To turn this feature on, go to Settings > Touch ID & Passcode > Unlock with Apple Watch. Rest finger to Open : This is an optional setting, not necessarily a “must” like the above, but we’ve found it useful. The “rest finger” setting is actually an accessibility feature, but it can double as a usability feature, too. When enabled, you only have to rest your finger lightly on the Touch ID sensor to unlock the device, instead of having to press down. Those who prefer this setting find it can make unlocking the phone faster and more convenient, but others may disagree, as they like the more tactile sensation of a button press. Try it both ways and see which one fits you best. To enable this one, go to Settings > Touch ID & Passcode > Rest Finger to Open . There are a few settings that could also improve your experience with the iPhone Duo, as they may make it easier to perform certain everyday tasks, like taking screenshots or reaching different parts of the screen, among other things. Turn off Fixed Volume Controls : This is a favorite hack for new Duo owners, as it makes using the device in any orientation much easier. By default, the iPhone Duo’s volume buttons are “fixed,” which means that no matter how you rotate the device, the Volume Up button remains the button that increases the volume and the Volume Down button decreases it. But many people find it’s easier if the buttons’ functionality rotates with the device. That is, the buttons re-orient themselves based on how you are holding the phone, making the “up” option always on the top or right. As you fold, unfold, and flip the phone, having buttons that flip with you actually makes more sense. To turn off the fixed volume controls, go to Settings > Sounds & Haptics > Fixed Position Volume Controls . Back Tap for Screenshots : The Duo tries to make it easier to take a screenshot by pressing the side button and either the Volume Up or Volume Down button at the same time. However, you still might find the process a two-handed affair (unless you just ask Siri to do it for you). That’s why many Duo owners are turning to a buried Accessibility feature to make taking screenshots a bit less complicated. In the phone’s accessibility settings, you can configure whether a double tap or triple tap on the back of the device triggers a particular action — which you can set to ‘take a screenshot.’ (Some people prefer the triple tap so they don’t accidentally trigger the feature.

events.title: Transportation secretary blames ‘routine’ equipment upgrade for grounding flights nationwide
events.summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday that a nationwide ground stop halting flights across the United States was caused by seemingly routine maintenance work. Duffy said that during “routine maintenance,” copper wire at a remote location was upgraded to fiber optic cable by L3Harris, a longtime contractor for the Federal Aviation Administration. After the upgrade, a router overloaded a critical communication system, leading to the ground stop. “It’s pretty straightforward work that we were doing yesterday at, again, a very remote location,” Duffy said during a Saturday press conference that appeared to have technical issues of its own . “What we’re working to determine was whether we had incompetence — meaning, was it user error or [installer] error from L3Harris? Or did they install a faulty router?” The FAA’s acting CTO Rebecca Guy added , “When we started to see the occurrence where our network was having instability, we started to look at what was the cause. And as such, we saw two places that were actually pinging our network at a very high rate — a thousand connections over every four to five seconds.” Guy said the FAA disabled “both of those, right away and were able to stabilize our network,” and is now performing a root cause analysis. Duffy has repeatedly insisted, at multiple press conferences, that Congress needs to provide more funding for aviation equipment upgrades. Asked why the upgrades were made at 3pm on a Friday afternoon — rather than, say, at midnight on a Saturday — he responded that while “switchovers” at bigger airports will take place late at night, remote switchovers happen during the day. “There will be reevaluation of when we do this work,” he said. This was only the third nationwide ground stop of the 21st century. More than 8,200 flights were canceled on Friday evening, according to aviation data firm Cirium . And the effects continued after the ground stop was lifted, with at least another 3,000 flights canceled on Saturday. The ground stop came just a day after the FAA announced the rollout of an AI tool for air traffic controllers; the air traffic controllers union said it was not consulted in designing the system. However, FAA administrator Bryan Bedford said the agency sees “zero evidence of anything nefarious and zero evidence of anything AI-related.” “We want to be clear that we have an equipment issue, and we’re working through what this defective piece of equipment was,” Bedford said. When Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin was asked earlier if the ground stop was caused by AI, he replied , “We call it SI [ super intelligence ] around here, remember? events.title: The AI graveyard: a running list of projects and startups that didn’t make it
events.summary: Last month, chatbot platform Character.ai filed for bankruptcy just five years after launching. Soon after, privacy-focused AI assistant Ollie announced its shutdown, too, citing competition in the market. “We got close, but ultimately couldn’t keep up,” co-founder and CEO Bill Lennon said on X . Aside from Character.ai and Ollie, plenty of AI bets never even survive inside the companies that build them. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence , about 42% of AI initiatives are ultimately abandoned by their corporate parents. The reasons vary: insufficient funding, technical challenges, competition, difficulty scaling, or just weak user demand. The result is a growing AI graveyard. Below is a look at some of the most notable AI products, startups, launches, and bets that have shut down, pivoted, or significantly missed expectations. Think of it less as a scorecard of flops than as a record of what these attempts can (hopefully) teach the rest of the industry. Even the biggest players aren’t immune. OpenAI, one of the most valuable private companies in the world, has had its own share of casualties and missteps. One of the more recent examples was its attempt to turn ChatGPT into a broader “ super app .” On July 9, OpenAI updated the app to combine several experiences, including separate “Chat,” “Codex,” and “Work” modes, while renaming the traditional, familiar version “ChatGPT Classic.” The redesign quickly drew criticism from users who found the new interface confusing and cluttered, and OpenAI rolled back the change soon after , bringing the familiar ChatGPT interface back. That wasn’t OpenAI’s only attempt to pull everything under one roof. The company has also shut down several stand-alone apps and folded their features directly into ChatGPT — a strategy that’s worked out better than the redesign did. ChatGPT Atlas, a stand-alone AI-powered web browser, lasted less than a year before being discontinued on August 9, with its most useful features absorbed into ChatGPT. The company did the same thing with Operator , an AI agent that could browse the web and complete tasks on a user’s behalf, and OpenAI has increasingly built image generation directly into ChatGPT, shrinking the role of DALL-E as its own separate destination for creating images. We also can’t forget its video-sharing platform, Sora , which struggled with high operating costs and user-retention challenges and shut down in March 2026. When Apple unveiled Apple Intelligence in 2024, an improved Siri was one of the highlighted features. The pitch promised a Siri that could understand context, know what was happening across apps, and get tasks done effectively. However, Apple repeatedly pushed back the release of the new Siri, citing various reasons like engineering issues and bugs . This delay eventually contributed to a $250 million settlement over claims regarding how Apple marketed the AI capabilities of the iPhone 16. Siri AI finally appeared in the iOS 27 beta this past July, with the new AI-powered version rolling out to English-language users first this month; support for other languages is expected to follow. Founded in 2021 by former Google researchers Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, Character.ai was a consumer AI app that let people chat with customizable bots, many of them modeled on celebrities and fictional characters. It raised $150 million at a $1 billion valuation in 2023. Then, the next year, Google paid a reported $2.7 billion to license its technology and bring its founders back into its orbit, leaving the startup to carry on without them. Character.ai has run into a lot of trouble over the years. Families have sued, alleging the chatbots contributed to teen suicides and self-harm, and Disney sent a cease-and-desist letter over unauthorized use of its characters. Character.ai barred under-18 users from open-ended chats late last year and agreed to settle several of the suits, along with Google, in early 2026. But it wasn’t enough. The company filed for bankruptcy in early October, citing legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds. In an ironic twist, Disney is now the opening bidder, offering $20 million for a license to some of its intellectual property. The app is still running during the process, and the sale is expected to wrap up by late November or early December. Relay, an AI-powered workflow automation tool built as an alternative to Zapier, shut down entirely in August 2026. The product let users automate email and task workflows using AI agents, but as OpenAI, Google, and other larger platforms built similar automation directly into their own tools, five-year-old Relay struggled to hold on to a reason to exist as a stand-alone product. Ollie launched in June 2026 as one of the first mainstream apps to achieve SOC 2, a privacy compliance standard.

events.title: Retail sales and Fed minutes in focus next week
events.summary: A report on retail sales will anchor the calendar of economic updates this week, which also includes details about the most recent Federal Reserve meeting and the latest take on consumer sentiment NEW YORK -- New data on retail sales will headline U.S. economic updates this week, but there will also be details from the most recent Federal Reserve meeting and a new read on consumer sentiment. The latest economic data showed that inflation remains hot . High prices on everything from groceries to clothing and gas have squeezed millions of Americans and cast a shadow over the broader economy. Democrats swept Congress in midterm elections and for many voters, the cost of living was the top issue. Here’s a look at some of the key reports coming in the week ahead. Retail activity may have slowed last month. Economists expect a 0.2% overall increase, easing back from 0.8% in September and 1.3% in August. At the same time that overall retail sales are slowing, spending at gas stations has surged amid persistently higher fuel costs because of the U.S. war with Iran. The war disrupted shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, slashing global oil supplies and raising prices. That has made gasoline more expensive and indirectly raised costs for anything that is shipped. Shoppers have been pulling back on spending just as retailers head into the vital holiday shopping season . The squeeze from stubbornly high inflation is expected to persist as long as the war stifles global oil supplies and tariffs from the U.S. trade war with much of the world keep putting pressure on prices. Details from the Federal Reserve's latest policy meeting will be released Wednesday. The minutes from that meeting could shed more light on the central bank's decision-making process as it tries to cool inflation. It held rates steady at its October meeting following the first rate hike in three years at its September meeting. Raising the benchmark interest rate can help slow economic growth and cool inflation by making borrowing more expensive. Timeline of the FAA nationwide ground stop: How it developed India seeks to triple clean energy capacity to 900 gigawatts by 2035, but major hurdles remain 20- to 30-foot waves pound the West Coast as storms continue Higher interest rates, though, could also stunt job growth, which has been strong but is showing some signs of weakening. Supporting the labor market is also part of the Fed's mandate along with taming inflation and taking action to support one can often be detrimental to the other. Inflation has remained stubbornly above 3%, which puts it well above the central bank's 2% target rate. The Fed is expected to raise rates again at its December meeting and anxiety over stubborn inflation likely means more rate hikes to follow in 2027. The latest weekly update on unemployment claims, which are a proxy for layoffs, will be released Thursday. Economists watch them closely because they can provide signs of where the job market is headed. Claims have remained at historically low levels amid a broader jobs market that has remained a strong point in an economy pressured by rising inflation. The resilient jobs market has made it easier for the Fed to focus on raising interest rates to cool inflation. The last broad employment update for October showed that U.S. employers created a surprising 165,000 new jobs and the unemployment rate dipped to 4.1%. The reports have shown that the job market remains solid, but unspectacular. Employers have added an average of 86,000 jobs a month throughout the year, which is modest by historic standards. The University of Michigan on Friday will release an update to its November consumer sentiment survey. It is expected to remain unchanged from its initial reading, which continued to show that consumers remain pessimistic as they deal with pressure from inflation on household budgets. Other reports on consumer confidence revealed similar concerns about inflation. The Conference Board's consumer confidence index for October showed some improvement in confidence levels, but they still remain on an overall downward trend. events.title: FAA back at "full operations" after Friday outage, Transportation Sec. says
events.summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday that all FAA systems are back to "full operations" after an hours-long outage Friday evening that grounded all air traffic across the U.S. The big picture: Duffy reiterated his plea to Congress to fund upgrades to the nation's air traffic control equipment, explaining that proper upgrades could have prevented the ground stop. Driving the news: Duffy explained that the outage was caused when a contractor performed routine maintenance on a telecommunications line to upgrade a copper wire to fiber-optic cable and install a new router. "It was such an old wire that it was being discontinued, meaning that line was going to get shut down. So we had to switch it over from old copper," Duffy said. Duffy said it's unclear whether the outage occurred because of contractor error or faulty equipment, but they are working to figure that out. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford warned that up to 5,000 flight cancellations will remain throughout today, but airlines have assured the agency that they should return to normal operations by the end of the day Sunday. "I do think the worst is behind us, but we still do have a significant amount of recovery work to do," Bedford said. According to numbers from FlightAware , over 4,700 international and domestic flights have been canceled, and over 13,500 delayed, as of 11:50 am ET. Zoom out: Bedford and Duffy both said the ground stop was ordered out of an abundance of caution for the safety of passengers and airplane crews. Bedford added that they have no reason to believe a cyberattack or an AI issue prompted the outage. "We see zero evidence of anything nefarious," Bedford said. Zoom in: Duffy used the press conference to again plead with Congress to fund upgrades for the aging air traffic control system. Duffy has previously said the FAA needs $30 billion to update airports and air traffic control. Congress had previously awarded $12.5 billion in July 2025 for upgrades into 2030. After Friday's outage, Duffy upped the funding request to $50 billion. "For me, it gets to be frustrating where everyone says they want to do it, and the president is pushing it, but we don't get the resources," Duffy said. "And I think this is the moment. If we don't start to switch out our systems, how long are we going to wait, America and Congress? And I think this is a sign for them to lean in. This is bipartisan." Bedford offered a blunt assessment when reporters asked about the system's function, saying it's the "worst-kept secret in government" that it needs an upgrade. "We have to keep the existing system operating at the very best of our ability," with the funding they have, he said. "But," Bedford continued, "let's not kid ourselves. It will continue to break until we replace it."

events.title: Asian governments react to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s exit
events.summary: Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia has drawn a range of responses across Asia, with some governments moving to confirm chip supply commitments, while others are monitoring the impact on local projects or addressing ongoing investigations. On Sunday, November 8, Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation after reports that Huang was targeted by a Chinese spy operation; Huang admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based chip company Megaspeed. Nvidia’s influence extends far beyond the United States. The chip giant has built close ties with companies worldwide, particularly in Asia, where many of its key partners play important roles in the global AI industry. China’s foreign ministry rejected allegations on November 10 that a Chinese businesswoman linked to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a spy, calling them groundless and a smear against Beijing. On Friday , a spokesperson reiterated opposition to export controls that disrupt global supply chains and stated the ministry was not aware of reports linking restricted Nvidia chips to a Shanghai data center associated with Alice Huang. Huang’s exit has also raised uncertainty over more than $3 billion in Chinese AI computing projects reliant on Nvidia’s restricted processors, according to Reuters. Many of these chips are subject to U.S. export controls, making them difficult for Chinese companies to obtain. In Singapore, authorities seized the passport of Alice Huang, former CEO of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, in June 2025 as part of an investigation into possible false declarations regarding server purchases, according to the Ministry of Home Affairs. The Singapore ministry said police took her passport to ensure she remained available for questioning, as she was not based in Singapore. The investigation examined whether servers shipped from Singapore to Malaysia were later sent to other countries without proper declaration. In February 2026, police found insufficient evidence to establish that Alice Huang had committed offenses related to the suspected false declarations, according to the ministry. However, authorities said she had knowingly provided inaccurate information about her role at Megaspeed. She was issued a warning and barred from re-entering Singapore. Her passport was returned that month. Singapore also said it received limited assistance from U.S. authorities despite repeated requests for information about U.S. server maker Supermicro. Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said its investigation into Megaspeed and six other individuals remains ongoing. The ministry did not identify the six individuals or specify their alleged roles in the case. South Korea has close ties to Nvidia, with major chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix playing important roles in supplying memory chips used in its AI processors. Following Huang’s exit, South Korea’s Science Ministry said Nvidia had reaffirmed its plan to supply 260,000 advanced GPUs to the country and to continue joint AI projects. Apart from that, South Korea’s government AI strategy council held an emergency meeting on Friday to assess the potential impact of Huang’s departure on the country’s AI industry, per a local media report. Taiwan’s Economy Minister Kung Ming-shin said Huang’s departure was unlikely to significantly change the growth of the global AI industry, according to local media . Meanwhile, Taipei’s city government said Nvidia’s planned overseas headquarters in the city remained on track despite the leadership change. The company has met its contractual obligations so far, and officials said they would continue to support the project. In Japan, the Industry Ministry said the government would closely monitor Nvidia following Huang’s resignation, describing the chipmaker as an important player in Japan’s AI semiconductor industry, Reuters reported. Deputy chief cabinet secretary Masanao Ozaki said it was too early to assess the impact on the global AI industry, while stressing Japan’s commitment to ensuring a stable supply of semiconductors. events.title: Fitch expects UAE GDP to rise this year and maintains high-grade credit rating
events.summary: Fitch Ratings is expecting the UAE's economy to expand in 2026 and has maintained the country's high-grade credit rating, citing resilient fiscal buffers. Real gross domestic product in the Arab world's second-largest economy will grow by 0.5 per cent this year, despite an estimated 1.5 per cent contraction in non-oil GDP, the New York-based agency said on Friday. Analysts at Fitch said Dubai's real GDP would remain below its 2025 level next year, "shrinking by close to 5 per cent", as it continues to recover from the effect of the Iran war, as "tourism and expat inflows return only slowly". The emirate's economy hit Dh473 billion ($128.8 billion) in the first half of 2026, down 2.3 per cent from a year earlier, as growth in financial services, health care and construction helped offset weakness in other sectors, government data showed last month . For the UAE, Fitch expects hydrocarbon GDP to rise by about 7 per cent in 2026 and surge by 26 per cent next year, with oil production no longer constrained by Opec+ quotas. The Emirates formally withdrew from the oil group in May . “Fitch expects all the emirates will put recovery programmes in place, but non-oil trend growth will be below prewar levels over our forecast period,” the Fitch analysts wrote. Fitch also kept the UAE's sovereign credit rating at AA-, with a stable outlook, reflecting low consolidated government debt, strong net external asset position and high GDP per capita. An AA- rating is the fourth-highest on Fitch's rating scale. Investment grade makes it easier to access capital markets and raise funding when the need to borrow arises. Fitch said the Emirates benefits from Abu Dhabi's sovereign net foreign assets which, at 180 per cent of UAE GDP in 2026, are among the highest Fitch-rated sovereigns, it said. Fitch had rated Abu Dhabi AA in May . “The stable outlook reflects demonstrated resilience of oil export revenues during the Iran war, which largely offsets the immediate negative impact of the war, as well as abundant fiscal and external buffers, and our expectation that individual emirates will bear the cost of the war rather than the federal government,” Fitch said. The UAE economy has fared relatively well despite geopolitical headwinds. GDP grew 0.4 per cent annually to Dh961.9 billion in the first half of 2026, driven by non-oil business activity, despite the impact of the Iran war . The non-oil sector's contribution to GDP during the first six-month period increased by 1.8 per cent to 79.2 per cent, the Federal Competitiveness and Statistics Centre revealed last month. Last week, Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Vice President and Ruler of Dubai, said the UAE’s foreign trade rose close to a record Dh3 trillion in the first nine months of the year, despite the challenges. Fitch added that Abu Dhabi's export revenue in 2026 is expected to be higher compared to its prewar forecasts despite the disruption, reflecting elevated crude prices and higher export volumes via pipeline to Fujairah and the Strait of Hormuz. “Crude oil constitutes the bulk of exports, and we consider Abu Dhabi's oil export infrastructure less vulnerable to long-term damage than more concentrated and bespoke downstream oil or liquefied natural gas plants,” Fitch said.

events.title: AI's four colliding crises
events.summary: AI's titans were handed an extraordinary mandate: Police yourselves. But the industry faces a four-pronged crisis of trust as Democrats surge to power and many Americans rebel over AI and data centers. Guardrails for the industry will be a priority for the new Congress, with some populist Republicans eager to pile on. Why it matters: The collision of safety scares, political blows, financial turmoil and leadership scandals threatens to derail AI's once seemingly unstoppable ascent. The big picture: Just six weeks ago, President Trump announced that top AI CEOs had agreed to a voluntary safety accord . But cracks were already showing and, since then, four crises have converged. 🏛️ 1. The political crisis: AI was on the ballot for the first time during the midterm elections through a series of data center measures across America. People voted against data centers in 40 out of 41 cases, and swing-state incumbents linked to the facilities, including Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) and Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R), were voted out. Now Democrats are planning a flood of AI bills once they take control of Congress in January, Reuters reports . They'll also bring some of the most powerful AI executives to D.C. to testify. 🦺 2. The safety crisis: OpenAI's Hugging Face breach , revealed in July , was a terrifying look at what could happen if machines operate beyond humans' control — and it was the first in a wave of revelations through the summer and fall. AI CEOs and engineers came forward with stark warnings about the dangers of the tech they've been building, including its potential to destroy humanity. Axios' Madison Mills reported that OpenAI and Anthropic are investigating tens of thousands of security incidents and that unvetted AI agents are accessing U.S. bank accounts. 💰 3. The financial crisis: The AI trade is looking more vulnerable as investors question when or whether the industry's sky-high spending will deliver sky-high returns. Tech stocks tumbled , with Nvidia falling 13% this week amid the ouster of founder and CEO Jensen Huang. The stock has lost nearly 25% of its value since the first New York Times report in late October about Huang's links to a suspected Chinese spy. Anthropic's IPO may not be what some hoped, with its projected valuation coming in roughly $600 billion below what investors envisioned just months ago. 🧐 4. The leadership crisis: Huang's stunning resignation, following revelations about affairs, is raising new questions about the vulnerability of the people running America's most powerful companies. Nvidia's stock slide exemplifies the risk of putting so much power in the hands of so few AI executives. Pop culture has turned on the AI titans , with three year-end films — " The Social Reckoning " and " Musk ," out last month, and " Artificial ," opening Christmas Day — savaging Mark Zuckerberg, Elon Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. Reality check: The AI industry's hurdles are partly growing pains — investors start demanding returns, lawmakers seek accountability, the public grows skeptical. The trust collapse echoes the moment social media companies went from Silicon Valley darlings to public enemies. But AI's reckoning — just like its rise — has come much faster.

events.title: MAGA turns on Lutnick amid China spy scandal
events.summary: Commerce Secretary Lutnick has become the face of the Trump administration's troubled response to Chinese espionage and potential national security threats. The most intense scrutiny is coming from Republicans on the Hill, fellow Cabinet members and the MAGA base. Why it matters: Regulators and policymakers on both sides of the aisle want someone's head for an affair that may have exposed sensitive technology to the nation's top foreign adversary. Two names are currently at the top of that list: former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang — and now Lutnick. The big picture: Over the past year, Lutnick slow-walked broader administration efforts to address suspicions that Singapore-based company Megaspeed was illegally diverting chips to China, Axios first reported . Administration officials had pushed to place Megaspeed on the Commerce Department's Entity List, which would have restricted exports of U.S. tech to the company. Driving the news: On Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confirmed as much. "Treasury, War, USTR, and State — they were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the Entity List for months, but Commerce has the pen," Bessent said on CNBC . Trump himself supported taking action on three occasions, but those efforts were delayed by Lutnick, Axios reported . There's a widespread belief in Trump's broad circle of advisers that the Nvidia scandal might be too much for Lutnick to survive — but Trump is standing beside him for now. Behind the scenes, the White House has not expressed concern regarding efforts to have Lutnick testify before Congress. MAGA commentators are also tearing Lutnick apart on shows like "War Room with Steve Bannon," while Republican senators openly take him to task. For the record: " Secretary Lutnick plays a fundamental role in advising the President across many different industries. The reports you have issued are inaccurate and false and literally misstate the topic, creating a false impression," the Commerce Department said in response to Axios' inquiries. Friction point: The brewing scandal hangs in part on a CIA warning that Jensen Huang was having an affair with Alice Huang, who ran Megaspeed and was also alleged to be a Chinese spy. That warning appears to have been ignored by Commerce Department officials, sources told Axios. Context: Last fall, CIA intelligence indicated Huang was the target of the espionage, which was reported in a "book" assembled by the Office of the Director of National Intelligence for a small circle of administration officials with top secret clearance, according to sources familiar with the matter. In March, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who's also White House national security adviser, compiled a memo about the issue to ensure that Cabinet officials with "equities" in Nvidia and AI were informed, one of those sources said. "The memo was made so that Lutnick and Bessent and others knew what was up," said one source. "Howard was given the memo. He ignored the memo," a second source said. In May, as Trump traveled to China aboard Air Force One, Rubio verbally briefed the president as a "reminder," one of the sources said. Reality check: Through it all, Trump has repeatedly been in Lutnick's corner. The president has defended Lutnick time and again, whether over tariffs, immigration or the latest China tussle. There are no indications Trump has changed his stance since publicly defending Lutnick on Thursday. The bottom line: While Trump continues to defend Lutnick, administration officials and congressional Republicans have clearly picked a target.

events.title: Wholesale food prices are on the rise
events.summary: Food prices are rising sharply even before they reach supermarket shelves. Why it matters: Americans are already paying more for groceries. New inflation data this week suggests that the pressure is not letting up. Wholesale fresh and dry vegetable prices surged 27% last month, adding to a 31% price jump the previous month. These are the prices paid by food distributors, grocery chains and other businesses to farmers and other producers for eventual sale to consumers. Wholesale food prices overall are up 1.7% from a year earlier, ending a three-month streak of annual price declines. Zoom in: Unusually warm weather, crop disease and insect infestations have reduced lettuce and other leafy green harvests in California. The Iran war, meanwhile, has driven up the cost of fertilizer and fuel, making it more expensive to grow and transport food. A regional grocery chain recently told Federal Reserve officials that it now costs more to transport a head of lettuce from California than to buy the lettuce itself, citing high diesel fuel prices. Truck freight costs are up almost 25% over the past year, the largest annual increase since 2022 and on par with the surge seen during the pandemic-era inflation shock. The big picture: It's unclear how much of the surge in producer prices will be passed along to consumers. But steeper price increases were already showing up at supermarket checkout counters last month. Grocery prices rose 0.4%, the biggest monthly increase in 6 months, driven by higher prices for meat, dairy products and snack foods. Fresh vegetable prices climbed 2%, including a nearly 8% jump in lettuce prices.

events.title: U.S. loses measles elimination status
events.summary: An international health organization has determined that the United States has lost its measles elimination status, according to multiple news reports. Why it matters: It's an official recognition of how much the country's public health has deteriorated due to a rolling series of outbreaks since early last year. Increased public skepticism about the safety and effectiveness of vaccines, a barrage of distrust from federal officials like Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and funding cuts for response efforts have all factored in the surge of cases, according to public health experts. The big picture: The Pan American Health Organization concluded there has been sustained transmission of the highly contagious virus for longer than 12 months, bringing the U.S. case count to its highest level in 35 years. The measles elimination status hinges on whether the same strain of measles stays in circulation for 12 months or longer without a break. The overwhelming majority of cases are in unvaccinated people. While overall measles vaccination rates remain relatively high, public health officials say they have to remain above 95% to maintain herd immunity. Driving the news: An expert panel convened by the Pan American Health Organization made the widely expected decision following a three-day meeting in Washington, D.C. What they're saying: "It is no surprise that the resurgence of measles has coincided with an administration that has inflicted significant damage to our health care system while spreading false claims about vaccines," said Richard Besser, president and CEO of the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation and a former acting director of the Centers for Disease Control. "It is unthinkable that people in the United States should be dying from measles in 2026," the Infectious Diseases Society said in comments prior to the decision. The group cited the potential long-term toll on infants infected this year, some of whom could develop serious neurologic disease years after the initial infection. By the numbers: There have been 5,412 confirmed cases so far this year, compared to 2,289 for all of 2025, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's latest tally. The last time measles cases were higher was in 1991, when the U.S. had 9,643 cases. Pennsylvania is in the grip of an outbreak that has accounted for more than 1,500 cases so far and six measles-associated deaths. Those reports are widely considered to be an undercount, due to the lack of widespread testing and unreported instances of mild illness. While most measles cases aren't severe, they can have long-lasting effects because of the way the virus can suppress the body's immune responses, leaving people more susceptible to other infections. About 1 in 5 unvaccinated people in the U.S. who get measles is hospitalized, per the CDC. How it works: Experts rely on disease tracking by local health departments and genetic sequencing, and can also factor vaccination rates and surveillance efforts. Canada and the United Kingdom have both lost their measles elimination status over the past year. The determinations are largely symbolic, but mean the virus has become endemic and is spreading freely in pockets of unvaccinated people, according to Yale epidemiologist Katelyn Jetelina. Since early 2025, there have been large-scale outbreaks in West Texas, along the Utah-Arizona border and in South Carolina.

events.title: Consumer Fight Back
events.summary: Radio Ulster , · 14 Nov 2026 , · 56 mins Black Friday - are you really saving money? Black Friday promises huge savings, but are the deals really as good as they seem? Before you click 'buy' Linzi Lima discusses the misleading discounts and marketing tactics that could leave shoppers paying more than they bargained for. Luxury serums, miracle ingredients and skincare routines costing hundreds of pounds. But when it comes to healthy skin, does a bigger price tag really mean better results? We separate the science from the hype... Why do some products just not last like they used to? Like trainers that fall apart after a few wears - many consumers feel quality is slipping. As trusted heritage brands change hands and manufacturing is outsourced, we investigate what's driving the decline and hear from the founder of the website 'Worse on Purpose' about the growing problem. Would you rather stream your music or own it? In an age of playlists and subscriptions, more people are returning to vinyl records, CDs and other physical formats. We'll explore what's behind the revival and why music fans are once again choosing something they can hold in their hands. Complaints about parcel deliveries are on the rise, and now Ofcom is warning companies to raise their game or face tighter regulation. We hear from James Stinson of Ofcom in Belfast. And if you've got a consumer issue, a story to share, or a question you'd like us to investigate, get in touch: cfb@bbc.co.uk

events.title: No Pilots. Few Air Traffic Controllers. What Could Go Wrong?
events.summary: On September 27, US transportation secretary Sean Duffy posted a video on X with the words “GAME CHANGER.” “Introducing ‘SMART’—the new air traffic management tool that saves YOU time, cuts back DELAYS, and makes your flying experience BETTER,” he wrote. This was a new AI-infused air traffic control system. Almost three weeks later, that post would get a new life, as a nervous joke, as the FAA issued a national groundstop on Friday the 13th that instantly threw the world’s airline schedules into chaos. The administration quickly announced that there was no evidence of a cyberattack, and no sign that SMART had anything to do with the communications failure at the heart of the government’s decision to suspend flights. But when asked on Friday night whether he could definitively rule out AI failure, Homeland Security secretary Markwayne Mullin could only say, “There’s nothing certain right now.” New systems like SMART are only the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the AI aviation revolution currently underway. Take, for instance, the Cessna Caravan that took off from Buchanan Field Airport in Concord, California, and flew south to Phoenix on a calm September morning. The plane, a single-engine turboprop, then turned east to Fort Worth, stopped at Shaw Air Force Base in South Carolina, and finally arrived at Dare County Regional Airport off the coast of North Carolina. The zigzag, coast-to-coast trip covered 3,200 miles; along the way, the aircraft navigated busy airspace and maneuvered to avoid storms. None of this would be remarkable, save for one fact: The entire journey took place without a single human hand touching the plane’s controls. According to Joby Aviation, the company that carried out the project, a safety pilot was aboard the Cessna at all times—but never needed to intervene. The pilotless trip marked a major milestone in aviation. The air travel industry has long been technologically conservative, and with good reason: When human lives are at stake, it’s better to be time-tested and a little dated than cutting-edge and unpredictable. But AI is making inroads into aviation with unprecedented speed. The effects now are hard to see, but the changes in the offing are huge, promising to remake the economics of air travel and transform how people and things move around in the sky. A big question remains, though: Can we trust this technology to be reliable and safe? Depends who you ask. “We're introducing all this new technology to improve the system, and it's going to be a disaster,” says a recently retired FAA employee. “This is literally a Pandora's box that we are going to regret.” Aviation’s embrace of AI traces back to the early 2000s, when advances in batteries and microelectronics suddenly made drones much more capable and inexpensive. The surge convinced officials that robots and humans would eventually need to share the airways, and that new infrastructure would be necessary to allow that. At the time, virtually all aircraft were human-piloted, and there was no way for drones to avoid human-flown planes or each other. In 2007, the federal government rolled out a sweeping project called Next Generation Air Transportation System—NextGen, for short—that mandated broad changes to the air travel system over the decades to come. Among its provisions was the requirement that, by 2020, aircraft in the United States be equipped with ADS-B, a system that constantly sends radio signals telling everyone in the vicinity where you are and where you’re headed. Joby’s aircraft flying past Lower Manhattan, New York, in April. With a road map to robot-friendly skies in place, big players like Amazon and Walmart began working on ambitious plans for drone delivery services. In 2014, Google unveiled Project Wing, a drone delivery offering that by 2018 was ferrying food, coffee, and medication to 164 homes near Canberra, Australia . The next year, the pilot program was expanded to Christiansburg, Virginia . Costs were high and service slow, but those early programs weren’t meant to become viable businesses. Instead, they were providing Google with operational experience for the years to come. Around the same time, a host of startups began working on a related kind of vehicle: electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft, or eVTOLs, also known as electric air taxis. These are, essentially, oversized drones (with room for pilots, for now) designed to carry a small number of people a short distance. By 2022 there were 600 different models under development. Soon, their manufacturers promised, cheap, short aerial hops would be commonplace. Joby was among those leading the charge: In 2020, the company unveiled the design of its S4 model, which it said would be able to carry a pilot and four passengers 100 miles or more at speeds of up to 200 mph. The S4’s maiden flight took place last year. For more than a decade, various eVTOL builders have been promising that production models were just around the corner .

Nearly 1,000 flights already had delays. Between the lines: The most heavily impacted airports were Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson, New York's JFK and Boston Logan. Among the major airlines, FlightAware's data showed Delta more affected than United or American. events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Supercomputing BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features SC 26 Supercomputing Month 2026 Nvidia GTC Berlin 2026 Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Collabora and Nextcloud pitch alternatives as education customers weigh the cost of losing free services Google: AI agent turned a security patch into a working exploit with no human help now Marvell and Penguin Solutions aim to end the RAMpocalypse with photonic memory fabric now The Jensen Huang saga could be the beginning of the end of the AI bubble – or just a boon for competitors 30 minutes ago Los Alamos boffins to put NextSilicon's Maverick-2 through natural selection in Darwin testbed 1 hour ago How many times are you paying to store the same file? 1 hour ago The fallout from Microsoft's education price rises and service cuts continues as institutions weigh the prospect of bigger bills, and the Windows maker's rivals struggle not to pull "I told you so" faces. The main takeaways are that free student email and collaboration services are being retired, and storage entitlements are changing. These changes generally apply at institutions' first renewal or extension on or after January 1, 2028. Microsoft announced the new plans last week, and the UK's Department for Education described itself as "disappointed" at the news. As well it might be, although the UK government has rarely seen a deal from Microsoft that it didn't like . Or, for that matter, other US tech giants . Exactly how much educational institutions will have to spend remains unclear. Mary Jo Foley of Directions on Microsoft put indicative student pricing at $2 per year for Microsoft 365 Education A2, $4 for A3, and $6 for A5, with Teams adding another dollar annually. Faculty licenses cost considerably more, while the new A7 student tier jumps to $385 a year before Teams. Foley cautioned that these were approximate figures, with actual prices set by Microsoft's partners. The new no-cost student tier, Microsoft 365 Education A0, is a poor replacement for Office 365 A1: it excludes Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, and Teams. Eligibility also requires full paid faculty coverage on A2 or higher and students who actively use Windows devices for education – potentially awkward for institutions running fleets of Chromebooks. A few dollars per student might not sound alarming. Multiply that across an institution, however, and something that used to be free becomes a recurring bill. Michael Meeks, CEO of Collabora Productivity, told The Register: "Free was the bait on the hook, and Microsoft spent years reeling in schools' email accounts, documents, identity management and classrooms onto its cloud." A poster on the edugeek.net forums commented: "This was always going to happen, I remember thinking this when we moved over to the MS free cloud solution. It will be free until they decide it isn't." The risk for Microsoft is that there are options. Meeks told us: "Schools now have a year to plan, and, in our experience with other large-scale educational projects, such as the University of Lille, that can be enough time to migrate properly." Other options include Nextcloud, which will be rolled out as part of Germany's Educational Cloud Infrastructure . Several Swiss universities also migrated to the service over an August weekend. According to Nextcloud, 39,500 students, teachers, and researchers, along with 585 terabytes of data, were shifted. Both Nextcloud and Collabora Productivity also highlight another factor that could drive educational institutions away from Microsoft: sovereignty. Dr Patrick Alberts, managing director of messaging provider Element, told The Register : "When an organization is locked to a vendor, it should be no surprise when that vendor takes advantage. When switching is made difficult, the vendor holds all the leverage. They can raise prices or slash services on a whim, knowing customers will swallow the pain rather than rip out the infrastructure. "Yet it's a bold move, given European governments are proactively following a digitally sovereign strategy.

events.title: I Investigated the Online Sports Betting Industry. DraftKings Shut Down My Account.
events.summary: ProPublica reporter Jake Pearson tests DraftKings’ guardrails at a Manhattan bar this spring. After a ProPublica investigation published this fall, the company closed Pearson’s account. Gerardo del Valle/ProPublica Late last month, I was getting dinner on the table when an email hit my inbox with some bad news. “Upon review your account has been closed at DraftKings’ discretion,” the message read. “We understand that this is not the decision that you were hoping for but this decision is final.”  I hadn’t bet on sports in months and had withdrawn all but a few cents of my balance. Why, I wondered, would my account even be under review? Was it something I’d said? In September, I’d published an investigation into how online sports betting companies like DraftKings court customers — and whether the internal guardrails they’ve put in place to stop their users from spiraling out of control are firm enough. For that piece, I’d intentionally bet like a problem gambler , recklessly escalating my betting behavior over 10 weeks. My wagering had been informed by a panel of professional sports bettors, recovering addicts and addiction specialists. As I flagrantly waved the red flags, DraftKings made me a VIP and assigned me my very own personal host. My recklessness was being rewarded. It just took three weeks and about $6,000 of losses. What Does Your Data Reveal About Sports Betting Apps? Help ProPublica Find Out. If you’ve bet on sports with FanDuel or DraftKings, you can help ProPublica understand how these apps work. Use our browser extension to download your betting history, then upload your files. Share Your Experience The company, like the rest of the industry, says it doesn’t want to profit off of addiction, and has invested heavily in a system of tools and in-app prompts designed to help bettors put conditions on their gambling and slow them down. But my experiment raised serious questions about the effectiveness of this system, what’s known as “responsible gaming.”   So on one hand, I could understand how a story like mine, which scrutinized a core business function, might rankle company executives. But on the other hand, DraftKings had been downplaying the significance of my story for weeks.  In an interview for the piece, the company’s chief responsible gaming officer, Lori Kalani, had told me that the system “worked the way it was supposed to” in my case by feeding me some 30 responsible gaming messages over the course of my 10-week betting spree. And on Oct. 22, about a month after publication, DraftKings CEO Jason Robins doubled down, telling a CNBC journalist that he had “personally looked” at my entire betting history and was “pretty proud of how we handled it.” (He also made false claims about my reporting, but I’ve already addressed that on X .) So as I read the notice of my account closure, I wondered: What changed, exactly? DraftKings didn’t respond when I asked. All I got was a check in the mail for 94 cents, the remainder of my balance. But what was clear was that my investigation was reaching more and more people — including state regulators and federal lawmakers. Since publication, it had gone viral. A 27-minute, behind-the-scenes documentary of our work that we posted on YouTube on Oct. 10 had been viewed more than 6 million times in just three weeks. Watch: Inside Our $22K Sports Betting Experiment Lisa Seville and Nadia Sussman/ProPublica The video offered viewers who may not be familiar with ProPublica (or perhaps not inclined to read 4,000-word stories) a way to learn about the reporting in the venue where so much sports betting content lives. Most of our viewers were young men — the prime sports betting demographic. And boy did they engage, leaving 3,500 comments on YouTube and flooding my inbox with messages about the same features and VIP perks detailed in my story. Regulators from across the country were citing my investigation when announcing that they were going to take a look for themselves at how DraftKings and its ilk incentivize users to keep betting. Federal and state officials were also demanding answers about how the company lures in its customers and keeps them in the action . In Ohio, regulators were even proposing a rule to restrict the apps’ marketing practices that spoke directly to one of the findings in my piece.   On the morning of Oct. 27, I sent DraftKings a series of questions for a story about that impact .  That evening is when the unsigned notice from DraftKings Support about my account closure appeared in my inbox. Two hours later, the company sent me a formal response to my questions, writing, in part, that “regular conversations and check-ins with regulators are normal course of business” and denying that the company improperly targets losing gamblers. I may no longer be able to access my account, but I’m still reporting on DraftKings and the online gambling industry. In fact, right now, we’re collecting wagering data from bettors to better understand how the major operators handle problem gambling. You can help by submitting your data here . If you’ve got a tip, you can also reach me directly at 917-512-0276 and jake.pearson@propublica.org . The post I Investigated the Online Sports Betting Industry. DraftKings Shut Down My Account. appeared first on ProPublica .
